Introduction: Why This Book Exists

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Electricity runs far more than your lights. It pumps and treats tap water, keeps food and medicine cold, and runs fuel pumps and card payments.12
  • Long blackouts are real and recent. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, Puerto Rico took about 11 months to restore power to the whole island.3
  • Many blackout deaths come days or months later, from things you can plan for. Cold, interrupted medical care and suspected generator fumes killed people in Texas, Puerto Rico and Spain.4515
  • This book prints only sourced facts. Every number has a citation, and every source shows its year. No theories and no predictions.
  • In the next hour: store water and check your carbon monoxide (CO) alarm. Aim for 1 gallon (3.8 liters) per person per day, for 2 weeks if you can.67
50 Mpeople lost power in the 2003 US and Canada blackout16
11 mofor Puerto Rico to restore power everywhere after Maria3
246deaths in Texas linked to the February 2021 winter storm4
3 M+US Medicare patients use electricity-dependent medical equipment10

#⚡ What electricity actually runs

The power grid is a hidden life-support system. Most of what keeps your household alive either arrives through wires or depends on something that does.

When the power stops, each system fails on its own clock. Some stop in seconds. Others hold out for hours or days on backup batteries and fuel.

Tap water

Your tap water is moved by electric pumps. Water and wastewater plants are often the biggest energy users in a town. They use about 30–40% of the energy a municipality uses, says the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA, 2024).1

In the February 2021 Texas freeze, more than 14 million people were hit by water outages and boil-water notices after days of power cuts and frozen pipes.8 Store water before you need it: see Storing Water for Months & Years.

Cold food and medicine

A closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds about 48 hours and a half-full one about 24 hours, if the doors stay shut.9

Some medicines must stay cool. Find out now how long yours stay safe at higher temperatures.11 Part 3 (Food) and Part 4 (Medicine) cover both in detail.

Medical care

Medical care depends on power too. After Hurricane Maria, a household survey found that about one third of deaths after the storm were attributed to delayed or interrupted health care.5

In the US, more than 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment. More than 4.6 million rely on that equipment or on services such as dialysis, oxygen or home health care (HHS emPOWER).10

Fuel, phones and money

Gas station pumps need electricity. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) lists fuel pumps, lighting and payment systems among the systems hit by power and telecom outages (2025).2

Phone service fails too. After Maria, surveyed households in Puerto Rico went an average of 41 days without cell phone service.5

Cash machines stop too. The April 2025 blackout in Spain and Portugal knocked out ATMs, traffic lights and subway networks.14

🧓 Elderly & disabled

People on powered medical equipment

Oxygen concentrators, ventilators, powered wheelchairs and home dialysis all need electricity. In the US, over 3 million Medicare patients use electricity-dependent equipment.10 List everyone in your family and street who does. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

#🌍 Real grid failures: dates, durations, deaths

Big blackouts are not rare and not only in the past. Here are the documented events this book learns from, in date order.

  1. Sept 1859

    The largest geomagnetic storm on record sets telegraph paper on fire.22

  2. Mar 1989

    A solar storm blacks out Quebec: 6 million people, 9 hours.23

  3. Aug 2003

    Northeast US and Ontario: about 50 million people lose power.16

  4. Sept 2017

    Hurricane Maria hits Puerto Rico. Full restoration takes about 11 months.3

  5. Feb 2021

    Texas freeze: more than 4.5 million people lose power; 246 deaths.174

  6. 2022–2025

    Ukraine: occupation and attacks cut available power capacity from about 38 GW to 12 GW.20

  7. May 2024

    The first G5 "extreme" geomagnetic storm in over 20 years.24

  8. Sept 2024

    Hurricane Helene: 5.9 million customers lose power; at least 250 US deaths.1918

  9. Apr 2025

    Mainland Spain and Portugal lose power at 12:33 Spanish time.12

Spain and Portugal, April 2025

On April 28, 2025, at 12:33 Spanish time, mainland Spain and Portugal lost power.12 Subways, traffic lights and ATMs stopped working.14

Full restoration took about 16 hours.13 Early reports linked at least three deaths to the blackout. In Galicia, police investigated carbon monoxide from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.15

The expert panel's final report, published in March 2026, found no single cause. It described a chain of failures with voltage control problems at its center.1213

Texas, February 2021 (Winter Storm Uri)

More than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for as long as 4 days. Federal investigators found that frozen equipment at power plants was the largest single cause.17

Texas officially linked 246 deaths to the storm. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.4 Water systems failed too, affecting more than 14 million people.8

Hurricane Helene, September 2024

Helene came ashore in Florida's Big Bend as a Category 4 hurricane on September 26, 2024.18 It left 5.9 million electricity customers without power across 10 states.19

The National Hurricane Center counted at least 250 US deaths. That made Helene the deadliest hurricane in the mainland US since Katrina in 2005.18

The Northeast blackout, August 2003

On August 14, 2003, about 50 million people in the US and Canada lost power. The outage cut 61,800 megawatts of electric load across eight US states and Ontario.16

Some parts of the US waited 4 days for power. Parts of Ontario had rolling blackouts for more than a week.16

Ukraine, 2022–2025: a grid under attack

Before 2022, Ukraine had about 38 gigawatts (GW) of dispatchable power capacity. It lost 19 GW to occupation, destruction and damage in the first year of the full-scale war. After more attacks in spring 2024, about 12 GW was left (IEA, 2025).20

That is about two-thirds of its capacity gone. Attacks on Ukraine's energy system continued through 2025.20

Grids only fail because of war or sabotage.

In Texas in 2021, the largest single cause was frozen power plant equipment.17 Quebec 1989 failed from a solar storm.23 The Iberian blackout had no single cause; voltage control problems were central.12

For full case studies of these and older events, see Real Long Blackouts: Lessons Learned.

#🏝️ Puerto Rico after Maria: 11 months to restore power

Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico on September 20, 2017.5 About 11 months later, officials said power had been restored to the whole island.3

A Harvard-led team surveyed 3,299 randomly chosen households. Through the end of 2017, homes averaged 84 days without electricity, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell phone service (NEJM, 2018).5

Interrupted medical care was a major killer. About one third of the deaths after the storm in surveyed households were attributed to delayed or interrupted health care.5 The same study estimated 4,645 excess deaths to the end of 2017.5

Counting the dead took nearly a year. The first official toll was 64.5 A George Washington University study, commissioned by the governor, estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.21

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults faced the highest risk

The George Washington University study found that poor and elderly people were most at risk of dying after Maria.21 Plan medicines and care for older relatives first. See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Puerto Rico needed about 11 months to restore power to every area.3 This book plans for a much longer case: 30 years with no grid, with no repair crews or deliveries to count on. See What Fails When: The 30-Year Timeline.

#☀️ Solar storms: the facts

Solar storms have already caused real blackouts. A big eruption on the Sun can throw a fast cloud of charged gas, called a coronal mass ejection (CME), toward Earth. The great storm of 1859 was caused by a very fast CME.22

1859: the Carrington Event

On September 1, 1859, astronomer Richard Carrington saw a bright flare on the Sun. The next day, the largest geomagnetic storm on record reached Earth.22

Auroras were seen as far south as the tropics. Currents surged through telegraph wires and set recording paper on fire at telegraph stations.22

1989: Quebec goes dark in 90 seconds

In March 1989, a geomagnetic storm tripped protective equipment on Hydro-Québec's grid. Within 90 seconds, 6 million people lost power, and it stayed off for 9 hours (NOAA).23

May 2024: the strongest storm in 20 years

On May 10, 2024, a G5 storm arrived. G5 is the top level on the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) 5-level scale, and this was the first G5 in over two decades (NASA, 2025).24

Grid operators reported isolated effects on large power transformers, voltage support equipment, line breakers and filters (NERC, 2024).25 GPS errors sent some self-steering farm tractors off course during spring planting.24

Solar storms only make pretty auroras.

In 1989 a solar storm cut power to 6 million people in Quebec.23 In 1859, storm currents set telegraph paper on fire.22

The full science, warning systems and what helps are in Solar Storms & Grid Collapse: The Facts.

#☠️ The pattern: who died, and how

In Texas and Puerto Rico, most deaths did not happen when the lights went out. They came over the following days and months, from causes a household can plan for.

  • Cold: about two-thirds of the 246 Texas deaths in 2021 were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.4
  • Missed medical care: about one third of the deaths in the Puerto Rico survey were attributed to delayed or interrupted care.5
  • Generator fumes: in Spain in 2025, police investigated carbon monoxide after a family of three died with a generator running.15
  • Age and poverty: after Maria, poor and elderly people faced the highest risk.21

Every cause of death, ranked by speed, is in What Kills People First in Disasters.

☠️ Danger

Never run a generator indoors or in a garage

Not even with the doors and windows open. Run it outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 meters) from windows, doors and vents, and use a battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm.7 See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

Children depend completely on adults for warmth, safe water and safe food. Learn the danger signs in Part 6 before you need them, and plan feeding now: see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

🌸 Women & girls

Store extra water for pregnancy

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises storing more water for pregnant women, for sick people and for hot climates.6 Pregnancy, birth and breastfeeding each have their own chapter in Part 5, starting with Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and pets

Your dogs depend on the same water, food and shelter as you. Count every pet when you work out how much water and food to store. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

#📏 Why this book uses facts only

Every number in this book has a source you can check. The small number after a sentence links to the source list at the end of the chapter.

Official numbers change, so we give the year. Texas first counted 210 storm deaths, then 246 in its final report.4 Puerto Rico's first official count after Maria was 64.5 An independent study later estimated 2,975.21

⚠️ Caution

Early numbers can be far too low

The Texas count rose by 36 deaths between reports.4 The first Maria count of 64 later sat beside study estimates of 2,975 and 4,645.215 When you read a number, check its date.

The first official death toll tells you the real cost.

After Maria, the first official toll was 64.5 A study commissioned by the governor estimated 2,975 excess deaths.21

Where this book's facts come from, in order of preference
Source typeExamplesUsed for
Government and UN bodiesCDC, EPA, FEMA, NOAA, WHO, UNICEFHealth and safety guidance, official data
Professional bodiesAmerican Heart Association, Red Cross, AAP, ACOGFirst aid and medical guidelines
Peer-reviewed researchNEJM, Lancet, Cochrane reviewsWhat works, and how well
Official event reportsFERC, ENTSO-E, National Hurricane CenterCauses, durations, death tolls
Major news outletsAP and similarEvent facts only: dates, places, tolls

What we leave out: rumors, predictions, unsourced opinions, product claims, prepper blogs, forums and Wikipedia. If a claim could not be checked against a source like those above, it is not in this book.

Do

  • Check who said it and when
  • Prefer official agencies and studies
  • Write the date next to any number you note down
  • Expect early tolls to change

Don't

  • Act on a single unsourced post
  • Pass on rumors in a crisis
  • Trust "secret" cures or miracle gear
  • Treat a forecast as a fact

#⏱️ Your next hour First 72 h

Do these six things now, while the power and shops still work. Start the timer and go.

Timer: Your next hour: six steps. Interactive in the digital edition.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Fill water containers

    Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 liters) per person per day for 3 days. Work up to a 2-week supply.6

    Use clean, food-grade containers. Never use ones that held chemicals, including old bleach bottles.6

  2. Check your CO alarm

    Use a battery-powered or battery-backup alarm. Put one on every level of your home, where it will wake sleepers.711 Replace the alarm every 5 years.7

  3. List every medicine in the house

    Write down who takes it, how much is left, and whether it must stay cool. Ask a pharmacist how long it stays safe when warm.11

  4. Tape the fridge rule to the fridge

    Closed fridge: 4 hours. Full freezer: 48 hours. Half-full freezer: 24 hours. When in doubt, throw it out.9

  5. Write a paper contact list

    Phone numbers and addresses for family, neighbors, doctors and a contact outside your area. Phones can be out for weeks.5

  6. Check on one vulnerable person

    Find out who near you depends on powered medical equipment, and agree a plan together.10

#🧠 Remember this

How long is food safe in a closed fridge with no power?

About 4 hours. Full freezer about 48 hours; half-full about 24 hours.

Where must a generator go?

Outdoors, at least 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors and vents. Never inside or in a garage.

How much water per person per day?

At least 1 gallon (3.8 L). Store 3 days at minimum, 2 weeks if you can.

How long did Puerto Rico take to restore power everywhere after Maria?

About 11 months (2017 to 2018).

What killed most people in the Texas 2021 freeze?

Cold exposure, mostly hypothermia: about two-thirds of 246 deaths.

What did the March 1989 solar storm do?

The First 72 Hours: Exact Order of Actions

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 13 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Light the house with flashlights, not candles. Never run a generator inside a home or garage, even with the doors and windows open.15
  • Fill every clean container with tap water in the first hour. In the 2003 blackout, Cleveland's main water pumps lost power and taps dropped to a trickle.9
  • Keep the fridge and freezer shut. A closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.2
  • Read every medicine label for "refrigerate". Insulin in vials or cartridges can stay at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days.7
  • Keep phones charged and the gas tank full. Then check on your neighbors.1
4 ha closed fridge keeps food safe without power2
48 ha full, closed freezer holds its temperature (24 h if half full)2
28 daysinsulin vials and cartridges can stay unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F)7
20 ft(6 m) minimum distance from a generator to doors, windows and vents4

#⏱️ The order of actions at a glance First 72 h

Work in this order: people, light, water, cold food, air, medicines, contact. The fastest dangers come first, and the slow ones wait their turn.

Every clock in this chapter comes from official power outage guidance: Ready.gov, the US Department of Agriculture (USDA), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).12

Write down the time the power went out. Tape it to the fridge door. The food and medicine decisions below all count from that moment.

  1. Minute 0

    Safety check. Flashlights on, not candles. Count every person. Make sure no generator, grill or stove is running indoors.14

  2. Hour 1

    Fill water containers while the taps still run. Read medicine labels. Unplug electronics to protect them from surges when power returns.1

  3. Hour 4

    The closed fridge reaches its safe limit. If the outage will last longer, move fridge food into coolers with ice.2

  4. Hour 24

    A half-full freezer reaches its limit. Once the outage passes one day, Ready.gov's rule for refrigerated medicines applies.21

  5. Hour 48

    A full freezer reaches its limit with the door kept closed.2

  6. Hour 72

    Switch to the routine in The First 30 Days: water system, toilets, rationing and roles.

💡 Tip

Print this page

Tape the timeline inside a kitchen cupboard. In a real outage, your phone may be dead and this book offline.

#🔦 Minute 0 to 15: the safety check

Use flashlights, not candles. Ready.gov lists candles as a fire risk during power outages.1

Keep a flashlight with extra batteries for every household member, including children.1

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Count everyone

    Call each name out loud. If someone is missing, write down where they were last.

  2. Turn on flashlights

    Give each child their own light and keep them in the same room as an adult.

  3. Check the air

    If a carbon monoxide (CO) alarm sounds, or anyone feels dizzy, sick or confused, get everyone outside into fresh air and get medical help.4

  4. Unplug electronics

    Power can come back with surges or spikes. Disconnect appliances and electronics to avoid damage.1

  5. Write the time

    Note the time the power went out on paper. Every food and medicine decision counts from it.

☠️ Danger

Never heat the house with a gas oven or stove

Ready.gov and the CDC both say not to use a gas stove or oven to heat your home. It is a carbon monoxide risk.14 See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

🎯 Practice now

Run a 15-minute blackout drill

One evening, switch off the lights and phones. Find the flashlights, count heads and fill the water containers. Time it, then fix whatever slowed you down.

#🚰 Hour 1: capture water while the taps still run

Fill every clean container now, before the pressure drops. City water can stop when the pumps that move it lose power.9

What happened in the 2003 blackout

The Northeast blackout began on August 14, 2003.13 Cleveland's water system shut down when its four major water supply pumps lost power. Taps gave no more than a trickle.9

About 1.5 million people in the Cleveland area lost water. Residents used bottled water for drinking and bathing.1011

The danger did not end when pressure came back. Residents were told to boil drinking water, because the system could have been contaminated when pressure was lost.1011

In Detroit, a boil-water alert covered 4.3 million customers. It was not lifted until Tuesday, August 19, 2003, five days after the blackout began.1213

📊 Key fact

No one can tell you how long your taps will run

The 2003 blackout caused loss of water service in some areas, not all.9 Treat every minute of pressure as borrowed time. Fill first, then deal with everything else.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Fill drinking containers first

    Use clean bottles, jugs and pots with lids. Label them "DRINKING".

  2. Fill cooking pots and kettles

    Cover them so dust and insects stay out.

  3. Fill the bathtub and buckets

    Use this water for flushing and washing. Keep small children away from a full tub.

  4. Turn the taps off when flow slows

    Write down the time the pressure dropped.

  5. When water returns, follow boil-water notices

    Do not drink tap water until officials say it is safe, or until you have treated it.10 See Disinfecting Water.

How much does your family need? Use the calculator, then read Storing Water for Months & Years for safe containers and hidden water in the house.

Water calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

👶 Babies & children

Babies: keep separate water for formula

Fill and label one covered container only for mixing formula. If a boil-water notice is issued, do not use tap water for formula until the notice is lifted or the water is treated. See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

#🧊 Hours 0 to 48: the fridge and freezer clock

Keep the doors shut. A refrigerator keeps food safe for up to 4 hours during a power outage if you do not open the door.23

A full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours with the door closed. A half-full freezer holds about 24 hours.23

Use appliance thermometers. The fridge should be at 4°C (40°F) or below, and the freezer at −18°C (0°F) or below.2

What to do when each clock runs out (USDA, Ready.gov)
ApplianceSafe forThen
Fridge, door closedAbout 4 hoursThrow out perishable food: meat, poultry, fish, soft cheeses, milk, eggs, leftovers and deli items2
Freezer, half fullAbout 24 hoursCheck each item for ice crystals or a temperature of 4°C (40°F) or below2
Freezer, fullAbout 48 hoursSame check as above2
Food at 4°C (40°F) or warmerUnder 2 hoursThrow it away after 2 hours. Also throw out any food with an unusual smell, color or texture1

If the outage will last more than 4 hours, move fridge food into coolers with ice.2

Perishable food left in a fridge with no power for more than 4 hours goes in the trash: meat, poultry, fish, soft cheeses, milk, eggs, leftovers and deli items.2

Frozen food that still has ice crystals, or is at 4°C (40°F) or below, can be safely refrozen.2

If it tastes fine, it is safe to eat.

USDA says never taste food to decide whether it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.2

For which foods to eat first and what is safe at room temperature, see Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Two cheap thermometers

Buy one appliance thermometer for the fridge and one for the freezer. Without them, you are guessing at the 4°C (40°F) line.2

#💊 Medicines that need cold

Read every medicine label in the house. Look for the word "refrigerate". Do it in the first hour, while you can still reach a pharmacist.

If a medicine was not kept at its recommended temperature during an outage, the FDA says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, doctor or the maker whether it is still usable.8

The one-day rule: if the power is out for more than a day, discard medicine that should be refrigerated, unless the label says otherwise.1

If a life depends on that refrigerated medicine, talk to a doctor or pharmacist and use it only until a new supply is available.1

Insulin

Insulin does not fail the moment the fridge stops. Insulin in vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days and still work.7

Pens and some brands have different limits. Check the label of your exact product.7

Above 30°C (86°F), the 28-day figure no longer applies. The FDA gives it only for 15–30°C (59–86°F).7 Read the label for the words "do not freeze" too, and if you keep insulin in a cooler, do not let it touch the ice.

When properly stored insulin is available again, the FDA advises replacing vials that were exposed to extreme conditions.7

Once the fridge stops, all insulin is ruined.

The FDA says insulin vials and cartridges keep working for up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F).7 Replace vials exposed to extreme conditions once properly stored insulin is available.7

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Gather every medicine

    Put all of them on one table, including children's and pets' medicines.

  2. Sort by the label

    Make two piles: "refrigerate" and "room temperature".

  3. Write a list

    For each cold medicine, write the name, the dose and how many days of supply are left.

  4. Call while you can

    Ask a pharmacist or doctor about each cold medicine while the phones work.8

  5. Watch the clock

    Once the power has been out for more than a day, apply the one-day rule above to everything that is not life-saving.1

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Medical devices and older adults

Talk to your medical provider now about a power outage plan for medical devices that run on electricity and for refrigerated medicines.1 Older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.1 See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Insulin vials and cartridges last up to 28 days out of the fridge, and only at 15–30°C (59–86°F).7 In a grid-down life measured in years, anyone on daily cold medicines needs a written plan with their doctor before the outage, not after.

#☠️ Carbon monoxide: the danger you cannot see

Run a generator outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Never use one inside a home, garage or carport.4

The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is blunt: never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if the doors and windows are open. Point the exhaust away from the house and other buildings.5

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Place it outside

    At least 6 m (20 ft) from any door, window or vent.4

  2. Point the exhaust away

    Aim it away from your home and other buildings.5

  3. Use a long cord

    An extension cord longer than 6 m (20 ft) keeps the generator at a safe distance.6

  4. Turn on a battery-powered CO alarm inside

    Use one in your home whenever a generator runs. Ready.gov advises CO alarms with battery backup on every level of the home.61

  5. Never move it indoors

    Not into the garage, not into the carport, not even with the doors open.54

A generator is fine in the garage if you leave the big door open.

The CPSC says never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.5

Do

  • Light rooms with flashlights1
  • Keep generators outdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from openings4
  • Run a battery-powered CO alarm6
  • If home is too hot or cold, go somewhere with heat or cooling, if it is safe to travel1

Don't

  • Use candles for light1
  • Heat the house with a gas oven or stove1
  • Run a generator in a garage or carport4
  • Leave a car engine running in a garage4

Know the warning signs. CO poisoning can cause headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion.4 If you suspect it, get to fresh air first, then get medical help.

For alarms, symptoms and safe heating, read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

#⛽ Fuel, cash and phone power

Keep phones and other electric equipment charged, and keep gas tanks full. That is Ready.gov's power outage advice, and it only works if you do it before the outage.1

Cash

Ready.gov's outage supplies start with flashlights with extra batteries for every household member, plus enough nonperishable food and water.1

Card readers and cash machines need electricity. Keep cash at home in small bills.

Phones and batteries

Find out now whether your home phone works in a power outage, and how long its battery backup lasts.1

Make a plan for batteries and other alternatives to meet your needs when the power goes out.1

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Charge everything now

    Phones, power banks, radios and flashlights with rechargeable batteries.1

  2. Stretch the battery

    Turn on low-power mode, dim the screen and close apps you do not need.

  3. Send one message out

    Tell your out-of-area contact that you are safe and when you will check in next.

  4. Charge from a car only outdoors

    Never run a car or generator in a garage or carport.4

  5. Switch off between check-ins

    Agree on fixed times to turn phones on, so the batteries last for days.

⚠️ Caution

Fuel is a fire and CO hazard

A fuel-burning generator belongs outdoors only, with its exhaust pointed away from buildings.5 For storage and safe refueling, see Generators & Fuel Storage.

#📞 Contact, neighbors and when to leave

Check on your neighbors. Ready.gov puts this on its list of things to do during an outage.1

Start with older adults and families with young children. They are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.1

If your home becomes too hot or too cold, and it is safe to travel, go to a place that has heat or cooling.1 Decide this early, while roads and daylight allow it.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Use your family plan

    Follow your meeting points and contact list. No plan yet? See The Family Emergency Plan.

  2. Set check-in times

    Agree when everyone switches phones on. Write the times on paper.

  3. Listen for official updates

    Keep a battery or hand-crank radio on, so you are not relying on your phone alone.

  4. Visit, do not just call

    Knock on the doors of neighbors who live alone, use medical devices or have babies.1

  5. Keep a paper log

    Write the time of each event: power out, water pressure lost, fridge food thrown out.

Each person in your home has different needs in the first 72 hours. Use this table as a quick check, one row at a time.

Babies and young children

Young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures, so check them often.1 Give older children a job and a flashlight of their own: it keeps them busy and close to you.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Pack period products, pain relief and any pregnancy or contraceptive medicines into one bag in the first hour. Ready.gov advises a flashlight with extra batteries for every household member.1 Keep each one by its owner's bed so no one walks to the bathroom in the dark.

Dogs and pets

Fill and label a water container for each animal in the first hour. Count how many days of food you have. Keep pets out of garages and away from any running generator. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

#🧠 Remember this

What comes first when the power goes out?

Safety: flashlights, count heads, check for CO. Then fill water.

How long is a closed fridge safe?

About 4 hours. Then throw out meat, poultry, fish, soft cheeses, milk, eggs, leftovers and deli items.

How long does a closed freezer hold?

About 48 hours if full, 24 hours if half full.

Where does a generator go?

Outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Never in a garage, even with the door open.

How long can insulin vials go without a fridge?

Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Check the label for pens.

Refrigerated medicine after more than a day without power?

Discard it unless the label says otherwise. If a life depends on it, ask a doctor or pharmacist and use it until new supply arrives.

Can you taste food to check it?

No. Never taste. When in doubt, throw it out.

The First 30 Days

🔴 CriticalFirst 30 days📚 10 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Never ration water. Drink what you need today and look for more for tomorrow. That is FEMA and Red Cross guidance.1
  • Ration food, not water. Healthy people can live on half their usual food for an extended period. Do not cut food for children or pregnant women.1
  • Get a toilet and a handwashing station working in week 1. Outbreaks after disasters follow unsafe water, poor sanitation and crowding.4
  • Store at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day. At least 2 quarts (1.9 liters) of that is drinking water, and heat can double the need.316
  • Count everything on day 4, then every 7 days. Turn every count into one number: days left.
  • Start long-term systems in weeks 3 and 4, while stored supplies still cover you: rain catchment, garden, compost.
Neverration water: drink what you need today1
½of usual food: what healthy people can live on for an extended period12
2 qt(1.9 L) minimum drinking water a day, normally active person1
1 per 20people: toilet planning figure for shared toilets5

#🗓️ Your 30-day map First 30 days

The first 72 hours keep you alive tonight. Days 4 to 30 turn quick fixes into daily systems. If you have not done the first 72 hours yet, start with The First 72 Hours.

Work one week at a time. Each week has one main job. Finish it before you move on.

  1. Week 1 · Days 4–7

    Water and toilets. Build a daily water routine. Set up a toilet and a handwashing station. Do the first full inventory. Give everyone a role.

  2. Week 2 · Days 8–14

    Sanitation every day, rations set. Use the inventory numbers to set portions. Choose one warm or cool room. Meet your nearest neighbors.

  3. Week 3 · Days 15–21

    Security and community. Start a watch rota, build a neighbor network, repair what broke, recount.

  4. Week 4 · Days 22–30

    Long-term systems. Rain catchment, garden beds, a seed check, compost, and a written plan for month 2.

💡 Tip

One wall, one sheet

Tape the week's jobs, the roles and the inventory "days left" numbers on one wall. Everyone checks the wall, not their memory.

#💧 Week 1: Turn stored water into a water system

Never ration water. If supplies run low, drink the amount you need today and try to find more for tomorrow.1

Plan on at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day. That is the CDC minimum to store. The CDC says to store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates.3

Of that, a normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (1.9 liters) each day.12 In very hot weather, water needs can double. Children, nursing mothers and sick people may need more.6 See How Much Water You Really Need.

Stored water is a bridge, not a plan. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, surveyed Puerto Rico households went an average of 68 days without water.9 Week 1 is when you find the next source and a way to treat it, while your stores still cover you.

Water for 30 days (arithmetic from the planning and drinking figures above; double the drinking column in very hot weather)
PeoplePlanning: 1 gal (3.8 L) each a dayDrinking minimum: 2 qt (1.9 L) each a day
130 gal (114 L)15 gal (57 L)
260 gal (227 L)30 gal (114 L)
4120 gal (454 L)60 gal (227 L)
6180 gal (681 L)90 gal (341 L)

Water calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Measure what you have

    Write the volume on every container. Add it up in liters and gallons.

  2. Work out days left

    Total water ÷ (number of people × 3.8 L or 1 gal). Write the answer on the wall.

  3. Choose your next source

    Rain, a well, a spring or a stream. See Finding Water When the Taps Stop.

  4. Choose and stock a treatment

    Boiling, bleach or a filter. See Disinfecting Water.

  5. Separate clean from dirty

    Mark some containers "DRINKING ONLY". Never pour untreated water into them.

  6. Log it every day

    One line a day: liters in, liters used, days left.

⚠️ Caution

Do not wait for the last container

Start collecting and treating from your next source while you still have a stored reserve. Then one bad day does not become a dry day.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs drink from your stores too

Add a line for each dog on the water log. Measure what your dog drinks on a normal day now, so you have a real number. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

#🚽 Weeks 1–2: Toilets and handwashing before anything else

Disease outbreaks after disasters follow conditions, not the calendar. A review in CDC's journal Emerging Infectious Diseases linked outbreak risk to displacement, crowding, safe water and sanitation, the population's underlying health, vaccination coverage and access to health care.4

Displacement is the main risk factor. Disasters that did not displace people rarely led to outbreaks.4 If your home is safe, making it livable keeps your family out of crowded temporary shelters. See Stay or Go?

Diarrheal outbreaks can follow contamination of drinking water.4 So the toilet and the water system are one job: waste must never reach what you drink.

The same review found the risk of diarrheal outbreaks after disasters is higher in developing countries than in industrialized countries.4 If your water or sanitation was weak before the outage, treat this section as urgent.

📊 Key fact

Your alarm is a condition, not a date

Act on sanitation the day any of these happens: tap water is no longer safe, the toilet stops flushing, or extra people move in. Each is a risk factor named in the review.4 For how fast each disease appears, see Waterborne Diseases.

Why sanitation matters by week 2

Illness shows up after a delay. The delay between swallowing a germ and the first symptom is called the incubation period.

Cholera can start within hours. Symptoms usually begin 2 to 3 days after exposure, but can start in a few hours or take up to 5 days.7 Hepatitis A takes 15 to 50 days, 28 on average.8

Do the arithmetic. A water or toilet mistake on day 4 can bring cholera by day 9, and hepatitis A anywhere from day 19 to day 54. A week 1 mistake can still make someone sick 7 weeks later.

Time from exposure to first symptom (CDC and WHO)
IllnessFirst symptom afterSpread by
CholeraA few hours to 5 days (usually 2–3)7Contaminated food or water10
Hepatitis A15–50 days (average 28)8Close contact, or contaminated food or water8

How many toilets you need

Plan one toilet per 20 people, or one per household, when households share.5 In the first phase of an emergency, no toilet should serve more than 50 people.5

Put a handwashing station right next to every toilet. The Sphere humanitarian standards call for handwashing facilities close to latrines.5

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Pick the method

    Flush with non-drinking water, or switch to a bucket or dry toilet. See Toilets Without Water.

  2. Pick the place

    Private, and away from food, water containers and any well. The Toilets chapter gives distances.

  3. Add handwashing

    Water, soap and a basin beside the toilet.5 See Handwashing & Personal Hygiene.

  4. Make one house rule

    Wash hands after the toilet and before touching food or drinking water.

  5. Give it an owner

    One person empties, cleans and restocks on a fixed schedule. Rotate the job weekly.

  6. Light the way

    Keep a lamp or a light ready on the path for night trips.

Dead bodies left after a disaster cause epidemics.

A 2007 review found no evidence that dead bodies cause epidemics. Deaths in rapid-onset disasters are mostly from blunt trauma, crush injuries and drowning.4 See Handling the Dead Safely.

👶 Babies & children

Check vaccines this month

Measles risk after disasters depends on how many people were already vaccinated, especially children under 15.4 Find your family's vaccination records now. See Vaccine-Preventable Diseases.

🌸 Women & girls

Safe toilets for women and girls

Put the toilet where women and girls can reach it safely at night: a short, lit path and a door that locks from inside. Pair up for night trips. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

A toilet within reach

For anyone who cannot walk far, put a seat-height bucket toilet near where they sleep, with its own handwashing basin. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

#📋 Day 4: The first full inventory

You cannot ration what you have not counted. Do the first full count on day 4. Recount every 7 days.

Turn every count into "days left". Days left = amount on hand ÷ amount used per day. One number per item is easy to read when you are tired.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Clear one shelf at a time

    Group like items. Work in pairs: one person counts, one writes.

  2. Count food in person-days

    One person-day is enough food for one person for one day at their normal eating.

  3. Count water

    Liters or gallons, from the water log.

  4. Count medicines per person

    Doses left ÷ doses per day = days left. Do this first for anyone on daily prescriptions.

  5. Count everything else

    Fuel, batteries, lamp oil, soap, bleach, diapers, formula, menstrual products and dog food.

  6. Post the numbers

    Write each "days left" on the wall sheet. Circle the lowest three. Those are next week's problems.

Food calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Count daily medicines before food

Write each person's medicine "days left" at the top of the sheet. Then read Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies for what to do as that number falls.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get this before you need it

A clipboard, a paper notebook, pencils, a permanent marker and masking tape for labels. Paper inventory works with no power at all.

#🥫 Week 2: Rationing math (food yes, water no)

Food can be rationed. Water cannot. FEMA and the American Red Cross say food may be rationed safely, except for children and pregnant women.1

Healthy people can survive on half their usual food intake for an extended period, and without any food for many days.12

That guidance covers healthy people. For anyone with diabetes, kidney disease or another diet-sensitive condition, read Special Diets before you change what they eat.

Worked example: a family of 4

Two adults and two children have 120 person-days of food.

  • Everyone eats full portions: 4 person-days used a day. 120 ÷ 4 = 30 days.
  • Adults eat half, children eat full: 0.5 + 0.5 + 1 + 1 = 3 a day. 120 ÷ 3 = 40 days.

Halving adult portions bought this family 10 days. It did not make any food. Use those days to start growing and collecting it.

Do

  • Cut healthy adults' portions first
  • Keep children and pregnant women on full portions
  • Write portions down so everyone sees them
  • Recount every 7 days and adjust

Don't

  • Ration water
  • Cut food for children or pregnant women
  • Guess at stock levels
  • Let one person control food in secret
👶 Babies & children

Children are not rationed

FEMA and Red Cross guidance excludes children from food rationing.1 For babies on formula, see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnant women are not rationed

The same guidance excludes pregnant women from food rationing.1 For breastfeeding mothers, see Breastfeeding.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs are on the sheet too

Count dog food in days like everything else. If it runs out inside 30 days, read Feeding Dogs Without Kibble now.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Rationing stretches a store. It never refills one. Every number on the inventory sheet reaches zero unless a system replaces it.

#🧭 Routine and roles

Give every job a person and every person a job. A shared routine means fewer decisions when everyone is tired.

In a household of 2, each person takes 2 or 3 roles. Write them down anyway. Swap the hardest jobs each week.

For sleep and shift plans, see Stress, Sleep & Routines. If anyone in your house has ADHD, give them roles with a clear daily checklist and a visible result. See Surviving With ADHD.

👶 Babies & children

Jobs for children

Give children small daily jobs and a fixed bedtime. A job they can finish is part of the routine too. See Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Roles for elders

Many key jobs can be done sitting down: record keeper, inventory counter, teacher, night radio listener. Give elders a named role on the wall.

🎯 Practice now

Practice a no-power weekend

While help still exists, live by the routine table for one weekend without using grid power. Write down every problem, then fix it before you need to.

#🌡️ Week 2: One warm room or one cool room

Pick one room and live in it. One room is easier to keep warm or cool than a whole house, and easier to watch.

Heat for warmth competes with fuel for cooking and boiling water. Use the fuel "days left" from your inventory before you choose a method.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Choose the room

    Use Staying Warm Without Heat or Staying Cool Without Air Conditioning to pick it.

  2. Move sleeping there

    Babies, elders and sick people get the best spots.

  3. Check fuel days left

    Take the number from the wall sheet. Keep enough fuel to treat water.

  4. Read the carbon monoxide chapter

    Do this before any flame or engine is used indoors or near the house.

  5. Check people twice a day

    Morning and evening, check babies, elders, the sick and dogs. See Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke for warning signs.

☠️ Danger

Read this before you burn anything indoors

Heaters, stoves, lamps, grills and generators all burn fuel. Before you use any of them for heat, light or cooking, read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Who to watch most closely

See What Kills People First for the groups at highest risk from heat and cold, and check them first every day.

#🤝 Weeks 2–3: Security and neighbors

Your nearest neighbors are your first backup. They are close enough to help today, and you are close enough to help them.

Security in the first month is mostly quiet habits: locks, a watch rota, not showing what you have, and knowing who lives around you. Details are in Home Security & Deterrence and Keeping a Low Profile.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Visit in daylight, in pairs

    Start with the two or three nearest homes.

  2. Share names and needs

    Who has babies, elders, medical devices or dogs.

  3. Swap skills

    List who can do first aid, repairs, gardening and child care. See Organizing Neighbors.

  4. Set a weekly meeting

    Same place, same day, same time.

  5. Agree on a help signal

    A sound, a flag or a runner, so anyone can call for help without power.

Do

  • Lock doors and gates at dusk
  • Keep supplies out of sight from doors and windows
  • Keep a written night-watch rota
  • Talk problems down. See De-escalation

Don't

  • Tell people outside your group how much you have
  • Post about your supplies online
  • Confront strangers alone
  • Take from homes or stores without permission. That is theft. See Scavenging vs Looting
🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls in the plan

Make sure women and girls have a say in where the toilet, water point and sleeping spaces go. Use a buddy for night trips and night watch.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs on the rota

A dog that barks at strangers is an early alarm. Keep it fed, vaccinated and under control around neighbors. See Rabies & Diseases Animals Give Humans.

#🌱 Weeks 3–4: Start the long-term systems

Start long-term systems while stores still cover you. In the worked example, food lasted 40 days with adults on half portions. Anything you plant needs to be growing well before that day.

Seeds planted in week 4 do not feed you in week 4. Check each crop's days to harvest on the seed packet, and plan for the gap.

  1. Do the third inventory

    Around day 28, recount everything.

  2. Sort by days left

    Put the lowest numbers at the top of the list.

  3. Match each item to a system

    Use the table above. Some items have no replacement yet: note them.

  4. Give each system an owner

    Write a name and a start date next to it.

  5. Write the month-2 plan

    Put it on the wall. Then read Year 1 to Year 30.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

The habits from these 30 days carry on for decades: a daily water log, a weekly count, a toilet owner and a weekly meeting. What changes is where the supplies come from. For how each stored item ages, see What Fails When.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Download and print while the internet works

The FEMA and Red Cross brochure Food and Water in an Emergency (PDF), the CDC page How to Create an Emergency Water Supply, and the review Epidemics after Natural Disasters. Keep paper copies with this book.

#🧠 Remember this

Should you ration water?

No. Drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow.

How little food can healthy adults live on for an extended period?

About half their usual intake. Never cut food for children or pregnant women.

How much water do you plan per person per day?

At least 3.8 L (1 gallon) stored, with at least 2 quarts (1.9 L) for drinking. Very hot weather can double the need.

What drives outbreaks after disasters?

Displacement most of all, plus crowding, water and sanitation, underlying health, vaccination coverage and access to health care.

How soon after bad water can cholera start?

Within a few hours to 5 days, usually 2 to 3 days. Hepatitis A takes 15 to 50 days.

How many people per shared toilet?

Plan 1 per 20 people (or 1 per household). Never more than 50 in the first phase.

What is the days-left formula?

Amount on hand ÷ amount used per day.

Do dead bodies cause epidemics?

No. A 2007 review found no evidence that they do.

#📚 Sources

  1. FEMA and American Red Cross: Food and Water in an Emergency (n.d.). Never ration water: drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow; a normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (half gallon) a day; healthy people can survive on half their usual food intake for an extended period and without food for many days; food may be rationed safely except for children and pregnant women.
  2. American Red Cross: Food and Water in an Emergency (2009). Red Cross edition of the same brochure: never ration water; a normally active person needs at least one-half gallon of water a day just for drinking.
  3. CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply (2024). Store at least 1 gallon of water per person per day, for at least 3 days and 2 weeks if possible; store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates.
  4. Emerging Infectious Diseases (CDC): Epidemics after Natural Disasters, by Watson, Gayer and Connolly (2007). Outbreak risk is associated primarily with displacement, and with safe water and sanitation, crowding, the population's underlying health status and access to health care; disasters that do not displace people rarely lead to outbreaks; diarrheal outbreaks can follow drinking-water contamination and the risk is higher in developing countries; no evidence that dead bodies cause epidemics; rapid-onset disaster deaths are mostly from blunt trauma, crush injuries and drowning; measles risk depends on baseline immunization coverage, especially among children under 15.
  5. UNHCR: Water and sanitation guidance for field operations (PDF) (n.d.). Target of 1 latrine per 20 people or 1 per household; no latrine should serve more than 50 people in the first phase of an emergency; Sphere standards for handwashing facilities close to latrines.
  6. Ready.gov (FEMA): Water (n.d.). 1 gallon per person per day; children, nursing mothers and sick people may need more; in very hot temperatures water needs can double.
  7. CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Cholera (2024). Symptoms usually start 2 to 3 days after exposure, with a range of a few hours to 5 days.
  8. CDC Pink Book: Chapter 9, Hepatitis A (2024). Incubation averages 28 days (range 15–50 days); spread by the fecal-oral route through close contact or contaminated food or water.
  9. New England Journal of Medicine: Mortality in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria (Kishore et al.) (2018). Surveyed households averaged 68 days without water, 84 days without electricity and 41 days without cell service after Hurricane Maria, to December 31, 2017.
  10. WHO: Cholera fact sheet (n.d.). Cholera is caused by eating or drinking food or water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae; symptoms appear 12 hours to 5 days after exposure.

Mind & Plan

How people actually behave in disasters, how to plan as a family or group, and how to decide whether to stay or go.

🧠 Part 1 · Mind & PlanChapter 10
👥

Building Your Group: Size, Roles & Skills

🟢 CoreFirst 30 daysYear 1📚 24 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • One household cannot cover every job for years. The UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) plans 20 liters (about 5 gallons) of water per person per day for household use and hygiene, so a family of 5 must move about 100 kg (220 lb) of water every day.1
  • Write a skills inventory on paper. Map who can do medical, food, repair, child care, security and teaching work, then train to fill the gaps. Stop the Bleed alone has trained more than 5 million people.2
  • Give every job a lead and a named backup. Fire-safety planners already do this for anyone who needs help to escape.3
  • Plan around the most vulnerable first. Older adults and young children are most at risk from extreme heat and cold.4 After Hurricane Maria, the poor and the elderly had the highest risk of death.5
  • Put every dog in the plan. Temporary public shelters may not allow animals.6
11 mountil all of Puerto Rico had power again after Hurricane Maria7
20 Lwater per person per day for household use and hygiene (UNHCR)1
26%of US adults with disabilities had nowhere to go if they evacuated (2024)8
4.6 M+US Medicare users who rely on powered equipment, dialysis, oxygen or home health9

#🏚️ Why one household struggles alone Year 1

Long outages last months, not days. After Hurricane Maria hit in 2017, it took about 11 months before power was restored to the whole of Puerto Rico.7

The people with the least suffered the most. A George Washington University study, commissioned by Puerto Rico's governor, counted 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018. The poor and the elderly were at the highest risk.5

A household has a fixed number of hands. Every hour spent hauling water is an hour not spent cooking, nursing, teaching or keeping watch.

The daily workload, in numbers

Water is the heaviest daily job. UNHCR plans for 20 liters (about 5 gallons) per person per day for household use and personal hygiene.1 One liter of water weighs 1 kilogram (2.2 lb).

For a family of 5, that is 100 liters (26 gallons), or 100 kg (220 lb), every single day. Over a year it adds up to 36,500 liters (about 9,600 gallons).

Food is the second big job. The 2010 US Dietary Guidelines estimate that adult women need about 1,600–2,400 kilocalories (kcal) a day and adult men about 2,000–3,000, depending on age and activity.10 Two adults eating 2,000 kcal each need about 1.46 million kcal a year.

Then add cooking, firewood, washing, toilets, gardening, night watch, child care and nursing the sick. Each of those jobs takes hours every day. A bigger group shares them out.

📊 Key fact

Most households have no plan yet

In a June 2024 survey by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), only 46% of US adults without a disability and 48% of adults with a disability had an emergency plan.8 The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) 2023 national survey found that 37% of adults made a plan in the past year, down from 41% in 2022.11

So more than half of US adults had no emergency plan in 2024. Do not assume your neighbors have supplies or skills. Ask. How to start that conversation is in Organizing Neighbors: Mutual Aid & Watch.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Over 30 years, every person in your group changes role. Babies become workers. Strong adults become elders who need care. Review your group plan every year, the same way Ready.gov tells you to re-think your emergency kit every year.12

#📋 The skills inventory: who can do what

Write down every person's skills, honestly. A paper inventory shows you the gaps before an emergency does.

Use six areas: medical, food, mechanical, child care, security and teaching. For each person, mark one of three levels: can lead, can back up, or is learning.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. List every person

    Include babies, elders, guests and dogs. Everyone has needs. Most people also have skills.

  2. Ask, then watch

    Ask each adult what they can do. Then watch them do it once: dress a wound, fix a leak, cook a meal for ten.

  3. Fill the grid

    One row per person, one column per skill area. Mark lead, backup or learning in each box.

  4. Circle the gaps

    A column with no lead is your top training priority. A column with only one name means one illness can stop that job.

  5. Train to fill them

    Book classes while instructors and hospitals still exist. Start with the table below.

  6. Review every year

    People age, move away and learn new things. Redo the grid on the same date each year.12

The six skill areas and where to start
Skill areaWhat it coversTrain first inRead more
MedicalFirst aid, bleeding, cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), nursing the sickStop the Bleed, CPR and first aidStopping Severe Bleeding
FoodStorage, cooking without power, food safety, growingFood safety without a fridgeLong-Term Food Storage
MechanicalGenerators, tools, water systems, repairsGenerator and carbon monoxide safetyCarbon Monoxide
Child careFeeding, safety, illness signs, playInfant and child CPRSick Baby & Child: Danger Signs
SecurityWatch rota, locks, calm talkDe-escalationHome Security
TeachingReading, math, practical skillsTeaching your own skills to othersTeaching Kids

🩺 Medical: the skill everyone needs some of

Bleeding control is a course anyone can take. The Stop the Bleed course teaches direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets. The American College of Surgeons counts more than 5 million people trained.2

Children 12 and older can learn CPR, according to the American Heart Association's 2025 guidelines, published on October 22, 2025.13 Train your teenagers, not just the adults.

Everyone acts only within their training. The Red Cross first aid steps say to give care based on what you find, within your training.14 Your grid tells the group who that is.

🍲 Food and 🔧 mechanical

The food lead keeps people from getting sick. They know rules like these: a closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours without power, a full freezer about 48 hours and a half-full one about 24.15 More is in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

The mechanical lead keeps engines and fuel from killing anyone. Generators run outdoors only, more than 20 feet (6 meters) from windows, doors and vents.16

☠️ Danger

Never run a generator indoors

Never use a generator inside a home or garage. Fit battery-powered carbon monoxide (CO) alarms and replace them every 5 years.16 Make CO safety part of the mechanical lead's job, and teach every backup.

👶 Child care, 🛡️ security and 📚 teaching

Child care is a full job, not a side task. The person minding small children should not also be on watch or at the stove.

In this book, security means awareness, deterrence and calm talk. The security lead runs the watch rota and knows how to talk a tense person down. See De-escalation & Avoiding Violence.

Teaching keeps skills alive. Every lead teaches a backup. Children also need reading and math every week.

#🔄 Roles, backups and rotation

Every job gets a lead and a named backup. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) home fire escape advice assigns a helper to each person who needs help getting out, plus a backup in case the helper is not home.3 Use the same idea for every job in your group.

The backup steps in when the lead is sick, injured, asleep or away. Write both names on the rota so nobody has to guess.

Rotate the hardest jobs

Swap heavy and light jobs on a set day each week. Water hauling, night watch, nursing and small-child care are the hardest. Nobody should be stuck with one of them for months.

Match the job to the body. Pregnant women, elders and people getting over an illness can lead planning, teaching, record keeping and inventory while others carry loads.

One 8-hour night watch (10 p.m. to 6 a.m.) shared by adults: simple arithmetic
Adults on the rotaHours each, every nightOr: shift length if each stands every other night
24 hours8 hours
42 hours4 hours
81 hour2 hours

Group size buys sleep. With 2 adults, each gives up 4 hours of every night. With 8 adults, each gives 1. Sleep and shift plans are in Stress, Sleep & Routines.

Do

  • Write the rota on paper where everyone sees it
  • Name a backup for every job
  • Rotate the hard jobs on a set day each week
  • Pair each learner with a lead
  • Hold a short meeting every week

Don't

  • Let one person be the only medic or mechanic
  • Leave the same person on night watch for weeks
  • Give child care to someone who is also on watch
  • Hand out jobs by habit instead of by skill
  • Keep the plan only in one person's head
⚠️ Caution

The person who never stops

Watch for the lead who skips meals, sleep and their turn off. Take them off the rota for a day and let the backup run the job. Signs that someone is not coping are in Mental Health: Grief, Trauma & Suicide Prevention.

💡 Tip

Different brains, different roles

Give each person roles with a clear checklist and a result they can see. How to match roles to people with ADHD or autism is in Surviving With ADHD, Autism & Different Brains.

#👵 Elders, disabled people, children and dogs come first

Build the plan around the people who cannot fend for themselves. Ready.gov warns that older adults and young children are vulnerable to extreme temperatures, and tells you to check on neighbors during an outage.4

Elderly and disabled people

Disabled adults face bigger barriers to leaving. In the June 2024 CDC survey, 26% of adults with disabilities said they had nowhere to go, against 15% of adults without. 20% named the cost of evacuating, against 14%.8

They had also lived through more disasters: 80% of adults with disabilities had experienced a natural disaster, against 70% without.8

Millions depend on power to stay well. More than 3 million US Medicare beneficiaries have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment, and more than 4.6 million when dialysis, oxygen and home health services are included.9

  • Name a lead carer and a backup for each person who needs help.3
  • Make meeting places reachable with a wheelchair or walker. FEMA's family plan says to make them accessible for people with disabilities.17
  • List every powered device, medicine and supply each person uses, and how long it lasts without power. Ready.gov tells you to plan for medical devices that need power.4
🧓 Elderly & disabled

Elders hold skills too

Put elders' skills in the inventory, not just their needs. Teaching, mending, cooking, record keeping and minding children are jobs that need no heavy lifting. Care details are in Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

Babies and children

👶 Babies & children

Children are not small adults in the plan

FEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can survive on half their usual food for an extended period, but food should not be rationed for children and pregnant women.18

Name one adult responsible for each child in any emergency, plus a backup. Reunion plans are in The Family Emergency Plan.

Children grow into helpers. Teenagers 12 and older can learn CPR.13 Age-by-age jobs are in Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Store extra water for pregnant women: the CDC names them among those who need more.19 Do not ration a pregnant woman's food.18

Make sure women and girls help decide where toilets, water points and sleeping areas go. Use a buddy for night trips. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

Dogs and other pets

Ready.gov says to include pets in your family emergency plan and to have your vet microchip them.20

Do not count on a public shelter for your dog. The FDA warns that temporary public shelters may not allow animals.6 FEMA's 2024 Pet Preparedness Toolkit says to find pet-friendly shelters before an emergency.21

🐕 Dogs & pets

Every dog gets a lead and a backup

Name who feeds, waters, walks and treats each dog. The CDC says to store extra water for pets.19 Count dogs in your water and food math. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

A public shelter will take my dog if I have to leave.

Temporary public shelters may not allow animals.6 Find pet-friendly places before an emergency.21

In a shortage, share food out equally per head.

Healthy people can survive on half their usual food for an extended period, but food should not be rationed for children and pregnant women.18

Only adults can learn lifesaving skills.

The 2025 American Heart Association guidelines say children 12 and older can learn CPR.13

#👥 How big should your group be? Do the math

This book does not give a magic number. Every extra person adds hands and adds needs. Do your own arithmetic with official planning figures.

Three figures set the floor for any group:

  • Water: 20 liters (about 5 gallons) per person per day for household use and hygiene.1 The CDC says to store at least 1 gallon (3.8 liters) per person per day for emergencies.19
  • Toilets: UNHCR's target is 1 latrine per 20 people, or 1 per household. No latrine should serve more than 50 people in the first phase of an emergency.22
  • First aid: The Red Cross lists kit contents sized for a family of four.23
What a group needs, by size (arithmetic from UNHCR and Red Cross figures; round up)
PeopleWater a day at 20 L eachLatrines at 1 per 20Family-size first aid kits (1 per 4)
480 L (21 gal)11
12240 L (63 gal)13
25500 L (132 gal)27
501,000 L (264 gal)313

Bigger groups need more structure. More people means more decisions to make and more chances to disagree. Rules, decision methods and dispute resolution are in Group Rules, Decisions & Resolving Disputes.

Separate households can still work as one group. Each family keeps its own home and stores, and the households share skills, tools and night watch.

💡 Tip

Write the group's numbers on one page

Head count, babies, elders, pregnant women, dogs, daily water, daily calories, latrines and first aid kits. Recount every month. The full food math is in Calories & Nutrition.

#🤝 Forming the group and practicing together First 30 days

Start small and start now. A group is easier to build while phones, shops and classes still work.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Start with who you know

    Family first, then your nearest neighbors, then friends who have skills you lack.

  2. Talk about needs first

    Each household lists its people, health needs, medicines, pets and supplies.

  3. Fill the skills grid together

    Agree on a lead and a backup for every job. Write the gaps down.

  4. Write simple agreements

    Who decides what, how work and food are shared, and how disputes are settled. Put them on paper.

  5. Practice together

    The Red Cross advises practicing your plan at least twice a year.24 NFPA advises fire drills twice a year, once by day and once at night.3

  6. Review every year

    Update the grid, the rota and the numbers. Replace expired supplies.12

🎯 Practice now

Run a 24-hour no-power weekend

Pick a weekend. Use only stored water and food, run the rota and stand a night watch. Write down every problem, then fix one each week.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these for the group

  • A paper notebook for the skills grid, rota and head count
  • One family-size first aid kit per 4 people, checked for expiry dates23
  • Battery-powered CO alarms, replaced every 5 years16
  • Places in a Stop the Bleed, CPR or first aid class for at least two adults
▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Download and print while the internet works

FEMA's Family Emergency Communication Plan, the Red Cross Family Disaster Plan Template and FEMA's Pet Preparedness Toolkit (all PDFs). Keep paper copies with this book.

#⏳ How the group changes over 30 years Long haul

Your group ages one year every year. Plan the roles for the people you will have, not only the people you have today.

  1. Year 0

    Babies and toddlers need full-time care. Older adults and young children are most at risk from heat and cold.4

  2. Year 1

    Every lead has a trained backup. Every hard job rotates. The skills grid has no empty columns.

  3. Year 10

    A child who was 2 at the start is now 12: old enough to learn CPR under the 2025 guidelines.13 Teenagers become backups.

  4. Year 20

    Today's 50-year-olds are 70. Move them from heavy work to teaching, records and child minding.

  5. Year 30

    Children born after the outage are adults and leads. Skills must be taught, not just stored on paper.

How to pass skills on is in Passing On Skills to the Next Generation. Which trades to rebuild first is in Rebuilding Local Trades & Economy.
