The Family Emergency Plan

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 13 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Pick one out-of-area contact. Local phone lines tend to overload after an emergency, so everyone reports to the same faraway person.4
  • Choose four meeting places: inside the home, in the neighborhood, outside the neighborhood and out of town.5
  • Text, don't call. Texts may get through when calls do not.7
  • Put the plan on paper. Give every person a wallet card with the numbers and meeting places.8
  • Practice twice a year, once in daylight and once at night.9
  • Name a helper and a backup for every baby, older adult and person with a disability, and put your pets in the plan.911
<50%of US adults had an emergency plan (CDC survey, June 2024)1
5,192children reported missing after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita (2005)2
2× a yearhow often to practice your escape plan9
1–2 minmay be all the time you get to escape a home fire9

#🗺️ Why a written family plan matters First 72 h

A family plan answers five questions before you need them. Where do we meet? Who do we tell? Who gets the kids? Who helps the people who need help? What happens to the dog?

In a crisis there is no time to discuss these. A written plan means every person already knows their job.

Most adults do not have one. In a June 2024 CDC survey, only 46% of adults without a disability and 48% of adults with a disability had an emergency plan.1

This chapter builds your plan in order: the out-of-area contact, meeting places, school and work, the people and pets who need help, drills, and a fill-in template at the end.

Two decisions live in other chapters. Whether to shelter or leave is in Stay or Go?. What each person carries is in Go-Bags for Every Family Member.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view: build two layers

Official family plans lean on phones and texting. Keep that layer, because it is fast while networks work.

Then add a no-phone layer: fixed meeting places, set check-in times and paper notes. That layer still works when there is no power to charge anything. It is covered below in "When phones are down".

#📞 The out-of-area contact and the paper contact list

Choose one person who lives outside your area to be your family's message center. The American Red Cross advises this because local phone lines tend to be overloaded after an emergency.4

FEMA and Ready.gov give the same rule: pick someone outside town, because they may be easier to reach in a disaster.56

Everyone reports to the same person. Then one message to that person tells you where everyone is, and you do not have to reach five phones one by one.

Set up your out-of-area contact

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Ask a calm person far away

    Choose a friend or relative who lives outside your area. The Red Cross calls this your out-of-area contact.4 Ask them, and get a clear yes.

  2. Pick a backup in a different region

    If your main contact lives in the same disaster zone as you on the day, you still have a second person to reach.

  3. Agree on a short message format

    Who, where, condition, next move. Example: "Ana OK. At spot 3. Kids with me."

  4. Write both numbers on paper

    Put them on a wallet card for every person, including in each child's backpack.8

  5. Test it

    Have every person text the contact once. Fix any wrong number the same day.

Text first, keep calls short

Do

  • Text for anything that is not a life-threatening emergency57
  • Keep calls brief and give only vital information7
  • Limit non-emergency calls to save your phone battery7
  • Call 911 first for a life-threatening emergency7

Don't

  • Redial at once if a call fails; wait 10 seconds first7
  • Make non-emergency calls that tie up the network7
  • Count on texting 911; it only works in some places7

If something happens, we will just call each other.

Calls can fail even when the equipment works, because network congestion blocks them. The FCC advises texting instead, because texts may get through when calls do not.7 FEMA says the same.5

The paper contact list

Write every important number on paper. A contact list inside a dead phone cannot help you.

List the out-of-area contact and backup, close neighbors, each school or daycare, each workplace, your doctor or clinic, your vet, and the local animal shelter.

💡 Tip

Use the official wallet card

FEMA's family communication plan comes as a fillable, wallet-sized card.8 Fill one in for every person. Put copies in each go-bag, each car and each child's school bag.

🎯 Practice now

Practice this now while phones still work

This week, have every family member text the out-of-area contact: "Test. I'm OK. At home." Fix any wrong number on every card the same day.

#📍 Four meeting places, near to far

Pick safe, familiar places where your family can go for protection or to reunite. FEMA's plan uses four levels: indoors, in your neighborhood, outside your neighborhood and out of town.5

The Red Cross gives the reason for the two closest ones. One spot right outside the home is for a sudden emergency like a fire. A second spot is for when you cannot return home.4

What each meeting place is for
SpotUse it whenGood examples
1. Inside homeHigh winds or a storm: you must shelter indoors5A small, windowless inner room on the lowest floor5
2. Just outsideA sudden emergency like a fire4A big tree, the mailbox or a neighbor's house5
3. Out of neighborhoodYou cannot get home4Library, community center, house of worship, friend's home5
4. Out of townYou cannot get home or to spot 3, or your area is told to evacuate5A relative's or friend's home in another town5

Every spot must work for every person. FEMA says to make sure meeting places are accessible for household members with disabilities.5 Check steps, slopes, distance and whether there is shelter from rain and sun.

Every spot must work for your animals too. FEMA says to think about animal-friendly locations.5 Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, so line up pet-friendly options ahead of time.13

Measure the route to spots 3 and 4 on a paper map and write the distance in both kilometers and miles. See Map & Compass Navigation.

⚠️ Caution

Give each spot a backup

A library can flood. A friend's house can burn. For spots 3 and 4, write a second choice next to the first, and agree that whoever arrives first leaves a dated note if they have to move on.

#🏫 School, daycare and work plans

Disasters do not wait until everyone is home. Your plan must cover the hours when children are at school, adults are at work and someone is on the road.

The Red Cross says to know the evacuation sites at work and at school or day care.4 It also tells commuters to make a plan for how the family will stay in contact if separated.10

📊 Key fact

Separation is a documented risk

After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, 5,192 children were reported missing. Officials called it the largest child-recovery effort in US history, and it took more than six months.2 The last child was reunited in March 2006.3

Make the school and daycare plan

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Ask for the school's emergency plan

    Ask where children go if the building is evacuated, and how the school contacts parents.

  2. Update the pickup list

    Ask who the school will release your child to. Add at least two trusted adults besides the parents, and keep it current.

  3. Teach your child the pickup names

    Name the adults on the school's list out loud with your child. Teach them to go only with those people.

  4. Put a card in every backpack

    Parents' numbers, the out-of-area contact and the meeting places, on a wallet card.8

  5. Teach the plan at the child's level

    Ready.gov has a family plan page written for kids.6 Practice it together.

Work and commuting

Know your workplace evacuation site.4 Then decide now who leaves work to collect the children and who goes home to the animals and older relatives.

Write down a walking route home from work in case roads or transit stop. Keep walking shoes, water and a paper map at work, as part of your work go-bag.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and young children

Assign one adult to each baby, plus a backup in case that adult is away. NFPA gives this advice for infants in home escape plans.9 Do the same for every child too young to get out alone.

On the plan, write each child's feeding needs, formula type, medicines and allergies. Keep a current photo of each child with the wallet card.

#🔀 When phones are down: the no-phone plan

If the network is down, your plan must work on foot and on paper. That means fixed places, fixed times and written notes.

  • Fixed check-in times. Example: "If we cannot reach each other, go to spot 3. Be there at 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. every day."
  • Dated notes. Anyone who leaves home or a meeting spot leaves a note: date, time, names, where they went.
  • One direction. Always move outward through the spots in order: 1, 2, 3, 4. Then searchers know where to look next.

For ways to pass messages without phones, see Radios: Ham, GMRS, CB & Listening.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Plan routes so that no woman or girl has to walk alone to a far meeting place, especially at night. Pair people up in the plan.

If someone is pregnant, add her due date, her clinic and her prenatal records to the plan. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

⏳ The 30-year view

Keeping the plan alive for decades

Children grow up, people move and pets change. Review the whole plan at each twice-yearly drill, the same schedule NFPA gives for escape plan practice.9

Write in pencil so it is easy to update. Keep copies in sealed plastic bags, and give one to your out-of-area contact.

#🧑‍🦽 Babies, older adults, disabilities and pets

More adults with disabilities have lived through a disaster. In the CDC's June 2024 survey, 80% of adults with disabilities had lived through at least one natural disaster, compared with 70% of adults without disabilities.1

They also face more barriers to leaving. 26% said they had nowhere to go, compared with 15% of adults without disabilities. 20% named the cost of evacuating, compared with 14%.1

The CDC says accessible planning and communication may help close these gaps.1 That starts with your family plan.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults and people with disabilities

Name a helper and a backup for each person who needs help to move. NFPA says to plan for anyone with a disability and assign a backup in case the main helper is not home.9

List their medicines, devices (wheelchair, walker, hearing aids, glasses) and exactly how to move them. Check that every meeting place is accessible to them.5 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and other pets

Pets belong in the family plan. Ready.gov says to include them and to have your vet microchip each pet.11 If a lost pet is taken to a vet clinic or shelter, staff can scan it for the microchip number.13

Find pet-friendly places to stay before an emergency, because public shelters may not take animals.1213 Check the microchip registry has your current phone number. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

Example: who helps whom (fill in your own below)
Needs helpMain helperBackupMust bring
Baby, 8 monthsParent AGrandparentCarrier, feeding supplies
Grandparent with walkerParent BNeighborWalker, medicine list, glasses
Child, 6 yearsOlder siblingParent AWallet card
DogTeenParent BLeash, harness, photo

#🔁 Drills: how and how often

Practice twice a year. NFPA says to practice your home fire escape plan twice a year.9 The Red Cross plan also says to practice evacuating your home twice a year.4

Drill in daylight and at night. For young children, NFPA suggests telling them about a drill before bed, because the goal is practice, not fear.9

  1. Week 1

    Write the plan, fill in wallet cards and choose all four meeting places.

  2. Month 1

    Daytime drill: use both exits from each room, then text the out-of-area contact.9 Walk the routes to spots 3 and 4 with the children and write down the time and distance.

  3. Month 6

    Night drill, then review and update the whole plan.9

  4. Month 12

    Daytime drill again. Keep going: one day drill and one night drill every year.9

  5. Each new school year or job

    Update school, daycare and work details and the pickup list.

Run a home drill

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. Tell young children first

    Explain what will happen. For a night drill, tell them before bed.9

  2. Start the drill

    Press the smoke alarm test button so everyone learns the sound.

  3. Use the second way out

    Every room needs two ways out. Check that the doors and windows that lead outside open.9

  4. Get low under smoke

    Practice crawling low to the exit.9 Close doors behind you to slow the fire.9

  5. Meet at spot 2 and count heads

    Helpers arrive with their assigned baby, older adult and dog.

  6. Text the out-of-area contact

    "Drill. All OK at spot 2." This tests the contact's number as well as your exits.

  7. Fix what went wrong

    Talk about what was slow or confusing. Update the plan that day.

☠️ Danger

Never go back inside

Once you are out, stay out. Do not go back into a burning home for any reason.9 A fire can leave you as little as 1 or 2 minutes to escape once the smoke alarm sounds.9 Tell the fire department who is missing, including pets. Firefighters have the equipment to do rescues.9 Teach this rule to every child.

In an emergency you can always text 911.

Text-to-911 is only available in some locations. Always try to call 911 first.7

For a bigger household or group, give each adult a written role. See Building Your Group: Size, Roles & Skills.

#🧠 Remember this

Why an out-of-area contact?

Local phone lines tend to overload after an emergency. Everyone reports to one distant person.

What are the four meeting places?

Inside home, just outside, out of the neighborhood, out of town.

Call or text?

Text. Texts may get through when calls do not. Keep calls short.

How often do you drill?

Twice a year, once in daylight and once at night.

How long might you have to escape a home fire?

As little as 1 or 2 minutes. Never go back inside.

Who helps the baby, Grandma and the dog?

A named helper for each, plus a named backup.

Phones are down. Now what?

Go outward through the spots in order, show up at check-in times and leave a dated note.

Stay or Go? Sheltering in Place vs Evacuating

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 14 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Follow official orders first. Leave when your zone is told to evacuate. Get inside at once when you are told to shelter in place.76
  • Run from water. Hide from bad air. Storm surge is the greatest threat to life on the coast. In a radiation emergency: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.34
  • Leave early, or the road itself can kill. In the 2005 Hurricane Rita evacuation, over 100 of at least 119 storm deaths were linked to the evacuation.2
  • Keep at least half a tank of fuel at all times. Fill it up when an evacuation looks likely.1
  • Staying has its own killers. After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with carbon monoxide (CO) and killed 10.5
3.7 Mpeople left the Texas coast before Hurricane Rita in 20052
100+of at least 119 Rita deaths were linked to the evacuation2
49%of US hurricane deaths (1963–2012) came from storm surge9
½ tankof fuel to keep in your car at all times1

#🧭 The official rule: plan for both, then follow orders

Plan for staying and for leaving, before anything happens. An earlier Ready.gov page (archived 2008) called stay-or-go the first important decision in an emergency, and told you to plan for both.8

Stay inside when the outside is the danger. Officials recommend sheltering in place when there is little time to react and being outside would be more dangerous.6

Leave when the hazard will reach your home. For hurricanes, a National Hurricane Center (NHC) official put it simply: "We evacuate from the water, not the wind, and we have evacuation zones."7

Orders come first

If officials order you to shelter in place, act immediately.6 Do not finish chores or go outside to look.

If you are told to evacuate, follow the recommended routes. Do not take shortcuts. They may be blocked.1

Leave early enough that severe weather cannot trap you. Plan now how you will leave and where you will go.1

💡 Tip

Find your zone today

Hurricane evacuations are ordered by zone.7 Look up the zones for your home, work and school while the internet still works. Write them on your paper plan. See The Family Emergency Plan.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

If no official orders reach you, use the same tests officials use: get away from rising water, and get inside when the air outside is the danger.36

A safe, stocked home with water, food and a garden is a strong reason to stay. See Preparing Your Home for a Long Outage.

#🌊 When leaving is the right call

In hurricanes, water kills more people than wind. The NHC says storm surge and large waves pose the greatest threat to life and property along the coast.3

An NHC study of US storms from 1963 to 2012 found that 49% of deaths, nearly half, were blamed on storm-surge flooding.9

Inland, flooding is the major threat from tropical storms.3 See Floods.

Which hazards usually mean stay, and which mean go
HazardUsual moveWhere to be
Storm surge on the coastGo when your zone is ordered out7Outside the surge zone3
Radiation releaseStay: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned4Basement or middle of the building4
Chemical cloud (plume)Stay if told to shelter in place6Interior room above ground, sealed1011
Any danger with little warningStay when outside is more dangerous6Indoors

For other hazards, see Wildfire & Smoke, Nuclear & Radiation Emergencies and Chemical Spills & Industrial Accidents.

Hurricane wind is the main killer, so a strong house is enough.

Storm surge is the greatest threat to life on the coast.3 It caused 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths from 1963 to 2012.9

#🏠 When staying is the right call: shelter in place

Shelter in place means you stay inside, in the safest room, until officials say it is safe to go out.4 It is the right move when being outside is more dangerous than being inside.6

Chemicals: go up. Radiation: go down or to the middle. Ready.gov guidance sends you above ground for a chemical release, but below ground for a radiological one.104

Radiation: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Get inside now

    This is the first of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) three rules: get inside, stay inside, stay tuned.4

  2. Go to the basement or the middle

    Get to the middle of the building or a basement, away from doors and windows.4

  3. Shut out the outside air

    Close and lock windows and doors. Turn off fans, air conditioners and forced-air heaters that pull in outside air.4

  4. Stay tuned

    Listen for updated instructions from officials.4 Without grid power, that means a battery or hand-crank radio.

  5. Stay until officials say it is safe

    Sheltering usually lasts at least 24 hours.13 Keep everyone inside, pets included.12

Chemical cloud: an interior room above ground, sealed

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Bring everyone in, pets too

    Pets should not go outside during a chemical emergency.12

  2. Shut out the outside air

    Close and lock windows and outside doors. Close the fireplace damper. Turn off fans, heating and air conditioning.12

  3. Go to an interior room above ground

    Take everyone into an interior room with no or few windows and shut the door.12 For a chemical cloud, shelter above ground, not in the basement.10

  4. Seal the room

    Seal windows, doors and air vents with plastic sheeting and duct tape.11 Ready.gov cites studies showing that sealing a room with common materials makes it safer against a chemical plume.10

  5. Listen and wait

    Keep the radio on. Leave the room only when officials say the air outside is safe.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and pets come inside with you

Pets should not go outside during a chemical or radiation emergency. Bring them into the shelter room.12 Keep a leash, a water bowl and waste bags in that room. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

☠️ Danger

No generator near your shelter room

After Katrina and Rita, most generator CO poisonings involved generators placed outside but near homes.5 Outside is not enough. See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Shelter-in-place kit

Plastic sheeting and duct tape for sealing a room.11 Cut the sheets to fit your chosen room's windows, door and vents now, and label each one. Add a battery or hand-crank radio so you can stay tuned.4

#🚗 What really happened on the road: Hurricane Rita, 2005

In September 2005, nearly 3.7 million people left the Texas coast in the days before Hurricane Rita made landfall.2 A 2018 review calls it the largest emergency evacuation in US history.2

The evacuation killed more people than the storm did. Over 100 of the at least 119 deaths attributed to Rita were linked to the evacuation itself, about 107 by that count.2

Heat in stuck cars was a major killer. At least 10% of evacuation deaths were linked to hyperthermia (dangerous overheating) in vehicles.2

Medical examiners suspected overheating or a worsened chronic illness in about another 50% of evacuation deaths.2

A bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire in the evacuation traffic. About two dozen people died.2

Plans can be fixed. Texas revised its evacuation plans after Rita and used the changes successfully in later storms.2

Three lessons for your own plan

  • Leave early. Go early enough that severe weather cannot trap you.1 Long waits in traffic were where Rita evacuees overheated.2
  • Pack for a long, hot wait. Carry drinking water and a way to stay cool for every person and animal in the car. Overheating in vehicles was linked to at least 10% of evacuation deaths.2
  • Plan transport for frail people first. People with chronic illness were among those who died on the road.2 Arrange their ride and supplies before anyone else's.
  • No car? Arrange a ride now. Ready.gov says to make arrangements with family, friends or your local government.1
🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older, sick and disabled people

Rita's deaths show the danger: overheating and worsened chronic illness in vehicles, and a burning bus full of nursing-home residents.2

If someone in your home is frail, uses medical equipment or cannot cope with heat, plan to leave early, before roads fill.1 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children in the car

Overheating in vehicles was a recorded cause of Rita evacuation deaths.2 Pack water, feeds and diapers for a long delay, not just the planned drive time. Never leave a child alone in a car. See The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit.

#⚖️ Risks of leaving vs risks of staying

Neither choice is free of risk. Compare the documented dangers for your hazard, your home and your people. Then pick the smaller danger.

Documented risks on each side
If you goIf you stay
Heat in stalled traffic: at least 10% of Rita evacuation deaths2Storm surge: 49% of US hurricane deaths, 1963–20129
Vehicle fire: the Rita nursing-home bus2Carbon monoxide: 10 generator deaths in Alabama and Texas after Katrina and Rita5
Blocked shortcuts, washed-out roads, downed power lines and flooded roads1Inland flooding from tropical storms3
Being outdoors during a radiation or chemical release, when inside is safer46Being trapped by severe weather if you leave too late1

Leaving is always the safe choice.

In the Hurricane Rita evacuation, the evacuation itself was linked to over 100 of at least 119 deaths.2 Leave when your zone is ordered out, and leave early.1

A generator outside the house cannot hurt anyone inside.

After Katrina and Rita, most generator CO poisonings involved generators placed outside but near homes. At least 78 people were poisoned and 10 died.5

Do

  • Leave early when your zone is ordered out
  • Follow the recommended routes
  • Keep half a tank of fuel, always
  • Get inside fast for radiation or chemicals
  • Follow official instructions on a battery radio

Don't

  • Take shortcuts that may be blocked
  • Wait until severe weather traps you
  • Run a generator near the house
  • Go outside to look during a release
  • Drive into flooded areas

Each rule above comes from Ready.gov, the CDC or Ready Illinois guidance.1456

#⛽ If you go: fuel, timing and routes

Keep at least half a tank of fuel at all times. Ready.gov advises this in case you must leave without warning. Fill the tank when an evacuation seems likely.1

Do not count on buying fuel on the way. Gas stations may be closed during emergencies and unable to pump gas during power outages.1

Take one car per family if you can. Ready.gov advises this to reduce congestion and delay.1

Know your range before you need it. Multiply the fuel in the tank by your car's fuel economy. Use your own car's measured figures, not the sticker.

The formula: gallons × miles per gallon = miles. In metric: liters ÷ (liters per 100 km) × 100 = km.

Driving range: example arithmetic
CarHalf tankFull tank
45 L (12 gal) tank, 7.8 L/100 km (30 mpg)290 km (180 mi)580 km (360 mi)
57 L (15 gal) tank, 9.4 L/100 km (25 mpg)302 km (188 mi)604 km (375 mi)
76 L (20 gal) tank, 11.8 L/100 km (20 mpg)322 km (200 mi)644 km (400 mi)

The evacuation, step by step

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. Know your zone and destination

    Plan how you will leave and where you will go.1 Hurricane orders go by zone.7

  2. Keep half a tank, always

    That covers an unexpected order to leave.1

  3. Fill up when evacuation looks likely

    Do it before the order, not after.1

  4. Grab go-bags and leave early

    Leave early enough to avoid being trapped by severe weather.1 See Go-Bags for Every Family Member.

  5. Use the recommended routes

    Do not take shortcuts. They may be blocked. Never drive into flooded areas.1

  6. Follow official instructions

    Listen to a battery-powered radio and follow local evacuation instructions.1 Keep a paper map with your route marked.

  7. Tell your out-of-area contact

    Say where you are going, your route and when you expect to arrive.

  1. Every day

    Fuel stays at half a tank or more.1

  2. Evacuation looks likely

    Fill the tank.1 Load go-bags, medicines, documents and pet supplies.

  3. Your zone is ordered out

    Leave. Use the recommended routes.1

  4. On the road

    Watch for washed-out roads and downed power lines. Do not drive into flooded areas.1

  5. Shelter-in-place order instead

    Get inside immediately.6

🎯 Practice now

Drive it and drill it

Ready.gov advises getting to know alternate routes out of your area.1 Drive your evacuation route and one alternate route in daylight. Note the time it takes and where the route could flood.

Run a shelter-in-place drill: everyone, including the dog, into the chosen room with the door shut. Time it, then improve it.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Save these official pages now

Print or save while the internet works: Ready.gov Evacuation, CDC: What to Do in Radiation Emergencies and NHC: Hurricane Hazards.

#📍 Where to go: relatives, shelters, rural or urban

Decide where you will go before you need to. Ready.gov tells you to plan where you will go if you are told to evacuate.1

Pick several destinations in different directions. Ready.gov advises this so you still have options in an emergency.1

Your options, in planning order

  • Friends or relatives outside the hazard zone. Agree now, in writing, that you can come. Say how many people and animals.
  • Public shelters opened by officials. Listen to official instructions for which shelters are open. Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, so plan where your dog will stay.14
  • Any safe place you can reach on half a tank, by your own range math above.1

Rural or urban? What the evidence supports

We found no reliable study that ranks rural or urban places as safer in a long outage. So this book makes no such claim.

Instead, test any destination against facts you can check yourself:

  • Is it outside storm-surge and flood zones?3
  • Can you reach it on the fuel you will have?1
  • Does it have water you can make safe? See Finding Water When the Taps Stop.
  • Do people there know you and expect you?
  • Can your baby, your oldest relative and your dog cope with the trip?
🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Before you arrive, ask how sleeping areas and toilets work at your destination or shelter. Travel and use facilities in pairs. Pack menstrual supplies and any prescribed medicines in each go-bag. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

⏳ The 30-year view

Leaving for good

In a multi-year outage, leaving can mean leaving your stores, water system and garden behind. Weigh that against a hazard that will reach the house, such as storm surge.3

#📋 The stay-or-go decision checklist

Answer these questions in order. Stop at the first "yes". The diagram and table say the same thing two ways.

The decision checklist
AskIf yes
1. Is there an official order for your area?Follow it right away.61
2. Is the danger in the air right now (radiation or a chemical cloud)?Stay. Shelter in place in the right room.410
3. Is your home in a storm-surge or flood zone, with a storm on the way?Go, early, by the recommended routes.31
4. Can you stay safely: a safe room, water, and no generator near the house?Stay and prepare.5
5. You answered "no" to question 4?Go to your planned destination, with at least half a tank.1

Before you lock the door

  • Medicines, documents and cash are in the go-bags.
  • Every person is accounted for, plus the dog, leash and food.
  • Your out-of-area contact knows your plan.
  • You have a paper map with your route marked.

The evacuation was linked to over 100 of at least 119 deaths. Heat in stuck cars killed people.

Can you count on buying fuel on the way?

No. Gas stations may be closed or unable to pump during power outages.

Is a generator outside the house safe?

Not near the house. Most CO poisonings after Katrina and Rita came from generators outside but near homes.

#📚 Sources

Half a tank of gas at all times, full tank if evacuation seems likely; gas stations may be closed or unable to pump during power outages; one car per family; follow recommended routes, no shortcuts; watch for washed-out roads and downed lines, do not drive into floods; listen to a battery radio; know alternate routes and several destinations in different directions; arrange rides if you have no car; leave early.
  2. Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness: Reflection on Lessons Learned: An Analysis of the Adverse Outcomes Observed During the Hurricane Rita Evacuation (2018).   3. NOAA National Hurricane Center: Hurricane Hazards (n.d.). Storm surge and large waves are the greatest threat to life and property along the coast; flooding is the major threat for people living inland.
  4. CDC: What to Do in Radiation Emergencies (n.d.). Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned; middle of the building or a basement, away from doors and windows; close windows, turn off fans and forced-air systems; stay inside until officials say it is safe.
  5. CDC MMWR: Carbon Monoxide Poisonings After Two Major Hurricanes, Alabama and Texas, 2005 (2006). At least 78 poisoned and 10 deaths from portable generators; most involved generators placed outside but near homes.
  6. Ready Illinois (State of Illinois): Stay Put (n.d.). Shelter in place when there is little time to react and being outside is more dangerous; act immediately when officials order it.
  7. CBS News: National Hurricane Center Highlights Deadliest Problem Ahead Of What Forecasters Believe Will Be Active Season (n.d.). NHC official: "We evacuate from the water, not the wind, and we have evacuation zones."
  8. Ready.gov (archived): Deciding to Stay or Go (2008). Whether to shelter in place or evacuate is the first important decision after an incident; plan for both in advance.
  9. FOX Weather: Storm surge from hurricanes, tropical storms kills more in US than wind (n.d.). Reports the NHC study by Edward Rappaport: 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths (1963–2012) blamed on storm surge.

  13. State of Nevada Emergency Management: Types of Radiation Emergencies (n.d.). Sheltering in a radiation emergency usually lasts at least 24 hours.
  14. FDA: Take Care of Your Pets Before Disaster Strikes (n.d.). Temporary public shelters may not allow animals.
🧠 Part 1 · Mind & PlanChapter 14
🎒

Go-Bags for Every Family Member

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 15 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Pack one bag per person, sized to their body. Keep a child's pack at or under 10% of body weight. Even fit soldiers are advised to stay at or under 30%.89
  • Each bag covers 3 days away from home. The Red Cross evacuation supply is 1 gallon (3.8 liters) of water per person per day, plus easy food, for 3 days.2
  • Babies, elders and dogs need their own supplies. Formula and diapers; medicines, glasses and hearing-aid batteries; collar, leash, ID, food and a bowl.12
  • Copies of documents and cash go in a waterproof packet. ID, insurance, proof of address, birth certificates and a medication list.12
  • Check every bag at least once a year. Replace expired items and refit bags as children grow.1
3 daysof supplies in an evacuation bag2
3.8 L(1 gallon) of water per person per day2
≤10%of a child's body weight in a backpack8
≤30%of body weight: the recommended ceiling for soldiers9

#🎒 What a go-bag is for First 72 h

A go-bag is the bag you grab when you must leave home fast. Fire, flood, a chemical leak or a damaged house can all force you out in minutes. The American Red Cross says every household should pack one.3

It is not your home supply. The Red Cross uses two sizes: a 3-day supply to take when you evacuate and a 2-week supply to keep at home.2 Your long-term stores stay at home. See Storing Water and Long-Term Food Storage.

Ready.gov says to keep supplies at home, at work and in the car.1 At work, be ready to shelter for at least 24 hours, and keep comfortable walking shoes with your supplies.1

Ready.gov also says to store items in airtight plastic bags and keep the whole kit in one or two easy-to-carry containers.1 For a family on foot, that means one backpack for each person who can carry one.

Whether to leave at all is a separate decision. It is covered in Stay or Go?

A go-bag should hold everything you need to survive.

Official lists size it for 3 days of evacuation. The 2-week supply stays at home.2 Carrying heavy loads causes injuries: foot blisters, stress fractures and back strains are among the most common.10

Do

  • Pack one bag per person who can carry one
  • Keep bags in one known spot near the exit
  • Weigh every bag on a bathroom scale
  • Put the heavy shared gear on the strongest adults

Don't

  • Pack one giant family bag that only one person can lift
  • Hide bags where only one person knows to look
  • Guess the weight
  • Borrow from the bags for daily use and forget to refill

#🧾 The adult bag: what the official lists include

Ready.gov and the American Red Cross publish the two most-used kit lists. Their core items overlap. The table merges them so you can pack from one list.12

Adult go-bag core items (Ready.gov and American Red Cross)
NeedWhat to packSource
Water1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day; 3 days for evacuationRed Cross2
FoodNon-perishable, easy-to-prepare food; manual can openerRed Cross, Ready.gov21
Light and newsFlashlight; battery or hand-crank radio (NOAA Weather Radio in the US); extra batteriesReady.gov, Red Cross12
First aidFirst aid kit; 7-day supply of medicines and medical itemsRed Cross2
Signal and airWhistle to signal for help; dust mask to help filter contaminated airReady.gov1
ShelterPlastic sheeting, scissors and duct tape; emergency blanketReady.gov, Red Cross12
HygieneMoist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties; soap and hand sanitizerReady.gov1
ToolsMulti-purpose tool; wrench or pliers to turn off utilitiesRed Cross, Ready.gov21
Phone and mapsCell phone with chargers and a backup battery; local mapsReady.gov1
Clothes and sleepComplete change of clothes for your climate; sturdy shoes; sleeping bag or warm blanketReady.gov1
Papers and moneyCopies of key documents; family and emergency contacts; cashRed Cross, Ready.gov21
ExtrasSpare car and house keys; matches in a waterproof container; rain gear; work glovesRed Cross, Ready.gov21

The first aid kit, light, radio and navigation each have their own chapter. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit, Radios and Map & Compass Navigation.

Water is the heavy part

One liter of water weighs 1 kg (2.2 lb). So 1 US gallon (3.8 L) weighs about 3.8 kg (8.3 lb).

The Red Cross 3-day evacuation supply is 3 gallons (11.4 L) per person.2 That is 11.4 kg (25 lb) of water for one person, before food, clothes or anything else.

For a 60 kg (132 lb) adult, that water alone is 19% of body weight. Compare that with the limits in the next section.

💡 Tip

Split the water load

Ready.gov says to keep a kit in the car too.1 If you leave by vehicle, the extra water rides there. On foot, carry what you can and pack a way to treat water you find. See Disinfecting Water and Water Filters.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Ready.gov lists feminine supplies and personal hygiene items in the basic kit.1 Pack at least 3 days of products for every girl and woman who menstruates, plus spares and a few sealable bags for used products.

Reusable options are in Periods Without Stores. Safety while displaced is in Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Start with what you already have

The Red Cross suggests starting with what you already own, including a backpack or duffel bag, then adding a few useful items as your budget allows.4 A school backpack with two wide straps is a fine first go-bag.

#⚖️ How heavy is too heavy?

Weigh every bag, then compare it with the carrier's body weight. Most research on carrying loads comes from soldiers. It gives clear ceilings you can use.

Adults

A U.S. Army report gives the Infantry School's recommended limits: a fighting load of 22 kg (48 lb), about 30% of body weight, and an approach-march load of 33 kg (72 lb), about 45%.11

A 2018 study in Military Medicine notes that loads of 30% of body mass or less are recommended to avoid drops in performance.9 It tested soldiers on a 10 km (6.2 mi) mixed-terrain course carrying 30% and 45% of body mass.9

It found that standard equations underestimate the energy cost of carrying loads over rough ground.9 A pack that feels fine on a flat road costs more on trails, mud or rubble.

These numbers come from trained, fit soldiers. Treat 30% as a ceiling for healthy adults, not a target.

Children

The National Safety Council (NSC) says a child's backpack should weigh no more than 5–10% of the child's body weight.8

KidsHealth, from the Nemours children's health system, gives a wider range of 10–20%. Its example: an 80 lb (36 kg) child should carry no more than 8–16 lb (3.6–7.3 kg).7 For a long walk, use the lower number.

Pack weight at 10%, 20% and 30% of body weight (arithmetic)
Body weight10%20%30%
20 kg (44 lb)2 kg (4.4 lb)4 kg (8.8 lb)6 kg (13 lb)
35 kg (77 lb)3.5 kg (7.7 lb)7 kg (15 lb)10.5 kg (23 lb)
50 kg (110 lb)5 kg (11 lb)10 kg (22 lb)15 kg (33 lb)
60 kg (132 lb)6 kg (13 lb)12 kg (26 lb)18 kg (40 lb)
80 kg (176 lb)8 kg (18 lb)16 kg (35 lb)24 kg (53 lb)

Children use the 10% column. The 20% column is the top of the KidsHealth range.7 The 30% column is the soldiers' ceiling.9

What too much weight does

A 2004 review of soldier load carriage lists the common injuries: foot blisters, stress fractures, back strains, metatarsalgia (pain in the ball of the foot), rucksack palsy (numbness or weakness from strap pressure on nerves) and knee pain.10

The same review says loads are easier to carry when they are lighter, better distributed and carried in better-designed equipment.10

⚠️ Caution

Narrow straps cause numbness

Tight, narrow straps that dig into the shoulders can cause tingling, numbness and weakness in the arms and hands.7 Choose wide, padded straps and loosen them if hands start to tingle.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Weigh the person

    Step on a bathroom scale without the bag. Write the number down.7

  2. Weigh them wearing the bag

    The difference is the pack weight. Do this for every bag, including the dog's.

  3. Work out the limit

    Multiply body weight by 0.10 for a child or 0.30 for an adult ceiling. Example: 60 kg × 0.30 = 18 kg (40 lb).

  4. Cut the weight

    Remove duplicates. Move water to the car kit. Give heavy shared items to the strongest adults.

  5. Walk with it on real ground

    Rough ground costs more energy than standard equations predict, so test on hills, grass or gravel.9

🎯 Practice now

Walk your route with the bags

Once a season, walk part of your evacuation route with everyone wearing their bag. Note who struggles and rebalance the loads. Drills and meeting points are in The Family Emergency Plan.

#🧒 Children's go-bags

A child who walks well can carry a small, light bag of their own. It holds personal items. Adults carry the water and heavy gear.

Ready.gov lists books, games, puzzles or other activities for children.1 The Red Cross adds games and activities, plus family and emergency contact information.2

  • A contact card with parents' names, phone numbers and an out-of-area contact
  • A complete change of clothes and sturdy shoes1
  • A whistle to signal for help1
  • A small flashlight, a water bottle and a few snacks
  • One comfort item and one small game or book

Fit rules

Use two wide shoulder straps. Bags slung over one shoulder, across the chest, or with only one strap do not spread the weight as well.7

The pack should rest evenly in the middle of the back and should not sag down to the buttocks.7

Lighten or adjust the pack if a child struggles to put it on or take it off, has back pain, or leans forward to carry it.7

👶 Babies & children

Children grow out of their bags

Clothes, shoes and safe pack weight all change as a child grows. Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.1 Re-weigh the child and the bag at every check.

Skills children can learn by age are in Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age.

#👶 The baby's bag (carried by an adult)

A baby cannot carry anything, so the baby's supplies add to an adult's load. If you can, have one adult carry the baby and another carry the baby's bag.

Ready.gov lists infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.1 The Red Cross lists bottles, formula, baby food and diapers.2

  • 3 days of formula or baby food, plus bottles and a way to clean them
  • 3 days of diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream
  • Spare clothes and a warm layer
  • A sling or soft carrier, so your hands stay free
  • The baby's medicines, a thermometer and a copy of the vaccination record

Count the baby in the carrier's load. Weigh yourself holding the baby and wearing the bag, then compare the difference with your 30% ceiling.9

👶 Babies & children

Full lists and safe feeding

Quantities for 2 weeks, 3 months and 1 year are in The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit. Safe formula preparation without power is in Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

#🧓 Elderly and disabled family members

Pack the small medical items people forget. The Red Cross lists hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, syringes and a cane.2

Ready.gov adds prescription eyeglasses, contact lens solution, prescription medicines, and non-prescription medicines such as pain relievers, anti-diarrhea medicine, antacids or laxatives.1

How many days of medicine?

The current Red Cross survival kit list says a 7-day supply of medications and medical items.2 Its power outage checklist says the same.5

Another Red Cross emergency supply checklist says a 1-month supply.6 Ask the doctor or pharmacist how to build an emergency supply. See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

Pack a written medication list with medical information. The Red Cross lists it among the documents to copy.2

🧓 Elderly & disabled

If they cannot carry the bag

Weigh the bag while they wear it. Watch for the same warning signs used for children: struggling to put it on or off, back pain, or leaning forward.7 If you see them, move the weight to someone else.

Mobility aids, oxygen and dementia care are covered in Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

#🐕 The dog's go-bag

Your dog needs its own supplies. The Red Cross lists pet supplies: collar, leash, ID, food, carrier and bowl.2 Ready.gov adds pet food and extra water for your pet.1

Pack current photos of you with your pet.3 If you are separated, a photo helps you show that the dog is yours.

  • Collar with ID tag, plus a spare leash
  • 3 days of food in an airtight bag
  • Water and a collapsible bowl
  • Any medicines your dog takes
  • Copies of vaccination and medical records
  • Waste bags

The dog's food and water add to an adult's load. Weigh them into someone's budget.

🐕 Dogs & pets

More on dogs

Food and water needs by dog size are in Dogs in a Long Emergency and Feeding Dogs Without Kibble. A dog first aid list is in Dog First Aid.

#📄 Documents and cash

Pack copies of documents, sealed against water. The Red Cross lists copies of these: medication list and medical information, proof of address, deed or lease, passports, birth certificates and insurance policies.2

Ready.gov lists copies of insurance policies, identification and bank account records, saved electronically or in a waterproof, portable container.1

FEMA's financial first aid kit

The US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and Operation HOPE publish the Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (EFFAK) for free.12 It has sections for household information, professional advisors and health care providers, and a checklist of legal documents and financial statements.12

Its checklist includes items such as military ID and discharge papers (DD 214). If a document is missing, it says to contact the company or agency for a copy.13 Ready.gov's financial preparedness page links the kit and its forms.14

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Gather

    Use the EFFAK checklist to find each document.13 Ask the agency for copies of anything missing.

  2. Copy

    Photocopy each document. Add the family contact list and a current photo of each pet with you.3

  3. Seal

    Put the copies in airtight plastic bags or a waterproof container.1

  4. Split

    Give a packet to each adult bag, so one lost bag does not lose everything.

  5. Back up

    Ready.gov mentions saving records electronically.1 Keep paper as well, because phones need charging.

Cash

Both official lists include cash. Ready.gov lists cash or traveler's checks; the Red Cross lists extra cash.12

💡 Tip

Pack small bills

Ready.gov warns that ATMs and card machines may not work in a power outage.15 Small bills mean you do not depend on anyone having change. Split the cash between adult bags.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view: papers

Deeds, birth records and identity papers matter for decades, long after phones fail. See Preserving Knowledge & Records for paper and ink that last.

#🔁 Checking and rotating bags

A bag only works if what is inside still works. Ready.gov's maintenance advice is short:1

  • Keep canned food in a cool, dry place
  • Store boxed food in tightly closed plastic or metal containers
  • Replace expired items as needed
  • Re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family's needs change

Make sure every family member knows where the kits are kept.1

  1. Today

    Start with what you already have, including a backpack or duffel bag.4

  2. Then

    Add a few useful items at a time, as your budget allows.4

  3. Each check

    Replace expired items.1 Write the earliest expiry date on a tag on the outside.

  4. Every year

    Re-think everyone's needs and update the bags.1

  5. After any use

    Refill the bag before you put it away.

  6. Growth spurt

    Re-weigh the child and the bag against the 10% limit.8

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view: bags without stores

When stores are gone, you cannot buy replacements. Eat bag food at home before it expires and refill from your home stores. Choose bag items that do not expire, such as tools, whistles, cups and clothing.

The bag's job stays the same for decades: 3 days away from home. What changes is the family: children grow, elders need more help, and dogs age.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Download and print while the internet works

  • Ready.gov: Build a Kit
  • American Red Cross: What Do You Need in a Survival Kit
  • FEMA: Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (large print)
  • KidsHealth: Backpack Safety

Printable lists for every kit are in Master Checklists.

#🧠 Remember this

How many days does a go-bag cover?

3 days for evacuation. The 2-week supply stays at home (Red Cross).

How much water per person per day?

1 gallon (3.8 L). Three days weighs about 11.4 kg (25 lb).

How heavy can a child's pack be?

10% of body weight or less (NSC). A 20 kg child carries 2 kg.

What is the adult ceiling?

30% of body weight, the figure recommended for trained soldiers.

How many days of medicine?

At least 7 days (Red Cross). Another Red Cross checklist says 1 month.

Originals or copies of documents?

Copies, sealed in airtight or waterproof bags.

How often do you check the bags?

At least every year, and replace expired items.

Part 2

Water

A person dies of dehydration long before starvation. How much water you need, how to store it, find it, and make it safe for decades.

💧 Part 2 · WaterChapter 15
🥤

How Much Water You Really Need

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 12 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day. That is the CDC and Ready.gov (FEMA) minimum. Keep at least 3 days, and 2 weeks if you can.12
  • In very hot weather, plan for double. Official guidance says heat can double water needs.2
  • Store extra for pregnant and breastfeeding women, children, sick people and pets. The CDC names pregnant women, sick people and pets; extension guidance adds children and nursing mothers.16
  • One gallon is a floor, not a full day. The humanitarian Sphere standard is 15 L (4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and hygiene.3
  • Thirty years cannot come out of storage. At 1 gallon a day, a family of 4 uses 1,460 gallons (5,527 L) a year. You need a source that refills.1
3.8 L(1 gallon) per person per day: the CDC home minimum1
14 daysof stored water: the CDC goal if you can manage it1
×2how much water needs can rise in very hot temperatures2
15 Lper person per day: the Sphere humanitarian minimum3

#📏 The official numbers, side by side

Agencies give different numbers because they answer different questions. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Ready.gov tell households what to store at home for a short emergency.1 Sphere sets minimum standards for humanitarian aid after a disaster.4

Know both. The home number tells you what to store. The humanitarian number tells you what a household uses once drinking, cooking and washing all count.

Home storage: CDC and FEMA First 72 h

Store at least 1 gallon (3.8 L) of water per person per day. The CDC says to keep at least a 3-day supply, and a 2-week supply if possible.1

Ready.gov, the FEMA preparedness site, gives the same figure of 1 gallon per person per day.2 The CDC says this water covers drinking, cooking and brushing teeth.1

Notice the words "at least". Both agencies present the gallon as a minimum, and both say hot climates need more.12

Disaster relief: Sphere and UNHCR First 30 days

The Sphere standard is 15 L (about 4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene (Sphere Handbook, 2011 edition).3 That is almost 4 times the CDC home minimum.

Sphere training material says 7.5 L (2 gallons) per person per day may be appropriate only for a short time, in the acute phase of a drought.4 It also says a minimum is never a maximum.4

UNHCR, the UN refugee agency, plans for 20 L (5.3 gallons) per person per day for domestic needs and personal hygiene in refugee settings.5

Official daily water figures, per person
Who says itPer dayWhat it is for
CDC, Ready.gov (FEMA)At least 3.8 L (1 gal)Home emergency stock: drinking, cooking, brushing teeth
Ready.gov (FEMA)Up to doubleVery hot weather
Sphere, short term only7.5 L (2 gal)Acute phase of a drought, for a short time
Sphere minimum15 L (4 gal)Drinking, cooking and personal hygiene
UNHCR20 L (5.3 gal)Domestic needs and hygiene in refugee settings

Sources for each row: CDC and Ready.gov12, Sphere34, UNHCR.5

#🍽️ Where a day's water goes

Sphere splits basic daily water into three uses: drinking (including water in food), basic hygiene and basic cooking.3 Seeing the split shows why one gallon runs out fast.

Basic survival water needs per person per day (Sphere)
UseLitersUS gallonsDepends on
Drinking and food2.5–3 L0.7–0.8 galClimate and the person's body
Basic hygiene2–6 L0.5–1.6 galSocial and cultural norms
Basic cooking3–6 L0.8–1.6 galType of food and local norms
Total7.5–15 L2–4 gal

Figures from the Sphere water supply standard.3 Gallon values are conversions (1 US gallon = 3.785 L).

📊 Key fact

What is left of a gallon after drinking

Sphere puts drinking and food water at 2.5–3 L per person per day.3 Take that out of a 3.8 L gallon and only 0.8–1.3 L (about 1 quart) is left for cooking and washing. Sphere's own range for those two uses is 5–12 L (1.3–3.2 gal).3

When water is short, drinking comes first. Sphere calls drinking and food water "survival needs", while hygiene and cooking are "basic" needs.3

Do not plan for hygiene water to be zero for long. Clean hands and safe toilets are covered in Handwashing & Personal Hygiene.

#🔥 Who needs more water

The 1 gallon minimum is not enough for everyone. The CDC says to store more for pregnant women, people who are sick, pets, and anyone living in a hot climate.1

University of Florida (UF/IFAS) Extension guidance adds children and nursing mothers to the list.6

Heat, hard work and exercise

In very hot temperatures, water needs can double.2 Ready.gov also says people in warm climates may need more water.2

FEMA and the Red Cross say a normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (1.9 L) a day.7 They add that needs vary with age, physical condition, activity, diet and climate.7

Hauling water, cutting wood and long walks are more than normal activity. Plan extra drinking water for whoever does that work.

For a family of 4, that turns a 2-week store of 56 gallons (212 L) into 112 gallons (424 L).12 Heat exhaustion and heat stroke are in Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnant and breastfeeding women

The CDC lists pregnant women among the people to store extra water for.1 UF/IFAS Extension guidance adds nursing mothers.6

Give her a personal bottle with liter marks. Then everyone can see how much she has had, and nobody has to ask.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

Count every child as a full person in your plan. UF/IFAS Extension guidance says homes with children should store more, not less.6

A baby on powdered formula needs safe water for every bottle. The CDC says to use bottled water for formula until tap water is declared safe.9 Add it to the plan, and see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out. Dehydration warning signs in babies are in Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Sick and older relatives

The CDC says to store more for people who are sick.1 UF/IFAS Extension guidance says the same.6

Put any relative with a long-term illness in the "needs more" group. Keep a filled cup within their reach, and refill it on a schedule.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs, cats and other pets

The CDC lists pets as a reason to store more water than the people's minimum.1 Ready.gov says a pet's emergency kit needs a water bowl and several days' supply of water.10 Your dog's needs are real numbers you can measure, so measure them now.

Fill the bowl from a measuring jug. Each time you top it up, write down how much you added. Average 3 days. Do it again in the hottest month. Dog dehydration and heatstroke are in Dog First Aid.

Do

  • Count babies, children and older relatives as full people
  • Plan double for very hot weather
  • Add extra for pregnancy, breastfeeding and illness
  • Measure each pet's real daily drinking

Don't

  • Plan for healthy adults only
  • Use the same number in summer and winter
  • Forget the dog
  • Assume one gallon covers washing and cooking too

#🧮 Your household's number: 3 days, 2 weeks, 1 year

Work out one number and write it on your water store. Follow the steps, then check them with the calculator.

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. Count everyone

    Adults, children, babies and older relatives. Add anyone who may shelter with you. Write pets on a separate line.

  2. Multiply by 1 gallon (3.8 L)

    That is the minimum per person per day.1

  3. Adjust for heat

    If your summers are very hot, double the number for those months.2

  4. Add for higher-need people

    Pregnant or breastfeeding women, children and anyone sick get extra.16

  5. Add your pets

    Use the daily amount you measured for each animal.1

  6. Multiply by days

    3 days at least. 14 days if you can.1

  7. Write it down

    Mark the total on your containers and in the margin of this page.

The weight of water

One liter of water weighs 1 kg; one US gallon weighs about 3.8 kg (8.3 lb).11 Two weeks of minimum water for a family of 4 is 212 L, so it weighs about 212 kg (467 lb).

That fits in eleven 20 L (5.3 gal) jerrycans, or one 55-gallon (208 L) drum plus a little more. Container choice, placement and weight are in Storing Water for Months & Years.

💡 Tip

Store in sizes you can lift

A full 20 L jerrycan weighs 20 kg (44 lb).11 A full 55-gallon drum holds 208 L, so it weighs over 200 kg (450 lb): far too heavy to carry. Keep some water in small containers so a child or an older adult can pour a drink.

#🚩 Dehydration and "days without water"

Drinking water is a survival need, not a comfort. Sphere lists 2.5–3 L a day for drinking and food under "survival needs".3

Sphere also says that amount depends on the climate and the individual's body.3 That is why heat matters so much: very hot weather can double needs.2

Warning signs: the WHO scale

The World Health Organization (WHO) sorts dehydration into three levels: none, some and severe. It uses these signs to check people with diarrhea.8

WHO signs of dehydration (two or more signs place a person in a level)
LevelSigns
SevereVery sleepy (lethargic) or unconscious; sunken eyes; cannot drink or drinks poorly; pinched skin goes back very slowly (2 seconds or more)
SomeRestless or irritable; sunken eyes; drinks eagerly, thirsty
NoneNot enough signs for "some" or "severe"

Signs from the WHO diarrheal disease fact sheet (2024).8

☠️ Danger

Severe dehydration is an emergency

If anyone shows two or more severe signs, get medical care at once. Children are at high risk: WHO lists diarrheal disease as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1 to 59 months.8

Treatment and more warning signs

This book prints the treatment, and the signs for babies, dogs and heat illness, in these chapters:

  • Adults and children, by severity, with the oral rehydration solution (ORS) recipe: Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration
  • Babies and young children: Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs
  • Dogs: Dog First Aid
  • Heat exhaustion and heat stroke: Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke
⚠️ Caution

Why this page prints no "days without water" number

This book prints only numbers it can check against an official or peer-reviewed source. A reliable figure for how long people survive with no water at all could not be confirmed for this edition, so none is given here.

Plan so that nobody in your household ever goes a day without drinking. That is the whole point of the numbers above.

A short-term minimum is fine to live on for months.

Sphere says 7.5 L per person per day may be appropriate only for a short time in an acute drought, and that a minimum is never a maximum.4 Its standard for drinking, cooking and hygiene is 15 L.3

One gallon a day covers everything a person needs.

The CDC calls 1 gallon a minimum and says to store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates.1 Sphere's drinking figure alone is 2.5–3 L, leaving little of the gallon for anything else.3

#⏳ The 30-year math: why storage alone cannot last

A year of minimum water for one person is 365 gallons (1,382 L). That is 1 gallon a day for 365 days.1

Stored water is a bridge. It carries you from the first hour until a source that refills is working.

Real outages have lasted far longer than 2 weeks. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 households in Puerto Rico found they went an average of 68 days without water service (New England Journal of Medicine, 2018).12 That is almost 5 times the CDC 2-week goal.1

  1. Day 3

    3 gallons (11 L) per person. The CDC minimum stock.1

  2. Day 14

    14 gallons (53 L) per person. The CDC goal if you can store it.1

  3. Year 1

    365 gallons (1,382 L) per person. A family of 4 needs 1,460 gallons (5,527 L), about 27 drums of 55 gallons.

  4. Year 1 at Sphere level

    A family of 4 at 15 L each uses 21,900 L (5,785 gal), about 105 drums.3

  5. Year 30

    10,950 gallons (41,450 L) per person at the minimum. A family of 4 needs 43,800 gallons (about 165,800 L).

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

No household can store 30 years of water. The plan is a renewable source plus treatment, with stored water as the buffer for droughts, freezes and breakdowns.

Start with Rainwater Harvesting and Finding Water When the Taps Stop. Treat every new source using Disinfecting Water.

Size your source with the same math. If your household needs 840 L (222 gal) every 2 weeks at the Sphere level, your source and tanks must deliver at least that, every 2 weeks, all year.3

Then add a margin for the hot season, when needs can double.2

#📓 Track it, plan it, never guess

A written water log tells you how many days you have left. Write it down so nobody has to remember it or guess.

☠️ Danger

Never ration drinking water

FEMA and the Red Cross say: never ration water. Drink the amount you need today, and look for more for tomorrow.7 The log is there to warn you early, not to cut what people drink.

The rule is one division: liters left ÷ (people × liters per person per day) = days left. Example: 56 gallons (212 L) for 4 people at 1 gallon each per day lasts 14 days.1

The example assumes 4 people at the CDC minimum, about 15 L (4 gal) a day for the household, so 197 ÷ 15.2 = 12.96, rounded down to 12.1 Round "days left" down, never up.

🎯 Practice now

Do a 24-hour water audit now

While the taps still work, live for one day only on water you pour from marked containers. Write down every liter you use for drinking, cooking, washing and cleaning.

Compare your total with 3.8 L and 15 L per person.13 Your real number is the one to store and to plan your source around.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Mark your containers

    Write the volume in large numbers on each one, plus the fill date.

  2. Give each person a marked bottle

    Fill it each morning. You can see at a glance who is drinking too little.

  3. Drink first, then cook, then wash

    Sphere calls drinking water a survival need.3 Cooking and hygiene come next.

  4. Log every evening

    Measure what is left and update "days left".

  5. Act at 7 days left

    Start collecting and treating water from another source before you run out.

Get these before you need them

  • A 1 L (1 quart) measuring jug
  • A marker pen and tape for labels
  • One marked bottle per person
  • Enough containers for your 14-day number (see Storing Water)

Storing Water for Months & Years

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 hYear 1📚 24 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Use only food-grade containers. Never reuse bottles that held bleach, pesticides, milk or juice.12
  • Label every container "drinking water" with the date. Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months.1
  • Store it cool, dark and away from fuel. The CDC says 10–21°C (50–70°F), out of sunlight, away from gasoline and pesticides.1
  • Your house already holds water. A home water heater holds 30–80 gallons (114–303 L). The toilet tank (never the bowl) is a last resort, disinfected first.34
  • Bathtub water is for flushing and washing, not drinking. A filled tub is also a drowning risk for small children.56
  • A full 208 L (55-gallon) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb). Put it where it will stay before you fill it.7
6 moreplace water you stored yourself1
458 lbweight of a full 208 L (55 gal) drum7
30–80 gal(114–303 L) of water inside a home water heater3

#🚰 Why stored water comes first First 72 h

When the taps stop, stored water is what you drink while you find and treat more. The CDC calls unopened, commercially bottled water the safest and most reliable water in an emergency.1

Long outages happen. After Hurricane Helene, Asheville, North Carolina, did not lift its boil water notice for all customers until November 18, 2024.9 Local public radio called it a 53-day water crisis.8

The CDC minimum is 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day. Store at least 3 days, and a 2-week supply if you can.1 Store more in hot climates, and for pregnant women and people who are sick.1

📊 Key fact

Do the math once

At 1 gallon per person per day, a family of 4 needs 56 gallons (212 L) for 2 weeks.1 That is about one 208 L (55-gallon) drum. For heat, babies, nursing mothers and dogs, see How Much Water You Really Need.

2-week supply at the CDC minimum of 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day

228 gal (106 L)106 kg (233 lb)Six 19 L (5 gal) jugs
456 gal (212 L)212 kg (466 lb)One 208 L drum + one jug
