Amounts use the CDC daily minimum.1 Weights use 1 kg per liter and about 8.3 lb per gallon.7 Add more for dogs, heat and illness.

Water calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Stored water is a bridge, not a forever supply. Over years you will refill from rain, wells and other sources. See Rainwater Harvesting, Wells & Hand Pumps and Finding Water When the Taps Stop.

#🛢️ Choosing safe containers

Use containers made for food or water. The CDC says FDA-approved, food-grade water storage containers are best.1

Look for the number 2 inside the recycling triangle. Utah's emergency management agency calls food-grade high-density polyethylene (HDPE #2) containers your best choice.10 If you reuse bottles, Ready.gov says to choose 2-liter soft drink bottles (PETE #1), not milk or juice jugs.2

Which containers can hold drinking water?
ContainerUse it?Why
Sealed store-bought bottled waterYes, bestSafest, most reliable emergency water1
Food-grade HDPE #2 jugs and blue drumsYesThe recommended long-term choice10
2 L soft drink bottles (PETE #1)Yes, after cleaningReady.gov's choice for reused bottles; sanitize first2
Milk and fruit juice jugsNoProtein and sugar residue stay inside and bacteria grow2
Anything that held bleach, pesticides or other chemicalsNeverThe CDC says do not use them1
GlassAvoidNebraska Extension says use plastic, not glass, if water may freeze12

A well-rinsed milk jug is fine for drinking water.

Ready.gov says milk protein and fruit sugar cannot be fully removed from these jugs, so bacteria can grow.2 Utah's guidance adds that milk jugs break down quickly and turn brittle.10

☠️ Danger

Never reuse a chemical bottle

The CDC says containers that held toxic chemicals, such as bleach or pesticides, must not be used for drinking water.1 If you do not know what a container once held, do not use it.

📊 Key fact

55-gallon (208 L) drum facts

  • Food-grade HDPE #2 only. Look for the 2 in the recycling triangle.10
  • Place it before you fill it. Full, it weighs about 208 kg (458 lb).7
  • Keep it out of the sun. Barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.22
  • Raise it off concrete or dirt on a pallet or boards.1322
  • Draw water with a pump or siphon, never a cup or a hand.23
🛒 Get it before you need it

Get this before you need it

  • Food-grade HDPE #2 jugs or drums, in sizes your family can lift
  • A drum pump or siphon hose, and a bung wrench for drum caps
  • Plain, unscented liquid chlorine bleach
  • A waterproof marker and labels
  • Wood pallets or boards to keep containers off concrete

#🧼 Clean, fill and treat

Sanitize every container before its first fill. This is the CDC method. It needs only soap, water and plain unscented bleach.1

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Wash and rinse

    Wash the container with soap. Rinse it completely with water.1

  2. Mix the sanitizer

    Stir 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented liquid chlorine bleach (5–9% sodium hypochlorite) into 1 quart (about 1 liter) of water.1

  3. Coat every surface

    Pour it into the container, cap it and shake well so the solution touches all inside surfaces.1

  4. Wait, then empty

    Wait at least 30 seconds, then pour the solution out. Let the container air-dry, or rinse it with clean, safe water.1

  5. Fill with safe water

    Fill it with clean, safe water and screw the cap on tightly.1

  6. Label it

    Write "drinking water" and the date on the container.1

Know where your fill water comes from. Ready.gov says tap water from a utility that treats it with chlorine needs nothing added. Water from a well or other untreated source needs bleach.2 Utah State University Extension says water from wells, rivers or rainwater must be treated before you store it.13

To treat clear water with bleach, the EPA dose is 8 drops of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25% bleach, per gallon (3.8 L).14 Double the dose if the water is cloudy, colored or very cold.14

Stir, then wait 30 minutes before anyone drinks it. The water should smell slightly of chlorine. If it does not, EPA says to repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes.14

For a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum of clear, untreated water, scale up EPA's 8-gallon dose of 2/3 teaspoon. That is about 4½ teaspoons (23 mL) of 6% bleach, or about 3½ teaspoons (17 mL) of 8.25% bleach.14 Double it for cloudy water.14

Bleach calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

⚠️ Caution

Plain, unscented bleach only

The EPA says not to use scented or color-safe bleach, or bleach with added cleaners.14 Its method uses bleach stored at room temperature for less than a year.14 For more on fresh bleach, tablets and pool shock, see Disinfecting Water.

☠️ Danger

Bleach cannot fix chemical pollution

The CDC warns that water polluted with harmful chemicals or toxins cannot be made safe by boiling, disinfecting or filtering.15 Never store water from a source that may hold fuel or chemicals. See Chemical Contamination.

#🔄 How often to rotate Year 1

Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months. The CDC and Ready.gov both give this interval.111

For store-bought water, go by the date on the bottle. That is the CDC's household rule.1 Its planning guide for hospitals adds that commercial "sell by" dates mainly help stores rotate stock. They do not mean the water has gone bad.16

Water you disinfect and bottle yourself does not keep forever. The same CDC guide says to check it from time to time for leftover (residual) chlorine and to treat it again if needed.16

  1. Day 0

    Sanitize, fill and treat if needed. Label "drinking water" with the date.1

  2. Month 6

    Replace the water.1 Use the old water for flushing, washing or the garden. Check each empty container for cracks and leaks.

  3. Month 12

    Rotate again. Buy a fresh bottle of bleach at the same time: EPA's method uses bleach less than a year old.14 Use the oldest store-bought water first.

  4. Every rotation

    Write the next due date on a calendar on paper, not only on your phone.

💡 Tip

A label that answers every question

Write four lines on each container: DRINKING WATER, the fill date, the source (city tap, or well treated with how many drops of bleach), and the replace-by date. The CDC asks for "drinking water" and the date at minimum.1

Start rationing your stored water on day one.

FEMA, the Red Cross and county emergency managers say never ration drinking water unless authorities order it.2017 Drink the amount you need today and try to find more for tomorrow.20

#🏠 Hidden water already in your house First 72 h

Protect the water in your pipes first. If the public supply may be contaminated, find your home's incoming water valve and close it.17 That keeps dirty water out of your pipes and water heater.

The Red Cross lists the hot-water tank, the pipes and ice cubes as safe water inside the home.18 The CDC also lists the water heater tank, and melted ice cubes made with water that was not contaminated.19

The water heater: 30–80 gallons

A home water heater can hold 30–80 gallons (114–303 L).3 The CDC means the tank that supplies your taps, not a home heating system.19

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Turn off the power or gas

    Switch off the electricity or gas that heats the tank.420

  2. Let it cool

    Wait for the tank to cool before you open anything.4

  3. Close the cold-water inlet

    Turn off the water intake valve at the tank.20

  4. Let air in

    Turn on a hot-water faucet in the house so the tank can drain.20

  5. Drain into a clean container

    Put a clean container under the drain valve at the bottom of the tank, then open the valve.4

  6. Refill before you restart

    Refill the tank before you turn the power or gas back on.20 If the gas was shut off, a professional needs to turn it back on.20

☠️ Danger

Power off, then wait

FEMA's order is power off, let the tank cool, then open the drain.4 Keep children away from the drain valve while the water is still hot.

🎯 Practice now

Find your valves today

Find your main water valve and the water heater drain valve now, in daylight. Tag the main valve so anyone can find it in the dark. If you live in an earthquake zone, see Earthquakes for strapping the water heater.

Water in the pipes

Step by step · 3 steps

  1. Close the main valve

    Stop outside water from flowing in.17

  2. Open the highest tap

    Turn on the faucet on the highest floor to let air into the pipes. A small amount of water will trickle out.20

  3. Drain the lowest tap

    Collect the water from the lowest faucet in the house.20

The toilet: tank maybe, bowl never

Never use water from the toilet bowl. FEMA and the Red Cross both rule it out.418

The tank behind the toilet is different. FEMA's current guidance lists it only if the water is clear and has no chemical cleaners, such as colored tablets, and says to disinfect it before use.4 The older FEMA and Red Cross booklet says not to use flush tank water at all.1820

Use tank water for flushing and washing first.3 Drink it only as a last resort, and disinfect it before you do.4

Do

  • Drain the water heater after the power is off and it has cooled4
  • Melt ice cubes made with uncontaminated water19
  • Take pipe water from the lowest tap20
  • Use toilet tank water for flushing3

Don't

  • Drink from the toilet bowl4
  • Use water from radiators, waterbeds, swimming pools or spas18
  • Use a toilet tank that holds colored cleaning tablets4
  • Turn the heater back on before the tank refills20

#🛁 Bathtub storage: the facts

Fill the bathtub before a storm, but do not drink it. The National Weather Service says to fill bathtubs and large containers in case tap water stops. Use bathtub water for cleaning and flushing only.5

Clean the tub and test that the plug holds before the storm. Scoop the water out with a bucket when you need it. For flushing without running water, see Toilets Without Water.

A full bathtub is a drinking water reserve.

The National Weather Service says bathtub water is for cleaning and flushing only: do not drink it.5 Keep drinking water in sanitized, food-grade containers.1

👶 Babies & children

A filled tub or bucket can drown a toddler

From 2006 to 2010, CPSC counted 434 drowning deaths of children under 5 at home. 82% were under age 2, and 81% of the incidents involved bathtubs or bath products.6

Drowning can happen quickly and in very shallow water. Never leave a tub, bucket or any container of water unattended. Keep bathroom doors closed and use toilet-lid locks.21 See Keeping Kids Safe.

#📍 Where to keep it: heat, light, fumes and weight

Pick a cool, dark spot away from fuel and chemicals. The CDC says 10–21°C (50–70°F), out of direct sunlight, and away from toxic substances such as gasoline or pesticides.1

Fumes can pass through plastic. Nebraska Extension warns that vapors from gasoline, kerosene and pesticides can penetrate plastic containers.12 Do not keep water next to the fuel cans in the garage.

Light ruins containers and feeds algae. Be Ready Utah says sunlight, and even artificial light, makes containers brittle or leaky. Blue 208 L (55-gallon) barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.22 Sunlight also lets algae grow in stored water.22

Raise containers off bare concrete or dirt. Utah State University Extension says plastic absorbs odors there, which changes the taste.13 Be Ready Utah adds that air flow underneath limits moisture and mold.22

Good spots

  • An inside closet or under a bed, away from outside walls
  • A cool, dark ground floor, on a pallet122
  • Several places in the house, so one leak or break does not take it all

Bad spots

  • Next to gasoline, kerosene or pesticides12
  • In direct sun, such as a porch or window122
  • On bare concrete or dirt13
  • On a shelf that is not built for the weight12

Weight: choose the spot before you fill

Water weighs 1 kg per liter, or about 8.3 lb per gallon.7 So a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb). Once it is full, you will not move it.

Nebraska Extension says shelves must be sturdy and stable, because water weighs over 8 pounds per gallon.12 Put drums at ground level on a pallet, where a pump or siphon can reach them.

Do not dip cups or hands into stored water. CDC guidance on safe storage says hands, cups and dippers carry germs into open containers.23 Pump or siphon water from a drum into a smaller container that has a lid and a tap.23

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Carry less, store closer

A full 19 L (5-gallon) jug weighs about 19 kg (42 lb).7 If someone in your home cannot lift that, keep small jugs with a tap where they sleep, and refill them from the big containers. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

#❄️ Freezing, heat and the seasons

Leave 5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of air at the top of any container that might freeze. Water expands as it freezes and can burst a full container.12

Use freezer-safe plastic, not glass, for water that may freeze.12 If your storage spot freezes in winter, leave the headspace or move the water into the heated part of the house.

Pipes freeze too. See Preparing Your Home for a Long Outage and Winter Storms & Extreme Cold.

💡 Tip

Hot climates: store more, store lower

In the tropics, 10–21°C (50–70°F) may be impossible to reach. The CDC says to store more water in hot climates.1 Use the coolest, darkest room you have, away from sunny walls and tin roofs.

#⏳ The 30-year view Long haul

Every stored container is temporary. Sun-exposed barrels can start to fall apart within 5 years.22 Plan to replace containers, not only the water in them.

For daily drinking water over years, use a safe-storage container. CDC guidance describes one with a small opening and a lid, plus a tap or narrow spout, so no hands or cups go inside.23 Open buckets and pots let hands, cups and dippers carry fecal germs into treated water.23

⏳ The 30-year view

Build the refill loop

In year 1, stored water carries you until rain catchment, a well or a treated stream supply is working. Then stored water becomes your buffer for dry spells and broken pumps. See Water Filters & SODIS, Build a Biosand Filter and Pottery & Making Containers.

👶 Babies & children

Keep sealed water for the baby

For powdered formula, the CDC says use bottled water until officials say tap water is safe. With no bottled water, boil water for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m or 6,500 ft) and let it cool.15

For babies under 2 months, premature babies or babies with weak immune systems, do not let the boiled water cool below 70°C (158°F) before you mix in the powder. That heat kills Cronobacter germs.15 Then cool the bottle to body temperature, and test a few drops on your wrist before feeding.15 See Feeding Babies.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Count the dogs

Ready.gov's pet kit includes a water bowl and several days' supply of water.24 Store dog water in the same food-grade containers and add it to your totals. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy and periods

The CDC says to store extra water for pregnant women.1 Keep a small covered container in the bathroom for washing during periods. See Periods Without Stores.

Every 6 months. For store-bought water, follow the date on the bottle.

Which plastic is best for storing water?

Food-grade HDPE #2. Clean 2-liter soft drink bottles (PETE #1) also work.

Can you reuse a milk jug?

No. Residue stays inside, bacteria grow, and the plastic turns brittle.

How much water is in a home water heater?

30–80 gallons (114–303 L). Power off and let it cool before draining.

Toilet bowl or toilet tank?

Never the bowl. The tank only if clear and chemical-free, as a last resort, and disinfected first.

Can you drink bathtub water?

No. Use it for flushing and washing.

What does a full 55-gallon drum weigh?

About 208 kg (458 lb). Place it before you fill it.

How much headspace if water might freeze?

5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of air at the top.

Finding Water When the Taps Stop

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 hFirst 30 days📚 11 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Use your stored, bottled water first. FEMA calls bottled water the safest and most reliable option after a disaster.2
  • Look inside before you look outside. The water heater tank, ice made from clean water and the toilet tank (never the bowl) are usable.2
  • Treat every outdoor source. CDC lists rain, streams, rivers, ponds, lakes and springs as sources you must make safe before drinking.1
  • Never drink floodwater, seawater or urine. Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals, and your body cannot clear the salt in seawater.58
  • Boiling does not remove fuel or chemicals. If a source may hold fuel or toxic chemicals, do not use it.1
  • Pool and spa water is for washing and cleaning only. CDC says not to drink it.1
4 typesof outdoor source on CDC's list: rain, moving water, ponds and lakes, springs. All need treatment.1
3hidden indoor sources FEMA names: water heater, ice, toilet tank2
3.5%of seawater's weight is dissolved salt9
0.8–5 ppmchlorine range in Canadian pool rules: set for swimmers, not for drinking10

#🧭 Where to get water, in the right order

When the taps stop, work from the safest source outward. Stored water first, then hidden water inside the building, then outdoor water that you treat.

FEMA's advice is plain: use bottled water first when you have it, because it is the safest and most reliable option.2 Building that store is covered in Storing Water for Months & Years, and how much you need is in How Much Water You Really Need.

No official body publishes one safety ranking of rain, springs, wells, streams and ponds. CDC's rule is simpler: every outdoor source needs treatment before anyone drinks it.1

The table below puts every common source in one place. It runs from your first choice to the water you must never drink.

Water sources, from first choice to never (FEMA, CDC, EPA)
SourceWhat official guidance saysBefore you drink
Stored bottled waterSafest and most reliable option2Use first
Water heater tankUsable if it is part of the drinking water system, not the heating system2Use
Melted iceUsable if made with water that was not contaminated2Use
Toilet tank (not bowl)Only if clear and free of toilet cleaners2Disinfect
RainOn CDC's list of outdoor sources1Treat
Natural springsOn CDC's list of outdoor sources1Treat
Private wellsCan be contaminated during floods1Treat; test and disinfect after a flood7
Streams, rivers, ponds, lakesMay hold livestock waste, sewage and chemicals1Treat; reject if chemicals are possible
Pools and spasHygiene and cleaning only1Do not drink
Floodwater, seawater, urine, radiators, waterbeds, toilet bowlsUnsafe to drink358Never drink

The outdoor rows (rain to ponds) are not ranked against each other by any official source. Treat all of them the same way.

#🏠 Hidden water inside your home or building

Before you walk anywhere, check the building you are in. FEMA names three indoor sources you can use when the taps stop.2

  • Water heater tank. Use it only if it is part of your drinking water system, not your home heating system.2
  • Melted ice. Safe if the ice was made with water that was not contaminated.2
  • Toilet tank (the box behind the seat). Only if the water is clear and no toilet cleaner has been added, and disinfect it first.2

An older FEMA and Red Cross booklet ruled out toilet tanks completely.3 FEMA's current guidance allows clear, cleaner-free tank water once it is disinfected.2 When in doubt, treat it.

How to drain a water heater safely is covered step by step in Storing Water. Do it once now, while you can still call a plumber if something goes wrong.

Getting water out of a toilet tank

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Lift the tank lid and look

    Check for colored water, a cleaner tablet or a clip-on cleaner. If any toilet cleaner is in there, do not drink it.2

  2. Use it only if it is clear

    FEMA allows tank water only when it is clear.2

  3. Scoop it, do not flush it

    Ladle it into a clean container. Flushing sends it to the bowl, and bowl water is never drinking water.3

  4. Disinfect it

    Boil or treat it before anyone drinks it.2 See Disinfecting Water.

Do use (indoors)

  • Water heater tank on the drinking water line
  • Ice made from clean water
  • Clear toilet tank water, after disinfecting
  • Pool or spa water for washing and cleaning

Don't drink

  • Toilet bowl water
  • Radiator or hot water boiler water
  • Waterbed water
  • Pool or spa water
☠️ Danger

Heating systems and waterbeds are not drinking water

FEMA's emergency food and water guide says not to use water from radiators, waterbeds, toilet bowls, or swimming pools and spas for drinking.3 FEMA's older shelter guide gives the reason for waterbeds: fungicides added to the water, or chemicals in the vinyl, can make it unsafe.4

💡 Tip

Remove toilet cleaner tablets now

An in-tank cleaner tablet turns a usable tank into one you cannot drink from.2 Take tablets out today and flush a few times, so every tank in the house stays a backup supply.

#🌧️ Outdoor sources: rain, springs, wells, streams and ponds

CDC lists four kinds of outdoor water you can make safe: rainwater; streams, rivers and other moving water; ponds and lakes; and natural springs.1

All four must be treated to kill germs before anyone drinks them.1 No outdoor source gets a free pass, however clean it looks.

Rain

Rain is on CDC's list of outdoor sources, and it still needs treatment.1 Roof catchment, gutters, first-flush diverters and tank math are in Rainwater Harvesting.

Springs

Natural springs are on the same list, with the same rule: treat the water before drinking.1

Wells

Well water can be contaminated during floods.1 EPA says private wells need to be tested and disinfected after floodwaters recede.7

Well types, hand pumps and shock chlorination are in Wells & Hand Pumps Without Electricity.

Streams, rivers, ponds and lakes

CDC warns that rivers, streams and lakes may be contaminated with livestock waste, human sewage, chemicals and other contaminants.1

Treatment kills germs, but boiling does not remove chemical pollutants.1 That makes choosing the source your first filter. See Chemical Contamination for what filters can and cannot remove.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Look upstream first

    Note farms and animal pens, sewage pipes and septic systems, and factories, fuel stores or dumps. These match the livestock waste, sewage and chemicals CDC warns about.1

  2. Reject chemical water

    If the water may hold fuel or toxic chemicals, walk away. Boiling will not remove them.1

  3. Collect in a clean container

    Use a container that has only held food or water. Keep the cap and the rim clean.

  4. Clear cloudy water

    Settle and strain cloudy water before you treat it. Methods are in Water Filters & SODIS.

  5. Treat every liter

    Boil or disinfect it to kill germs.1 Doses and times are in Disinfecting Water.

  6. Store and label it

    Pour it into a clean, covered container. Write "TREATED" and the date on it so nobody mixes it up with raw water.

Clear, fast-running stream water is clean enough to drink as it is.

CDC lists streams and rivers among sources that must be treated, and warns they may carry livestock waste, human sewage and chemicals.1 How fast the water moves does not change that rule.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls: fetch water together

Go to water in pairs or groups, in daylight, with an agreed route and return time. Never send a girl alone to a distant source. Safe paths, lighting and latrine design are in Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older and disabled people: lighten the load

A full 19 L (5 gal) container weighs about 19 kg (42 lb), because each liter of water weighs about 1 kg (2.2 lb). Use 4 L (1 gal) jugs, a wagon or a garden cart. Give people who cannot carry a seated job, such as treating, labeling and logging water.

#🗺️ Map every water source near you, now

The best time to find water is before you need it. A paper map of nearby sources lets anyone in the family find water when you are sick, away or asleep.

Draw it on paper, so it works without a charged phone. See Maps & Compass for reading and marking maps.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Get a paper map

    A local street or topographic map, or a hand-drawn sketch. Mark your home in the center.

  2. Walk a circle around home

    Mark every stream, river, pond, lake and spring. Add wells, rain barrels, large clean roofs and public taps.

  3. Note what is upstream

    Mark farms, sewage pipes and fuel or chemical sites near each source.1

  4. Note who owns it

    Ask the owner now for permission to draw water in an emergency. Taking without permission can be a crime. See Scavenging: the Law & Ethics.

  5. Note the route and the carry

    Write the distance and how long the walk took with a full container. Pick the flattest route.

  6. Recheck after every flood

    Floods can contaminate wells, and floodwater can reach streams and lakes.15 Mark flooded sources as "test before use".

🎯 Practice now

Practice the carry this week

Fill a 19 L (5 gal) container, carry it 100 m (110 yd) and time yourself. Then try it with a cart. You will learn which containers, handles and routes work for your family before it matters.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • Food-grade water containers with handles and tight caps, in sizes each person can carry
  • A wagon, garden cart or wheelbarrow
  • A funnel and clean cotton cloths for straining
  • A bucket with 10 m (33 ft) of rope, for reaching water from banks and open wells
  • A waterproof paper map, pencils and labels
  • Treatment supplies from Disinfecting Water
⚠️ Caution

What this chapter leaves out, and why

This edition gives no methods or yield figures for finding water by plant or animal signs, dew collection, solar stills or plant bags. We could not verify published figures for this printing, and this book does not print unverified numbers.

Plan your supply around stored water, rain and treated surface water. Official guidance covers all three.12

#🏊 Pools, spas and other urban water

CDC says pool and spa water can be used for personal hygiene and cleaning, but not for drinking.1 FEMA's emergency guide also lists pools and spas among the sources not to drink from.3

Pool chemistry is set for swimmers. Canadian pool rules keep free chlorine between 0.8 and 5.0 parts per million (ppm), a level judged not harmful to bathers who swallow some water.10 That is a swimming standard, not a drinking-water standard.

Pool water is already chlorinated, so it is safe to drink.

CDC limits pool and spa water to hygiene and cleaning.1 Pool chlorine levels are set for swimmers who swallow a little, not for daily drinking.10

Good uses for pool water

  • Washing hands and bodies
  • Cleaning floors, tools and surfaces
  • Laundry (see Laundry Without Machines)

Every bucket of pool water you use for cleaning is a bucket of treated drinking water you save.

Tanks in apartment and office buildings

If your building has water tanks, find out now what each tank is for. Ask the building manager whether it is on the drinking water line, the heating system or the fire system.

Water from heating systems, such as radiators and hot water boilers, is not drinking water.3 A water heater tank on the drinking water line is.2

⚠️ Caution

Neighbors' pools and tanks

Ask before you take. Agree now, in writing if you can, who may use a pool or tank in an emergency and for what. Shared rules prevent fights later. See Community & Mutual Aid.

#🌊 Floodwater: water everywhere, none to drink

Never drink floodwater. CDC says it can contain sewage, and eating or drinking anything contaminated by it can cause diarrheal disease such as E. coli or Salmonella infection.5

Floods also move containers of chemicals away from where they were stored.5 So floodwater can hold germs and chemicals at once, and boiling does not remove chemical pollutants.1

Touching floodwater is a smaller risk than swallowing it. CDC says skin contact alone does not pose a serious health risk; eating or drinking anything contaminated with floodwater is what causes disease.6

☠️ Danger

Floods poison wells and streams too

Well water can be contaminated during floods.1 EPA says private wells must be tested and disinfected after floodwaters recede.7 CDC also warns against bathing in rivers, streams or lakes contaminated by floodwater.5

If you must work in or near floodwater

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Cover up

    Wear rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles.5

  2. Keep it out of your mouth

    Do not eat, drink or smoke with floodwater on your hands. Swallowing it is the main risk.6

  3. Do not bathe in it

    Not in floodwater, and not in rivers, streams or lakes it has reached.5

  4. Wash clothes hot

    Wash clothes that touched floodwater or sewage in hot water and detergent before wearing them again.5

  5. Check for advisories

    Ask your water utility or health department whether a boil water advisory is in force.7

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

CDC says toys that were in floodwater must be disinfected before children play with them.5 Keep children out of floodwater and away from cleanup work.

Mix infant formula only with your best water: stored bottled water first.2 See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs

Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals.5 Keep dogs out of it where you can, and give them the same treated water you drink. If a dog wades through floodwater, rinse its paws and coat with clean water before it licks itself. See Dog Health.

For the full picture of flood hazards, see Floods. For the diseases floodwater spreads, see Waterborne Diseases.

#🚫 Water you must never drink

Some water makes you worse off than drinking nothing. Learn these by heart and teach them to every child old enough to understand.

Seawater

Seawater is toxic to humans. USGS explains that your body cannot get rid of the salt: the kidneys cannot get enough fresh water to dilute it, and the body fails.8

About 3.5% of seawater's weight is dissolved salt.9 For every cup of seawater you drink, you would need at least the same amount of fresh water for your kidneys to flush that salt out.9

Urine

Do not drink urine. It carries salts and waste products your body has just removed. Drinking it hands that load back to your kidneys, which need more water to clear it again.11

Urine is also not sterile. It can contain bacteria, even in healthy people.11

Drinking your own urine stretches your water supply in an emergency.

Urine returns salt and waste to a body that is already short of water, so the kidneys need extra water to remove it again.11

Water with fuel or chemicals in it

CDC says do not use water contaminated with fuel or toxic chemicals. Boiling will not remove chemical pollutants.1 Find another source.

If you boil water long enough, any water becomes safe.

Boiling does not remove chemical pollutants such as fuel.1 Choose a different source when chemicals are possible.

Heating systems, waterbeds and toilet bowls

FEMA lists radiators, waterbeds, toilet bowls, and pools and spas as water not to use for drinking.3 Waterbed water can hold fungicides or chemicals from the vinyl.4

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Stored water is a bridge, not a supply. Any supply that lasts decades has to come from rain, springs, wells or surface water, and CDC says all of those need treatment.1

Use year 1 to build lasting systems: rain catchment, a hand-pumped well if you can, and a biosand filter. Keep your source map up to date every year.

Save these official pages while the internet works

  • FEMA: Where can I find clean drinking water after a disaster?
  • CDC: Safety Guidelines: Floodwater

Print them or save them as PDFs next to this book.

Stored bottled water. FEMA calls it the safest and most reliable option.

Name 3 hidden water sources at home.

Water heater tank, ice made from clean water, and the toilet tank (not the bowl).

Which outdoor sources need treatment?

All of them: rain, streams, rivers, ponds, lakes and springs.

No. Use it for hygiene and cleaning only.

Does boiling fix water with fuel in it?

No. Boiling does not remove chemicals. Find another source.

What must you do to a private well after a flood?

Disinfecting Water: Boiling, Bleach, Iodine & Tablets

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 7 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Boil clear water at a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil for 3 minutes. Boiling kills bacteria, viruses and parasites.1
  • Cannot boil? Use regular, unscented bleach. 8 drops of 6% or 6 drops of 8.25% per 3.8 liters (1 gallon). Double it for cloudy or very cold water, then wait 30 minutes.2
  • Bleach and iodine do not kill Cryptosporidium. Boiling does. Chlorine dioxide does too, but it needs hours.34
  • Boiling and disinfection do not make water with fuel or toxic chemicals safe. If you suspect them, find another source.1
  • No iodine for pregnant women or people with thyroid problems. CDC does not recommend it for them.3
  • Bleach weakens with age. EPA's method uses bleach stored less than a year. For the long haul, learn the pool shock method.2
1 minat a rolling boil kills germs in clear water1
8 dropsof 6% bleach per gallon (3.8 L) of clear water2
30 minwait after adding bleach before you drink2
Hourschlorine dioxide needs to kill Cryptosporidium4

#🧭 Pick your method in 10 seconds

Safe bottled water comes first. If you have none, EPA ranks boiling ahead of bleach. Bleach is the backup when you cannot boil.2

Boiling is the best way to kill germs, including viruses, bacteria and parasites.1 CDC notes that, except for boiling, few water treatment methods are 100% effective against all germs.3

Use the four steps below every time you treat water. Step 1 matters most, because no disinfectant fixes chemical pollution.

Quick picks

  • You have fuel: boil. It is the most reliable method.1
  • No fuel, clear water: unscented bleach, then wait 30 minutes.2
  • No fuel, unknown source or a sick person at home: chlorine dioxide tablets for the full label time, because they also kill Cryptosporidium.4
  • Cloudy water: clear it first, and double the bleach dose.2
  • Possible fuel or chemicals: do not treat it. Find another source.1
Disinfection methods at a glance (CDC, EPA)
MethodHowKills Crypto?Watch out
BoilingRolling boil 1 min (3 min above 2,000 m)YesNeeds fuel; leaves chemicals in
Bleach8 drops of 6% per gallon, wait 30 minNoUnscented only; replace yearly
IodineFollow the labelNoNot in pregnancy or thyroid disease
Chlorine dioxideFollow the label; hours for CryptoYes, slowlyKeep sealed from air and light
Pool shockMake stock, dilute 1 to 100NoStrong chemical; label the stock

Sources for the table: boiling1, bleach2, iodine and chlorine against Cryptosporidium3, chlorine dioxide14 and pool shock7.

This chapter is about killing germs. To remove dirt and parasites, see Water Filters & SODIS. To clean water for years, see Build a Biosand Filter.

#🔥 Boiling: the most reliable method First 72 h

A rolling boil for 1 minute makes clear water safe from germs. Above 6,500 ft (about 2,000 m), boil it for 3 minutes.1

The full minute is already a safety margin. CDC asks for a whole minute to allow for people misjudging when water is really boiling.5

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Clear cloudy water first

    Let it settle and draw off the clear water, or pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.1

  2. Bring it to a rolling boil

    A rolling boil means big bubbles that keep breaking the surface even when you stir.

  3. Hold the boil for 1 minute

    Hold it for 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft). Use the timer below.1

  4. Cool it with the lid on

    Do not add ice unless the ice was made from safe water.

  5. Store it clean and covered

    Pour it into clean, sanitized containers with tight covers.1 See Storing Water.

Timer: Rolling boil: 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m / 6,500 ft). Interactive in the digital edition.

You must boil water for 10 or 20 minutes to make it safe.

CDC says 1 minute at a rolling boil, or 3 minutes above 6,500 ft.1 Boiling kills germs quickly, and the full minute already adds a safety margin.5 Extra minutes only burn fuel you will need later.

Flat taste? Pour the cooled water back and forth between two clean containers a few times.1

☠️ Danger

Boiling does not remove chemicals

Water polluted with fuel or toxic chemicals cannot be made safe by boiling or disinfection.1

Use a different source. See Chemical Contamination.

💡 Tip

Save fuel for water

Boiling depends on fuel. Keep a pot with a lid and a fuel reserve that is only for water. See Cooking Without Power for stoves that run on wood and charcoal.

#🧴 Bleach: the right bottle, the right drops

Use regular, unscented chlorine bleach whose label says it is for disinfection and sanitizing.2

Do not use scented, color-safe or "with cleaner" bleach. EPA rules those out for drinking water.2

Read the strength on the label. EPA's table is for bleach with 6% or 8.25% sodium hypochlorite.2

Use fresh bleach. EPA's method calls for bleach that has been stored at room temperature for less than one year.2 That limit assumes room temperature, so keep bottles in a cool, dark place and date each one.

Unscented household bleach per volume of clear water (EPA)
Water6% bleach8.25% bleach
1 quart or 1 liter2 drops2 drops
1 gallon (3.8 L)8 drops6 drops
2 gallons (7.6 L)16 drops12 drops (⅛ tsp)
Cloudy, colored or very coldDouble itDouble it

EPA gives these doses for clear water and says to double them for cloudy, colored or very cold water.2 For bigger containers, multiply the 1-gallon dose, or use the calculator.

📊 Key fact

Bleach of another strength

EPA's table covers 6% and 8.25% bleach only.2 If your label shows another percentage, do the arithmetic from EPA's 6% dose: drops per gallon = 48 ÷ your %, rounded up.

For example, 5.25% bleach needs 10 drops per gallon and 4% bleach needs 12. The same formula gives EPA's 6 drops for 8.25%. Double it for cloudy, colored or very cold water.2

Bleach calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Clear the water

    If it is cloudy, murky or colored, let it settle or pour it through a clean cloth, paper towel or coffee filter.2

  2. Count the drops

    Use a clean dropper and the table above. Keep that dropper only for bleach.

  3. Stir and wait 30 minutes

    Do not drink it, cook with it or give it to pets during the wait.2

  4. Smell it

    It should smell slightly of chlorine. If not, repeat the dose and wait another 15 minutes.2

  5. Fix a strong taste

    Let it stand open to the air for a few hours, or pour it from one clean container to another several times.2

  1. Minute 0

    Add the drops and stir.

  2. Minute 30

    Smell test. A faint chlorine smell means it is ready.2

  3. Minute 45

    Only if there was no smell: you repeated the dose at minute 30, so it is ready now.2

  4. A few hours

    Optional: let strong-tasting water stand open to the air.2

Timer: Bleach contact time: 30 minutes. Interactive in the digital edition.

Do

  • Use regular, unscented bleach with the % on the label
  • Write the purchase date on every bottle
  • Clear cloudy water before dosing
  • Wait the full 30 minutes
  • Double the dose for cloudy or very cold water

Don't

  • Use scented, color-safe or "with cleaner" bleach
  • Use bleach stored over a year if fresh bleach exists
  • Guess the dose by pouring
  • Drink before the wait is over
  • Rely on bleach for Cryptosporidium
⚠️ Caution

Five common bleach mistakes

  • Wrong bottle: scented, color-safe or "with cleaner" bleach is not for drinking water.2
  • Old bottle: EPA's method uses bleach stored less than a year.2
  • Cloudy or icy-cold water at the normal dose: double it.2
  • Drinking early: the 30-minute wait is part of the treatment.2
  • Dirty containers: clean water poured into a dirty jug is no longer clean. Store it in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers.1

Just pour in a splash of bleach. More is always safer.

Measure it. EPA gives exact drops for clear water and says to double them only for cloudy, colored or very cold water.2 If the water then tastes too strong, let it stand open to the air for a few hours.2

#🦠 Cryptosporidium: the germ bleach cannot kill

Bleach and iodine kill most harmful bacteria and viruses. They are less effective against the tougher parasites Cryptosporidium and Giardia.1

Against Cryptosporidium ("Crypto"), iodine and chlorine are not effective. That is CDC's rating in its water treatment guide.3

Boiling kills it. So does chlorine dioxide, if you follow the maker's instructions.1 Chlorine dioxide is more potent than the same dose of chlorine and kills most waterborne germs, including Cryptosporidium.4

Layer your methods

A filter with pores of 1 micron or smaller, plus chlorine dioxide, has a "very high" rating against Cryptosporidium in CDC's guide.3

Filter first, then disinfect. CDC says to add a disinfectant after filtering to kill viruses and any remaining bacteria.13 Filter types and pore sizes are in Water Filters & SODIS.

📊 Key fact

Only boiling comes close to 100%

CDC states that, except for boiling, few water treatment methods are 100% effective at removing all germs.3 When someone in your home is very young, very old or sick, boil when you can.

Symptoms of Crypto, Giardia and other water germs are in Waterborne Diseases.

#💊 Iodine and chlorine dioxide tablets

Iodine: short-term only

Iodine does not reliably kill Cryptosporidium, and it works less well in cloudy water.4

Follow the manufacturer's instructions for the dose and the waiting time.3

⚠️ Caution

Who should not use iodine

CDC does not recommend iodine-treated water for:

  • Pregnant women
  • People with thyroid problems
  • People with a known iodine hypersensitivity
  • Anyone using it continuously for more than a few weeks at a time3
🌸 Women & girls

Pregnant? Skip iodine

CDC does not recommend iodine-treated water during pregnancy.3 Boil water instead, or use bleach or chlorine dioxide tablets.

Write "NOT FOR PREGNANCY" on the iodine bottle so no one forgets.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Thyroid disease or iodine allergy

CDC does not recommend iodine-treated water for people with thyroid problems or a known iodine hypersensitivity.3 Ask about thyroid conditions before you hand out iodine water.

Chlorine dioxide: slow but thorough

Chlorine dioxide kills most waterborne germs, including Cryptosporidium.4 The catch is time.

Tablets and drops need several hours of contact time. They also leave no lasting disinfectant in the water.4

📊 Key fact

Why the label wait matters

In a 2014 lab study of chlorine dioxide tablets, killing Cryptosporidium took hours, not minutes, and weaker doses took longer.6

Lab results are not a field promise. Always use the wait time on your product label.

Protect the tablets. Chlorine dioxide is volatile and breaks down in sunlight. Do not expose tablets to air, and use any mixed solution quickly.4

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Read the label

    Find the water volume per tablet and the wait time. Some labels give a longer time for Cryptosporidium.

  2. Clear the water first

    Settle it, then pour it through a clean cloth.1

  3. Add the tablet

    Use the exact volume on the label. Open one blister at a time.

  4. Wait the full time

    If you do not know the source, use the longest time on the label. Crypto needs hours.4

  5. Keep it covered

    Treated water has no lasting protection, so store it clean and closed.4

#🏊 Pool shock: EPA's long-term chlorine source Long haul

Granular calcium hypochlorite is dry chlorine. EPA's emergency disinfection guidance, as archived in 2013, uses it in two steps: make a strong stock solution, then dilute it into the water you drink.7

The method is written for high-test granular calcium hypochlorite with about 70% available chlorine.7 If the label lists a different active ingredient, this method does not apply.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Work outside, away from kids and dogs

    Use a measuring spoon and bucket that you keep only for chlorine.

  2. Make the stock

    Dissolve 1 heaping teaspoon (about ¼ oz, 7 g) in 2 gallons (7.6 L) of water. This gives about 500 mg/L of chlorine.7

  3. Label the stock

    Write "CHLORINE STOCK: DO NOT DRINK" and the date on the container.

  4. Dilute 1 part to 100

    Add 1 part stock to 100 parts clear water. That is roughly 1 pint (16 oz) of stock per 12.5 gallons (47 L).7

  5. Air out a strong smell

    If the chlorine smell is too strong, pour the water back and forth between clean containers.7

Stock to add at 1 part per 100 (arithmetic from EPA's ratio)
Water to treatStock to add
1 liter (about 1 quart)10 mL (about 2 tsp)
1 gallon (3.8 L)38 mL (1.3 fl oz)
20 liters (5.3 gallons)200 mL (6.8 fl oz)
12.5 gallons (47 L)1 pint (about 470 mL)
☠️ Danger

The stock is not drinking water

The stock is about 500 mg/L of chlorine, 100 times stronger than the water you drink after dilution.7 Keep it labeled, capped and locked away.

Never mix pool chemicals with other cleaners, and keep the granules dry and sealed. If someone swallows the stock, see Poisoning.

⚠️ Caution

Pool shock still misses Crypto

Calcium hypochlorite is chlorine. CDC rates chlorine as not effective against Cryptosporidium.3 Boil, or use chlorine dioxide, when Crypto is a concern.

#👶 Babies, children, dogs and elders

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

  • Lock up bleach, tablets and pool shock where children cannot reach them.
  • Keep children away from pots of boiling water. Let water cool on a back burner with the lid on.
  • For mixing formula and feeding bottles, follow Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.
  • Teach older children the 30-minute rule: no drinking from a bucket that is still "waiting".
🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and pets

Give your dog the same treated water your family drinks, in a bowl you wash daily.

Never leave stock solution or a dosing bucket where a dog can drink from it. Dog water diseases are covered in Dog Health.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older and disabled people

  • A full pot of boiling water is heavy. Let it cool, then ladle it out instead of lifting it.
  • Counting drops is hard with poor eyesight. Pre-mark a measuring spoon, or have one person do all dosing.
  • Check thyroid conditions before using iodine.3

#⏳ Disinfecting water for 30 years

⏳ The 30-year view

Plan for each method running out

  • Bleach: EPA's method uses bleach under a year old.2 Stored bleach is a first-year tool, not a 30-year one.
  • Iodine: CDC does not recommend continuous use for more than a few weeks at a time.3
  • Chlorine dioxide: Tablets must stay sealed from air and light.4
  • Boiling: Works for decades if you have fuel.1

The arithmetic for one household

Say your household drinks and cooks with 15 liters (4 gallons) a day. That is about 5,500 liters (1,460 gallons) a year. Your real daily need depends on climate, work and family size.

Bleach: at 12 drops (⅛ teaspoon) of 8.25% bleach per 2 gallons, 1,460 gallons takes about 91 teaspoons.2 That is about 450 mL (15 fl oz) of fresh bleach a year, for clear water.

Pool shock: 1 heaping teaspoon makes 2 gallons of stock, which treats 200 gallons at 1 to 100.7 So 1,460 gallons needs about 7 heaping teaspoons (about 50 g, 1.8 oz) a year.

This is dosing arithmetic only. It is not a promise of shelf life. Store granules dry, sealed and dated, and check the label.

💡 Tip

Use more than one barrier

Clear water first, then kill germs. Over the years, pair a biosand filter or a certified filter with boiling or chlorine.3

Keep a simple water log

Write down every batch: the date, the container, the method and the dose. When someone gets sick, a log shows which water they drank.

Add a line when you open a new bleach bottle or tablet pack. That tells you when the bleach passes one year.2

🎯 Practice now

Practice this now

  • Dose 1 gallon of tap water with bleach. Count the drops, wait 30 minutes and learn the faint chlorine smell.2
  • Time a 1-minute rolling boil on your emergency stove and note how much fuel it uses.
  • Look up your home's altitude and write "1 min" or "3 min" on your pot lid.1
🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • Regular, unscented bleach with the strength on the label (date every bottle)
  • A glass or plastic dropper and a measuring spoon set used only for chemicals
  • Chlorine dioxide tablets, kept sealed
  • A large pot with a lid, and fuel set aside for water
  • Granular calcium hypochlorite labeled about 70%, stored dry and locked
  • Coffee filters or clean cotton cloth for clearing water
▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print or download these official pages now

  • CDC: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency
  • EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
  • CDC guide: what each treatment method removes
  • CDC Yellow Book 2026: Water Disinfection for Travelers

#✅ Do this now

0 / 10 done

#🧠 Remember this

How long do you boil water?

1 minute at a rolling boil. 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).

How much 6% bleach per gallon (3.8 L)?

8 drops for clear water (6 drops of 8.25%). Double for cloudy or very cold water.

How long after adding bleach?

30 minutes. No chlorine smell? Repeat the dose and wait 15 more minutes.

Which germ do bleach and iodine not kill?

Cryptosporidium. Boil, or use chlorine dioxide with a long wait.

Who should avoid iodine water?

Pregnant women, people with thyroid problems or iodine allergy, and anyone using it for more than a few weeks.

Pool shock ratio?

1 heaping tsp in 2 gallons makes stock. Then 1 part stock to 100 parts water.

Does boiling remove fuel or chemicals?

No. Find another source.

How old can stored bleach be?

EPA's method uses bleach stored at room temperature for under a year.

  2. EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (n.d.). 🦠

Waterborne Diseases: Recognize, Prevent, Treat

🔴 CriticalFirst 30 days📚 20 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Start oral rehydration solution (ORS) right away. Most people with cholera can be treated with ORS.4 See Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.
  • Cholera can kill within hours. Watch for milky "rice-water" diarrhea, vomiting and leg cramps.46
  • Chlorine alone does not stop Cryptosporidium. It survives 3.5–10.6 days in properly chlorinated water.13 Boiling kills it.19
  • Toilets, treated water and clean hands save lives. Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene were linked to at least 1.4 million deaths in 2019.3
  • Count back from the first symptom. Cholera starts within hours to 5 days; hepatitis A takes 15–50 days. The gap tells you where to look.616
443,832children under 5 killed by diarrhea each year1
1.4 Mdeaths in 2019 linked to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene3
1 in 10people with cholera get severe symptoms6
10.6 daysupper end of how long Cryptosporidium survives in chlorinated water13

#🦠 Why these diseases matter so much

Diarrhea is one of the top killers of young children. Diarrheal disease is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months.1

Each year it kills about 443,832 children under 5 and another 50,851 children aged 5 to 9.1 There are nearly 1.7 billion cases of childhood diarrheal disease every year.1

Water is a main route. The World Health Organization (WHO) says contaminated drinking water can spread diarrhea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio.2 It causes about 505,000 diarrheal deaths each year.2

A 2023 WHO report added up the cost of unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH). In 2019, safe WASH could have prevented at least 1.4 million deaths.3

More than 1 million of those deaths were from diarrhea.3

📊 Key fact

Children pay the highest price

Among children under 5, unsafe WASH caused 395,000 deaths in 2019.3 Diarrhea caused 273,000 of them.3

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

In a grid-down life, your household does the work of the water plant, the sewer and the first clinic, for decades. This chapter is the "why". Disinfecting Water, Toilets Without Water and Handwashing & Personal Hygiene are the "how".

#🔍 Know the diseases: signs and timing

Learn the first signs and how long each germ takes to show. Use the table as a quick guide. The details follow below it.

Five waterborne diseases at a glance (CDC)
DiseaseGermFirst signsStarts after
CholeraBacteriumWatery "rice-water" diarrhea, vomiting, leg crampsA few hours to 5 days (usually 2–3)6
CryptosporidiumParasiteDiarrhea2–10 days (average 7)12
GiardiaParasiteDiarrhea, gas, greasy floating stools, cramps1–2 weeks11
TyphoidBacteriumFever, headache, stomach problems6–30 days10
Hepatitis AVirusTiredness, nausea, dark urine, yellow skin or eyes15–50 days (average 28)16

Cholera

Cholera can kill within hours. WHO calls it a severe diarrheal disease that can kill within hours if it is not treated.4

You catch it by drinking or eating something that contains cholera bacteria. Symptoms usually start 2–3 days later, but can start within a few hours or as late as 5 days.6

Early signs are watery diarrhea, vomiting, leg cramps and restlessness. The diarrhea often looks milky white and is called "rice-water stool".6

About 1 in 10 people get severe symptoms. Untreated severe dehydration can lead to kidney failure, shock, coma and death.6

☠️ Danger

Cholera: act in hours, not days

If someone has large amounts of watery diarrhea, start ORS immediately and get them to any working clinic. With early and proper treatment, even people with severe cholera can survive.6

Typhoid fever

Typhoid spreads through sewage. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) says it spreads through food, drinks and water contaminated by sewage, and through food rinsed in contaminated water.9

Symptoms usually appear 6–30 days after infection.10 They include fever, headache and stomach problems such as constipation or diarrhea.910

Feeling better does not mean the danger is over. CDC says people can keep carrying and spreading the bacteria after their symptoms go away.9

Dysentery (bloody diarrhea)

Dysentery is diarrhea with blood in it. WHO calls acute bloody diarrhea dysentery.1 It lists dysentery among the diseases that contaminated drinking water spreads.2

Blood in the stool is a reason to get professional care. See when diarrhea becomes an emergency in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.

E. coli

E. coli is a leading cause of serious diarrhea. WHO names rotavirus and Escherichia coli (E. coli) as the two most common causes of moderate-to-severe diarrhea in low-income countries.1

It spreads through sewage. CDC warns that floodwater can contain sewage, and that swallowing water or food it has contaminated can cause diarrheal disease such as E. coli infection.20

Boiling and chlorine both kill bacteria such as E. coli.19 Treat it like any diarrhea: ORS first, and professional care if the stool turns bloody.

Giardia

Giardia is a parasite that causes long, draining diarrhea. Symptoms usually start 1–2 weeks after you swallow the germs and last 2–6 weeks.11

Look for diarrhea, gas, smelly greasy stools that can float, stomach cramps, nausea and dehydration.11

Symptoms can last longer than 6 weeks, especially in people with weak immune systems. Some infected people have no symptoms at all.11

Cryptosporidium ("Crypto")

Crypto is the germ that chlorine does not stop. Its tough shells (oocysts) can survive 3.5–10.6 days in water with 1–3 mg/L (1–3 ppm) of free chlorine.13 CDC rates iodine and chlorine as not effective against it.19

Illness starts on average 7 days after exposure, with a range of 2–10 days.12 In healthy people it usually clears up within 2–3 weeks.14

In people with weak immune systems it can cause watery diarrhea for weeks to months, and even life-threatening malnutrition and wasting.14

⚠️ Caution

Bleach alone is not enough for Crypto

Boil the water: a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).5 CDC rates boiling as very effective against parasites such as Crypto.19

No fuel? A filter with an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller removes Crypto.19 Compare your options in Water Filters & SODIS and Disinfecting Water.

Hepatitis A

Hepatitis A is a liver virus that spreads from stool to mouth. It passes from person to person, or through contaminated food or water.16

Symptoms include tiredness, nausea or vomiting, stomach pain, fever, joint pain, loss of appetite, dark urine, clay-colored stools and jaundice (yellow skin or eyes).17

Most young children show nothing. About 70% of infections in children under 6 cause no symptoms,16 so you cannot tell who carries it by looking.

  1. Day 0

    The virus is swallowed in food or water, or passed on by close contact with an infected person.16

  2. Day 15–50

    Symptoms begin, on average around day 28. Many young children never show any.16

  3. While ill

    Tiredness, nausea, stomach pain, dark urine, clay-colored stools, yellow skin or eyes.17

  4. Under 2 months

    Symptoms usually last less than 2 months.17

#⏱️ Water or food? Use the clock

The same germs travel by water, food and hands. The true source is always someone's stool.

CDC lists food, drinks and water contaminated by sewage as typhoid routes.9 For hepatitis A it lists close contact and contaminated food or water.16

So the useful question is: which water, which food, which hands? The incubation period, the time from swallowing a germ to the first symptom, tells you when the exposure happened.

Do the arithmetic. If a child's first hepatitis A symptoms start on day 60, the exposure was between day 10 and day 45 (60 minus 50, and 60 minus 15).16

If cholera-like diarrhea starts on day 60, look at what people drank and ate from day 55 to day 60.6

Look-back windows: if symptoms started today, search this far back
Suspected diseaseLook backMost likely
CholeraA few hours to 5 days62–3 days ago6
Cryptosporidium2–10 days12About 7 days ago12
Giardia1–2 weeks111–2 weeks ago
Typhoid6–30 days10Anywhere in that window
Hepatitis A15–50 days16About 4 weeks (28 days) ago16

Long windows mean a wide search. For typhoid and hepatitis A, the source can be a meal or a water run from weeks ago, so a written log matters more than memory.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Write it down

    For every sick person, note the day and hour of the first symptom, and what the symptoms are.

  2. Match the disease

    Use the table above to find the most likely germ.

  3. Count back

    Subtract the incubation range from the first-symptom day. That gives the exposure window.

  4. List shared sources

    Every water source, drink, shared dish and food handler in that window.

  5. Compare sick and well

    The source the sick people shared and the well people did not is your lead suspect.

  6. Cut it off

    Stop using it. Treat all drinking and rinse water. See Epidemics: Quarantine, Isolation & Infection Control for caring for the sick safely.

💡 Tip

Clues: water, food or hands?

  • Water: the sick people all drank from one source, even if they ate different meals.
  • Food: the sick people all ate one dish, whatever they drank. See Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.
  • Hands and close contact: cases follow one another inside a household. Hepatitis A spreads from person to person.16
  • No germ pattern fits: think about fuel, pesticides or other chemicals. See Chemical Contamination.

#🚰 Break the chain: toilets, water, hands, food

Every disease in this chapter starts in someone's stool. Typhoid travels through sewage,9 and hepatitis A moves from stool to mouth.16 Block each route and the germ cannot reach a mouth.

Hands matter as much as water. WHO linked about 384,000 diarrheal deaths in 2019 to poor hand hygiene alone.3 It linked another 356,000 deaths from respiratory infections to poor hand hygiene.3

The four barriers

  • Toilet: keep stool far from water and food. See Toilets Without Water for distances from wells.
  • Treat water: every drop for drinking, brushing teeth, mixing baby formula and rinsing food. See Disinfecting Water.
  • Wash hands: after the toilet and diaper changes, and before touching food. See Handwashing & Personal Hygiene.
  • Food: rinse it in treated water only. CDC lists food rinsed in contaminated water as a typhoid route.9

Chlorinated water is safe from every germ.

Cryptosporidium survives 3.5–10.6 days in water held at 1–3 mg/L of free chlorine.13 Chlorine still kills most bacteria and viruses; for Crypto, boil or use a 1-micron filter.19

Do

  • Drink, cook and brush teeth with treated water only
  • Rinse fruit and vegetables in treated water9
  • Wash hands after the toilet, diapers and caring for the sick
  • Keep the toilet away from wells and streams
  • Start ORS at the first watery stool

Don't

  • Rely on bleach alone for Cryptosporidium13
  • Let anyone with diarrhea cook for others
  • Let someone who had typhoid cook for others without a clinician's advice9
  • Use one dipper for both raw and treated water
  • Guess with antibiotics

#💧 Treatment: oral rehydration first

Replace lost fluid first. That is what keeps people alive. WHO says most people with cholera have mild or moderate diarrhea and can be treated with ORS.4

CDC adds that with early, proper treatment, even people with severe cholera can survive.6

Start at the first watery stools. WHO defines diarrhea as 3 or more loose or liquid stools in a day.1

For children with diarrhea, WHO and UNICEF recommend low-osmolarity ORS plus zinc supplements.18 Zinc shortens an episode of diarrhea by 25%.1 Take the zinc dose from a clinician or the package label. The full method and home recipe are in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Start ORS right away

    Give small sips often. Use sachets, or the recipe in the ORS chapter.18

  2. Keep feeding

    Babies keep breastfeeding. Children keep eating their normal food.18

  3. Check for dehydration

    Fast heartbeat, dry mouth, skin that is slow to flatten after a pinch.6

  4. Protect everyone else

    One carer, one toilet or bucket for the sick person, handwashing after every contact, and no cooking for others.

  5. Get professional care for danger signs

    Use the table in the next section. Go early, not late.

Caring for a sick person without spreading it

The carer is the person most exposed. Hepatitis A spreads by close contact,16 and typhoid can spread even after the patient feels better.9 Set up the sickroom before you need it.

  • One carer where possible, who washes hands after every contact, every bucket and every diaper.
  • One toilet or lidded bucket for the sick person, emptied into the latrine, never near water.
  • Separate cup, plate and towel, washed apart from the family's.
  • Soiled bedding and clothes handled with gloves and washed away from the water source.
  • No food preparation by the sick person or, ideally, by the carer.

Disinfectant strengths for surfaces and laundry are in Epidemics: Quarantine, Isolation & Infection Control. Day-to-day nursing is in Nursing the Sick at Home.

Oral rehydration calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Cholera is a death sentence without a hospital.

Most cholera patients can be treated with ORS.4 Early treatment is what matters; even severe cases can survive with it.6

☠️ Danger

Do not guess with antibiotics

Never give leftover, fish or animal antibiotics. ORS comes first; antibiotics are a clinician's decision. Read the facts in Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts and get a clinician's advice wherever one exists.

#🚨 Danger signs: get help fast

Move fast when fluid loss is heavy. Cholera can kill within hours.4 Other diseases are slower, but still need professional care.

What you see, what it can mean, what to do
SignCan meanDo this
Large amounts of watery, milky stool; vomiting; leg crampsCholera6ORS now; clinic fast
Fast heartbeat, dry mouth, slow skin pinch, low blood pressureDehydration6More ORS; clinic
Blood in the stoolDysentery2Professional care
Fever and headache 6–30 days after unsafe water or foodTyphoid10Professional care; keep away from food prep
Yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, clay-colored stoolsHepatitis A17Professional care; strict handwashing
Greasy, floating diarrhea that goes on for weeksGiardia11Professional care; check your water
Diarrhea for weeks in someone with a weak immune systemCryptosporidium14Professional care; ORS

For babies and children, also use the danger-sign list in Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs.

#👪 Protect the people most at risk

The same germ hits some people much harder. Plan your best water, your ORS and your fastest trip to care around them.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and young children

Diarrhea kills about 443,832 children under 5 every year.1 In 2019, unsafe WASH caused 273,000 diarrheal deaths in this age group.3

Wash hands after every diaper change: 70% of young children with hepatitis A show no symptoms.16 Mix formula only with safe water (see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out).

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Elderly people and weak immune systems

In people with weak immune systems, Crypto can cause diarrhea for weeks to months and life-threatening wasting.14 Even nitazoxanide, a drug used for Crypto, has not been shown to work in these patients.15

Giardia can also last beyond 6 weeks in them.11 Give them boiled water, because boiling kills Crypto,19 and watch them closely for dehydration.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnant women

If you are pregnant and get heavy diarrhea, vomiting, fever or yellow eyes, get professional care as early as you can. Keep drinking ORS meanwhile, and see Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs

Your dog shares your floor, your hands and often your water. Give dogs clean water, keep them out of the latrine and away from the drinking-water source, and bury or bag their feces away from water. See Rabies & Diseases Animals Give Humans.

#⏳ The long haul: outbreaks keep coming

Cholera is not a disease of the past. In 2024, 60 countries reported 560,823 cholera cases and 6,028 deaths to WHO.8

Cholera deaths rose for the second year in a row: 2024 deaths were about 50% higher than in 2023.7 By WHO's September 2025 report, 31 countries had reported outbreaks that year.7

⏳ The 30-year view

Keep a sickness log for 30 years

A paper notebook beats memory. Record each case: name, date of first symptom, symptoms, and what the person drank and ate. It turns the arithmetic above into a real early warning. See Public Health for a Small Community.

🎯 Practice now

Vaccinate while clinics still exist

CDC recommends typhoid vaccination for travelers to high-risk areas.9 Hepatitis A is a vaccine-preventable disease covered in CDC's vaccine reference, the Pink Book.16 Ask a clinician now which vaccines fit your family.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • ORS sachets, low-osmolarity formula18
  • Zinc for children, to use as a clinician or label directs18
  • A water filter with an absolute pore size of 1 micron or smaller, which removes Cryptosporidium, plus spare parts19
  • Fuel set aside only for boiling drinking water
  • A thermometer, gloves and a notebook for the sickness log
  • A lidded bucket set aside for a sick person
▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Read and save while the internet works

  • CDC: Signs and Symptoms of Cholera
  • CDC: Symptoms of Giardia Infection
  • WHO: Cholera fact sheet
  • CDC: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency

#✅ Do this now

0 / 9 done

#🧠 Remember this

How soon can cholera cause symptoms?

Within a few hours to 5 days; usually 2–3 days.

What do cholera stools look like?

Milky white, watery "rice-water" stools.

What is the first treatment for watery diarrhea?

Oral rehydration solution (ORS), started right away.

Does chlorine kill Cryptosporidium?

Not reliably. It survives 3.5–10.6 days at 1–3 mg/L free chlorine. Boil the water instead.

Hepatitis A incubation?

15–50 days, average 28.

Classic Giardia signs?

Gas, cramps, smelly greasy floating stools, 1–2 weeks after exposure.

Deaths linked to unsafe WASH in 2019?

At least 1.4 million, over 1 million of them from diarrhea.

  2. WHO: Drinking-water fact sheet (2023). Contaminated drinking water can transmit diarrhea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid and polio; about 505,000 diarrheal deaths a year.

  4. WHO: Cholera fact sheet (n.d.). Cholera can be fatal within hours if untreated; most cases are mild or moderate and can be treated with ORS.
