Calories & Nutrition: How Much Food Keeps You Alive

🔴 CriticalFirst 30 days📚 14 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Plan 2,100 kcal per person per day. It is the minimum planning figure that food aid uses for general rations (the Sphere standard).1
  • Hard work needs more. Adult men need about 2,000–3,000 kcal a day and adult women about 1,600–2,400, depending on age and activity.4
  • Get 10–12% of calories from protein and about 17% from fat. That is the Sphere split for a 2,100 kcal ration.2
  • Adult protein floor: 0.8 g per kg of body weight a day. The 2025–2030 US Dietary Guidelines now advise 1.2–1.6 g/kg.97
  • Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more protein: 71 g a day in the US reference tables.10
2,100kcal per person per day: the emergency planning minimum1
766,500kcal per person per year at 2,100 a day (2,100 × 365)1
0.8 g/kgadult protein RDA per day, nearly unchanged since 19419
71 gprotein a day in pregnancy and breastfeeding (US tables)10

#🔢 The planning number: 2,100 kcal a day First 30 days

Start every food plan at 2,100 kilocalories (kcal) per person per day. In this book, "calories" means kilocalories.

The Food Security Cluster, which coordinates humanitarian food aid, calls 2,100 kcal the minimum planning figure for general rations and asks partners to align with Sphere.1 Its 2025 emergency guidelines call it the Sphere standard and ask all groups to harmonize around it.2

A 2002 National Academies report on emergency relief food also used 2,100 kcal per day as its planning basis.5

It is a floor for planning, not a perfect fit for each body. The guidance says to adjust the requirements to the context.1 WFP and UNHCR guidance calls 2,100 kcal the initial reference value for the early stage of an emergency, when people have no other food.3

Calories needed at 2,100 kcal per person per day (simple multiplication)
Period1 personFamily of 4Family of 6
1 day2,1008,40012,600
1 week14,70058,80088,200
30 days63,000252,000378,000
1 year766,5003,066,0004,599,000
30 years22,995,00091,980,000137,970,000

Every number in the table is 2,100 × people × days.1 Use it to see the scale of the job before you buy anything.

📊 Key fact

One average, many bodies

2,100 kcal is a planning average for a whole group. Adult needs alone run from 1,600 to 3,000 kcal a day, depending on sex, age and activity.4 Plan the group total first, then check each person.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

One person eating 2,100 kcal a day for 30 years needs about 23 million kcal (22,995,000).1 Plan stored food as the bridge while you build food production. Read Feeding a Family Forever: The Land Math.

#👪 Real needs: sex, age and workload

Adult women need about 1,600–2,400 kcal a day. Adult men need about 2,000–3,000 kcal a day.4 Where a person falls in that range depends on age and how physically active they are.4

The US Dietary Guidelines give estimates by age, sex and three activity levels: sedentary, moderately active and active.6 In the 2015–2020 edition this table is Appendix 2, "Estimated Calorie Needs per Day, by Age, Sex, and Physical Activity Level".14

The estimates are rounded to the nearest 200 kcal. One person's real needs may be higher or lower than the average in the table.6

Adult calorie ranges (US Dietary Guidelines) compared with the 2,100 kcal plan
Whokcal per dayGap at the active end
Adult women1,600–2,400Up to 300 kcal short
Adult men2,000–3,000Up to 900 kcal short

The gaps are simple subtraction: 2,400 − 2,100 = 300, and 3,000 − 2,100 = 900.4

⚠️ Caution

Averages can hide a hungry worker

A household that averages 2,100 kcal a day can still leave its most active man up to 900 kcal short every day.4 Set a target for each person, not just for the group.

Without power, many chores are done by hand: hauling water, cutting wood, washing clothes, digging. Put anyone who does them every day at the active end of their range when you plan.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. List everyone

    Write each person's name, age, sex and body weight on one page.

  2. Pick an activity level

    Mark each person sedentary, moderately active or active.6 Be honest about the work they do now, not last year.

  3. Look up the estimate

    Find their age, sex and activity level in the printed calorie table.13

  4. Add the household up

    Total the daily targets. Compare the total with 2,100 × the number of people.

  5. Plan with the bigger number

    Use whichever total is higher for buying and storing.

  6. Recheck every season

    Redo the list when work, ages, pregnancies or body weights change.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print these while the internet works

Download or print the full tables so you can plan offline:

  • Merck Manuals: Estimated calories needed by age, sex and activity level
  • Dietary Guidelines 2015–2020 (archived), Appendix 2 calorie table
  • Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 (PDF)
  • Food Security Cluster Handbook: Food Assistance

#🥩 Protein: the floor and the new target

Adults need at least 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight per day. This US recommended dietary allowance (RDA) has changed very little since the RDA idea began in 1941.9

The number comes from nitrogen balance studies. They gave an estimated average requirement (EAR) of 0.66 g/kg and an RDA of 0.83 g/kg, which was rounded down to 0.8.9

The same 0.8 g/kg RDA applies to every adult age group from 19 to over 70.12

The 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines for Americans raise the target to 1.2–1.6 g/kg a day, adjusted to each person's calorie needs.78 That is 50–100% more than the old RDA (1.2 ÷ 0.8 = 1.5; 1.6 ÷ 0.8 = 2).

The new guidelines appeared in January 2026.11 Harvard's Nutrition Source points out that protein needs vary a lot between people, that the National Academies set wider ranges, and that needs are best set with a health professional.11

Daily protein for adults by body weight (body weight × g/kg)
Body weightRDA 0.8 g/kg2025–2030 DGA 1.2–1.6 g/kg
50 kg (110 lb)40 g60–80 g
60 kg (132 lb)48 g72–96 g
70 kg (154 lb)56 g84–112 g
80 kg (176 lb)64 g96–128 g
90 kg (198 lb)72 g108–144 g

The new guidelines base protein on body weight because protein needs vary with age, body size and physical activity.7 The g/kg figures come from the RDA and the new guidelines.97 This table is for adults only. Do not use it for babies or children.

Protein foods named in the 2025–2030 guidelines: eggs, poultry, seafood and red meat, plus beans, lentils, nuts and soy.7 The guidelines say to put a high-protein food in every meal.8

For which of these keep for years, read Long-Term Food Storage.

💡 Tip

Use kilograms for protein math

Divide pounds by 2.2 to get kilograms. A 154 lb adult is 70 kg, so the RDA is 70 × 0.8 = 56 g a day.9

#🧈 Fat, carbohydrate and the Sphere split

Sphere puts 10–12% of a ration's energy from protein and 17% from fat.2 The Food Security Cluster calls these the minimum nutritional requirements for planning general rations.1

In a 2,100 kcal day, that is 210–252 kcal from protein and 357 kcal from fat.2 The remaining 1,491–1,533 kcal (71–73%) come from carbohydrate foods.

⚠️ Caution

Calories and protein are not the whole diet

This chapter covers energy and protein. Vitamins and minerals need their own plan. Read Deficiency Diseases: Scurvy, Pellagra, Beriberi & More before you finish your food list.

#🧮 From people to kilograms: label math

Turn your calorie total into kilograms of food with the label on each package. A calorie plan only helps once you know how many kilograms (or pounds) of each food to store.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Read the label

    Find the energy per serving (Calories or kcal) and the serving size in grams.

  2. Work out kcal per kg

    kcal per serving ÷ grams per serving × 1,000.

  3. Choose the food's share

    Decide what part of your calories this food will supply, for example one third.

  4. Work out the kilograms

    Total kcal × share ÷ kcal per kg. Multiply by 2.2 for pounds.

  5. Round up and write it down

    Write the target on your inventory sheet and on the storage bin.

Worked example with a made-up label (not a real product)
StepWorkingResult
Label160 kcal per 45 g serving160 ÷ 45 × 1,000
kcal per kg3,556 kcal in each kg3,556
Family of 4, 1 year4 × 2,100 × 3653,066,000 kcal
Food gives one third3,066,000 ÷ 31,022,000 kcal
Kilograms needed1,022,000 ÷ 3,556 = 287.4Round up: 288 kg (635 lb)

The 2,100 kcal starting figure is the planning minimum from the Food Security Cluster.1 Swap in your own household total if it is higher.

How many days will your food last?

Days of food = total kcal you have stored ÷ your household's kcal per day. Count every food, using the kcal per kg from its label.

Example: a family of 4 at 2,100 kcal each needs 8,400 kcal a day.1 If the inventory adds up to 500,000 kcal, that is 500,000 ÷ 8,400 = 59.5, so 59 full days.

  1. Day 1

    List everyone with age, sex, weight and activity level. Set each person's calorie and protein target.

  2. Week 1

    Do the label math (kcal per kg) for every stored food. Write it on each container.

  3. Month 1

    Add up total kcal on hand. Divide by the household's daily total to get days of food.

  4. Every season

    Reweigh people, update targets for work and pregnancy, and redo the days-of-food count.

Food calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

The calculator multiplies people × days × kcal per person per day. Change the kcal box to match your household's own targets.

🎯 Practice now

Practice the label math this week

Pick three foods you already store. Work out kcal per kg for each and write it on the container with a marker. Next time you shop, you can compare foods by kcal per kg and price. See Prepping on a Budget.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • A mechanical kitchen scale (no batteries) for weighing portions
  • A mechanical bathroom scale for weighing people
  • A notebook and pencils for the household food log
  • A printed copy of this chapter and the calorie tables

#🤰 Who needs extra: pregnancy, breastfeeding, children and elders

Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more protein than other adults. The US reference tables set 71 g a day in pregnancy and in breastfeeding, for ages 19–30 and 31–50.10

Those tables base adult protein on 0.8 g per kg of a reference body weight.10 An AHRQ research protocol lists pregnancy and lactation at 1.1–1.3 g/kg a day, above the adult 0.8 g/kg.12

For a 60 kg (132 lb) woman, 0.8 g/kg is 48 g. The 71 g figure is 23 g more each day.10

These protein reference values were published in 2005. AHRQ notes they had not been updated for nearly two decades.12

🌸 Women & girls

Plan her extra share first

When food is short, set aside the extra protein for pregnant and breastfeeding women before you split the rest of the household's food. Read Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital and Breastfeeding: The Survival Superpower.

👶 Babies & children

Babies are not small adults

Do not plan a baby's food from the adult numbers in this chapter. Read Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out and the First Foods chapter. For children, use the age rows in the printed calorie table.13

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults: protein does not shrink with age

The adult protein RDA stays at 0.8 g/kg from age 19 to over 70.12 Calorie needs change with age and activity, so check each older person's row in the table.4 For diabetes, kidney disease and other special needs, read the Special Diets chapter.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs need their own plan

The human calorie and protein numbers in this chapter do not apply to dogs. Plan their food separately with Feeding Dogs Without Kibble.

#📋 Share food fairly and keep records

Write down each person's daily target and weigh what they actually get. A plan on paper does nothing if portions are guessed.

Weigh people on the same scale, at the same time of day, about once a month. Write it in the food log next to their target. A falling weight tells you to recheck their share and their workload.

Do

  • Set a calorie and protein target for each person
  • Plan active workers at the top of their range
  • Set aside extra protein for pregnant and breastfeeding women first
  • Weigh portions with a scale
  • Keep a dated food log and inventory
  • Re-plan when the work or the season changes

Don't

  • Give everyone the same portion by habit
  • Plan below 2,100 kcal a head without a reason
  • Use adult tables for babies or dogs
  • Guess food stocks by eye
  • Forget to count yourself in the plan

Everyone needs 2,000 calories a day.

Adult estimates run from about 1,600 to 3,000 kcal a day, by sex, age and activity.4 Any one person may need more or less than the table average.6

2,100 kcal a day is enough for anyone.

2,100 kcal is a minimum planning figure that aid planners adjust to the context.1 Active adult men can need up to 3,000 kcal.4

Protein advice is settled and never changes.

The 0.8 g/kg RDA held almost unchanged from 1941, but the 2025–2030 US guidelines now advise 1.2–1.6 g/kg.97 Harvard notes that individual needs vary widely.11

💡 Tip

Make it a routine

Pick one day a week to update the food log and inventory. Assign it to one person as a job, and rotate the job each month.

🌾 Part 3 · FoodChapter 29
🧊

Food Safety Without a Refrigerator

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 15 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Keep the fridge and freezer doors shut. A closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours. A full freezer holds about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.12
  • Perishables above 4°C (40°F) for 2 hours or more go in the trash. That means meat, poultry, fish, eggs and leftovers. Above 32°C (90°F) the limit is 1 hour.1513
  • Eat in this order: fridge food first, then freezer food, then non-perishable pantry food.7 Within the fridge, perishables go before the foods the USDA chart lets you keep.3
  • Never taste food to check it. When in doubt, throw it out.2
  • Get medical help for danger signs: bloody diarrhea, diarrhea with a fever over 38.9°C (102°F), vomiting that stops you keeping liquids down, dehydration, or diarrhea longer than 3 days.11
4 ha closed fridge keeps food safe without power2
48 ha full freezer holds, door shut (24 h if half full)1
2 hmost time perishables may sit above 4°C (40°F)1
20 minbacteria can double in the danger zone4

#⏱️ The countdown starts when the power stops First 72 h

A closed refrigerator keeps food safe for up to 4 hours. After 4 hours without power, throw out refrigerated meat, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers.2

A full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours if the door stays shut. A half-full freezer holds for about 24 hours.12

These times come from the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). They only hold if the doors stay closed.1

Keep an appliance thermometer in both the fridge and the freezer. Safe readings are 4°C (40°F) or colder in the fridge and −18°C (0°F) or colder in the freezer.12

The first 30 minutes of an outage

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Write down the time

    Put it on the fridge door. Your 4-hour fridge clock and 24 to 48-hour freezer clock start now.2

  2. Keep both doors shut

    Open them only to read the thermometer or move food out. The safe times assume closed doors.113

    Tape a list of what is in the freezer to its door, so no one opens it to look.7

  3. Read both thermometers

    Write down the readings. The fridge should be 4°C (40°F) or colder and the freezer −18°C (0°F) or colder.2

  4. Pack the freezer tight

    Group frozen food together. Food packed close stays cold longer.1

  5. Get coolers and ice ready

    If the outage may last more than 4 hours, plan to move fridge perishables into a cooler with ice.1

⚠️ Caution

Two numbers, two different clocks

4 hours is how long a closed fridge stays cold enough. 2 hours is how long a perishable food may sit above 4°C (40°F).1

No thermometer? Use the 4-hour rule.2 Have a thermometer? Use the 2-hour rule on what it reads.3

💡 Tip

Freeze water now, while you have power

Freeze containers of water and gel packs ahead of time. They keep the freezer, fridge or cooler cold after the power goes.1 Full jugs also fill empty freezer space, and a full freezer holds twice as long as a half-full one.1

#🌡️ The danger zone and the 2-hour rule

Bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F and 140°F). USDA calls this range the "Danger Zone."4

In that range, bacteria can double in number in as little as 20 minutes.4

Never leave perishable food in the danger zone for more than 2 hours. If the air is above 32°C (90°F), the limit is 1 hour.56

Keep hot food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter, and cold food at 4°C (40°F) or colder. USDA lists chafing dishes, warming trays, slow cookers and ice as ways to do it.4

Why 2 hours matters: the math

At the fastest rate, one doubling every 20 minutes, 2 hours is 6 doublings.4 That turns 1 germ into 64.

  1. 0 min

    1 germ on the food

  2. 20 min

    2

  3. 40 min

    4

  4. 1 hour

    8 (the hot-weather limit above 32°C / 90°F)5

  5. 80 min

    16

  6. 100 min

    32

  7. 2 hours

    64 (the normal limit: throw out perishables)1

📊 Key fact

Hot weather cuts your time in half

Above 32°C (90°F), perishable food may sit out for only 1 hour, not 2.5 In a hot climate with no ice, plan every meal around this limit.

⚠️ Caution

Lost track of the time?

If you do not know how long food has been out of the cold, you cannot apply the 2-hour rule. Follow the official fallback: when in doubt, throw it out.2

#🧊 Stretching the cold: coolers, block ice and dry ice

If the power will be off longer than 4 hours, move fridge perishables into a cooler with ice or frozen gel packs.1 Do it before the 4 hours run out.

Keep the cooler at 4°C (40°F) or colder.6 Add ice as it melts to hold that temperature.

Pack a cooler

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Pick the riskiest foods first

    Meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers. These are the foods USDA says to discard after 2 hours above 4°C (40°F).1

  2. Layer food with ice

    Use ice cubes, block ice or frozen gel packs.1

  3. Put a thermometer inside

    The target is 4°C (40°F) or colder.6

  4. Keep the lid shut

    Open it only to take food out or read the thermometer.

  5. Add ice as it melts

    Top it up before the reading climbs above 4°C (40°F).6

  6. Apply the 2-hour rule

    Perishables that sat above 4°C (40°F) for 2 hours or more go in the trash.1

Dry ice and block ice for longer outages

About 23 kg (50 lb) of dry ice should hold a full 510-liter (18-cubic-foot) freezer for 2 days.1

USDA advises getting dry ice or block ice if the power will be out for a long time.1 Find out now where you can buy it locally.

☠️ Danger

Dry ice burns skin

Never touch dry ice with bare hands.16 Use thick gloves or a towel. Keep it where children and pets cannot reach it.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • 2 appliance thermometers: one for the fridge, one for the freezer1
  • A third thermometer for the cooler
  • At least one good cooler1
  • Gel packs and jugs to freeze water in1
⚠️ Caution

Running a fridge on a generator

A generator can keep a fridge cold, but it brings its own dangers. Read Carbon Monoxide before you start one.

#🍽️ Eat in this order

Eat the food that spoils fastest first. The American Red Cross order is: food from the refrigerator first, then food from the freezer, then non-perishable food.7

The official clocks explain why: about 4 hours for the fridge, 24 to 48 hours for the freezer.12

  1. First: hours 0–4

    Fridge perishables: meat, poultry, fish, milk, eggs, leftovers, cut fruit and cooked pasta. Cook and eat them, or move them to a cooler with ice.23

  2. Second: days 1–2

    Freezer food as it thaws. Food that still has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder can be refrozen or cooked.12

  3. Third

    Fridge foods the USDA chart lists as safe to keep even after 2 hours above 4°C (40°F): hard cheese, butter, whole fresh fruit, dried fruit, whole raw vegetables, bread, peanut butter and condiments.3

  4. Last

    Non-perishable pantry food: cans, dry grains, beans and other long-life stores.7 See Long-Term Food Storage and Shelf-Life Tables.

💡 Tip

Cook only what you will eat at one meal

Without a working fridge, leftovers are on the 2-hour clock (1 hour above 32°C / 90°F).5 Cooking smaller amounts means less to throw away. For safe ways to cook without power, see Cooking Without Power.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and young children

Opened baby formula is on the USDA discard list once it has been above 4°C (40°F) for more than 2 hours.3 Children under 5 are more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.11

Worldwide, diarrheal disease is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1 to 59 months.15

Give them the safest food first, and never the doubtful item. For feeding without power, see Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs: do not feed them the trash pile

The USDA rules in this chapter are written for people, and no official rule here says thrown-out food is safe for dogs. Bag or bury discarded food so dogs cannot get it. See Feeding Dogs Without Kibble.

#✅ Keep or throw out: the USDA tables

Judge each food item separately. The official FoodSafety.gov power outage chart is built for exactly this.3

The chart's fridge rule applies to food that sat at 4°C (40°F) or above for more than 2 hours.3

When the power comes back (or at the 4-hour mark)

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Read the freezer thermometer

    At 4°C (40°F) or below, the frozen food is safe and may be refrozen.2

  2. Read the fridge thermometer

    No thermometer? Count the hours. Past 4 hours, perishables go.2

  3. Go item by item

    Use the table below. Each food gets its own decision.3

  4. Check smell, color, texture and warmth

    Anything that seems wrong or feels warm goes, even if the table says keep.3

  5. Bag the discards securely

    Keep them away from children and dogs. See Garbage & Waste Management.

Fridge food above 4°C (40°F) for more than 2 hours (FoodSafety.gov, USDA and CDC, short version)2310
FoodDecision
Raw or cooked meat, poultry, fish, seafood❌ Throw out
Milk, cream, yogurt❌ Throw out
Soft cheese (Brie, cream cheese, cottage cheese)❌ Throw out
Eggs and egg dishes❌ Throw out
Leftovers, casseroles, soups, stews, potato salad❌ Throw out
Cooked pasta, rice, potatoes❌ Throw out
Cut fresh fruit❌ Throw out
Cooked vegetables, tofu, pre-cut packaged greens❌ Throw out
Opened baby formula❌ Throw out
Hard cheese (cheddar, Colby, Swiss, Parmesan, provolone, Romano)✅ Keep
Butter, margarine✅ Keep
Whole fresh fruit, dried fruit, raisins, dates, coconut✅ Keep
Whole raw vegetables (not cut)✅ Keep
Bread, rolls, muffins, tortillas✅ Keep
Peanut butter, jelly, ketchup, mustard, pickles, olives✅ Keep

Not on this list? Check the full chart. If you still cannot tell, throw it out.2

Frozen food

Thawed food can be refrozen if it still has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder.13

If the freezer thermometer reads 4°C (40°F) or below when power returns, the food is safe and may be refrozen.12 No thermometer in the freezer? Check each package on its own.1

Frozen meat, poultry, fish and other perishables that thawed and stayed above 4°C (40°F) for more than 2 hours go in the trash.3

Any food, any time

Throw out any food with an unusual smell, color or texture, or that feels warm to the touch.313

Never taste food to decide if it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.12

If it looks and smells fine, a small taste will tell you if it is safe.

USDA and CDC both say never taste food to decide if it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.12

Food that has started to thaw must never be refrozen.

It is safe to refreeze if it still has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder.13

A closed fridge keeps food safe for a day or two.

A closed fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours. After that, meat, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers go.214

Do

  • Write down when the power went off
  • Read the thermometers before you decide
  • Check each item on its own
  • Move perishables to a cooler before 4 hours pass
  • Throw out anything doubtful

Don't

  • Open the fridge "just to look"
  • Taste food to test it
  • Trust smell alone
  • Touch dry ice bare-handed
  • Leave cooked food out past 2 hours
▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print these official charts now

Print both pages while you still have power, and tape them inside a kitchen cupboard:

  • FoodSafety.gov: Refrigerated Food and Power Outages8
  • FoodSafety.gov: Frozen Food and Power Outages9
  • CDC: Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency2

#🤢 Food poisoning: symptoms and danger signs

The common symptoms are diarrhea, stomach pain or cramps, nausea, vomiting and fever.11

Food poisoning is common even with working fridges. A CDC study published in 2025 estimated that major germs in food caused about 9.9 million illnesses in the US in 2019.12

📊 Key fact

What the US numbers show (CDC study, 2025)

The same study estimated 53,300 hospital stays and 931 deaths from food eaten in the US in 2019.12 Norovirus alone caused about 5.5 million of the illnesses.12

☠️ Danger

Get medical help now for any of these

  • Bloody diarrhea11
  • Diarrhea with a fever over 38.9°C (102°F)11
  • Vomiting so often that you cannot keep liquids down11
  • Signs of dehydration11
  • Diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days11

Botulism and home-canned food are covered in Home Canning Safely. Danger signs in babies are in Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs.

Watch for dehydration

Signs of dehydration include little or no urine, a very dry mouth and throat, and feeling dizzy when standing up.11

Replace lost fluid early. How to mix and give oral rehydration solution (ORS) is in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.

Who gets sickest

Some people are more likely to get food poisoning and to get seriously ill: adults 65 and older, children under 5, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems.11

Check people in these groups often for the danger signs above, and get help at the first one.11 Give them the safest food in the house.

When someone gets sick

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Start fluids at once

    Drink plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.11 Use ORS if you have it.15

  2. Check the danger signs

    Bloody diarrhea, diarrhea with fever over 38.9°C (102°F), can't keep liquids down, dehydration, or diarrhea past 3 days means get help.11

  3. Find and remove the suspect food

    Throw out anything else from the same batch so no one else eats it.

  4. Keep the sick person out of the kitchen

    Have someone else cook. Wash hands after every bathroom trip and cleanup; see Handwashing & Personal Hygiene.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy

Pregnant people are in a higher-risk group for food poisoning.11 CDC advises a pregnant person with fever and flu-like symptoms to talk to a doctor.11 See Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults

Adults 65 and older are more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.11 Check them often for dehydration and the other danger signs, and get help at the first one.11

#⏳ No fridge for years: the daily rules Long haul

Without power, a fridge is just an insulated box. It keeps food safe for about 4 hours after the power goes, and no longer.2

After the first days, the 2-hour rule governs every meal you cook. Perishable food may sit in the danger zone for 2 hours at most, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F).5

Three safe choices for any cooked food

Step by step · 3 steps

  1. Eat it now

    Serve within 2 hours of cooking, or 1 hour in heat above 32°C (90°F).5

  2. Keep it hot

    Hold it at 60°C (140°F) or hotter, for example in a covered pot over low heat.4

  3. Or throw it out

    When time is up and it is not hot, discard it.1

For the long haul, your food has to be safe at room temperature from the start. These chapters cover the methods:

Ways to keep food without a refrigerator
MethodWhere to learn it
Dry goods in sealed containersLong-Term Food Storage
Canning in jarsHome Canning Safely
Drying, smoking, salting, fermentingDrying, Smoking, Salting & Fermenting
Cool storage for roots and fruitRoot Cellars & Cold Storage
⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

The rules in this chapter do not expire. The danger zone, the 2-hour rule and "never taste to test" apply in year 30 exactly as on day 1.45

What changes is your tools. Look after your thermometers, because they are the only way to know a temperature instead of guessing it.

🎯 Practice now

Run a cooler test this month

Fill a cooler with ice and a thermometer, then note the reading every few hours. Record how long it stays at 4°C (40°F) or colder in your climate.6 Now you know your real number, not a guess.

💡 Tip

Label cooked food with the time

Write the cooking time on the pot lid with chalk or tape. Then anyone can see when the 2-hour limit runs out.5

#✅ Do this now

0 / 10 done

#🧠 Remember this

How long does a closed fridge keep food safe without power?

About 4 hours.

How long does a freezer hold with the door shut?

About 48 hours if full, 24 hours if half full.

What is the danger zone?

4–60°C (40–140°F). Bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes.

How long can perishables sit in the danger zone?

2 hours. Only 1 hour above 32°C (90°F).

When can thawed food be refrozen?

If it still has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder.

Can you taste food to check it?

No. When in doubt, throw it out.

Which fridge foods can you keep after an outage?

Hard cheese, butter, whole fruit, whole raw vegetables, bread, condiments.

Five food poisoning danger signs?

Bloody diarrhea, diarrhea with fever over 38.9°C (102°F), can't keep liquids down, dehydration, diarrhea over 3 days.

🌾 Part 3 · FoodChapter 30
🍳

Cooking Without Power

🟠 HighFirst 72 hFirst 30 days📚 22 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Cook outdoors only with camp stoves and charcoal grills, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows. That is the Ready.gov (FEMA) rule for power outages.1
  • Never use a gas stove or oven to heat your home. It is a carbon monoxide (CO) risk.13
  • Put a battery-powered CO alarm near every sleeping area. People who are asleep can die from CO before they feel any symptoms.2
  • Keep cooked food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter, or eat it within 2 hours. In heat above 32°C (90°F), the limit is 1 hour.45
  • Save fuel for drinking water. A rolling boil for 1 minute makes water safe from germs, or 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).7
6 m(20 ft) from windows for camp stoves and charcoal grills1
60°C(140°F) or hotter keeps cooked food out of the danger zone4
1 minat a rolling boil makes water safe from germs7
3–6 Lof water per person per day just for cooking (Sphere)9

#🚫 Rule one: every flame cooks outside First 72 h

Every cooking fire makes carbon monoxide (CO). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) lists stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces and gas ranges among the things that make it whenever fuel burns.2

You cannot see or smell CO. It builds up in enclosed or partly enclosed spaces and poisons the people and animals who breathe it.2

Camp stoves and charcoal grills go outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 A garage, carport, tent or camper is an enclosed or partly enclosed space, not "outdoors".23

If your gas range still works, use it for cooking only, then turn it off. Never use a gas stove or oven to heat the home.13

Where each way of cooking is allowed
CookerSafe placeNever
Camp stove (propane, butane, liquid fuel)Outdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from windows1Inside a home, garage, tent or camper
Charcoal grillOutdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from windows1Inside, even "just to finish cooking"
Gas range or ovenCooking only, then offHeating the home1
Wood fire or rocket stoveOutdoors, away from the houseAn open fire indoors
Solar cookerA sunny spot outdoorsLeaving food in it after the sun goes
☠️ Danger

Outside but close is not enough

After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people in Alabama and Texas and killed 10. Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.21

Stoves and grills make CO too.2 Keep the full 6 m (20 ft) from windows,1 and set up so the smoke blows away from the house.

Know the warning signs

CO poisoning causes headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion.3 CDC notes that people often describe these as "flu-like".2

If anyone feels this way while a stove, grill or fire is burning nearby, get everyone into fresh air first. Then get medical help.3

Fit CO alarms with battery backup,1 and replace each alarm every 5 years.2 The full story is in Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Pick the spot

    Open air, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 Keep it away from doors and vents too.

  2. Check the wind

    Set up so smoke blows away from the house and from where people sit.

  3. Clear the ground

    Bare soil, gravel or paving. Nothing that can burn underneath or hanging overhead.

  4. Mark a no-go zone

    Lay a rope or a ring of stones around the cooker. Children and dogs stay outside it.

  5. Keep fire tools within reach

    A metal lid that fits your pan, a bucket of sand or soil, and a flashlight.

  6. Never leave it alone

    An adult stays with a lit stove or fire until it is fully out.

💡 Tip

Rain is not a reason to cook inside

When the weather is too wet to cook outdoors, eat a no-cook meal instead. Keep a few days of ready-to-eat food for exactly this. See Long-Term Food Storage.

#🔥 Your cooking options, side by side

You have five main ways to cook without the grid. Three of them burn fuel and make CO. A solar cooker and a retained-heat box burn nothing themselves, because CO comes from burning fuel.2

Camp stove (propane, butane or liquid fuel)

Best for: boiling water and quick meals in the first days and weeks. Rule: outdoors only, 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1

Limit: its fuel comes from stores. Fuel pumps are among the systems FEMA lists as hit by power outages (2025).13

Charcoal grill

Same rule as the camp stove: outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1 Never bring it indoors to keep warm or to finish cooking.

Once bought charcoal runs out, you can make your own from wood. See Charcoal, Lime, Ash & Useful Low-Tech Materials.

Wood fire and rocket stove

Wood is a cooking fuel you can gather locally, year after year. A rocket stove is a small stove with an insulated, L-shaped burn chamber that you feed with sticks.

Wood smoke still carries CO: CDC lists fireplaces and stoves among CO sources.2 Cook on wood outdoors. For indoor wood stoves and chimneys, read Heating With Wood. To light fires for decades, read Fire Starting Methods That Last Decades.

Solar cooker

No fuel, no flame, no CO.2 It cooks only while the sun shines on it.

Retained-heat box ("haybox")

You boil the pot on a stove, then let insulation finish the cooking. No flame goes in the box. The safety rules are in the no-flame section below.

Do

  • Cook in the open air, 6 m (20 ft) from windows1
  • Keep a lid on every pot
  • Use the sun on sunny days
  • Finish long dishes in an insulated box
  • Keep a battery CO alarm by every bed2

Don't

  • Use a grill or camp stove in a home, garage, tent or camper
  • Heat the house with a gas stove or oven1
  • Leave a fire alone
  • Let kids or dogs inside the no-go ring

#⛽ Fuel: count it, store it, stretch it

Stored fuel is all you can count on. FEMA lists fuel pumps, lighting and payment systems among the systems hit by power outages (2025).13

Outages can last months. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, surveyed households in Puerto Rico went an average of 84 days without power.14 Hurricane Helene in 2024 cut power to 5.9 million customers across 10 states.15

So measure how much fuel your family uses per day, while you still have a scale and time to practice.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Weigh the fuel

    Weigh a full canister, bag of charcoal or bundle of dry wood on a kitchen scale. Write it down.

  2. Boil 1 liter (about 1 quart)

    Lid on. Time how long it takes to reach a rolling boil.

  3. Weigh again

    The difference is your fuel per liter boiled.

  4. Cook a normal day

    Breakfast, dinner and drinking water. Weigh the fuel before and after.

  5. Do the math

    Fuel stored ÷ fuel per day = days of cooking you have.

  6. Post the number

    Write "days of fuel left" on the fuel shelf and update it every week.

📊 Key fact

Worked example (use your own numbers)

These numbers are made up to show the math. Say your test shows one day uses 300 g (0.66 lb) of fuel, and you have 10 kg (22 lb) stored.

10 kg ÷ 0.3 kg per day = about 33 days of cooking.

Store fuel away from water and food

Fuel vapors can pass through plastic. University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension warns that gasoline, kerosene and pesticide vapors can penetrate plastic water containers.16 Keep stored water, and anything you eat or drink from, well away from fuel.

For storing and rotating liquid fuels, read Generators & Fuel Storage.

⚠️ Caution

Fuel handling habits

  • Change or refill fuel canisters only when every flame nearby is out.
  • Close valves fully after each use.
  • Store fuel where children cannot reach it.
  • Keep matches and lighters in a closed metal tin.
⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Bought fuel runs out first. Plan to move, step by step, to fuels you can renew: dry wood you cut and season, charcoal you make, and the sun.

Every liter of fuel you save with a lid, a solar cooker or an insulated box is a liter you still have next winter.

#💧 Water first: the biggest fuel job

Boil drinking water at a rolling boil for 1 minute. Above 2,000 m (6,500 ft), boil it for 3 minutes.7

Longer is not needed. CDC's Yellow Book says boiling kills organisms quickly, and the full minute already adds a margin of safety.8 Every extra minute burns fuel you need later.

Boiling does not remove fuel or chemicals.7 For other methods, read Disinfecting Water.

Timer: Rolling boil: 1 minute. Interactive in the digital edition.

You must boil drinking water for 10 minutes or more.

CDC says 1 minute at a rolling boil, or 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).7 The full minute already includes a safety margin.8

Cooking needs water too

Plan 3–6 L of water per person per day just for cooking. That is the Sphere humanitarian figure, on top of 2.5–3 L for drinking and food.9

The CDC home minimum of 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day covers drinking, cooking and brushing teeth.10 Sphere's cooking figure alone, 3–6 L, can use up that whole gallon.9

📊 Key fact

Cooking water for a family of 4

4 people × 3–6 L = 12–24 L (3.2–6.3 gal) a day, using the Sphere range.9

Over 30 days that is 360–720 L (95–190 gal), just for cooking.

👶 Babies & children

Keep fuel for the baby's water

For powdered formula, CDC says to use bottled water until officials say tap water is safe. With no bottled water, boil water for 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m or 6,500 ft).11

For babies under 2 months, premature babies or babies with weak immune systems, mix the formula with water that is still about 70°C (158°F).11 Cool the bottle before feeding. Set aside fuel that is only for this. See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

#🌡️ Cook it safe: heat, time and leftovers

Bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F and 140°F). USDA calls this the "Danger Zone". In that range, bacteria can double in as little as 20 minutes.4

Keep hot food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter until you serve it.4

Cooked food left in the danger zone has 2 hours. If the air is above 32°C (90°F), it has 1 hour.5 After that, throw it out.

Never taste food to check whether it is safe. When in doubt, throw it out.6

  1. 0 min: off the heat

    Serve it now, or keep it at 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4

  2. 20 min

    In the danger zone, bacteria can already have doubled.4

  3. 1 hour

    Limit in hot weather, above 32°C (90°F).5

  4. 2 hours

    Limit in cooler weather. Throw out what is left.5

Leftover starches count too. FoodSafety.gov lists cooked pasta among foods to discard after more than 2 hours above 4°C (40°F) in a power outage.22

💡 Tip

Cook one meal at a time

Without a fridge, cook only what your household will eat at that meal. Write the time on the pot lid with chalk or tape, so anyone can see when the 2-hour limit runs out.5 For storing food without power, read Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get two food thermometers

A thermometer shows whether food is still at 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4 Buy a dial or glass one that needs no battery, plus a spare.

When food makes someone sick

Get medical help for these signs: bloody diarrhea, fever over 38.9°C (102°F), frequent vomiting, signs of dehydration, or diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days.12

Some people get much sicker: adults 65 and older, children under 5, pregnant people and people with weak immune systems.12 For fluids, read Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.

#📦 No-flame cooking: insulated boxes and the sun

Retained-heat ("haybox") cooking

Bring the pot to a full boil on a safe outdoor stove, then put the lidded pot into a well-insulated box. The insulation holds the heat in, so you stop burning fuel to keep it simmering.

The one rule: the food must stay at 60°C (140°F) or hotter. That is USDA's hot-holding temperature. Below it, bacteria grow fastest.4

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Build the box

    Use a box, basket or cooler. Line every side, the bottom and the top with thick insulation: blankets, pillows, a sleeping bag, straw or crumpled paper.

  2. Choose the pot

    A pot with a tight lid and handles, that fits the hollow with insulation pressed all around it.

  3. Boil it hard

    Bring the food to a full rolling boil on the outdoor stove. Stir so it is hot all the way through.

  4. Move it fast

    Lid on, straight into the box, insulation over the top. Close every gap.

  5. Leave it closed

    Do not open it to peek. Every opening lets heat out.

  6. Check before eating

    60°C (140°F) or hotter: serve it.4 Cooler, and for under 2 hours: boil it again, then eat. Longer, or you do not know: throw it out.56

☠️ Danger

Keep the box away from flames

Blankets, straw and paper burn. Take the pot off the stove before it goes into the box, and keep the box well away from the fire.

🎯 Practice now

Test your box with water now

Boil 2 L (about 2 quarts) of water, box it, and check it with a thermometer every hour. Write down how many hours it stays at 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4

That is your box's safe time. Never leave food in it longer than that.

⚠️ Caution

Beans and grains in the box

Always bring them to a full boil first. Do not leave them in the box overnight unless your water test shows the box holds 60°C (140°F) or hotter that long.4

Solar cookers

A solar cooker burns nothing, so it makes no CO.2 It needs direct sun and a cook who checks the food.

  • Set it up in full sun, outside the children's and dogs' play area.
  • Use a dark pot with a lid.
  • Turn the cooker to face the sun as it moves across the sky.
  • Do not stare into the shiny reflector.
  • Check the food with a thermometer before you eat it: 60°C (140°F) or hotter.4
  • If clouds come and the food cools, the 2-hour clock starts.5 Finish it on the stove.

#🫘 Beans, rice and grains on less fuel

Humanitarian food planning starts at 2,100 kcal per person per day.19 The 2025–2030 Dietary Guidelines list beans and lentils among protein foods.20

Your fuel decides how often you can cook them. Use the habits below, then measure what works with your own stove and food.

Six fuel-saving habits

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. One pot, one fire

    Cook beans, grain and vegetables together, or one after another on the same fire.

  2. Lid on, always

    Keep the lid on from the moment the water goes in.

  3. Boil, then box

    Bring the pot to a full boil, then finish the long, slow part in a retained-heat box, using the safety checks above.4

  4. Use only the water you need

    Every extra liter heated is fuel wasted. Cooking water is already 3–6 L per person per day.9

  5. Cook while the sun is out

    Put slow dishes in the solar cooker on clear days, and save stove fuel for water and bad weather.

  6. Cook only what you will eat

    Leftovers have 2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F).5 Food you throw away is fuel thrown away.

🎯 Practice now

Run a soak test now

Take two equal cups of the same dried beans. Soak one in clean, treated water overnight; leave the other dry.

Cook both on the same stove. Write down the minutes until soft and the fuel used for each. Now you know, for your beans and your stove, what soaking saves.

Soak and cook with safe water. CDC counts cooking in the clean water you need each day.10 If you are unsure about a source, treat it first with the methods above.

For growing and processing these crops, see Growing & Processing Grains and Beans.

#👪 Children, elders, women and dogs at the cooking fire

The cooking spot puts flames, hot pots, fuel and CO in one place. Plan for each person who comes near it.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

Infants are among those at higher risk from CO.2 Keep babies and young children indoors or well away from the cooker, never inside the no-go ring.

Give older children safe jobs away from the flame: carrying water, washing vegetables, setting out bowls. Cook full portions for children; FEMA and the American Red Cross say food may be rationed except for children and pregnant women.17 See Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age and Burns.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Elders and people with heart or lung disease

Older people and people with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are at higher risk from CO.2 Seat them upwind and away from the smoke.

Adults 65 and older are also more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.12 Serve them food hot, straight from the pot.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy

Pregnant people are in a higher-risk group for food poisoning.12 Give them freshly cooked, hot food, not leftovers.

Do not cut a pregnant woman's portion: FEMA and the Red Cross exclude pregnant women from food rationing.17 CDC also says to store extra water for pregnant women.10

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs

CO poisons animals as well as people.2 If the dog and people feel unwell at the same time while something is burning nearby, treat it as CO and get everyone into fresh air.3

Keep dogs out of the no-go ring, tied or shut away while you cook. For feeding dogs from the family pot, read Feeding Dogs Without Kibble.

If a fire gets away

Plan two ways out of every room. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) says to practice the plan twice a year, during the day and at night.18

You may have only 1 to 2 minutes to escape once a home fire starts. Get out and never go back inside.18

Use flashlights, not candles, for light while you cook and clean up after dark.1

Ready.gov's Power Outages page, CDC's Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics, and USDA's Danger Zone page. Keep paper copies with this book.

#🧠 Remember this

Where do camp stoves and charcoal grills go?

Outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.

Can you heat the house with a gas stove or oven?

Never. It is a carbon monoxide risk.

Someone has a headache and dizziness near a burning stove. First move?

Everyone into fresh air first, then medical help.

How hot must food stay until it is served?

60°C (140°F) or hotter.

How long can cooked food sit out?

2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F). Then throw it out.

How long do you boil drinking water?

1 minute at a rolling boil. 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).

The haybox rule?

Boil first, lid on, box closed, check 60°C (140°F) before serving.

How much cooking water per person per day?

3–6 L (Sphere), on top of drinking water.

Part 4

Medicine & First Aid

First aid that saves lives in minutes, treating injuries and infections when no hospital is coming, and keeping medicines working for as long as possible.

🩺 Part 4 · Medicine & First AidChapter 50
🧰

Building a Long-Term Medical Kit

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 hYear 1📚 12 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Build three tiers, not one big box. A personal kit on each adult, a household kit at home and in the car, and a shared group store. The Red Cross says to keep a kit both at home and in the car.1
  • Start the household kit from the Red Cross family-of-four list. It includes 2 absorbent compress dressings, 25 adhesive bandages and 1 roll of cloth tape.1
  • Personal kits are for bleeding first. The US Army built its soldier kit around severe bleeding and airway problems, two leading causes of battlefield death, and added a second tourniquet.2
  • Use the WHO Essential Medicines List (2025) as a planning map, not a shopping list. It names 523 medicines for adults and 374 for children, and it is written for working health systems.34
  • Skills beat gear. More than 5 million people have taken Stop the Bleed training: direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets.5
  • A kit is a living inventory. Check expiration dates and replace anything used or out of date.1
25adhesive bandages in the Red Cross family-of-four kit1
2tourniquets in the US Army IFAK II soldier kit2
523adult medicines on the WHO 2025 Essential Medicines List3
5M+people trained in Stop the Bleed worldwide5

#🧰 Three tiers: who carries what

One kit cannot do every job. A box at home does not help on the road. A pocket kit cannot treat a whole family for a month.

So split your supplies into three tiers. Each tier copies an established model: the US Army's Improved First Aid Kit (IFAK) for personal kits, the American Red Cross family list for households, and the World Health Organization (WHO) essential medicines idea for the group store.614

The three tiers at a glance
TierWhere it livesBuilt fromMain job
1. PersonalOn your body or beltArmy IFAK ideaStop severe bleeding fast
2. HouseholdHome and carRed Cross family listCuts, burns, sprains, fever
3. GroupOne locked, shared storeWHO essential medicines idea + a clinicianRestock tiers 1 and 2; long-term medicines
💡 Tip

Color-code the tiers

Use a red pouch for bleeding gear, a clear box for the household kit and labeled tubs for the group store. A tired person can then grab the right thing in the dark.

#🩸 Tier 1: the personal bleeding kit

The personal kit solves one problem: bleeding that can kill before help arrives. The US Army says severe bleeding and airway problems are two of the leading causes of death on the battlefield, and its kit targets both.2

In 2013 the Army introduced a redesigned kit, the IFAK II.6 The redesign drew on soldier feedback and added a second tourniquet.2

The civilian version

You are not a soldier, but the logic carries over: small, light, always on you, and focused on bleeding. Carry only items you have been trained to use.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Put the tourniquet where both hands reach it

    An outside pocket or belt pouch, not the bottom of a bag. Learn it first in a class. See Stopping Severe Bleeding.

  2. Add a pressure bandage and gauze

    These are for wounds a tourniquet cannot reach. Stop the Bleed teaches wound packing alongside tourniquets.5

  3. Add gloves

    At least 2 pairs. The Red Cross kit specifies nonlatex gloves.1

  4. Add a few days of your own medicines

    Keep them in labeled containers with a written list of names, doses and allergies.

  5. Add a card and a marker

    Write what you did and the time. The Army kit carries a casualty card and marker for the same job.6

  6. Make every kit the same

    Same pouch, same layout, same place on every adult. Anyone can then find anything in the dark.

Do

  • Carry it on your body
  • Keep the tourniquet reachable with either hand
  • Train before you rely on the gear
  • Replace anything you use the same day

Don't

  • Bury it in a backpack
  • Carry gear you have never practiced with
  • Add "nice to have" items until it is too heavy to carry daily
  • Share one personal kit across the family
⚠️ Caution

A tourniquet is a skill, not a gadget

Stop the Bleed courses teach tourniquets together with direct pressure and wound packing.5 Take the course before you trust the gear, and practice only the way your instructor shows you.

#🏠 Tier 2: the household kit

Start with the American Red Cross list. It is written for a family of four. The Red Cross says to keep one kit at home and one in the car.1

Copy the list exactly first. Add your family's extras after. The Red Cross also says to include personal items such as medicines and emergency phone numbers, or other items your health care provider suggests.1

Red Cross first aid kit for a family of four1
ItemAmount
Absorbent compress dressings, 5 × 9 in (13 × 23 cm)2
Adhesive bandages, assorted sizes25
Adhesive cloth tape, 10 yd × 1 in (9 m × 2.5 cm)1 roll
Antibiotic ointment packets, about 1 g each5
Antiseptic wipe packets5
Aspirin packets, 81 mg each2
Emergency blanket1
Breathing barrier with one-way valve1
Instant cold compress1
Nonlatex gloves, size large2 pairs
Hydrocortisone ointment packets, about 1 g each2
Scissors1
Roller bandage, 3 in (7.5 cm) wide1
Roller bandage, 4 in (10 cm) wide1
Sterile gauze pads, 3 × 3 in (7.5 × 7.5 cm)5
Sterile gauze pads, 4 × 4 in (10 × 10 cm)5
Oral thermometer, non-mercury and nonglass1
Triangular bandages2
Tweezers1
First aid instruction booklet1

Only four items are medicines or antiseptics: antibiotic ointment, antiseptic wipes, hydrocortisone ointment and low-dose aspirin.1 Everything else is dressings, tools and protection.

The aspirin in the kit is fine for anyone in pain.

Never give aspirin to children.7 Do not give it to teenagers either unless a doctor says so. If you are allergic to aspirin, have a bleeding problem or take a blood thinner, do not take the kit aspirin unless a clinician tells you to. Read the warnings on the label first.

Add these for your household

  • Each person's prescription medicines and a written medicine list
  • Children's versions of any OTC medicines you use, in their own pouch
  • Menstrual supplies, including reusable ones
  • Extra gloves, tape and gauze
  • Elastic bandages and splint material
  • A printed copy of this book's medical chapters
👶 Babies & children

Children get their own pouch

Never give aspirin to children.7 WHO keeps a separate children's list, the EMLc, with 374 medicines in 2025.3

Keep children's medicines apart from adult ones, write each child's weight on the pouch, and dose only as the label says. See The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Pack menstrual products for every woman and girl, plus pain relief used only as the label directs. If anyone is pregnant or breastfeeding, read the warnings on every label first and ask a clinician whenever one is available.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

One medicine list per person

Write each person's medicines, doses, times, allergies and prescriber on one card. Tape it inside the kit lid. Anyone on a blood thinner should ask a clinician before taking the kit aspirin. For long-term illness, see Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs need a separate kit

Pack the dog's supplies in their own box marked DOG, so human and dog medicines never mix. Give a dog medicine only when a veterinarian has told you to. See Dog First Aid.

#🏘️ Tier 3: the group store

A group store is a small supply room, not a bigger first aid kit. It refills the personal and household kits, and it holds what one family cannot.

The model is how health systems plan. WHO says essential medicines are meant to be available within functioning health systems at all times, in adequate amounts.4 A group store tries to keep that promise on a small scale.

What goes in it

  • Bulk consumables: multiples of every Red Cross item, especially gloves, gauze and tape
  • Durable tools: tweezers, scissors, splints and spare thermometers (the Red Cross specifies non-mercury, nonglass)1
  • The medicine plan made with a doctor or pharmacist (next section)
  • Printed references and the supply log
  • Separate shelves for children's and dogs' supplies

Do the arithmetic. The Red Cross list covers 4 people.1 For a group of 12, three lists give 75 adhesive bandages, 6 compress dressings, 30 gauze pads and 6 pairs of gloves. That is only a starting point. The quantities section shows how to scale it from your own use.

💡 Tip

Give the store one keeper

Name one person to run the log and a second person to check it. Every item that leaves gets written down: what, how many, for whom, and the date.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Even today, with power and pharmacies, WHO reports that availability and affordability of essential medicines remain problems in many countries.4 Over decades, plan for supplies running out: keep reusable tools, learn the skills, and stay connected to any clinic that still works.

#💊 Essential medicines (WHO 2025) and what "OTC" means

WHO's Model List of Essential Medicines (EML) names the medicines a health system needs most. WHO defines essential medicines as those that satisfy the priority health-care needs of a population.4

WHO published the current edition on 5 September 2025: the 24th adult list and the 10th children's list (EMLc).3 Together they name 523 medicines for adults and 374 for children.38

The 2025 update by the numbers (WHO)3
MeasureNumber
New medicines added to the adult list20
New medicines added to the children's list15
Listed medicines given new uses7
Total adult medicines523
Total children's medicines374

The 2025 update added key cancer treatments.3 It also added diabetes and obesity medicines in the GLP-1 class (semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide) and the dual-action medicine tirzepatide.3

Core and complementary lists

The core list covers the minimum medicine needs of a basic health-care system. The complementary list covers priority diseases that need specialist diagnosis, monitoring or care.4

WHO chooses each medicine by public health relevance, evidence of efficacy and safety, and comparative cost-effectiveness.4 That is a good test for your own plan too: what problems are common in your group, and what is proven to help?

The WHO list is a home stockpile list. Buy everything on it.

It is written for health systems. Even the core list is the minimum for a basic health-care system, and complementary items need specialist diagnosis, monitoring or care.4 Use it as a map to discuss with a doctor or pharmacist.

What "OTC" means

Over-the-counter (OTC) medicines are sold without a prescription. Each country decides which medicines are OTC, so check your local rules with a pharmacist.

Give OTC doses only as written on the label. For what each common OTC medicine does, see Over-the-Counter Medicines.

Sort every medicine into one of three groups
GroupExamplesHow to get moreWho decides the dose
OTCThe kit ointments and aspirinPharmacy or storeYou, by the label
Prescriptions you take nowBlood pressure, diabetes, thyroidYour prescriber and pharmacyYour prescriber
Prescriptions you might needAntibiotics, strong pain reliefOnly through a clinicianA clinician
☠️ Danger

Never self-prescribe

Do not take prescription medicines that were not prescribed for you. Do not use veterinary, fish or aquarium antibiotics. This book never recommends either.

The facts on why are in Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts.

#📦 Quantities for long durations

Size your kit from your own use, not from a guess. We could not find an official kit list sized for decades without power. So use arithmetic on two numbers you control: how many people, and how much you actually use.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Count your people

    List adults, children, babies, elders and dogs separately. Each group needs different items.

  2. Set the baseline

    One Red Cross list per 4 people, rounded up.1 A family of 6 needs 2 lists.

  3. Log your use for 3 months

    Write down every bandage, glove, wipe and dose you use. Real numbers beat guesses.

  4. Multiply to a year

    3 months × 4 = 1 year. Example: 10 bandages in 3 months is 40 a year, or 1,200 over 30 years.

  5. Do the medicine math

    1 tablet a day is 365 a year and 10,950 over 30 years. Show that number to your prescriber and plan together.

  6. Split durable from consumable

    Buy durable tools once, plus a spare. Buy consumables in bulk and rotate them.

Durable versus consumable
Durable: buy once, plus a spareConsumable: buy in bulk and rotate
TweezersAdhesive bandages
ThermometerSterile gauze pads and compress dressings
Scissors and splintsGloves
Instruction bookletTape, wipes and ointments
📊 Key fact

The medicine math, in one line

The Red Cross kit holds 2 packets of 81 mg aspirin and 5 packets of antibiotic ointment.1 Compare that with your usage log before you assume it will last. Medicines also expire: see Medicines: Shelf Life & Expiration Facts.

  1. This week

    Check your home kit against the Red Cross list. Put a second kit in the car.1 First 72 h

  2. This month

    Build one personal bleeding kit per adult. Book a Stop the Bleed class. First 30 days

  3. Month 3

    Finish your usage log. Scale your household kit to one year.

  4. Month 6

    Set up the group store and the medicine plan with a clinician. Year 1

  5. Every check date

    Count, date, replace. Repeat for as long as you need the kit. Long haul

#🌡️ Storage conditions and rotation

A kit you cannot find, cannot open or that has expired is the same as no kit. The Red Cross says to check expiration dates and replace any used or out-of-date contents.1

Follow the storage line on each label. Read it on every medicine and sterile pack, and copy any temperature limit onto your inventory sheet.

If a medicine got too hot or too cold, do not guess. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, health care provider or the manufacturer.10

📊 Key fact

Insulin without a fridge

The FDA says insulin vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days.11 Pens and other products can differ, so check each leaflet, and replace insulin exposed to extreme conditions as soon as you can.11 See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

Review the whole kit at least once a year. Ready.gov says to replace expired items as needed and to re-think your needs every year as your family changes.12

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Use hard, sealed containers

    Use tubs with tight lids to keep out water, insects and rodents.

  2. Label the outside

    Write the tier, the contents and the earliest expiration date on the lid.

  3. Lock medicines away from children

    Store them high and locked. Keep the key where every adult knows to find it.

  4. Keep boxes off the floor and away from heat

    Not by the stove, not in the sun, not on a damp floor. Follow each label's storage line.

  5. First in, first out

    New stock goes to the back. Use the oldest first so nothing expires unseen.

  6. Keep the log with the box

    Every item in or out gets a line: what, how many and the date.

Do

  • Keep a kit at home and in the car1
  • Pick one fixed check date and stick to it
  • Keep sterile packs sealed and dry
  • Read the storage line on every label

Don't

  • Store medicines where children can reach them
  • Mix loose pills in unlabeled bags
  • Use a sterile pack that is wet or torn as if it were sterile
  • Leave the only kit in a car that might be gone
👶 Babies & children

Child safety

Children explore boxes and bags. Keep every medicine, including the kit aspirin, in a locked box. Aspirin is never for children.7

#🎓 Skills matter more than gear

Training turns a box of supplies into care. The Army rebuilt its kit from soldier feedback.2 Your family's kit should follow the same rule: carry what you know how to use.

The American College of Surgeons (ACS) Stop the Bleed program has trained more than 5 million people worldwide. It teaches three techniques: direct pressure, wound packing and tourniquets.5

Training options, in a sensible order
CourseWhat you learnWhen
Stop the BleedPressure, wound packing, tourniquets5Before you buy a tourniquet
CPR and first aidCPR, choking, everyday injuriesEvery adult and teen, first year
Wilderness first aidCare when help is hours or days awayAfter the basics
Pharmacist or doctor reviewYour family's medicine planBring your medicine lists

For CPR steps and the current guidelines, see CPR & Choking. The Red Cross includes a first aid instruction booklet in its kit list, so keep a printed guide in every kit.1

🎯 Practice now

Practice with your own kit

  • Empty the kit on a table. Name every item and say what it is for.
  • Repack it with your eyes closed. Then repack it in the dark.
  • Ask each adult to find the tourniquet in under 10 seconds.
  • Teach children where the kit lives and how to bring it to an adult.

Download while the internet works

  • WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines: the current adult and children's lists.9
  • Red Cross: Anatomy of a First Aid Kit: print it and tape it inside your kit lid.1
🛒 Get it before you need it

Buy these first

  • The full Red Cross family list, times your household size
  • One tourniquet per adult, after a Stop the Bleed class
  • Extra gloves, gauze and tape
  • Hard, sealable tubs and a notebook for the log
