🩻

Assessing a Sick or Injured Person

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 19 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Protect yourself first. Check the scene for safety, form a first impression, ask permission and put on gloves if you have them.1
  • Not responding and not breathing, or only gasping? Start CPR now. Spend no more than 10 seconds on that check.319
  • In an injury, heavy bleeding comes first. Military medicine works in the order MARCH: Massive bleeding, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia.5
  • Count, don't guess. A resting adult: pulse 60–100, breathing 12–20 a minute, nail refill under 2 seconds.91012
  • Children run faster. A newborn's resting pulse is 70–190.10 WHO counts 50 or more breaths a minute as fast breathing in babies aged 2–11 months.1617
  • Write the time next to every number. Then check again and compare.
10 seclongest you should take to check if a collapsed person responds3
60–100normal resting pulse for adults and children aged 10 and up10
12–20breaths per minute for a resting adult9
<2 secnormal time for a pressed nail bed to turn pink again12

#🧭 The whole check at a glance

Work in the same order every time, so you never have to stop and decide what comes next.

The chart shows the order this chapter teaches. Each step has its own section below.

#🦺 Scene safety: protect yourself first

Stop before you rush in. The American Red Cross starts every emergency the same way: check the scene for safety, form an initial impression, get consent and put on personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves.1

Keeping yourself safe is what lets you help others.2 If you get hurt too, your family has two patients and one less helper.

Look for anything that could hurt you

  • Fire, smoke or fumes from a stove, heater or generator
  • Walls, roofs, trees or vehicles that could fall or roll
  • Fast or deep water
  • Broken glass, sharp metal and needles
  • Blood, vomit and other body fluids: glove up first
  • A frightened or protective animal
  • An angry or violent person: back away and get help
Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Stop and look

    Scan the whole area before you step in. Is anything still dangerous?1

  2. Form a first impression

    As you walk up, notice: Is the person moving? Making sounds? Bleeding heavily? Is the skin an odd color?1

    If blood is pooling or spurting, control it first.5

  3. Ask permission

    Say your name and "I know first aid. Can I help?" Get consent before you touch them.1 For a child, ask a parent or caregiver if one is there.

  4. Protect your hands and eyes

    Put on gloves and eye protection if you have them.1

  5. Get help and gear moving

    Shout for help and send someone for the medical kit. The Red Cross says to get equipment and give care based on what you find, within your training.1

☠️ Danger

Collapsed and not breathing? Do not finish this chapter first

Check for a response and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If the person is unresponsive and not breathing, or only gasping, that is cardiac arrest: start CPR and use an AED (automated external defibrillator) right away.319 See CPR & Choking.

Timer: Responsiveness and breathing check: 10 seconds at most. Interactive in the digital edition.

Do

  • Pause and scan before you go in
  • Ask "Can I help?" first
  • Wear gloves for any body fluid
  • Send someone for the kit

Don't

  • Run into smoke, water or a collapse zone
  • Touch blood with bare hands
  • Spend more than 10 seconds deciding about CPR3
  • Leave the person alone to fetch gear if someone else can go

#🔺 The primary survey: find the fastest killer

The primary survey is a quick first check for the most urgent problems. Fix each problem as you find it, then move to the next one.

ABC: the classic order

The Canadian Red Cross builds its first check around the ABCs: Airway, Breathing and Circulation.4

  • Airway: Is it open? Can they talk or cry?
  • Breathing: Is the chest rising and falling?
  • Circulation: Is there a pulse? Any major bleeding? What color is the skin?

MARCH: when there is heavy bleeding

Tactical Combat Casualty Care (TCCC) is the accepted standard for prehospital care on the battlefield.5 It divides care into three phases: Care Under Fire, Tactical Field Care and Tactical Evacuation Care.5

MARCH sets the order of care. While still in danger, the only treatment is control of life-threatening bleeding. Once you are safe, you work through all five letters.6

The five MARCH parts were shaped by battlefield limits such as delayed evacuation and limited supplies.7 Those are the same limits a household faces when no ambulance is coming.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. M: Massive bleeding

    Look and sweep your gloved hands over the body for pooling or spurting blood. Stop it now: see Stopping Severe Bleeding.

  2. A: Airway

    Can they talk or cry clearly? If not, look in the mouth for anything blocking it. See CPR & Choking.

  3. R: Respiration

    Watch both sides of the chest rise. Count breaths for a full minute. Look for wounds on the chest and back.

  4. C: Circulation

    Feel the pulse, press a nail bed and look at the skin. A slow nail refill can point to shock.13

  5. H: Hypothermia and head injury

    Get them off cold ground and covered. Note how alert they are. See Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke and Head & Spine Injuries.

First aid always starts with the airway.

It depends on the emergency. For a person who is unresponsive and not breathing, the Red Cross says to start CPR and use an AED immediately.3 The American Heart Association's 2025 guideline starts CPR with chest compressions.19 For an injured person, TCCC's MARCH puts massive bleeding before the airway.56

#💓 Vital signs with no machines

Vital signs are numbers you can count with a watch, your fingers and your eyes. Normal values change with age, sex, weight, fitness and overall health.8

So compare every reading with two things: that person's own normal, and the last reading you took.

Pulse

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Find the pulse

    Use your index and middle fingers. Press gently with flat fingers on the inner wrist below the base of the thumb, or at the side of the neck beside the windpipe.10

    Check one side of the neck only. Pressing both sides at once can slow blood flow to the head and cause fainting.10

  2. Count for a full minute

    Use a watch or clock that shows seconds. Count every beat for 60 seconds.

  3. Judge rhythm and strength

    Write "regular" or "irregular", and "strong" or "weak".

  4. Compare

    Check the number against the age table below and against the person's own normal.10

Breathing

Watch or feel the chest. One rise and one fall is one breath. Count for a full 60 seconds.

Also note how hard they work to breathe: noisy breaths, flaring nostrils, or skin pulling in between the ribs. WHO uses fast breathing and chest indrawing as signs of pneumonia in young children.16

Timer: Count breaths or pulse: 60 seconds. Interactive in the digital edition.

⚠️ Caution

Short counts multiply your mistakes

Counting for 15 seconds and multiplying by 4 is quick, but miss just one breath and your answer is off by 4 per minute. When the number matters, count the full minute.

💡 Tip

Count breaths without moving

Keep your fingers on the wrist after you finish the pulse, and watch the chest. You can count breathing straight away without a break.

Capillary refill (the nail-bed test)

Press a fingernail until it turns white, then let go. Normal pink color should return in under 2 seconds.12

A time over 2 seconds can be a sign of dehydration, hypothermia, narrowed arteries in the limbs (peripheral vascular disease) or shock.1213

💡 Tip

Cold hands give slow results

Hypothermia is one of the listed causes of slow refill.13 If the hand is cold, warm it and test again, and test more than one finger. Remove colored nail polish first, or you cannot see the color change.12

Skin, alertness and the rest

Skin: write three words. Color (pink, pale, gray, blue, flushed), temperature (warm, cool, hot) and moisture (dry or sweaty).

Alertness: write one letter of AVPU. A = alert and talking. V = responds only to your voice. P = responds only to a painful touch. U = no response.

Temperature: if you have a thermometer, write the number and where you took it (mouth, armpit, ear or rectum).

Blood pressure: only with a cuff. The average healthy adult reads between 90/60 and 120/80 mmHg (millimeters of mercury).8

🛒 Get it before you need it

Assessment tools that need no power

  • A wind-up or mechanical watch with a second hand
  • Notebooks and pencils (several of each)
  • Disposable gloves and eye protection
  • A manual blood pressure cuff and stethoscope, if you will train to use them
  • A thermometer and a small flashlight

Full kit lists are in Building a Long-Term Medical Kit.

#👶 Normal ranges by age

Babies and children have faster pulses than adults. Use the row that matches the person in front of you.1011

Normal resting pulse by age (MedlinePlus)
AgeBeats per minute
Newborn, 0–1 month70–190
Infant, 1–11 months80–160
1–2 years80–130
3–4 years80–120
5–6 years75–115
7–9 years70–110
10 years to adult, including seniors60–100
Well-trained athletes40–60
Breathing rates at rest, and WHO "fast breathing" levels for children aged 2 months to 5 years
AgeTypical at restWHO: fast breathing
2–11 months30–45 (age 3–6 months)50 or more
12 months to 5 yearsn/a40 or more
6–11 years18–25n/a
12–18 years12–18n/a
Adults12–20n/a

Table sources: WHO fast-breathing levels;1617 ages 3–6 months and 12–18 years;15 ages 6–11 years;14 adults.9 "n/a" means our sources did not list a figure for that age.

📊 Key fact

Children's "normal" ranges are softer than they look

A 2011 systematic review in The Lancet found that the reference ranges in common use for children were not based on evidence. It pooled 69 studies, with heart rate data from 143,346 children and breathing data from 3,881 children, to build new age charts.18

A pulse under 60 always means something is wrong.

Well-trained athletes can have a normal resting pulse of 40–60.10 That is why you record each person's own baseline while they are well.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

  • Count breaths when the child is calm, for a full minute, and write down if they were crying.
  • Sleeping children run slower. One school-age chart lists an awake pulse of 75–118 and a sleeping pulse of 58–90 for ages 6–11.14 Write down whether the child was awake or asleep.
  • Know the WHO fast-breathing levels: 50 or more breaths a minute at 2–11 months, 40 or more from 12 months to 5 years.1617
  • Babies under 2 months have their own danger signs. For the full lists, see Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs.

#🗣️ SAMPLE: the questions to ask

Once the urgent problems are handled, ask questions. If the person cannot answer, ask family or bystanders, and look for medical ID tags, notes or medicine bottles.

Use the six letters of SAMPLE as a checklist. Write each answer down as you go.

The SAMPLE history: what to ask and write
LetterAskWrite down
S: Signs and symptoms"What is wrong? Where does it hurt?"What you see, and what they feel, in their words
A: Allergies"Are you allergic to any medicine, food or insect stings?"The allergy and what happened last time
M: Medicines"What do you take? When was the last dose?"Names, doses and times, including herbal products
P: Past history"Any heart, lung, diabetes, seizure or other health problems? Could you be pregnant?"Conditions, past operations, pregnancy
L: Last in and out"When did you last eat, drink and pee?"Times and amounts; for babies, last feed and last wet diaper
E: Events"What happened just before this started?"A short story of the event, with times
💡 Tip

Ask about pain the same way every time

Ask them to rate their pain from 0 (none) to 10 (the worst they can imagine). Write the number and the time. Repeat the same question later so you can compare like with like.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Ask about a possible pregnancy and the date of the last period in private, without family listening. Explain each step before you touch, offer a woman helper if one is there, and keep the person covered as much as you can.

#🔍 The head-to-toe check

Look, ask, then gently feel, working from the head down. Compare the left side with the right side as you go.

Do this after the primary survey, and only once any heavy bleeding is controlled.5 Tell the person what you are about to do before every step.

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. Head and face

    Look for cuts, bumps, bruises, and blood or clear fluid from the ears or nose. Look at both pupils: are they the same size?

  2. Neck

    Look and feel for wounds and swelling. If they fell, were hit or have neck pain, keep the head still and read Head & Spine Injuries.

  3. Chest

    Watch both sides rise together. Press gently on the ribs and ask about pain.

  4. Belly

    Press gently in each of the four quarters. Note pain, hardness or swelling.

  5. Hips

    Look for wounds and ask about pain. If they fell or were crushed, do not rock or squeeze the hips: keep them still.

  6. Legs and arms

    Check each limb for wounds, swelling or odd shape. Ask them to wiggle fingers and toes, and test feeling and nail refill on each side.

  7. Back

    Slide a gloved hand under the back where you can, then look at your glove for blood.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older and disabled people

Normal vital signs change with age and overall health.8 Ask a caregiver or family member what is normal for this person: their usual alertness, speech, mobility and pulse. Make sure hearing aids and glasses are in place before you judge confusion.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs

A dog guarding a hurt owner can stop you helping. Ask someone the dog knows to hold it away while you work. Dogs have their own normal ranges and checks: see Dog First Aid.

#🚩 Findings that mean act now

Some findings mean you stop assessing and start treating. These are the ones this chapter covers.

Act on these straight away
You findIt can meanDo
No response, and no breathing or only gaspingCardiac arrest3Start CPR and use an AED now
Pooling or spurting bloodMassive bleeding, the first letter of MARCH5Stop the bleeding before anything else
Nail refill over 2 secondsDehydration, hypothermia or shock1213Look again for bleeding, keep them warm, recheck often
Young child breathing at or above the WHO level, or chest pulling inSigns WHO uses for pneumonia16Follow the child danger-sign chapter
Pulse or breathing outside the range for the ageA change from normal10Recount for a full minute, look for the cause, recheck soon
🎯 Practice now

Learn the official warning-sign lists now

This chapter teaches you how to measure. Stroke, heart attack and sepsis each have their own official warning-sign lists. Print them from your national health service while the internet works, and keep them with your notes. For sepsis, also read Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts. For babies and children, read Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print and save while the internet works

  • American Red Cross: Adult Ready Reference Cards (PDF)
  • MedlinePlus: Vital Signs
  • Canadian Red Cross: Check, Call, Care poster (PDF)

The Canadian Red Cross notes that its poster does not replace formal first aid and CPR training.4

#📒 Written patient notes

Write everything down, with the time. A written record shows whether the person is getting better or worse, and lets another caregiver take over without starting again.

Keep one page per patient. Start a new line every time you recheck.

What goes on a patient note
SectionWhat to write
WhoName, age, rough weight, date
What happenedThe SAMPLE answers, in short lines
Vital signsTime, pulse, breaths, nail refill, skin, AVPU, temperature if known
FindingsWhat the head-to-toe check found, side by side
Care givenEvery treatment and medicine, with dose and time
ChangesBetter, worse or the same, compared with the last check
Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Write the time first

    Every line starts with the clock time. Numbers without times cannot show a trend.

  2. Write what you counted, not what you guessed

    "Pulse 112, regular, weak" beats "fast pulse".

  3. Use their words for symptoms

    Write "crushing pain in chest" in quotes, exactly as they said it.

  4. Recheck and add a new line

    Repeat the vital signs and write them under the last set, so the change is easy to see.

  5. Keep the note with the patient

    If they move or a new caregiver takes over, the note goes with them.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Battlefield care was shaped around delayed evacuation and limited supplies.7 In a long grid-down life, your notebook becomes the only medical record. Keep a binder with one section per family member: allergies, medicines, past illnesses, baseline vital signs and every illness or injury.

🎯 Practice now

Record everyone's baseline now

Vital signs vary with age, sex, weight, fitness and health.8 Once a year, sit each family member down at rest. Count pulse and breathing for a full minute, test nail refill, and write the numbers with the date. A sick person's numbers mean far more when you know their healthy ones.

🎯 Practice now

Get hands-on training

The Red Cross teaches that you should give care based on what you find, within your level of training.1 Take a first aid and CPR course while classes still exist, and practice this whole chapter on each other.

What do you check before you touch anyone?

That the scene is safe for you. Then get consent and put on gloves.

How long do you spend checking a collapsed person for a response?

No more than 10 seconds. Not breathing or only gasping: start CPR.

What does MARCH stand for?

Massive bleeding, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia (and head injury).

Normal adult resting pulse and breathing?

Pulse 60–100. Breathing 12–20 a minute.

Normal nail refill time?

Under 2 seconds.

WHO fast breathing for a baby aged 2–11 months?

50 or more breaths a minute.

What does SAMPLE stand for?

Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medicines, Past history, Last in and out, Events.

What goes next to every number in your notes?

The time.

🩺 Part 4 · Medicine & First AidChapter 52
❤️

CPR & Choking: Adults, Children, Infants

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 18 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Not responding and not breathing normally? Start CPR now. Gasping is not normal breathing. Shout for help, then push.1
  • Push hard and fast in the center of the chest. Aim for 100–120 a minute, at least 5 cm (2 in) deep in adults but not more than 6 cm (2.4 in).1
  • Babies, children, drowning, overdose: give breaths too. Use 30 compressions, then 2 breaths.51
  • Choking adult or child who cannot cough or speak: alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out. If they go limp, start CPR.3
  • Choking baby under 1: 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand. Never abdominal thrusts.3
100–120chest compressions per minute, every age12
5–6 cmadult push depth (2–2.4 in)1
30:2compressions to breaths for one rescuer1
5 + 5back blows, then thrusts, for choking (2025)3

#🆕 What changed in the 2025 guidelines

This chapter follows the newest rules. The American Heart Association (AHA) published its 2025 Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care (ECC) on October 22, 2025, in the journal Circulation.318

CPR means cardiopulmonary resuscitation. It is chest compressions, with or without rescue breaths, for a person whose heart has stopped pumping.1

The guideline for babies and children was written by the AHA together with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).2 International experts in the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) reviewed the same science in 2025.7

What is new in 2025 (AHA and AAP)
Topic2025 rule
Choking, awake adult or childAlternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts3
Choking, infant5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand32
Infant CPR hands2 thumbs with your hands around the chest, or the heel of one hand. The 2-finger method was removed.9
Chain of survivalOne chain for all ages, in and out of hospital3
Opioid overdoseGuidance now includes naloxone use by the public3
⏳ The 30-year view

Keep a paper copy

Guidelines change. The 2025 version replaced earlier advice on choking and on infant CPR.3 Print this chapter now, while you can still check it against the official pages.

#🔎 Spot cardiac arrest and get help

Check fast, then act. A person in cardiac arrest does not respond and is not breathing normally, or is only gasping.1

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Make sure the scene is safe

    Look for danger to you first: traffic, fire, live wires, deep water, smoke. The AHA choking algorithm starts with this check too.10

  2. Tap and shout

    Tap their shoulders hard and shout, "Are you OK?" No answer means unresponsive.1

  3. Look at the chest and face

    No breathing, or only gasping, means start CPR.1

  4. Shout for help

    Send one person for help and for an automated external defibrillator (AED), if one exists.5

  5. Start pushing right away

    Do not wait for help to arrive. Begin chest compressions now.5

☠️ Danger

Gasping is not breathing

Slow, noisy gasps can happen after the heart stops. Treat "only gasping" the same as "not breathing" and start CPR.1

⚠️ Caution

Do not hunt for a pulse

The public is not asked to check a pulse. Unresponsive and not breathing normally is enough to start.1 Feeling for a pulse wastes seconds.

In a long outage, "call for help" may mean a two-way radio, a whistle or a runner. Plan this now in Radios: Ham, GMRS, CB & Listening. If the person is breathing, use Assessing a Sick or Injured Person instead.

#👐 Adult CPR, step by step

Your hands do the pumping. Good CPR is deep, fast, steady and has very few pauses.14

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Lay them on their back on something firm

    A floor or flat ground works. Compressions work best on a firm surface.1

  2. Place your hands

    Put the heel of one hand on the lower half of the breastbone, in the center of the chest. Put your other hand on top.1

  3. Lock your arms

    Kneel close. Keep your elbows straight and your shoulders right over your hands, so your body weight does the work.

  4. Push deep and fast

    Push at least 5 cm (2 in) but not more than 6 cm (2.4 in), 100 to 120 times a minute.1

  5. Let the chest rise all the way

    Do not lean on the chest between pushes. Full recoil lets the heart refill.1

  6. Add breaths if you can

    If you are trained and willing, give 2 breaths after every 30 pushes.1 If not, keep pushing without stopping.5

CPR metronome: CPR compressions: 100–120 per minute (set to 110). Interactive in the digital edition.

💡 Tip

Push to a song

The AHA says people remember the right pace better when they train to the beat of "Stayin' Alive" or another familiar song at 100–120 beats a minute.6

Do

  • Push on the lower half of the breastbone
  • Use a firm floor or the ground
  • Let the chest come all the way back up
  • Swap pushers about every 2 minutes
  • Keep pauses for breaths very short

Don't

  • Lean on the chest between pushes
  • Push shallow "polite" compressions
  • Push deeper than 6 cm (2.4 in) on an adult
  • Stop to check for a pulse
  • Do CPR on a soft mattress

Every item above comes from the 2025 adult guideline.1 Keep any pause under 10 seconds.1

Timer: 2 minutes: swap who is pushing. Interactive in the digital edition.

Swap pushers about every 2 minutes. That keeps compressions strong as people tire.1 Swap fast, during the breaths if you can.

📊 Key fact

UK guidance matches

The Resuscitation Council UK 2025 adult guideline also sets a depth of at least 5 cm and no more than 6 cm.8

🌸 Women & girls

CPR on women and girls

The hand position is the same for everyone: the center of the chest.5 Do not let worry about touching a woman's chest delay CPR. Push on the breastbone, between the breasts.

#🫁 Hands-Only CPR or CPR with breaths?

Hands-Only CPR has two steps. Call for help (or send someone), then push hard and fast in the center of the chest.5

The AHA recommends it for teens and adults who suddenly collapse outside a hospital, such as at home, at work or in a park.5

Some people need breaths as well. The AHA recommends compressions plus breaths for all infants (up to age 1), children (up to puberty), drowning victims, drug overdose victims and people who collapse from breathing problems.5

If you are trained and willing, give 30:2 to adults too.1 ILCOR still suggests the 30:2 ratio in its 2025 review.7

How to give rescue breaths

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Open the airway

    Tilt the head back with one hand on the forehead. Lift the chin with two fingers of the other hand.1

  2. Seal your mouth over theirs

    For an adult or child, pinch the nose shut. For a baby, cover the mouth and nose with your mouth.2

  3. Breathe for 1 second

    Blow just enough to see the chest rise.1

  4. Give a second breath, then push again

    Go straight back to compressions. The two breaths should take less than 10 seconds.1

☠️ Danger

Opioid overdose

For a suspected opioid overdose, the 2025 guidelines include naloxone use by the public.3 Give naloxone if you have it, and give CPR with breaths.5 See Poisoning & Toxic Exposures.

You need a certificate before you are allowed to do CPR.

Hands-Only CPR is two steps: call for help, then push hard and fast in the center of the chest.5 An AHA consumer survey found many people still wrongly believe CPR requires special training.13

CPR on TV shows you how it is done.

The AHA reports that TV depictions of Hands-Only CPR are often misleading.12 Learn from the official guideline numbers and hands-on practice instead.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • A CPR face shield or pocket mask for every first aid kit
  • A CPR training manikin, adult and infant if you can
  • Naloxone, if anyone in your group uses opioids, through a doctor or pharmacy where it is legal
  • A printed copy of this chapter in each kit

#👶 Children and babies: what is different

Babies and children need breaths with compressions. The AHA recommends CPR with breaths for all infants and for children up to puberty.5

CPR by age (AHA 2025)
WhatAdultChildInfant
AgeAfter puberty1 year to pubertyUnder 1 year
Rate100–120/min100–120/min100–120/min
Depth5–6 cm (2–2.4 in)About 5 cm (2 in)About 4 cm (1.5 in)
Hands2 hands1 or 2 hands2 thumbs around chest, or heel of 1 hand
1 rescuer30:230:230:2
2 rescuers30:215:215:2

Adult figures come from the adult guideline.1 Child and infant figures come from the pediatric guideline, which sets the depth at at least one third of the chest's front-to-back depth.2

Alone with no phone? If you did not see the child collapse, give about 2 minutes of CPR before you leave to get help.2

Infant CPR (under 1 year)

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Lay the baby on a firm, flat surface

    A table or the floor works. Compressions need a firm surface.2

  2. Wrap your hands around the chest

    Put both thumbs side by side on the center of the chest, just below the nipple line. Wrap your fingers around the back.2

  3. Or use the heel of one hand

    If your hands cannot reach around the chest, push with the heel of one hand.2

  4. Push about 4 cm (1.5 in)

    That is at least one third of the chest depth, at 100–120 a minute. Let the chest rise fully.2

  5. Give gentle breaths

    Cover the mouth and nose. Puff just enough to make the chest rise. Use 30:2 alone, 15:2 with two rescuers.2

Push on a baby's chest with two fingers.

The 2025 guidelines removed the two-finger method because it often failed to reach the right depth.29 Use two thumbs with your hands around the chest. If you cannot reach around, use the heel of one hand.2

👶 Babies & children

Newborns at birth are different

A baby who needs help in the first minutes after birth follows a separate neonatal guideline. There, the two-thumb method with hands wrapped around the chest is preferred.11 See Newborn Care: The First 28 Days.

🎯 Practice now

Practice on a doll, not a baby

Never practice compressions or back blows on a real child. The AHA's Infant CPR Anytime kit has a practice infant manikin and was updated for the 2025 guidelines.15

#🆘 Choking: adults and children over 1

Severe choking is silent. The person cannot speak, cough or breathe. They may clutch their throat with their hands.1

Mild choking is noisy. If they can cough hard or speak, let them keep coughing and stay with them. Act if the cough becomes weak or stops.8

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Ask "Are you choking?"

    If they nod and cannot speak, act now. Tell them you are going to help.

  2. Shout for help

    Send someone for help. Do not leave the person.10

  3. Give 5 back blows

    Stand behind and to the side. Support their chest with one hand and lean them forward. Strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand.8

  4. Give 5 abdominal thrusts

    Stand behind them and wrap your arms around the waist. Put a fist just above the belly button, well below the breastbone. Grab it with your other hand and pull sharply in and up.1

  5. Repeat 5 and 5

    Keep alternating until the object comes out or the person stops responding.3

  6. If they go limp, start CPR

    Lower them to the ground and begin compressions. Each time you open the airway, look in the mouth. Remove an object only if you can see it.117

Back blows are outdated. Only use abdominal thrusts (the "Heimlich").

Since 2025 the AHA says to alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts for awake adults and children.3 The UK guideline also starts with back blows.8

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnant and choking

Do not press on a pregnant belly. Give chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts: hands on the center of the breastbone, pulling straight back.110

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Larger or seated people

If you cannot get your arms around someone's waist, use chest thrusts instead.1 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

⚠️ Caution

No blind finger sweeps

Do not poke your fingers into the throat to search for the object. You can push it deeper. Remove it only if you can see it.12

#🍼 Choking: babies under 1 year

Babies get back blows and chest thrusts only. Abdominal thrusts are not recommended for infants.3

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Lay the baby face down on your forearm

    Hold the jaw with your hand to support the head. Keep the head lower than the chest. Rest your arm on your thigh.2

  2. Give 5 back blows

    Strike firmly between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.3

  3. Turn the baby face up

    Support the back of the head and sandwich the baby between your arms. Keep the head lower than the chest.2

  4. Give 5 chest thrusts

    Use the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, just below the nipple line.32

  5. Repeat 5 and 5

    Keep going until the object comes out or the baby stops responding.3

  6. If the baby goes limp, start infant CPR

    Use the infant CPR steps above. Look in the mouth before each set of breaths and remove only what you can see.2

☠️ Danger

Never give abdominal thrusts to a baby

For any baby under 1 year, use back blows and chest thrusts only.3 The chest thrusts now use the heel of one hand, not two fingers.2

👶 Babies & children

Prevent it first

Rescue is the backup plan. The prevention side (food sizes, small objects, supervision at meals) is in Keeping Kids Safe: Drowning, Fire, Poison, Strangers.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs are not small people

All the numbers in this chapter come from human guidelines.12 Dog CPR and dog choking use different positions and methods. A frightened, choking dog may also bite. Learn the dog methods in Dog First Aid, and keep children back.

#⏱️ How long to keep going, and when to stop

Keep pushing until help takes over. The AHA tells the public to continue chest compressions until help arrives.5

If an AED arrives, turn it on and follow the voice prompts.5 Keep pushing while someone else sets it up.

If the person wakes, moves with purpose or starts breathing normally, stop compressions. Stay with them and watch their breathing closely.1 A breathing person who is not awake can be rolled onto their side in the recovery position.8

⚠️ Caution

You may stop CPR when

  • The person shows clear signs of life, such as normal breathing or purposeful movement1
  • A trained helper takes over5
  • An AED is ready: follow its voice prompts5
  • The scene becomes unsafe for you10
  • You are too exhausted to continue and no one can take over8

The public guidance gives no time limit. It says to keep going until help arrives.5 It does not set a rule for a place where no help can come. Decide in advance, as a household, who will make that call.

Use teams. Swap pushers about every 2 minutes so compressions stay strong for as long as you continue.1

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

CPR is one link in a chain of survival that the AHA now uses for every age and setting.3 If no ambulance or hospital can be reached, the links after CPR are not available. Back blows, thrusts and CPR need nothing but trained hands, so train every capable person.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Talk about wishes now

Some older or very ill people have clear wishes about resuscitation. Ask while they can tell you, and write it down. When CPR does not work, see Death, Dying & Handling the Dead Safely.

#🎯 Practice and teach your household

Train your older kids. The 2025 AHA guidelines say children 12 years old or older can learn CPR.3

Choking can turn into cardiac arrest. The AHA says knowing how to help someone who is choking, and when to start CPR, can prevent a heart crisis.17

🎯 Practice now

Practice while help still exists

  • Use an AHA Hands-Only CPR kiosk if one is near you.14
  • Use the AHA Family & Friends CPR course materials, updated for 2025.16
  • Practice infant CPR and choking on a manikin with Infant CPR Anytime.15
  • Push to the metronome above for 2 full minutes. Feel how tiring it is.
▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Watch and download while the internet works

  • AHA: Learn Hands-Only CPR (video and pace guide)
  • AHA: Hands-Only CPR kiosk locations
  • AHA: 2025 adult choking algorithm (PDF)
  • AHA: Highlights of the 2025 Guidelines (PDF)
☠️ Danger

Never practice on a real person

Do not push on the chest, or give real back blows or thrusts, to anyone who is breathing and well. Use a manikin, a doll or a firm cushion.

💡 Tip

Run a two-minute family drill

One person lies on the floor as the patient. Others practice: check, shout, send a runner. Then push on a manikin or firm cushion beside them, and swap at 2 minutes. For choking, only mime the hand positions on a standing adult.

#✅ Do this now

0 / 10 done

#🧠 Remember this

How fast do you push?

100–120 times a minute, for every age.

How deep for an adult?

At least 5 cm (2 in), but not more than 6 cm (2.4 in).

Who needs breaths with compressions?

Babies, children, drowning, overdose and breathing problems. 30:2.

Choking adult who cannot cough or speak?

Alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts.

Choking baby under 1?

5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts with the heel of one hand. Never abdominal thrusts.

How do you push on a baby's chest since 2025?

Two thumbs with your hands around the chest, or the heel of one hand. Not two fingers.

Pregnant and choking?

Chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.

The choking person goes limp?

Lower them down and start CPR. Look in the mouth before breaths. No blind finger sweeps.

🧓

Caring for Elderly & Disabled People

🟠 HighFirst 72 hFirst 30 days📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Older people face the highest risk when the grid fails. After Hurricane Maria, poor and elderly people had the highest risk of dying, and older men had a 35% higher death risk than expected.1
  • Interrupted care kills slowly. A survey after Maria linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted medical care.2
  • List every powered medical device now. Over 3 million US Medicare patients use electricity-dependent equipment. Ask each person's provider for a power outage plan.34
  • Name a main helper and a backup for every person who cannot move fast, and practice twice a year, by day and by night.5
  • Pack the small aids people forget: hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, a cane and a written medicine list.6
35%higher death risk for older men after Hurricane Maria1
1 in 3Maria excess deaths linked to interrupted medical care2
3M+US Medicare patients on electricity-dependent equipment3
26%of adults with disabilities had nowhere to go (vs 15%)9

#📉 Who dies first when the power fails

The disaster record points one way. Older and chronically ill people carry the most risk when power, water and medical care stop.18

This chapter covers what that means for the people in your care. It gives the documented facts first, then the actions.

Hurricane Maria, Puerto Rico, 2017

Surveyed households went an average of 84 days without power, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell phone service.2 In remote areas, 83% of homes had no electricity for the whole period studied, from landfall to December 31, 2017.2

The first official death toll was 64.2 A George Washington University study, commissioned by the governor, estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.1

Many of those people were not killed by wind or water. The household survey linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted medical care.2 Poor and elderly people faced the highest risk.1

The official death toll shows who a disaster killed.

After Maria the first official count was 64.2 The George Washington University study estimated 2,975 excess deaths, with poor and elderly people at highest risk.1 Deaths from missed care kept coming for months: the study counted through February 2018.

Texas winter storm, February 2021

Texas health officials counted 246 storm-related deaths. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia (dangerously low body temperature).7

The final count rose from 210 to 246.7 Cold exposure killed more people than every other cause combined.

The Hurricane Rita evacuation, 2005

The evacuation killed more people than the storm did. Over 100 of the at least 119 deaths attributed to Rita were linked to the evacuation itself.8

At least 10% of evacuation deaths were linked to overheating in vehicles. Medical examiners suspected overheating or a worsened chronic illness in about another 50%.8

A bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire in the evacuation traffic, and about two dozen people died.8 More on this in Stay or Go?

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view: everyone becomes the elder

Over 30 years, a 45-year-old parent becomes 75 and a 60-year-old becomes 90. Plan as if every adult in your group will need this chapter one day.

Write each person's needs down now, while they can tell you, and update the list at every family drill. See Building Your Group.

#🔌 Oxygen, CPAP and other powered equipment

Many people stay alive or mobile on machines that plug into the wall. In the US, over 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment.3

Over 4.6 million rely on that equipment or on services such as dialysis, oxygen or home health care.3 Oxygen concentrators, powered wheelchairs and home dialysis all depend on electricity.3

Other common examples are continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machines for sleep apnea, electric hospital beds, and feeding or suction pumps. Each one stops when its battery is empty.

Make the plan before the outage. Ready.gov says to talk to your medical provider about a power outage plan for medical devices that run on electricity.4

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. List every device and every user

    Include your family and your street. Write the person's name, the device, and what the provider says happens if it stops.

  2. Find the real battery time

    Read the manual and write the hours on a label on the device. Then test a full charge while the device runs, and write that time too.

  3. Ask the provider for an outage plan

    Cover each device and each refrigerated medicine.4 Ask what to do if the device cannot run at all.

  4. Choose one safe power source

    A generator runs outdoors only, more than 6 m (20 ft) from windows, doors and vents.10

  5. Decide where to go

    If the home gets too hot or too cold, and it is safe to travel, go to a place with heat or cooling.4 Choose it now, with a route.

☠️ Danger

Generators kill families who run them indoors

Never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if the doors and windows are open.11 In the April 2025 Spain blackout, police in Galicia investigated carbon monoxide from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.12

Put a battery-powered carbon monoxide (CO) alarm near every sleeping area, and replace it every 5 years.10 See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

⚠️ Caution

Oxygen and open flames

Light the house with flashlights, not candles. Ready.gov lists candles as a fire risk during outages.4

Keep every flame, stove and smoker away from oxygen equipment. Ask the oxygen supplier now for its written fire-safety rules and keep them with the equipment.

💡 Tip

Label every oxygen cylinder

Ask the supplier how long each cylinder lasts at the person's prescribed flow rate. Write that time and the fill date on a tag tied to the cylinder, so any helper can read it in the dark.

⏳ The 30-year view

Powered devices over 30 years

Every machine that needs electricity depends on your power system for as long as the grid is down. Ask the provider now what non-powered options exist for each device.

For power you can make yourself, see Small Solar & Batteries and Low-Tech Power for the Long Haul.

#💊 Medicines: the clock starts when the power stops

Start with a written list. The Red Cross lists a medication list and medical information among the documents to copy for your kit.6 Write each medicine's name, dose, times and what it is for.

Keep at least 7 days on hand. The current Red Cross survival kit list says a 7-day supply of medications and medical items.6 An older Red Cross checklist says a 1-month supply.15

Ask the doctor or pharmacist how to build a larger emergency supply legally. Ready.gov also lists non-prescription medicines: pain relievers, anti-diarrhea medicine, antacids and laxatives.16

Medicines that need a fridge

The one-day rule: if the power is out for more than a day, throw away medicine that should be refrigerated, unless the label says otherwise.4

If a life depends on that medicine, talk to a doctor or pharmacist and use it only until a new supply is available.4

Insulin has its own rule. Vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days. Pens and other products differ, so read the label.13

Replace insulin that has been exposed to extreme heat or cold.13 For any other medicine kept at the wrong temperature, check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, provider or the maker.14

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Long-term medicine plans

Medicines for heart disease, diabetes, lung disease and other long-term conditions are covered in Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies. How long stored medicines stay good is in Medicines: Shelf Life & Expiration Facts.

#🌡️ Heat and cold hit older bodies hardest

Older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures, says Ready.gov.4 The record agrees.

In the 2021 Texas storm, about two-thirds of 246 deaths came from cold exposure.7 In the Rita evacuation, at least 10% of evacuation deaths were linked to overheating in vehicles.8

Move early, not late. If the home becomes too hot or too cold and it is safe to travel, go to a place with heat or cooling.4 Decide while roads and daylight still allow it.

Never heat a home with a gas oven or stove. Ready.gov warns against it because of carbon monoxide.4

Do

  • Use flashlights, not candles4
  • Move frail people early to a place with heat or cooling4
  • Check on older neighbors in person4
  • Keep a battery CO alarm by each bed area10

Don't

  • Heat the house with a gas oven or stove4
  • Run a generator inside, even with doors open11
  • Leave a frail person in a hot, stuck car8
  • Wait until the roads are full to leave
👶 Babies & children

Babies and elders in one room

Ready.gov names both older adults and young children as especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.4 Keep them together in the warmest room in winter, or the coolest in summer, so one adult can watch both.

See Staying Warm Without Heat and Staying Cool Without Air Conditioning.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Visit, do not just call

Ready.gov puts checking on neighbors on its list of things to do in an outage.4 Knock on the doors of older people who live alone or use medical devices. A dead phone tells you nothing.

Signs and treatment of hypothermia and heat stroke are in Hypothermia, Frostbite & Heat Stroke.

#🦯 Mobility, hearing, vision and communication aids

Small aids decide whether someone can walk, hear a warning or read a label. The Red Cross kit list includes hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, syringes and a cane.6

Ready.gov adds prescription eyeglasses and contact lens solution.16 It also says to replace expired items and to re-think your needs every year.16

Aids to pack for each older or disabled person
ItemPack thisListed by
Hearing aidsThe aids plus extra batteriesRed Cross6
GlassesPrescription eyeglassesRed Cross, Ready.gov616
Contact lensesLenses plus lens solutionRed Cross, Ready.gov616
CaneThe cane the person usesRed Cross6
SyringesThe syringes they needRed Cross6
Medicines7-day supply and a written listRed Cross6

Communication

Make the plan usable by the person it is for. The CDC says accessible planning and communication may help close the preparedness gaps for people with disabilities.9

Write a card for each person. Put their name, conditions, medicines, allergies and devices on it, and how they communicate best: speech, writing, sign language or pictures. Keep one copy on them and one in the kit.

Know what is normal for them. Normal vital signs change with age and overall health.17 Ask family what this person's usual alertness, speech and walking look like, and write it on the card.

Before you decide someone is newly confused, check that their hearing aids and glasses are in and working. How to check a sick person step by step is in Assessing a Sick or Injured Person.

Light, water and a toilet within reach

Give each person their own flashlight with extra batteries, and keep it within reach of the bed. Ready.gov says to use flashlights, not candles.4

Water is heavy. One liter weighs 1 kg and one US gallon weighs 8.33 lb.18 So a full 19 L (5-gallon) jug weighs about 19 kg (42 lb). Keep small containers within reach of anyone who cannot lift that.

Put a toilet within reach of anyone who cannot walk far, with its own handwashing water. See Toilets Without Water.

🎯 Practice now

Learn the hands-on skills now

Ask the person's nurse, doctor or therapist to show you, while help still exists:

  • How to move them from bed to chair
  • How to prevent pressure sores
  • How to make their home safer against falls
  • How to handle dementia day to day

Write down what they teach and keep it with this book. Bed care and pressure sores are also in Nursing the Sick at Home.

#🚪 Moving people who cannot move fast

People with disabilities face disasters more often. In a June 2024 CDC survey, 80% of adults with disabilities had lived through at least one natural disaster, against 70% of adults without disabilities.9

They also have fewer ways out. 26% said they had nowhere to go, against 15%. 20% named the cost of evacuating, against 14%.9

Plans were rare on both sides: only 48% of adults with disabilities and 46% without had an emergency plan.9

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Name a main helper and a backup

    NFPA says to plan for anyone with a disability and to assign a backup in case the main helper is not home.5

  2. Check every meeting place

    FEMA says to make meeting places accessible for household members with disabilities.19 Check steps, slopes and distance.

  3. Keep the car ready

    Keep at least half a tank of gas at all times, and a full tank if an evacuation seems likely.20

  4. Leave early

    Go early enough that severe weather cannot trap you.20 Long waits in traffic were where Rita evacuees overheated.8

  5. Pack for a long, hot wait

    Carry water and a way to stay cool for every person in the car, plus the aids and medicines listed above.86

  6. Practice with them

    Run the drill twice a year, by day and by night, as NFPA advises for fire escape plans.5

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Two ways out of every room

NFPA's escape plan asks for two ways out.5 For someone who uses a wheelchair or walker, check that both ways are actually usable: no steps, no narrow gaps, nothing stacked in the way.

Full family plans are in The Family Emergency Plan, and grab-and-go lists in Go-Bags for Every Family Member.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Assistance dogs and pets

Pack the dog's own kit. The Red Cross lists a collar, leash, ID, food, carrier and bowl.6

Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, so find pet-friendly places to stay before you need them.21 See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

#🍲 Food, water, choking and infection

Older adults get sicker from food poisoning. Adults 65 and older are in the CDC's higher-risk group.22

Get care early for severe signs: bloody diarrhea, a fever over 38.9°C (102°F), frequent vomiting, signs of dehydration, or diarrhea that lasts more than 3 days.22 Safe food without a fridge is in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

Give them your best-treated water. In people with weak immune systems, the parasite Cryptosporidium can cause diarrhea for weeks to months, with wasting.23 See Disinfecting Water.

Protein does not shrink with age

The adult recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for protein stays at 0.8 g per kg of body weight from age 19 to over 70.24

For a 60 kg (132 lb) person, that is 48 g of protein a day. For calories and special diets, see Calories & Nutrition and Special Diets.

Choking in a chair or wheelchair

If you cannot get your arms around someone's waist, use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts.25 Full adult choking steps are in CPR & Choking.

Save or print these official pages and keep them with this book:

#🧠 Remember this

Who had the highest risk of dying after Hurricane Maria?

Poor and elderly people. Older men had a 35% higher death risk than expected.

What share of Maria's excess deaths was linked to interrupted care?

About one third.

Refrigerated medicine after more than a day without power?

Throw it away unless the label says otherwise. If a life depends on it, ask a doctor or pharmacist and use it until new supply arrives.

How long can insulin vials stay out of the fridge?

Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Pens differ: read the label.

Where does a generator go?

Outdoors, more than 6 m (20 ft) from windows, doors and vents. Never in a garage, even with the door open.

How many helpers for each person who cannot move fast?

Which small aids do people forget?

Over 100 of at least 119 deaths linked to the evacuation; at least 10% hyperthermia in vehicles; about another 50% suspected overheating or worsened chronic illness; nursing-home bus fire.
  9. CDC: Emergency Preparedness Behaviors Among Adults With and Without Disabilities, United States, June 2024 (2024 data). 48% vs 46% had a plan; 80% vs 70% had experienced a natural disaster; nowhere to go 26% vs 15%; evacuation cost 20% vs 14%; accessible planning and communication.
  10. CDC: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics (2024). Generators outdoors more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents; never in a home or garage; battery CO alarms; replace every 5 years.
  11. US Consumer Product Safety Commission: What to Know About Generators (2022). Never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if doors and windows are open; point exhaust away from buildings.
  12. heise online: Blackout in Spain and Portugal, at least three dead after power outage (2025). At least three deaths; Galicia family deaths and generator carbon monoxide investigation.
  13. FDA: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency (n.d.). Vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, may be left unrefrigerated at 59–86°F for up to 28 days; pens and products differ; replace insulin exposed to extreme conditions.
  14. FDA: Safe Drug Use After a Natural Disaster (n.d.). If a medicine was not stored at the right temperature, check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, provider or manufacturer.
  15. American Red Cross: Emergency Supply Kit Checklist (n.d.). Medical items and medications (1-month supply).
  16. Ready.gov (FEMA): Build a Kit (n.d.). Prescription eyeglasses and contact lens solution; prescription and non-prescription medicines; replace expired items; re-think needs every year.
  17. MedlinePlus (NIH): Vital signs (n.d.). Normal vital signs change with age, sex, weight, exercise capability and overall health.
  18. USGS Water Science School: Facts About Water (n.d.). Water weighs 8.33 pounds per gallon and 1 kilogram per liter.
  19. FEMA: Family Emergency Communication Plan (n.d.). Meeting places should be accessible for household members with disabilities.
  20. Ready.gov (FEMA): Evacuation (2025). Half a tank of gas at all times, full if evacuation seems likely; leave early enough to avoid being trapped by severe weather.
  21. FDA: Take Care of Your Pets Before Disaster Strikes (n.d.). Temporary public shelters may not allow animals.
  22. CDC: Food Poisoning Symptoms (2024). Severe signs (bloody diarrhea, fever over 102°F, frequent vomiting, dehydration, diarrhea over 3 days); higher-risk groups including adults 65 and older.
  23. CDC: Cryptosporidiosis Summary Report, National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (2013 data). Weeks to months of diarrhea and wasting in immunocompromised people.
  24. AHRQ Effective Health Care Program: Dietary Protein Intake, Research Protocol (n.d.). Adult protein RDA 0.8 g/kg for ages 19 to over 70.
  25. American Heart Association: Part 7, Adult Basic Life Support, 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC (Circulation) (2025). Adult choking care, including chest thrusts when abdominal thrusts are not possible.

Babies & Children

Keeping newborns, babies and children alive and healthy: feeding, warmth, hygiene, danger signs, safety, education and emotional health.

👶 Part 6 · Babies & ChildrenChapter 93
🎒

The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit

🟠 HighFirst 72 hFirst 30 days📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Build the kit in three tiers: 2 weeks, 3 months, 1 year. The Red Cross advises a 2-week supply at home, and Puerto Rico households averaged 84 days without power after Hurricane Maria.12
  • Measure first, then multiply. Count what your child really uses in a day, then multiply by 14, 91 and 365. Your child's own count beats any average.
  • Formula needs safe water and fuel. CDC says to use bottled water until tap water is declared safe, and water at about 70°C (158°F) for young or vulnerable babies.3
  • Children's medicines get their own pouch. Never give aspirin to children. Pack a non-mercury, non-glass thermometer.45
  • Every bucket and basin needs a lid. Of the children under 5 who drowned at home in a CPSC count, 82% were under age 2.6
2 weekshome supply the Red Cross advises1
84 daysaverage time without power, Puerto Rico 20172
70°C(158°F) water to mix formula for young babies3
82%of child drownings at home were under age 26

#🎒 The kit at a glance: eight bins

Pack the kit by job, not by store aisle. When you are tired and it is dark, you want to grab "the diaper bin", not search five boxes.

Start from the official lists. Ready.gov names infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.8 The Red Cross adds baby food and says to copy important documents.1

Ready.gov also says to keep supplies in airtight plastic bags, packed in one or two easy-to-carry containers.8 One bin per job does that for a baby.

0 / 8 done
💡 Tip

Label the outside, three times

Write the bin number, its job and the clothing size or date on two sides and the lid. You should be able to read it by flashlight from across the room.

⏳ The 30-year view

A 3-year kit, not a 3-day kit

A newborn becomes a 3-year-old who walks, eats family food and may be out of diapers. Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.8

In a long outage there is no calendar reminder. Tie the full review to a fixed date, such as the child's birthday.

#📦 How much: 2 weeks, 3 months, 1 year

Use three tiers, and tie each one to a real event.

  • 2 weeks: the Red Cross advises a 2-week supply for home and 3 days for evacuation.1
  • 3 months: after Hurricane Maria in 2017, surveyed Puerto Rico households averaged 84 days without power and 68 days without water.2
  • 1 year: power came back to the whole island about 11 months after the storm.9

Short outages happen too. In the February 2021 Texas freeze, more than 4.5 million Texans lost power, some for up to 4 days.10

Measure, then multiply

Your child's real daily count is the only number that fits your child. Get it in 3 days.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Count for 3 days

    Tally every diaper, wipe, feed, outfit and bib. Tape the tally sheet inside a cupboard door.

  2. Find the daily average

    Add the three days and divide by 3. Round up, never down.

  3. Multiply for each tier

    Times 14 for 2 weeks, times 91 for 3 months, times 365 for 1 year.

  4. Fill the 2-week tier first

    Finish one tier before you start the next. A full 2 weeks beats a half-filled year.

  5. Re-count every month

    Write the new count and date on the tally sheet. Adjust the next purchase.

Daily count times days (arithmetic only: use your own child's count)

A year of single-use items is a large pile. At 8 diapers a day, a year is 2,920 diapers. Compare that with a reusable stash (see the diaper section below).

Water for the baby

Count the baby as a full person in your water plan. CDC advises at least 4 liters (1 gallon) per person per day, for 2 weeks if possible, and more for pregnant women, sick people and hot climates.11

University of Florida Extension says to store more water when children or nursing mothers live in the home.12 Ready.gov says very hot weather can double water needs.13

The arithmetic per person: 4 liters (1 gallon) a day is 53 liters (14 gallons) for 2 weeks, 344 liters (91 gallons) for 3 months and 1,382 liters (365 gallons) for a year. Storage methods are in Storing Water for Months & Years.

#🍼 Feeding supplies

Pack for how your baby eats today, and pack a backup. Feeding changes fast between birth and age 3.

Breastfed babies

Direct breastfeeding needs no mixing water, no bottles and no fuel. The nursing mother does need extra water, so plan more for her.12

The facts on supply, latch, blocked ducts and relactation are in Breastfeeding: The Survival Superpower.

🌸 Women & girls

The mother is part of the baby kit

Put her water bottle, snacks, breast pads and nursing clothes in the feeding bin, within reach of where she feeds. UF Extension lists nursing mothers among the people who need more stored water.12

Formula-fed babies

Formula is only as safe as the water you mix it with. CDC says to prepare formula with bottled water until officials say tap water is safe.3

If you must boil water, CDC says to boil it for 1 minute. For young or vulnerable infants, mix powdered formula with water at about 70°C (158°F).3

Boiling does not remove chemicals. CDC says chemically contaminated water cannot be made safe by boiling, disinfecting or filtering.3

So the formula bin holds more than formula:

  • Formula of the exact type your baby uses, with the use-by date written on the lid
  • Bottled water marked "formula only"
  • A pot with a lid, a stove and fuel to boil water
  • Bottles or cups, a bottle brush, dish soap and a washing basin
  • A clean towel and a lidded box for drying clean parts

The full method, and what to do when formula runs out, is in Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

⚠️ Caution

Stored water has a date

CDC says to label and date stored water and replace it every 6 months. Keep it at 10–21°C (50–70°F), out of sunlight.11 Rotate the "formula only" water on the same day you rotate the rest.

Toddlers and solid food

The Red Cross lists baby food in the kit.1 Add spoons, bowls and an open cup your child can hold. First foods and foods to avoid are in First Foods for Babies Without Stores.

Learn infant choking first aid before solids start. The 2025 AHA guidelines use back blows and heel-of-hand chest thrusts for infants.25 Practice the steps in CPR & Choking.

Do

  • Keep a separate stock of bottled water for formula3
  • Store fuel for boiling with the feeding bin
  • Pack two of every bottle part
  • Empty and turn over the washing basin after use

Don't

  • Mix formula with water that may hold fuel or chemicals, even boiled3
  • Leave a basin of wash water standing where a toddler can reach it7
  • Switch formula types in a crisis without a reason

#🧷 Diapers, wipes and hygiene

Diaper supplies are health supplies. Ready.gov lists diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream in the basic kit.8

A healthy-looking child can still spread germs. CDC says hepatitis A spreads by the fecal-oral route, and 70% of infections in children under 6 cause no symptoms.16

So wash your hands with soap after every change. WHO estimates that poor hand hygiene caused 384,000 diarrhea deaths in 2019.17 Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene caused 395,000 deaths in children under 5 that year.17

What goes in the diaper bin:

  • Diapers in the current size and the next size up
  • Wipes, or washcloths and a small water bottle
  • Diaper rash cream8
  • Bar soap and a handwashing jug
  • A wipeable changing mat
  • A pail with a tight lid, plus trash bags

If the baby seems well, you can skip handwashing after a diaper change.

Most hepatitis A infections in children under 6 (70%) have no symptoms, and the virus spreads by the fecal-oral route.16 Wash every time.

☠️ Danger

A diaper pail can drown a toddler

CPSC counted 434 in-home drowning deaths of children under 5 in 2006–2010. 82% were under age 2, and 81% involved bathtubs or bath products.6

KidsHealth says drowning can happen in less than 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water. Never leave water containers unattended.7 Put a lid on every pail and empty basins straight away. More in Keeping Kids Safe.

Cloth stash math, washing with little water and rash treatment are in Cloth Diapers & Baby Hygiene.

#👕 Clothes that grow with the child

Children grow out of clothes, so store sizes ahead. Ready.gov says to re-think kit needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.8

Temperature is the reason clothes matter. Ready.gov notes that young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures during power outages.14

How many outfits

Outfits needed = outfits used per day times days between washes, plus spares for wash day. Example: 3 a day, washing every 3 days, is 9 outfits plus spares.

Use your 3-day tally for the "per day" number. If you wash less often, the outfit count goes up by the same arithmetic.

Sizes, by fit

  • Pack by fit, not by the age on the label. Try clothes on the child when you can.
  • Weigh and measure monthly. Write the numbers on the health card.
  • Keep outgrown clothes clean and labeled. They serve a younger child, a trade or cloth for repairs.
  • Warm layers and sun layers both. Cold-house methods are in Staying Warm Without Heat.
  1. Every day

    Dress the child for the room you are in, not for the season on the calendar.

  2. Every month

    Weigh, measure and check fit. Shift bins when clothes get tight.

  3. Every season

    Before the cold or hot season, check the layers you need.

  4. Every birthday

    Do the full kit review Ready.gov advises each year.8

🛒 Get it before you need it

Buy bigger sizes while stores exist

Secondhand children's clothes in the next sizes up cost little now. Wash, label by size and pack them in airtight bags, as Ready.gov advises for kit supplies.8

#😴 Sleep, light and air at night

Night feeds and changes need light that cannot start a fire. Ready.gov advises flashlights, not candles, in a power outage.14 A headlamp keeps both hands free for the baby.

What goes in the night bin:

  • A headlamp and a flashlight, with spare batteries
  • The baby's own sleep space, set up to the safe-sleep rules
  • Sleep clothing for the season
  • A battery carbon monoxide (CO) alarm

Put a battery CO alarm near where the baby sleeps. CDC advises battery-operated CO alarms and says to replace them every 5 years.15

☠️ Danger

Generators stay outside

CDC says to run generators outdoors, more than 6 m (20 feet) from windows, doors and vents, and never in a home or garage.15 A baby cannot tell you they feel ill. Read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

Safe-sleep facts on the sleep surface, position and bedding are in Newborn Care: The First 28 Days. Read them before you choose what goes in this bin.

#🚗 Car seats, carriers and moving with a child

Your car kit is a second baby kit. Ready.gov advises keeping kits at home, at work and in the car.8

Car seats

  • Photograph every label on the seat. Keep the photos with your kit papers.
  • Keep the manual in a zip bag in the car kit. It is the only instruction book written for that exact seat.
  • Write the seat's limits on the health card, next to the child's latest weight and height. Compare them at each monthly weigh-in.
  • If a used seat has no labels or manual, you cannot check its limits. Do not rely on it.

Carriers and loads

A carrier keeps your hands free, but the baby counts as load. Military research recommends loads of 30% of body mass or less to avoid a drop in performance.22

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Weigh yourself

    Use a bathroom scale. Write the number down.

  2. Weigh the full load

    Step on again holding the baby in the carrier and wearing the bag.

  3. Subtract and divide

    The difference divided by your weight is your load share.

  4. Lighten if over 30%

    Move items to another adult or a cart.22

Example arithmetic: 30% of 60 kg (132 lb) is 18 kg (40 lb). A 9 kg (20 lb) baby plus a 9 kg (20 lb) bag reaches that line.

A walking toddler can carry a little. The National Safety Council says a child's backpack should weigh no more than 5–10% of the child's weight.23 For a 14 kg (31 lb) child, that is 0.7–1.4 kg (1.5–3 lb).

👶 Babies & children

What a toddler can carry

A small water bottle, a snack, a comfort toy and a copy of their ID card. Keep it within the 5–10% line.23 Full family bags are in Go-Bags for Every Family Member.

#💊 Infant medicines, thermometer and health card

Give children's medicines only as the label or a clinician says. Doses depend on the product and the child, so this chapter lists none. Use professional care whenever it exists.

Never give aspirin to children.4 Keep the adult kit's aspirin out of the children's pouch.

The children's medicine pouch
ItemWhy
Non-mercury, non-glass thermometer, plus a spareThe type the Red Cross specifies for first aid kits5
Oral rehydration solution (ORS) packetsWHO and UNICEF advise low-osmolarity ORS for children with diarrhea19
Zinc, as a clinician directsWHO and UNICEF pair zinc with ORS and continued feeding19
Diaper rash creamOn the Ready.gov kit list8
The child's own prescriptionsRed Cross: pack a 7-day medication supply1
Children's fever or pain medicine labeled for the child's ageDose only by the label
Dose card and penRecords each dose, time and who gave it
📊 Key fact

Why ORS is in every baby kit

WHO lists diarrheal disease as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months, with about 443,832 deaths in children under 5 each year.18 How to use ORS is in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.

WHO keeps a separate Essential Medicines List for children (EMLc). The 2025 edition lists 374 medicines.20 Use it as a map when you talk with your clinician, not as a shopping list. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit.

Store and check

Check dates at every kit review. The Red Cross advises checking expiration dates and replacing used or out-of-date items.5

If a medicine was not stored at the right temperature, FDA says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist.21 Ready.gov says to throw out refrigerated medicine after an outage of more than a day, unless the label says otherwise.14

The health card

Write one card per child and keep it in the medicine pouch.

  • Name, date of birth, latest weight and the date it was taken
  • Allergies and medical conditions
  • Each medicine: name, strength, label dose for this child, times given
  • Normal temperature and breathing rate, measured when the child is well
  • Vaccine dates and clinician contacts
  • Car seat limits and the latest height

Record "normal" while the child is healthy, so you can compare when they are sick. Danger signs are in Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs. Fever care is in Fever, Coughs & Common Childhood Illnesses.

🎯 Practice now

Practice with the thermometer now

Take your child's temperature while they are well, by daylight and then by headlamp. Write the reading and time on the health card. A skill you have practiced is easier at 3 a.m.

#🪪 Papers, ID and comfort

Pack proof of who your child is and who they belong to. After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita, 5,192 children were reported missing. Reuniting all of them with family took more than six months.24

  • A child ID card: recent photo, name, parents' names and an out-of-area contact
  • Copies of the birth certificate and vaccination record (the Red Cross says to copy important documents)1
  • The health card
  • Extra cash, which the Red Cross includes in its kit list1
  • A familiar comfort toy for awake time

Update the photo at every kit review. Reunification planning is in Keeping Kids Safe.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Download these while the internet works

  • Ready.gov: Build a Kit: the official basic kit list, including infant items.
  • CDC: Prepare and Store Powdered Infant Formula in an Emergency: print it and put it in the feeding bin.
  • WHO Model Lists of Essential Medicines: the adult and children's lists.

#✅ Do this now

What are the three kit tiers?

2 weeks, 3 months and 1 year.

Why plan for 3 months?

After Hurricane Maria, Puerto Rico households averaged 84 days without power.

How do you size the kit?

Count 3 days of real use, average it, then multiply by 14, 91 and 365.

What water goes in formula?

Bottled water until tap water is declared safe. About 70°C (158°F) for young or vulnerable babies.

Aspirin for children?

Never.

Which thermometer?

How much can a toddler carry?

Biggest water danger to toddlers at home?
