Part 8

Shelter, Heat & Light

Staying warm, cool, dry and lit without electricity, and doing it without poisoning yourself with carbon monoxide or burning the house down.

🔥 Part 8 · Shelter, Heat & LightChapter 104
🏠

Preparing Your Home for a Long Outage

🟠 HighFirst 72 hFirst 30 days📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Choose one warm, safe room now. Few windows, two ways out, and space for everyone, pets included.12
  • Never heat with a gas stove or oven. Never run a generator indoors. A generator goes outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.34
  • Use flashlights, not candles. Fit carbon monoxide (CO) alarms with battery backup. Replace each CO alarm every 5 years.35
  • Practice your fire escape twice a year, by day and by night. You may have only 1–2 minutes to get out.2
  • Find your main water valve today. To empty the pipes, close it, open the highest tap and drain from the lowest.67
  • After a flood, wear rubber boots, gloves and goggles. Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals.8
246deaths in the Texas freeze of February 2021, about two-thirds from cold9
84 daysaverage time without power for Puerto Rico homes after Hurricane Maria10
1–2 minmay be all the time you get to escape a home fire2
6 m(20 ft): the least distance from a generator to doors, windows and vents4

#🏠 Your house has to stand on its own First 72 h

In a long outage, your home must keep you warm, keep fire out and hold your water. This chapter shows how to set it up before you need it.

In February 2021, more than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for up to 4 days.11 Texas later linked 246 deaths to the storm. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.9

The water failed too. Water system problems affected more than 14 million Texans during the same storm.12

Outages can last for months. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 Puerto Rico households found that homes went 84 days without power on average.10

📊 Key fact

Hurricane Helene, 2024

Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states.13 That was one storm, in one recent year.

Plan to live at home for at least 2 weeks. The American Red Cross advises a 2-week supply for home and a 3-day supply if you must leave.14 For a 30-year outage, that is only the base you build on.

Water comes first: see Storing Water for Months & Years. If your house is not safe to stay in, read Stay or Go?

#🛋️ Choose one warm, safe room First 72 h

Live, sleep and keep watch in one room. Close off the rest of the house and use it for storage.

For chemical and radiation emergencies, the CDC's shelter-in-place advice is an interior room with no or few windows, with everyone inside, pets included.1 Pick your warm room by the same rule, and one room can do both jobs.

Add one rule from fire safety: know two ways out of every room.2 In a small room, plan on the door plus a window that opens.

What to look for in your warm room
Look forWhy
Few windowsThe CDC's shelter-in-place room has no or few windows1
Two ways outNFPA's escape rule for every room2
Space for everyone, dogs tooThe CDC brings pets into the shelter room with you1
Far from the generator spotA generator must sit at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents4
A place for a CO alarmReady.gov advises CO alarms with battery backup3
Above the flood lineFloodwater can carry sewage and chemicals8

Set up the room

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Pick it today

    Walk the house with the table above. Write the room into your Family Emergency Plan.

  2. Close off the rest

    Shut the doors to rooms you are not using. Lay rolled towels along the gaps under them.

  3. Cover the windows at night

    Hang blankets or heavy curtains, but keep the exit window easy to open. Ready.gov's basic kit includes plastic sheeting and duct tape.16

  4. Insulate the floor

    Put rugs, mats or folded blankets under every sleeping place.

  5. Fit the alarms

    Add a CO alarm with battery backup.3 Add a battery smoke alarm too.

  6. Move everyone in

    Babies, elders and sick people get the warmest spots. Dogs sleep inside too.

⚠️ Caution

Any flame changes the rules

Never seal a room around a flame or an engine. Before you use any stove, heater, lamp or generator for warmth, read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer. For warmth with no heat at all, see Staying Warm Without Heat.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and small children

Ready.gov warns that young children and older adults are vulnerable to extreme temperatures.3 Give small children a warm place in the warm room, where an adult can see them.

For safe sleep and keeping newborns warm, see Newborn Care.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Elders and people on medical devices

Check on older neighbors. Ready.gov lists older adults as vulnerable to extreme temperatures.3 More than 3 million US Medicare beneficiaries have claims for medical equipment that runs on electricity.17

Ready.gov says to plan now for any medical device that needs power.3 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs come inside

The CDC's shelter-in-place advice brings pets into the room with you.1 Ready.gov says to include pets in your family plan, with a bowl and several days of water in their kit.18

Temporary public shelters may not take animals.19 Your warm room may be your dog's only shelter. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

💡 Tip

Hot climate?

In the tropics you may need a cool room more than a warm one. The safety rules stay the same: two ways out, working alarms, and the generator far from the house. See Staying Cool Without Air Conditioning.

#🔥 Heat and light without fire or fumes First 72 h

Use flashlights, not candles. It is one of Ready.gov's basic power outage rules.3 For lamps and lanterns that last for decades, see Light Without the Grid.

Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven. Ready.gov and the CDC both say so.34

Fit CO alarms with battery backup.3 The CDC says to replace each CO alarm every 5 years.5 Write the date you fitted it on the back.

☠️ Danger

Generators kill, even outside

Never run a generator inside a home or garage, even with the doors and windows open.15 The CDC adds carports, and says to keep it at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4

After the 2005 hurricanes in Alabama and Texas, at least 78 people were poisoned by generator CO and 10 died. Most cases involved generators placed outside, but near the home.20

Do

  • Use flashlights for light3
  • Fit CO alarms with battery backup3
  • Run a generator outside, 6 m (20 ft) from openings4
  • Point generator exhaust away from buildings15
  • Unplug electronics during the outage3
  • Check on older neighbors3

Don't

  • Light the house with candles3
  • Heat with a gas stove or oven34
  • Run a generator in a home, garage or carport4
  • Trust open doors or windows to clear the fumes15

A generator in the garage is fine if the garage door is open.

The US Consumer Product Safety Commission says never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.15

For wood stoves, see Heating With Wood. For fuel storage and running a generator safely, see Generators & Fuel Storage.

#🚪 Fire safety: alarms and two ways out

A home fire can leave you as little as 1–2 minutes to escape.2 Every flame you add for heat, light or cooking is one more way for a fire to start.

Plan as if no fire truck is coming. Prevention, working alarms and a practiced escape are your fire service now.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Know two ways out of every room

    Usually a door and a window. Check that both open from the inside.2

  2. Practice twice a year

    Run the drill by day and by night.2

  3. Get low and close doors

    Crawl low under smoke. Close doors behind you to slow the fire.2

  4. Meet outside

    Go straight to your outside meeting place and count heads.

  5. Never go back in

    Not for people, pets or things.2 Tell rescuers who is missing instead.

Alarms that work without the grid

Put a battery smoke alarm in the warm room and outside every sleeping area. Press the test button at every drill so everyone knows the sound.

Keep spare batteries for every alarm, sealed and dated. Store them with your flashlight batteries.

Keep a fire extinguisher near where you cook and heat. Learn to use it from your local fire service while classes still run.

👶 Babies & children

Babies, children and anyone who needs help

Assign one adult to each baby and to anyone who cannot get out alone, plus a backup.2 Carry them in the night drill too.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print these while the internet works

  • NFPA: How to Make a Home Fire Escape Plan (PDF)
  • NFPA Sparky: Home Fire Escape Plan grid for kids
  • Ready.gov: Power Outages
  • CDC: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics

#🚰 Pipes: protect the water inside your walls

Your pipes and water heater hold water you can use. FEMA and the Red Cross explain how to get it out.7

In Texas in 2021, water system problems hit more than 14 million people.12 Learn your own pipes before the taps stop.

Find the main water valve and learn to close it. If the public water may be contaminated, closing it keeps dirty water out of your pipes.6

Emptying the pipes before a hard freeze

If you cannot keep the house above freezing, empty the pipes into clean containers. Water expands as it freezes. That is why stored water needs 5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of space at the top of the container.21 A full pipe has no space at all.

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Close the main valve

    This stops outside water from flowing in.6

  2. Open the highest tap

    Open the faucet on the top floor to let air into the pipes.7

  3. Drain the lowest tap

    Catch the water from the lowest faucet in clean containers.7

  4. Label and store it

    Write the date on each container. Use plastic, not glass, where it may freeze.21

The water heater holds more. For the safe order (power off first, then drain), see Storing Water.

⚠️ Caution

Gas turned off? Call a professional

If the gas to the water heater was shut off, a professional needs to turn it back on.7 Refill the tank before the power or gas goes back on.7

Shelves must be strong. Water weighs over 8 lb per gallon (about 1 kg per liter), so stored containers need sturdy shelving.21

A full bathtub is your drinking supply.

The National Weather Service says to use bathtub water for cleaning and flushing only, not for drinking.22

👶 Babies & children

Tubs and buckets drown toddlers

From 2006 to 2010, 434 children under 5 drowned in US homes. 82% were under age 2, and 81% of the deaths involved bathtubs or bath products.23

Drowning can happen in less than 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water. Never leave water containers unattended, use toilet-lid locks and keep bathroom doors closed.24

#🌀 After a storm: check the house before you trust it

Check the house from outside first, in daylight, before anyone moves back into damaged rooms. Keep children and dogs back until you are done.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Look from outside

    Walk all the way around. Look for a sagging roof, cracked or leaning walls, and trees resting on the building.

  2. Stay away from fallen wires

    Keep everyone, children and dogs included, well back.

  3. Smell gas? Get out

    Leave the house. Do not light flames or use switches. Stay out until it has been checked.

  4. Dress for floodwater

    Wear rubber boots, gloves and goggles.8

  5. Check your water

    Ask about boil water advisories. A private well must be tested and disinfected after floodwater goes down.25

  6. Clean what floodwater touched

    Disinfect children's toys. Wash clothes in hot water with detergent.8

Floodwater can contain sewage. Swallowing contaminated water or food causes diarrheal disease.8 Floods also move chemical containers.8

☠️ Danger

Do not bathe in floodwater

The CDC says not to bathe in water that may be contaminated.8 Keep children from playing in it.

If you run a generator during cleanup, the same rule applies: outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4

Hazard by hazard, see Floods and Hurricanes & Tornadoes. For collapse and debris dangers, see Salvage Hazards.

🎯 Practice now

Walk the house now

Do the outside walk-around today, while the house is fine. Photograph the roof, walls and nearby trees so you can spot changes after a storm.

#🗓️ Home prep, stage by stage

Do the slow jobs now. Leave only quick jobs for the storm warning and the outage itself.

  1. Now

    Choose the warm room. Fit CO alarms with battery backup.3 Find the main water valve.6 Practice the fire escape.2

  2. Storm warning

    Fill the bathtub and large containers for washing and flushing.22 Charge phones and keep gas tanks full.3

  3. Power out

    Flashlights on, no candles, no gas oven for heat.3 Generator outside, at least 6 m (20 ft) away.4

  4. Hard freeze

    If the house cannot stay above freezing, empty the pipes: main valve closed, top tap open, drain the lowest.67

  5. After the storm

    Boots, gloves and goggles for floodwater.8 Test and disinfect a private well.25

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • CO alarms with battery backup3
  • A flashlight for every person3
  • Plastic sheeting and duct tape16
  • Rubber boots, gloves and goggles8
  • Battery smoke alarms, spare batteries and a fire extinguisher
  • Food-grade water containers: see Storing Water
⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

CO alarms need replacing every 5 years.5 Over 30 years, that is 6 alarms for each spot in the house. Count them into your long-term plan.

Two drills a year2 adds up to 60 drills in 30 years. Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and replace expired items.16 Children grow, elders age and dogs change.

How often do you replace a CO alarm?

How do you empty the pipes?

What makes a good warm room?

Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer

🔴 CriticalFirst 72 h📚 15 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Never run a generator, grill, camp stove or car engine inside a home, garage or carport. Open doors and windows do not make it safe.146
  • Put the generator outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Point the exhaust away from buildings.14
  • Fit a battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm near every sleeping area. Sleeping people can die before they feel any symptoms.2
  • Alarm sounding, or headache and dizziness? Get everyone outside into fresh air first. Then get medical help.1
  • Never heat your home with a gas oven or stove. It is a carbon monoxide risk.61
6 m(20 ft) minimum from a generator to doors, windows and vents1
78+people poisoned by generator CO in Alabama and Texas after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita (2005); 10 died3
5 yrsreplace every CO alarm after this long2
3family members died at home in Galicia during Spain's 2025 blackout; police investigated generator CO7

#💨 The killer you cannot see or smell First 72 h

Carbon monoxide (CO) is a gas with no color and no smell, and it can kill you.2 You will not notice it building up.

Every flame and every engine makes it. CO is in the fumes whenever fuel burns in cars and trucks, small engines, stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces, gas ranges and furnaces.2

Indoors, it collects. CO builds up in enclosed or partly enclosed spaces and poisons the people and animals who breathe it.2

With no grid power, generators, grills, camp stoves, gas ovens and car engines become the tools for power, cooking, charging and heat. Official outage guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and Ready.gov (FEMA) warns against each of them used the wrong way.16

☠️ Danger

Outside is not automatically safe

After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people in Alabama and Texas and killed 10. Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.3

#📅 What recent blackouts show

Generators have killed people after hurricanes, and police investigated a generator CO case after the 2025 blackout in Spain. Below are documented events and the scale of recent outages. Every entry is a recorded fact, not a forecast.

  1. 2005

    Alabama and Texas, after Hurricanes Katrina and Rita: portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with CO and killed 10. Most of the generators were outside but near homes.3

  2. 2017

    Puerto Rico, after Hurricane Maria: surveyed households went an average of 84 days without power.11 Long outages mean the rules in this chapter apply for months, not days.

  3. Feb 2021

    Texas winter storm: more than 4.5 million Texans lost power, some for up to 4 days.9 The state counted 246 storm-related deaths, about two-thirds of them from cold.10

  4. Sep 2024

    Hurricane Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states.12

  5. Apr 2025

    Spain and Portugal: a widespread blackout on April 28 stopped subways, traffic lights and ATMs.8 In Galicia, police investigated CO from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.7

The lesson from 2005: outside was not enough. Most of those generators were outdoors but near the home.3 The CDC rule is outdoors and at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.1

In a cold outage, choose only safe heat. Staying Warm Without Heat shows how to keep warm without burning anything.

#🤒 Symptoms, and why sleeping people die

The warning signs are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion.1 The CDC notes that people often describe them as "flu-like".2

Breathing in a lot of CO can make you pass out or kill you.2

People who are asleep or drunk can die from CO before they have any symptoms.2 No headache wakes them up. A CO alarm can.

Who is at higher risk

Everyone is at risk. Infants, older people, and people with chronic heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are more likely to get sick from CO.2

⚠️ Caution

Do not try to tell CO from flu

CO can poison every person and animal who breathes it in the same space.2 If several people, or the dog, feel unwell at once while an engine, grill, stove or heater is running, treat it as CO. Get everyone outside first.1

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

Infants are more likely to get sick from CO.2 A baby cannot tell you about a headache, so put a CO alarm near where the baby sleeps, as you would for every sleeping area.2

Let older children hear the CO alarm's test sound. Teach them one rule: when it sounds, go straight outside to the family meeting spot.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older and disabled people

Older people and anyone with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are more likely to get sick from CO.2 During an outage, check on older neighbors.6

If someone cannot get out of bed alone, decide now who helps them outside when the alarm sounds.

#⛽ Generators: outdoors and far away

Run a portable generator outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.1

Never run one in a home, garage or carport. Open doors and windows do not make it safe.14 Point the exhaust away from your house and any other building.4

Distance matters as much as "outside". Most generator poisonings after Katrina and Rita involved generators placed outdoors but close to homes.3

Set up a generator, step by step

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Choose the spot now

    Outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from every door, window and vent.1 Mark it with a stake or paint so nobody guesses in the dark.

  2. Aim the exhaust away

    Point it away from your home and from any other building.4

  3. Run a long cord

    Use an extension cord longer than 6 m (20 ft), so the generator can stay far away.5

  4. Switch on a battery CO alarm inside

    Keep a battery-powered CO alarm running in the home whenever the generator runs.5

  5. Never move it closer

    Not into the garage or carport, not even in rain or to stop theft.14

A generator is fine in the garage if the big door is open.

The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) says never use a generator inside a home or garage, even if doors and windows are open.4

If the generator is outside the house, everyone inside is safe.

Most generator CO poisonings after Katrina and Rita involved generators outside but near homes.3 Keep it at least 6 m (20 ft) from openings.1

💡 Tip

Agree on generators with your neighbors

Your neighbors' doors and windows count too. Agree as a street that nobody runs a generator within 6 m (20 ft) of any home's doors, windows or vents.1 See Organizing Neighbors: Mutual Aid & Watch.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and other pets

CO poisons animals as well as people.2 Keep dogs away from generator exhaust, and never keep a pet in a garage or carport with an engine running.

If your dog seems weak or sick at the same time as people, take everyone, dog included, into fresh air. Then see Dog First Aid.

For fuel storage, refueling, cords and transfer switches, see Generators & Fuel Storage.

#🔥 Grills, camp stoves, ovens and cars

Use charcoal grills and camp stoves outdoors only, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.6

Never heat your home with a gas oven or stove.61 A gas range burns fuel, and burning fuel makes CO.2

Never run a car or truck in a garage or carport.1 If you charge phones from a car, park it in the open first.

Fuel-burning devices: the rules (CDC, CPSC, Ready.gov)
DeviceSafe useNever
Portable generatorOutdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents; exhaust pointed away14In a home, garage or carport, even with doors open14
Charcoal grill, camp stoveOutdoors, 6 m (20 ft) from windows6Indoors
Gas oven or stovetopCooking, then turn it offHeating the home6
Car or truckEngine on only in the open airIn a garage or carport1
Fireplace, wood stoveMakes CO too2; follow the chimney rules in Heating With WoodBurning when fumes stay in the room, where CO builds up2
Fuel lantern or lampMakes CO too2; battery lights burn no fuelLeft burning while people sleep, since sleepers get no warning2
☠️ Danger

Tents, campers and cars are enclosed spaces too

CO builds up in enclosed and partly enclosed spaces.2 A grill or camp stove inside a tent, camper, boat cabin or parked car is the same danger as one inside your kitchen.

Cook outdoors with the methods in Cooking Without Power. For stove installation, clearances and chimney care, see Heating With Wood. For safe light at night, see Light Without the Grid.

#🚨 CO alarms: your night watch

Use a battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarm.26 An alarm that runs only on mains power goes silent in a blackout.

Put one near every sleeping area.2 That is where people are when they cannot notice symptoms.2 Ready.gov also advises alarms in central locations on every level of the home.6

Replace every alarm after 5 years.2 Keep one switched on whenever a generator is running.5

Set up your alarms

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Check the label

    It must say carbon monoxide. A smoke alarm is a different device unless its label says it detects both.

  2. Choose battery power

    Battery-powered, or plug-in with battery backup. Nothing that dies with the grid.2

  3. Mount one near each sleeping area

    Include the places where babies and older relatives sleep.2

  4. Write two dates on it

    The install date, and a replace-by date 5 years later.2

  5. Test it and teach the sound

    Press the test button as the manual says. Let every family member, including children, hear what it sounds like.

🎯 Practice now

Run a night-time get-out drill

The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) advises practicing a home escape plan twice a year, during the day and at night, with two ways out of every room.13 Use the same drill for the CO alarm: wake up, get out, meet outside, count heads.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • Battery-powered or battery-backup CO alarms, one per sleeping area2
  • Spare batteries in the size each alarm takes
  • One extra battery CO alarm to run whenever the generator runs5
  • An extension cord longer than 6 m (20 ft)5

#🩺 If someone may be poisoned: fresh air first

Fresh air is the first treatment. If the alarm sounds, or anyone feels dizzy, sick or confused, get everyone outside into fresh air. Then get medical help.1

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Get everyone out now

    People and pets, straight outside into fresh air.1 Do not stop to hunt for the source.

  2. Keep yourself safe

    Do not go back in for belongings. The Red Cross notes that keeping yourself safe helps you take care of others.15

  3. Get medical help

    Call emergency services, or get the person to medical care as fast as you can.1

  4. Check anyone who does not respond

    Check quickly. If they do not respond and are not breathing normally, or are only gasping, start CPR and use an automated external defibrillator (AED) as soon as one is available (AHA, 2025).14

  5. Stay out while the source runs

    Do not go back in while the engine, grill or stove is still burning. Where responders exist, let them say when it is safe.

Learn CPR before you need it: see CPR & Choking: Adults, Children, Infants.

Do

  • Get everyone outside first1
  • Take the pets too2
  • Get medical help1
  • Start CPR if a person does not respond and is not breathing normally, or only gasping14

Don't

  • Search the house for the source
  • Go back in for belongings15
  • Put a sick person to bed in the same house
  • Shrug it off as flu while engines or burners are running
⏳ The 30-year view

When no ambulance is coming

Fresh air is the one first step every household can always take.1 In a long grid-down life, prevention is the whole plan: correct placement, working alarms and a family that gets out fast.

#🛏️ The CO-safe bedtime check

Night is when CO kills quietly. Sleeping people can die before they notice symptoms.2 Do this check every night that anything has burned fuel.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Walk the house

    No generator, grill, camp stove or engine running inside, in the garage or in the carport.16

  2. Check the generator spot

    Outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents, with the exhaust pointed away.14

  3. Put out lanterns and fuel lamps

    Lanterns make CO too.2 Switch to battery lights for the night.

  4. Check every alarm

    One near each sleeping area, battery in, working.2

  5. Agree who does what

    Name the adult who wakes the children, who carries the baby, who helps older relatives and who takes the dog.

💡 Tip

Make it a habit, not a decision

Tie the check to something you already do every night, such as locking the door. A routine you do without thinking still happens when you are exhausted.

#⏳ The 30-year view Long haul

CO risk lasts as long as you burn anything. Fireplaces, stoves, lanterns and furnaces all make CO, not just generators.2

If your heat, cooking and light come from wood, charcoal or oil, the same rules apply every single day. Burn outdoors, or in a stove with a properly installed, clean chimney. See Heating With Wood.

Alarms wear out on a schedule. Replace them every 5 years,2 so a 30-year plan needs several generations of alarms.

⏳ The 30-year view

30 years of alarms: the math

At one replacement every 5 years,2 each sleeping area needs 6 alarms over 30 years. A home with 3 sleeping areas needs 18.

Store spares with the batteries they take. Check the date printed on each spare before you fit it.

The rules never expire. Teach them to every child in the household, so the next generation runs the home the same way.

  9. FERC: Final Report on February 2021 Freeze Underscores Winterization Recommendations (2021). More than 4.5 million Texans lost power, some for up to 4 days.
  10. Texas Department of State Health Services: February 2021 Winter Storm-Related Deaths (2021). Final count of 246 deaths; about two-thirds from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.
  11. New England Journal of Medicine: Mortality in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria (Kishore et al.) (2018). Household survey: an average of 84 days without power.
  12. EIA: Today in Energy, US electricity outages in 2024 (2025). Hurricane Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states.
  13. NFPA: How to Make a Home Fire Escape Plan (n.d.). Practice twice a year, day and night; two ways out of every room; never go back inside.
  14. American Heart Association: Part 7, Adult Basic Life Support, 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC (Circulation) (2025). Start CPR when a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally or only gasping; use an AED as soon as one is available.
  15. American Red Cross: Check, Call, Care: 3 Emergency Action Steps to Take to Save Lives (n.d.). Keeping yourself safe helps you take care of others.

Security & Community

Staying safe through deterrence, a low profile, de-escalation and strong neighbors, plus trade, group rules and safe firearm storage.

🛡️ Part 11 · Security & CommunityChapter 134
🤝

Organizing Neighbors: Mutual Aid & Watch

🟢 CoreFirst 30 daysYear 1📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Check on your neighbors first. Ready.gov puts it on the power outage to-do list, because older adults and young children are most at risk from heat and cold.1
  • Hold a block meeting in week 1. Write one paper sheet: who lives where, who needs help, who has which skills, and one meeting place everyone can reach.10
  • Register anyone who depends on powered medical equipment. After Hurricane Maria, about 1 in 3 excess deaths was linked to delayed or interrupted health care.2
  • Watch in pairs. Observe, write it down, report. Never chase or confront. Six 4-hour shifts of 2 people need 12 person-shifts a day.
  • Shared kitchens: keep hot food at 60°C (140°F) or hotter. Bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F–140°F) and can double in 20 minutes.15
  • Generators, grills and camp stoves stay outdoors, more than 6 m (20 ft) from any window, door or vent, including your neighbor's.121
84 daysaverage time without power for surveyed Puerto Rico homes after Hurricane Maria (2017)2
1 in 3Maria excess deaths linked to delayed or interrupted health care2
3M+US Medicare patients with claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment12
37%US adults who made an emergency plan in the past year (2023)5

#🏘️ Why your neighbors are your first backup

In a long outage, outside help is slow and far away. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 households in Puerto Rico found they went an average of 84 days without power, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell service.2

Hurricane Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states in 2024.6 In Asheville, North Carolina, the water crisis that followed lasted 53 days.7

Without electricity, fuel pumps do not work. Outages also knock out lighting and payment systems.8 Driving away to find help is often not an option.

The people who die are often the ones nobody checked on. In the February 2021 Texas winter storm, 246 people died. About two-thirds of those deaths came from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia (dangerously low body temperature).4

After Maria, the poor and the elderly had the highest risk of dying, and older men had a 35% higher risk of death.3 Those are the neighbors a street can reach on foot every day.

📊 Key fact

Most households are not ready

FEMA's 2023 national survey found that only 37% of US adults made an emergency plan in the past year, down from 41% in 2022.5 Expect most of your neighbors to start with little. Organizing early turns their gaps into a shared plan.

For what research shows about how people behave in disasters, see How People Really Behave in Disasters. For group size and roles, see Building Your Group.

#🗺️ Map your block: the first meeting First 72 h

Start with the homes you can walk around in a few minutes. A small block that actually meets beats a big network that only exists on paper.

Everything you learn goes on one paper block sheet and one hand-drawn map. Paper works when phones are dead.

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. Knock and introduce yourself

    Go in daylight, with a partner. Give your name and house, and invite them to a short block meeting.

  2. Pick one meeting place

    Choose a spot everyone can reach. FEMA's family plan includes a neighborhood meeting place and says meeting places should be accessible to people with disabilities.10

  3. Hold a 30-minute meeting

    Agree on three jobs: check on each other, share news, keep watch. Keep it short so people come back.

  4. Fill in the block sheet

    For each home: adults, children, babies, elders, pets, medical needs, skills, and tools they are willing to lend.

  5. Draw the map

    Houses, the meeting place, water sources, and who checks on whom (buddy pairs).

  6. Choose a block captain and a backup

    The captain keeps the sheet. The backup keeps a copy in a different house.

  7. Set the next date

    Meet often at first, then settle into a fixed weekly time.

⚠️ Caution

Keep the block sheet private

Medical details and supply lists stay on paper with the captain and the backup. Do not post them on the notice board or online. See Keeping a Low Profile.

💡 Tip

Ask, do not demand

Let each household choose what to share. People who feel respected at the first meeting come to the second one.

#📡 Talking without phones or power

Text instead of calling while the network still works. The FCC and FEMA advise texting for non-emergency messages, keeping calls short and not redialing again and again, because networks get congested in emergencies.9

Limiting calls also saves your phone battery.9 Then plan for no phones at all: after Maria, homes averaged 41 days without cell service.2

Block communication methods, from most to least dependent on power
MethodNeeds power?Best for
Text messagePhone battery and a working networkShort updates while networks last
Two-way radioBatteriesWatch posts talking to each other
Runner (2 people)NoUrgent messages inside the block
Notice boardNoRotas, news, lost and found, meeting times
Window signNo"OK" or "HELP" seen from the street
WhistleNoAlarms using a code you agree on

Agree on a window sign. A green "OK" sheet or a red "HELP" sheet in the front window lets the morning check-in walker see at a glance which doors to knock on first.

A whistle is on Ready.gov's basic kit list.11 Agree on a short block code, write it on the notice board, and teach it to the children.

For licenses, ranges and batteries, see Radios: Ham, GMRS, CB & Listening.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Communication kit for the block

  • A whistle for every adult and older child
  • A notice board, pins, and a waterproof cover
  • Clipboards, pencils and a sharpener
  • Red and green sheets of paper or card for window signs
  • Spare batteries for any radios
▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print these while the internet works

FEMA Family Emergency Communication Plan (PDF): print one for each household on the block. FCC/FEMA tips for communicating in an emergency.

#🔦 Watch rotas people can keep up First 30 days

A block watch is eyes and ears, not a fighting force. Its job is to notice, write it down, report, and wake people up when something is wrong.

The rota must be fair and simple, or it falls apart within weeks. Do the math before you start.

Rota math for your block

  • Person-shifts per day = number of shifts × people per shift. Six 4-hour shifts × 2 people = 12.
  • Shifts per adult = person-shifts per day ÷ adults on the rota. 12 ÷ 24 adults = 0.5, so one shift every 2 days.
  • With only 12 adults, everyone stands one 4-hour shift every day, on top of water, food and child care.
Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Choose your posts

    One or two spots that see the street entrances and the meeting place. Fewer posts means a lighter rota.

  2. Always work in pairs

    One watches while the other writes or goes for help. Nobody stands a night shift alone.

  3. Keep a logbook

    Time, what you saw, what you did. Plain facts, no guesses about people.

  4. Hand over properly

    The next pair arrives a few minutes early and reads the log before the old pair leaves.

  5. Report, then rest

    Tell the captain anything unusual. Nobody stands two shifts in a row.

Do

  • Watch, write it down, report
  • Work in pairs with a whistle
  • Wake the captain when unsure
  • Rotate shifts fairly, including weekends
  • Give tired people a night off

Don't

  • Chase, follow or confront anyone
  • Punish or detain people yourselves
  • Stand a post alone at night
  • Talk about supplies at the post
  • Warm up with a grill or heater in a closed shed
⚠️ Caution

Observe and report: never confront

The watch calls people together; it does not fight. Avoidance and calm talk come first. See De-escalation & Avoiding Violence.

☠️ Danger

Cold watch posts and carbon monoxide

Never run a generator, grill, camp stove or fuel heater in a shed, garage, tent or car to stay warm. Carbon monoxide (CO) is colorless and odorless, and sleeping people can die before they feel symptoms.21 Dress warmly instead, and swap shifts more often in the cold.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Put women on the planning team and let them say which posts, paths and pairings feel safe. Nobody, and especially no woman or girl, should walk alone at night to a post, water point or latrine. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

#🧰 Sharing tools, skills and supplies Year 1

Not every house needs every tool. One shared, logged collection keeps each saw, ladder and wheelbarrow working for the whole block.

The same goes for skills. A nurse, a mechanic and a gardener on one street can cover gaps that no single household could.

Set up a tool library

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. List what people will lend

    Each household writes down tools it is willing to share. Owners keep ownership.

  2. Mark every tool

    Paint, scratch or tag the owner's house number on the handle.

  3. Keep a sign-out log

    One notebook, kept by one keeper. Every loan gets a line.

  4. Set three rules

    Return it clean. Report damage the same day. Bring it back by the due date.

  5. Hold a repair day

    Once a month, sharpen, oil and fix the shared tools together.

Tool library sign-out log (copy this into a notebook)
ToolOwnerBorrowerDue backCondition
Bow sawHouse 5House 2FridaySharp, clean
LadderHouse 3House 1Today, 5 pmGood
     

Share skills and trips

  • Skills board: list who can give first aid, fix bikes, mind babies, read a map or repair a roof.
  • Pool trips: fuel pumps stop working without electricity,8 so one cart or car trip should carry errands for several homes.
  • Child care rota: one adult minds several children so other parents can haul water or stand watch.

For trading with people outside the block, see Barter, Trade & Money.

#🍲 Running a communal kitchen safely

One kitchen for several homes means one fire, one cook rota and one set of hygiene rules. It also means one mistake can make everyone sick at once.

Food safety numbers for a shared kitchen (USDA, FoodSafety.gov)
RuleMetricUS
Danger zone: bacteria grow fastest154–60°C40–140°F
Hold hot food at or above1560°C140°F
Keep cold food and coolers at or below164°C40°F

Bacteria in the danger zone can double in as little as 20 minutes.15 Cook in batches you can serve hot, right away.

Plan portions with real numbers. Humanitarian food aid uses 2,100 kcal per person per day as its minimum planning figure.17 A kitchen feeding 30 people needs 30 × 2,100 = 63,000 kcal a day.

Food calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Cook outdoors, away from homes

    Ready.gov says camp stoves and charcoal grills belong outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.1

  2. Wash hands at a set station

    Soap and water before cooking, after the latrine and after handling raw meat. See Handwashing & Personal Hygiene.

  3. Sick cooks stay out

    Anyone with diarrhea or vomiting does not cook or serve until they are well.

  4. Serve hot, serve fast

    Keep food at 60°C (140°F) or above until it is served.15

  5. Do not keep risky leftovers

    Perishable food that sat out more than 2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F), gets thrown out.16

  6. Clean and dry everything

    Wash pots, ladles and boards with hot soapy water and let them dry in the air.

Disasters always cause epidemics.

A review in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases found that disasters which do not displace people rarely lead to outbreaks. The risk rises with crowding, poor water and sanitation, poor nutrition and lost access to health care.19 A clean, uncrowded shared kitchen helps keep that risk low.

Shared toilets need numbers too. UNHCR's target is 1 latrine per 20 people (or 1 per household), and no latrine should serve more than 50 people in the first phase of an emergency.20 Put latrines well away from the kitchen and water. See Toilets Without Water.

👶 Babies & children

Babies, children and pregnant women

Children under 5, pregnant people and adults 65 and older are at higher risk from food poisoning.18 Serve them first, straight from the hot pot. Rope off the fire area so toddlers cannot reach it, and give one adult the job of watching children during cooking.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs at the kitchen and meeting place

Keep dogs leashed and out of the cooking area. Feed them separately, away from people eating. Carbon monoxide poisons animals as well as people,21 so never shut a dog in a garage or shed with a running engine or heater.

☠️ Danger

Never cook indoors with a grill or camp stove

Ready.gov says to use generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills only outdoors, and never to use a gas stove or oven to heat a home.1 See Carbon Monoxide.

#🧓 Nobody left behind: vulnerable neighbors

Make a private list of every neighbor who could die without help. Then make sure someone checks on each of them every day.

More than 3 million US Medicare beneficiaries have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment. Counting dialysis, oxygen and home health services, it is more than 4.6 million.12

In a June 2024 CDC survey, 26% of adults with disabilities said they had nowhere to go in an evacuation, against 15% of adults without disabilities. 20% named the cost of evacuating, against 14%.13

Moving frail people can kill them too. Nearly 3.7 million people evacuated ahead of Hurricane Rita in 2005. Over 100 of at least 119 deaths were linked to the evacuation itself, including heat in vehicles and a nursing-home bus fire.14

The vulnerable-neighbor register: what to ask and what the block does
NeedAsk aboutBlock plan
Oxygen, CPAP, dialysis or other powered deviceBackup power, the provider's outage planFirst on the morning check; first call on any shared power
Lives alone, or has dementiaWho has a spare key; usual routineDaily knock and talk; buddy sleeps over in extreme heat or cold
Cannot walk far, or uses a wheelchairCan they reach the meeting place?Two named helpers; plan routes early
Babies and toddlersFormula, diapers, medicinesShared "baby shelf" of spare supplies
Pets and service dogsFood, leash, vaccination papersPet buddy who can feed and walk them

The daily check-in walk

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Walk the route every morning

    Two people, same time each day. Look for the OK or HELP sign in each window.

  2. Knock at priority homes first

    Elders living alone and anyone on powered equipment. Ready.gov names older adults and young children as most at risk from extreme temperatures.1

  3. Talk, do not just wave

    Ask about warmth, water, food, medicines and sleep. Look inside if you can.

  4. Write it on the sheet

    Name, time, how they are, what they need.

  5. Act the same day

    Bring in the medic, move the person somewhere warmer or cooler, or call help if it exists.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Elders and disabled neighbors

After the 2021 Texas freeze, about two-thirds of the 246 deaths came from cold exposure.4 A warm shared room at night and a daily visit cost little. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

👶 Babies & children

Children: ID and a reunion plan

After Hurricane Katrina, 5,192 children were reported missing; the last were reunited with family by March 2006.25 Give every child a card with their name, parents' names, house and the block meeting place. Ready.gov's kit list includes formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream:11 pool spares on a shared baby shelf.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and pets

Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, and vet clinics and shelters scan microchips to find owners.24 Keep a "lost and found pets" corner on the notice board, with a photo of each block pet.

#🩹 Train the block and keep it going Long haul

Every adult on the block should know how to stop bleeding and do CPR. Teach it at block meetings and practice it on a schedule. See CPR & Choking.

You need a certificate before you are allowed to do CPR.

An American Heart Association survey found many people still wrongly believe CPR requires special training.23 Learn it now, but never hold back in an emergency because you lack a card.

A generator is safe as long as it is outside.

After two 2005 hurricanes, at least 78 people were poisoned and 10 died from portable generators, and most cases involved generators outside but near the home.22 Keep them more than 6 m (20 ft) from every window, door and vent on the street.21

  1. Day 1

    Check on the neighbors on each side and across the street. Put up OK or HELP signs.

  2. Week 1

    First block meeting. Block sheet, map, captain, backup, meeting place.

  3. Week 2

    Watch rota starts. Daily check-in walk. Notice board up.

  4. Month 1

    Shared kitchen and latrine rules. Tool library log. Skills board.

  5. Year 1

    Monthly first aid practice. Rotate captains. Recount adults and redo the rota math.

  6. Year 5 and beyond

    Teenagers learn each role. Written rules and records outlast any one leader.

🎯 Practice now

Practice this now while help still exists

Ask your local emergency management office or Red Cross chapter what volunteer disaster and first aid training they offer, and go with a neighbor. Then run one practice: a 30-minute block meeting and one full day of the check-in walk.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Over decades, people tire, fall ill, move away and die. Rotate every role, write the rules down, and keep the block sheet updated each season. When disputes come, use agreed rules, not the loudest voice. See Group Rules, Decisions & Resolving Disputes.

#✅ Do this now

0 / 10 done

#🧠 Remember this

After Maria, how long were homes without power on average?

84 days. Also 68 days without water and 41 without cell service.

What share of Maria's excess deaths was linked to interrupted health care?

About 1 in 3. Register neighbors on powered equipment and check them first.

How do you work out a watch rota?

Shifts × people per shift = person-shifts. Divide by the adults on the rota.

What does the watch do when it sees trouble?

Observe, write it down, report and wake people up. Never chase or confront.

What temperature should shared hot food stay at?

60°C (140°F) or hotter until served.

How far must generators and grills be from windows?

More than 6 m (20 ft) from any window, door or vent, including your neighbor's.

How many people per latrine?

Target 1 per 20 people; never more than 50 in the first phase.

Scavenging & Salvage

Finding and reusing what is left lawfully and safely: what to look for first, what is still usable, and the hazards that injure scavengers.

🔎 Part 12 · Scavenging & SalvageChapter 139
📋

What to Salvage First: The Priority List

🟢 CoreFirst 30 daysYear 1📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Salvage only what you have the right to take. Your own things, things people give or trade you, and items covered by a community agreement. Taking without permission is theft. See Scavenging vs Looting.
  • Water containers first, medical supplies second, warmth third. After Hurricane Maria, homes averaged 68 days without water, and about one third of excess deaths were tied to interrupted health care.1 In the 2021 Texas freeze, about two-thirds of deaths were from cold.2
  • Only food-grade containers hold drinking water. Never use one that held bleach, pesticides or other toxic chemicals.4
  • Leave what has spoiled. Fridge food is safe for only about 4 hours without power. Refrigerated medicine is thrown out after more than a day unless its label says otherwise.1816
  • Weigh before you carry. Water weighs 1 kg per liter. Keep loads at or under 30% of body weight.823
  • Log every item, where it came from and who allowed it. Date it, check it, and replace what is used or out of date.1213
68 daysaverage time without water after Hurricane Maria1
53 daysAsheville's water crisis after Hurricane Helene, 20243
1 kgweight of 1 liter of water (8.33 lb per gallon)8
≤30%of body weight: the load ceiling for fit adults23

#📋 The priority list: what to look for first First 30 days

Salvage in the order that things kill. Records from long outages point to three big killers: no safe water, missed medical care and cold.12

After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a survey of 3,299 Puerto Rico households found they averaged 68 days without water and 84 days without power (NEJM, 2018).1 About one third of excess deaths were tied to delayed or interrupted health care.1

Texas linked 246 deaths to the February 2021 winter storm. About two-thirds were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.2

After Hurricane Helene in 2024, Asheville, North Carolina, went through a 53-day water crisis before its boil-water notice was lifted.3

So this book ranks salvage in that order: hold water, treat injury and illness, stay warm. Light, tools and materials come next. The ranking is guidance built from those records.

The salvage priority list
RankLook forWhy it ranks here
1Food-grade water containers with lidsMaria homes averaged 68 days without water1
2First aid supplies, medicines, soapAbout 1 in 3 Maria excess deaths: interrupted care1
3Blankets, sleeping bags, plastic sheeting, duct tapeAbout 2 in 3 Texas 2021 storm deaths: cold2
4Flashlights, batteries, battery CO alarmsCandles are a fire risk; CO alarms need battery power1622
5Wrench, pliers, multi-tool, manual can openerListed in the Ready.gov and Red Cross kits1314
6Fasteners, wire, rope, clothing, glass jarsRepairs, clothing and storage for the long haul

#🪣 Water containers: the number-one find

A clean container is worth more than the water in it. Rain, streams and wells can refill it again and again. Without one, you cannot carry, treat or store water.

Use only food-grade containers. The CDC says never to use a container that held toxic substances such as bleach or pesticides.4

Look for the number 2 inside the recycling triangle. Utah's emergency management agency calls food-grade high-density polyethylene (HDPE #2) the best choice.5 It also says milk jugs break down and become brittle.5

A lid and a tap beat an open bucket. CDC safe-storage guidance favors a small opening, a lid and a tap or spout. Hands, cups and dippers carry germs into wide-open containers.10

How many containers?

The Sphere humanitarian standard is 15 L (about 4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and hygiene.9 For a family of 4, that is 60 L (about 16 gallons) every day.

Arithmetic: two 20 L (5.3 gallon) jugs per person hold 40 L. That is about 2.5 days at the Sphere amount. Aim for enough containers to carry today's water and store tomorrow's.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Ask what it held

    Read the label and smell it. Reject anything that held bleach, pesticides, fuel or other chemicals.4

  2. Check the plastic

    Look for HDPE #2.5 Reject milk jugs and anything brittle or cracked. Light makes containers brittle and leaky.6

  3. Wash and rinse

    Wash with soap and water, then rinse well.4

  4. Sanitize

    Stir 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented liquid bleach into 1 quart (about 1 L) of water. Pour it in, cap, shake to coat every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, then pour it out.4

  5. Fill and label

    Fill with safe water. Write "drinking water" and the date on it.4

☠️ Danger

Fumes pass through plastic

Nebraska Extension warns that vapors from gasoline, kerosene and pesticides can penetrate plastic containers.7 Treat a jug found sitting beside fuel or pesticides as a non-drinking container. Store your water away from them.4

👶 Babies & children

Lids on, always, around toddlers

Drowning can happen quickly in less than 2.5 cm (1 inch) of water. Never leave a bucket or any container of water unattended.24 Salvaged buckets need tight lids before they come home.

Any big plastic jug or drum is fine for drinking water.

Only food-grade containers are safe, and never one that held bleach or pesticides.4 Milk jugs break down and turn brittle.5 Full storage rules are in Storing Water.

#🩹 Medical and hygiene supplies

Use the American Red Cross first aid list as your salvage list. It is written for a family of 4.12

  • Dressings: 2 absorbent compress dressings, 25 adhesive bandages, 10 sterile gauze pads, 2 roller bandages and 2 triangular bandages12
  • Tape and protection: 1 roll of adhesive cloth tape, 2 pairs of nonlatex gloves and a breathing barrier12
  • Ointments and wipes: antibiotic ointment, antiseptic wipes, hydrocortisone ointment and 81 mg aspirin12
  • Tools: tweezers, an emergency blanket, an instant cold compress, a non-mercury nonglass thermometer and an instruction booklet12

Most of the list is dressings and protection. Only four items are medicines or antiseptics.12 Sealed bandages, gauze and gloves are light, compact and worth taking in bulk. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit.

Hygiene supplies prevent illness. Ready.gov lists soap, hand sanitizer, moist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties in its basic kit.13

Found medicines: read the storage line first

Insulin: the FDA says vials, opened or unopened, may be kept unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days. Replace insulin that was exposed to extreme heat or cold.15

Other refrigerated medicines: Ready.gov says to throw them out if the power has been out for more than a day, unless the label says otherwise.16

The safety rules for found medicines, including expiration dates, are in Found Food & Medicine.

⚠️ Caution

Prescription medicines belong to one patient

A prescription was written for one person's body and illness. Before anyone takes a found prescription medicine, ask a doctor, nurse or pharmacist whenever one can be reached. Antibiotic facts are in Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and children

Never give aspirin to children.17 Keep salvaged aspirin with adult supplies only.

Ready.gov's baby items are infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.13 Put them at the top of the list for any household with a baby.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Elderly and disabled people

The Red Cross lists hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, syringes and a cane.14 These are small, light and very hard to replace.

In the US, more than 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment (HHS emPOWER).25 Batteries for that equipment are a top find.

#🔧 Tools, fasteners, fabric, glass and batteries

Hand tools

Take tools that need no power. Ready.gov lists a wrench or pliers to turn off utilities and a manual can opener.13 The Red Cross adds a multi-purpose tool.14

Saws, hammers, axes, shovels and files let one person do far more work. Choosing and caring for them is in The Essential Hand Tools.

Fasteners, tape and sheeting

Nails, screws, bolts, wire and hinges are small and light. Sort them by size into lidded jars or tins so you can find them in the dark.

Ready.gov lists plastic sheeting, scissors and duct tape in its basic kit for sheltering in place.13 Sheeting and tape also patch broken windows and leaking roofs until a proper repair.

Fabric and clothing

Blankets and sleeping bags come first. Ready.gov lists a sleeping bag or warm blanket, a complete change of clothes and sturdy shoes for each person.13 The Red Cross first aid list includes an emergency blanket.12

Wash anything that touched floodwater. CDC says to wash clothes that touched floodwater or sewage in hot water and detergent. Disinfect toys before children use them.19

Clean cotton cloth is the raw material for reusable pads and cloth diapers. See Periods Without Stores.

Glass

Glass jars and bottles store dry food, seeds and liquids. Do not use glass for water that may freeze. Use freezer-safe plastic instead.7

The Red Cross specifies a non-mercury, nonglass thermometer for first aid kits.12 Handle old glass thermometers and broken glass as hazards: see Salvage Hazards.

Batteries and light

Light the house with flashlights, not candles. Ready.gov lists candles as a fire risk in power outages.16 Ready.gov also lists extra batteries in its basic kit.13

Battery CO alarms are high-value finds. The CDC advises battery-powered or battery-backup carbon monoxide (CO) alarms, replaced every 5 years.22 Look for a date on the alarm before you trust it.

Car batteries and damaged batteries need special handling. See Salvage Hazards.

A generator is the best thing you can salvage.

Fuel pumps do not work without electricity (FEMA, 2025).20 A generator must run outdoors, more than 6 m (20 feet) from windows, doors and vents, and never in a home or garage.22 See Carbon Monoxide.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Ready.gov lists feminine supplies and personal hygiene items in its basic kit.13 Sealed pads, tampons and menstrual cups are light and high value. The CDC says pregnant women need more stored water, so containers matter even more.4

Salvage in pairs, never alone. See Personal Safety for Women & Girls.

#🏚️ Where to look, with permission

Start with your own home. Walk it room by room before you go anywhere else. List what you already own before you ask anyone else.

Then ask. This chapter covers lawful salvage only: your own things, things people give or trade you, and items covered by a community agreement. Taking from homes, stores or vehicles without permission is theft, and looting is a crime. The law is in Scavenging vs Looting.

Where to look, and what to watch for
PlaceLook forWatch for
HomesFirst aid kits, blankets, containers, water heater water11Fridge food is unsafe after 4 hours without power18
Garages and shedsHand tools, fasteners, tarps, buckets, cartsFuel and pesticide vapors penetrate plastic7
FarmsDrums, tanks, fencing wire, feed bucketsAny container that held pesticides is not for drinking water4
Hardware and farm storesFasteners, tools, sheeting, containersStock belongs to the business: agree terms with the owner
Vehicles (owner's permission)First aid kit, blankets, tools13Fuel pumps do not work without power20
Flooded buildingsMetal tools, glass, sealed itemsFloodwater can carry sewage and move chemical containers19

Vehicle parts have their own chapter: Useful Parts From Vehicles. Ready.gov advises keeping a kit in the car, so ask the owner about the trunk first.13

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Get permission

    Write down the owner's name, the date and what they agreed to. If no one can give permission, follow your community's agreement.

  2. Go in pairs

    Tell someone where you are going and when you will be back.

  3. Gear up

    Work gloves, a dust mask and sturdy shoes.13 In flood-damaged places add rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles.19

  4. Check before you enter

    Look for structural damage, gas smells and spilled chemicals. If in doubt, stay out. See Salvage Hazards.

  5. Work the list from the top

    Water containers, then medical supplies, then warmth. Stop when your load limit is reached.

  6. Log it

    Record each item, the place and who allowed it, before it joins the group store.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs

Leave dogs at home or on a short leash during salvage. Floodwater can carry sewage and chemicals.19

Worth finding for your dog: collar, leash, ID tag, food, carrier and bowl (Red Cross).14 Ready.gov adds extra water for your pet, so count the dog when you count containers.13

#⏳ What spoils fast and what lasts

Time decides value. Some finds are unsafe within hours. Others keep their value for years if you store them well.

Food in a dead fridge is the fastest to go. USDA says a fridge keeps food safe for about 4 hours if the door stays closed. A full freezer holds about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.18 Days later, that food is not a salvage find.

Bleach weakens with age. EPA's emergency method calls for bleach stored at room temperature for less than one year.21 Use a found bottle with no date for cleaning, not for treating drinking water.

Plastic weakens in light. Be Ready Utah says sunlight, and even artificial light, makes containers brittle or leaky.6 A barrel that sat in a sunny yard is a lower-value find than one from a dark shed.

Short-lived: use now or leave

  • Food from a fridge or freezer without power18
  • Refrigerated medicines kept warm16
  • Undated bleach21
  • Milk jugs5

Keeps its value if stored well

  • Metal hand tools, kept dry and oiled
  • Glass jars and bottles
  • Fasteners in sealed tins
  • HDPE containers kept out of light6
  • Wool and cotton kept dry and away from pests
⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Even good finds wear out. Containers in sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.6 CO alarms need replacing every 5 years.22 Stored bleach is a first-year tool.21

Plan salvage as a cycle, not a one-time haul. Log a replace-by date for every item that wears out.

#⚖️ Weight vs value: carry it or leave it?

Water is the heaviest thing you will move. One liter weighs 1 kg (2.2 lb). One US gallon weighs 8.33 lb (3.8 kg).8

A 2018 study in Military Medicine notes that loads of 30% of body mass or less are recommended to avoid drops in performance.23 Those were fit soldiers. Treat 30% as a ceiling, not a target.

The 30% ceiling, and how much water that equals (arithmetic)
Body weight30% ceilingEquals this much water
50 kg (110 lb)15 kg (33 lb)15 L (4.0 gal)
70 kg (154 lb)21 kg (46 lb)21 L (5.5 gal)
90 kg (198 lb)27 kg (60 lb)27 L (7.1 gal)

Do the family math. At the Sphere amount of 15 L per person per day, a family of 4 needs 60 L (60 kg) of water a day.98 A 70 kg adult at the 30% ceiling carries 21 kg.23 That is 3 full loads every day. Carts and wheelbarrows are high-value finds. See Bicycles, Carts & Moving Loads.

Value per kilogram matters too. A pack of gauze, a pair of glasses or a box of batteries weighs little and is hard to replace. A heavy item you already own one of adds little.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Is it ours to take?

    No permission, no agreement: leave it.

  2. Is it safe to handle?

    Chemicals, fuel, flood soaking or damaged batteries: leave it and mark the spot.

  3. Does it meet a top-4 need?

    Water, medical, warmth or safe light: take it first.

  4. Will it spoil before we use it?

    If yes, take only what you will use now. Check the chart above.

  5. Can we carry it safely?

    If it pushes anyone past 30% of body weight, come back with a cart or a second person.23

Do

  • Carry containers empty and fill them close to where you use the water
  • Use carts, wagons and wheelbarrows
  • Split heavy loads between people
  • Mark heavy finds and come back

Don't

  • Walk long distances with full glass jars
  • Give children adult loads
  • Carry fuel or chemicals home in food containers
  • Take more than you can store dry

#📒 Inventory and sharing Year 1

If it is not written down, you do not have it. A log stops double counting, shows what is running out, and proves where each item came from.

The Red Cross says to check first aid kit expiration dates and replace anything used or out of date.12 Ready.gov says to replace expired items and re-think your needs every year.13 The CDC says to label stored water with the date.4

Example salvage log (one line per item)
Item and countFrom, and who allowed itCheck or replace by
2 HDPE #2 jugs, 20 LNeighbor's garage; owner, 3 MayRefill water every 6 months4
1 bottle liquid bleach, datedOwn home1 year from the date21
1 battery CO alarmGroup store, by agreement5 years from its date22
  1. Every day

    Check lids, water levels and that every log entry has a place.

  2. Every 6 months

    Replace water you bottled yourself.4

  3. Every year

    Replace bleach that is a year old.21 Re-think the group's needs and replace expired items.13

  4. Every 5 years

    Replace CO alarms.22 Inspect barrels and jugs for brittleness.6

Sharing by need

Share water by need, drinking first. Sphere puts drinking and food at 2.5–3 L per person per day, within basic survival needs of 7.5–15 L.9 The CDC says pregnant women, sick people and hot climates need more.4

Share heavy tools, not just food. A group can keep one set of saws, ladders and carts with a sign-out sheet. That leaves more carrying capacity for water and medical supplies.

Write the sharing rules before you need them. See Organizing Neighbors. Turning leftovers into tools is in Repurposing Junk.

🎯 Practice now

Do a salvage audit of your own home this week

Walk each room with the floor plan above. List every container, first aid item, blanket, tool and battery you already own. Then you know what is worth asking others for.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • Food-grade water jugs with a tap or spout10
  • Rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles19
  • Work gloves and dust masks13
  • A waterproof marker, labels and a notebook for the log4
▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print these while the internet works

  • Red Cross: Anatomy of a First Aid Kit, your medical salvage list12
  • Ready.gov: Build a Kit, the basic supply list13
  • CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply, container rules4

#✅ Do this now

0 / 9 done

#🧠 Remember this

What are the first three salvage priorities?

Water containers, medical and hygiene supplies, then warmth: blankets, sleeping bags and sheeting.

Which plastic number marks a good water container?

HDPE #2, food-grade. Never one that held bleach, pesticides or fuel.

How much water does Sphere set per person per day?

15 L (about 4 gallons) for drinking, cooking and hygiene.

How heavy is a liter of water?

1 kg (2.2 lb). A US gallon is 8.33 lb.

What is the load ceiling for a fit adult?

30% of body weight. A 70 kg adult: 21 kg.

How long is fridge food safe with no power?

About 4 hours with the door closed. Full freezer: about 48 hours.

What goes in the salvage log?

Item, count, where it came from, who allowed it, and the check or replace date.
