Repurposing Junk Into Useful Things

🔵 Long haulYear 1Long haul📚 20 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Know what it held before you reuse it. The CDC says a container that held toxic chemicals, such as bleach or pesticides, must never hold drinking water.1
  • For food and water, reuse only food-grade plastic. Look for the 2 in the recycling triangle: high-density polyethylene (HDPE). Heavy-duty, food-grade #1 (PETE) is also accepted.23
  • Milk and juice jugs get non-food jobs. Their residue lets bacteria grow, and they turn brittle.42
  • Boiling does not remove fuel or chemicals. If you do not know an item's past, keep it away from food, water and fire.5
  • Put a lid on every bucket and barrel. A child can drown in less than 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water.6
#2HDPE, the best plastic for stored water2
5 yrsblue barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart7
458 lba full 208 L (55 gal) drum, about 208 kg8
<1 in(2.5 cm) of water can drown a small child6

#♻️ Three questions before you reuse anything Year 1

Over 30 years, worn-out and salvaged things become your raw material. Repurposing works when the right material goes to the right job. It fails when the wrong material ends up next to food, water, fire or a child.

Ask three questions every time, in this order.

  • What is it made of? Plastic (find the code), glass, wood, metal, or something you cannot name.
  • What did it hold or touch? Food, water, fuel, chemicals, pesticides or floodwater.
  • What will it touch next? Drinking water, food, fire, skin, children or dogs.

The answers decide the job. The CDC rule for drinking water is short: use food-grade containers, and never use containers that held toxic chemicals such as bleach or pesticides.1

Plastic picks up what sits near it. University of Nebraska–Lincoln (UNL) Extension warns that fuel and pesticide vapors penetrate plastic.9 The CDC says to store water containers away from gasoline and pesticides.1

☠️ Danger

Chemical containers never hold food or water

The CDC says not to use containers that held toxic chemicals for drinking water.1 Boiling does not remove fuel or toxic chemicals from water.5

Mark these containers NOT FOR FOOD and give them a non-food job, or leave them.

⚠️ Caution

Salvage lawfully

Repurpose what you own, what you are given, or what you have clear permission to take. Taking other people's property is theft. Looting is a crime, and many places punish it more harshly during a declared emergency.

The law and the ethics are in Scavenging vs Looting.

#🧴 Plastics: read the code, then clean it

Turn the container over and find the number inside the recycling triangle. Utah's Division of Emergency Management says to look for the 2. Food-grade high-density polyethylene (HDPE #2) is its best choice for stored water.2

Oregon State University Extension also accepts heavy-duty, food-grade containers stamped PETE (#1, polyethylene terephthalate) or HDPE.3

Resin codes and reuse for food or water
CodeWhat it isFood or water?
#2HDPEYes, if food-grade. The best choice for water.2
#1PETEYes, if heavy-duty and food-grade.3
#3 to #7Other plasticsNot named by the agencies cited here. Non-food jobs, unless the maker labels it food-grade.1
Any codeMilk or juice jugNot for water. Residue feeds bacteria.4
Any codeHeld chemicals, fuel or pesticidesNever for food or water.1

The number alone is not enough. The CDC asks for food-grade containers.1 A #2 bucket that once held paint or pool chemicals is still a chemical container.

A well-rinsed milk jug is fine for storing water.

Ready.gov says milk and fruit juice containers keep protein and sugar residue that lets bacteria grow.4 Utah's guide adds that milk jugs break down and become brittle.2

Sanitize a reused food-grade container

This is the CDC method. You need soap, water and plain, unscented liquid chlorine bleach.1

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Wash and rinse

    Wash the container with soap and water. Rinse it completely.1

  2. Mix the sanitizer

    Stir 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of unscented liquid chlorine bleach into 1 quart (about 1 liter) of water.1

  3. Coat every surface

    Pour it in, cap it and shake so the solution touches every inside surface.1

  4. Wait, then empty

    Wait at least 30 seconds, then pour the solution out.1

  5. Fill and cap

    Fill with safe water and close it tightly. Ready.gov's version of these steps is written for chlorinated tap water.14

  6. Label it

    Write "drinking water" and the date on it.1

💡 Tip

Write the job on the container

Use a permanent marker: WATER, FOOD or NOT FOR FOOD. For water, the CDC asks at least for "drinking water" and the date.1 A clear label helps a tired family member grab the right jug.

#🛢️ Drums, buckets and rain barrels

A clean, food-grade HDPE drum becomes a water barrel. Utah's guidance names food-grade HDPE #2 as the best plastic for stored water.2

Place it before you fill it. Water weighs 1 kg per liter (8.33 lb per gallon).8 So a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb). UNL Extension advises sturdy shelving for stored water because of its weight.9

Raise it off concrete and keep it out of the sun. Be Ready Utah says to raise containers off concrete for air flow. It also says blue barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.7 Utah State University Extension adds that plastic on concrete or dirt absorbs odors.11

Give it a lid and a tap. CDC safe-storage guidance prefers a container with a small opening, a lid and a spigot (tap). Wide-mouth vessels let hands, cups and dippers contaminate the water.12 The CDC also says to keep treated water in clean, covered containers.13

Turn a food-grade drum or bucket into a water station

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. Check its history

    It must be food-grade and must never have held chemicals, fuel or pesticides.1

  2. Wash and sanitize

    Use the CDC steps in the plastics section above.1

  3. Fit a lid and a tap

    Keep the lid on. Draw water from the tap so no hand or cup goes inside.12

  4. Set it up high and dry

    Put it on a pallet or boards, in shade, away from fuel and pesticides.71

  5. Fill with safe water

    For a full 208 L (55-gallon) drum, Oregon State gives 2 tablespoons (30 mL) of unscented household bleach.3 For other amounts, see Disinfecting Water.

  6. Leave room to freeze

    Where it can freeze, leave 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of headspace.9

  7. Label and rotate

    Write "drinking water" and the date. Replace water you stored yourself every 6 months.1

Rain barrels

Rainwater must be treated before you drink it. The CDC lists rainwater among the outdoor sources that need treatment.5 Utah State University Extension says the same.11

A rain barrel is a food-grade drum under a downspout. Roof math, gutters, first-flush diverters, screens and mosquito control are in Rainwater Harvesting.

⚠️ Caution

Drum stoves and burn barrels

This chapter gives no plans for drum stoves or burn barrels. For heat, see Heating With Wood. Never cut, weld or heat a drum unless you know it never held fuel or chemicals.

If anything burns indoors, fit a battery-powered carbon monoxide (CO) alarm. The CDC says to replace CO alarms every 5 years.16 See Carbon Monoxide.

👶 Babies & children

Lids on every bucket and barrel

Drowning can happen quickly in less than 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water. Never leave a water container open and unattended.6

The US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) counted 434 in-home drowning deaths of children under 5 in 2006–2010. 82% were under age 2. Its warning names buckets as well as bathtubs.15

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Size containers for the person lifting

A 19 L (5-gallon) jug of water weighs about 19 kg (42 lb).8 For older or disabled people, use smaller jugs, or a drum with a tap so nobody has to lift it.

#🔄 High-value conversions at a glance

Match each item to a job the guidance supports. This table covers common household salvage.

Common salvage and the use the guidance supports
ItemBest useKey rule
Food-grade HDPE (#2) drumWater barrel or rain barrelShade it.7 Treat rainwater before drinking.5
Food-grade bucket with lidCovered water container with a tapLid on, no dipping.12
Heavy-duty PETE (#1) drink bottleDrinking-water bottleFood-grade only, sanitized first.31
Wood pallet or boardsPlatform under water containersKeeps plastic off concrete.711
Milk or juice jugNon-food jobsResidue feeds bacteria.4
Chemical, fuel or pesticide containerNon-food jobs, clearly markedNever food or water.1
Glass jarDry food storageNot for water that can freeze.9

Pallets

Use pallets and boards to lift water containers off concrete. Be Ready Utah and Utah State University Extension both advise it.711 Before you burn or build with any salvaged wood, read Salvage Hazards.

Bicycles

Keep bicycles whole and rideable. Do not strip a working bike for parts. Repairs, spare parts, trailers and handcarts are in Bicycles, Carts & Moving Loads.

Tires and car parts

Check the vehicle hazards first. Tires, wire, mirrors and seat fabric, plus battery acid and lead safety, are in Useful Parts From Vehicles.

Glass

Do not store water in glass where it can freeze. UNL Extension advises against glass for stored water. It says to leave 2–3 inches (5–8 cm) of headspace in containers that may freeze.9

Glass jars for dry foods are covered in Mylar, Buckets, Oxygen Absorbers & Pests. Handle broken glass with thick gloves and sweep it up at once.

Metal

Know the metal before it touches food or fire. Zinc-coated (galvanized) metal and its fumes are covered in Basic Blacksmithing & Metal Repair. Old paint is covered in Salvage Hazards.

#☠️ The red list: what not to reuse

When in doubt, keep it out of food, water and fire. Every rule below comes from the guidance cited in this chapter.

Do

  • Reuse food-grade #2 HDPE and #1 PETE for water23
  • Sanitize before the first fill1
  • Store water away from gasoline and pesticides1
  • Wear rubber boots, gloves and goggles for flood-soaked salvage10
  • Disinfect flood-soaked toys before children use them10

Don't

  • Put water in a container that held bleach, pesticides or other toxic chemicals1
  • Store water in milk or juice jugs4
  • Trust boiling to remove fuel or chemicals5
  • Store water in glass where it can freeze9
  • Leave plastic water containers in direct sun7

Boiling or bleach will make water from a fuel or chemical drum safe.

The CDC says not to use water that may hold fuel or toxic chemicals, because boiling will not remove them.5 Its infant-feeding guidance adds that chemical contamination cannot be removed by boiling, disinfecting or filtering.20

Floods move chemical containers. The CDC warns about this in its floodwater guidance.10 Treat any container that sat in floodwater as unknown until you know what it held.

The CDC also says to wash flood-soaked clothes in hot water with detergent.10 Do that before cloth goes to rags, bedding or patches.

Materials to identify first

Do not sand, cut, burn or cook on these until you have read the chapter named.

  • Old painted wood or metal: lead paint, in Salvage Hazards
  • Building materials and insulation: asbestos, also in Salvage Hazards
  • Zinc-coated (galvanized) metal: zinc fumes, in Basic Blacksmithing & Metal Repair
  • Car batteries: acid and lead, in Useful Parts From Vehicles
  • Wood of unknown treatment: do not burn it, and do not build food beds or animal feeders from it
🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and salvage

Keep salvaged chemical containers capped and out of a dog's reach. Disinfect anything that sat in floodwater before it becomes a dog bowl or toy, the same way the CDC advises for children's toys.10

#🧰 Organizing a salvage workshop

Run every item through the same line. A fixed path keeps unknown and dirty things apart from food, water and children.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Quarantine

    Bring salvage to an outdoor holding spot first. Wear rubber boots, gloves and goggles for anything flood-soaked.10

  2. Identify

    Find the resin code, the old label or the material. Ask what it held. If nobody knows, it is non-food.

  3. Clean

    Wash everything. Sanitize anything headed for food or water with the CDC method.1

  4. Sort

    Green bin: food and water. Yellow bin: non-food jobs. Red bin: marked NOT FOR FOOD, or discarded.

  5. Label and log

    Write the job and the date on the item. Record it in a paper notebook so the group knows what exists.

  6. Store and share

    Keep food and water containers away from fuel and pesticides.1 Share surplus through your group; see What to Salvage First.

Workshop safety rules

Keep generators outside. Never run one in a home, garage or carport. Place it at least 20 feet (6 m) from doors, windows and vents.17 The CPSC says never indoors, even with doors and windows open.18

Fit a battery-powered CO alarm anywhere a fire, stove or engine runs near people. Replace it every 5 years.16

Plan two ways out. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) home escape plan calls for two ways out.19 Keep both clear of stacked salvage.

🎯 Practice now

Practice this now

While hardware stores are open, sanitize one food-grade bucket and fit it with a tap. Then spend 10 minutes sorting your garage into green, yellow and red piles.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get this before you need it

  • Food-grade buckets with tight lids, and drum taps (spigots)
  • A bung wrench for drum caps
  • Permanent markers and tape for labels
  • Rubber boots, heavy gloves and safety goggles
  • Battery-powered CO alarms, with spare batteries
  • Plain, unscented liquid chlorine bleach

#⏳ Keeping plastic useful for 30 years Long haul

Shade protects plastic. Be Ready Utah says light makes containers brittle and grows algae in stored water.7

Every container you protect is one you do not have to replace. Keep plastic out of the sun, off bare concrete and away from fuel.71

  1. Day 0

    Sanitize, fill and label with "drinking water" and the date.1

  2. Month 6

    Replace water you stored yourself.114 Check each empty container for cracks.

  3. Every year

    Look for brittle plastic and algae. Light causes both.7 Move brittle containers to non-food work.

  4. Year 5

    Blue barrels kept in direct sun can start to fall apart.7 Replace battery CO alarms.16

  5. Years 5–30

    Down-cycle: water container, then dry non-food storage, then parts bin. Re-label it at every step.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Your stock of food-grade containers is limited, so guard it. Never let a food-grade drum be borrowed for fuel, paint or pesticide. Once it holds a chemical, the CDC rule takes it out of food and water use for good.1

#✅ Do this now

0 / 10 done

#🧠 Remember this

Which plastic code is best for stored water?

#2 HDPE, food-grade. Heavy-duty, food-grade #1 PETE is also accepted.

Can a rinsed milk jug store water?

No. Residue grows bacteria and the jug turns brittle.

Can boiling fix water from a chemical drum?

No. Boiling does not remove fuel or toxic chemicals.

How do you sanitize a container?

1 tsp (5 mL) unscented bleach per quart (1 L) of water. Shake to coat, wait 30 seconds, pour out.

How heavy is a full 55-gallon drum?

About 208 kg (458 lb). Place it before you fill it.

Why a tap instead of a dipper?

Hands, cups and dippers contaminate water in wide-mouth containers.

How much water can drown a toddler?

Less than 1 inch (2.5 cm). Lid every bucket.

Hurricanes & Tornadoes

🟠 HighFirst 72 h📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Evacuate from the water, not the wind. Storm surge and large waves are the greatest threat to life on the coast.12
  • Inland is not safe either. Flooding is the major hurricane threat inland. Hurricane Helene killed at least 250 people in the US in 2024.13
  • Generators go outside, at least 6.1 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents. Never in a home, garage or carport.4
  • The deaths do not stop when the wind stops. Hurricane Maria's official toll was 64. A later study counted 2,975 excess deaths.56
  • Bathtub water saved before a storm is for flushing and cleaning only. Do not drink it, and keep small children away from a filled tub.78

⚠️ Caution

Not yet in this edition

Tornado shelter, mobile homes, window protection, chainsaws and downed power lines are not covered here yet. Those sections are still being checked against official sources, and this book prints only checked facts.

Until they are added, save your national weather service's tornado and hurricane safety pages while the internet works. Two official hurricane pages are listed in the "Download now" box below.

#🌊 Storm surge: the deadliest hurricane hazard

In a hurricane, water kills more people than wind.9 The National Hurricane Center (NHC) says storm surge and large waves are the greatest threat to life and property along the coast.1

Storm surge is an abnormal rise of seawater generated by the storm, over and above the normal tide.1 It is the sea itself coming onto the land.

An NHC study by Edward Rappaport blamed 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths from 1963 to 2012 on storm surge.9

That is why an NHC official put it so simply: "We evacuate from the water, not the wind, and we have evacuation zones."2 Learn your zone before the season starts. For the full decision, see Stay or Go?

Hurricane wind kills most people, so a strong house keeps you safe.

Storm surge caused 49% of US hurricane and tropical storm deaths from 1963 to 2012.9 On the coast, surge and waves are the greatest threat to life.1

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Download now, while the internet works

Save these official pages to your phone, then print them:

  • NHC: Hurricane Hazards (storm surge and inland flooding)
  • NWS: Hurricane Safety Checklist (printable PDF)

#🚗 Leave early, leave safely

A late, crowded evacuation can kill too. When Hurricane Rita threatened Texas, nearly 3.7 million people evacuated in 4 days.11

More than 100 of at least 119 deaths were linked to the evacuation, not to the storm itself.11 At least 10% were heat illness (hyperthermia) in vehicles, and a bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire.11

Do not let this keep you in a surge zone. The lesson is to leave early, with a plan and fuel in the tank.12

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Know your zone now

    Find out before the season whether your home is in a storm surge evacuation zone.2

  2. Keep fuel in the car

    Keep at least half a tank at all times. Fill up when an evacuation seems likely.12

  3. Plan where you will go

    Decide how you will leave and where you will stay.12 Check that the place accepts your dogs, since public shelters may not.13

  4. Leave early

    Go early enough that severe weather cannot trap you on the road.12

  5. Use official routes

    Follow the recommended evacuation routes. Do not take shortcuts.12

  6. Carry water for the drive

    Pack drinking water for every person and pet in the car. Heat in vehicles killed people during the Rita evacuation.11

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and other pets

Temporary public shelters may not allow animals.13 Find a pet-friendly place to stay before the season, not on the day you leave.

Microchip your dog. Vet clinics and animal shelters scan for microchips.13 Store extra water for pets, too.14 See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

🎯 Practice now

Practice this now

Do a timed dry run on a calm day. Load the car with go-bags, water, medicines, dogs and leashes, and note how long it takes.

Then drive your official evacuation route once, so you know it in the dark and in the rain.

Next, test-run the generator at its marked spot with the CO alarms switched on, so the first time is not during a storm.

#⛰️ Inland flooding: Hurricane Helene, 2024

Hurricanes kill far from the beach. For people living inland, NHC says flooding is the major threat.1

Hurricane Helene came ashore as a Category 4 hurricane on September 26, 2024. It caused at least 250 deaths in the US, making it the deadliest hurricane on the US mainland since Katrina.3

Helene left 5.9 million customers without power across 10 states.15 In the mountain city of Asheville, North Carolina, a systemwide boil water notice followed, and the water crisis lasted 53 days.1610

  1. Sept 26, 2024

    Helene comes ashore as a Category 4 hurricane.3

  2. After landfall

    5.9 million customers lose power across 10 states.15 Asheville goes under a systemwide boil water notice.16

  3. Nov 18, 2024

    After 120 water samples are tested, Asheville lifts the notice for all customers. The water crisis lasted 53 days.1016

📊 Key fact

How people die in sudden disasters

In rapid-onset disasters such as storms and floods, most deaths come from blunt trauma, crush injuries and drowning.17

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Helene left millions without power and a whole mountain city without safe tap water for 53 days.1510 With no grid for decades, your household has to store, collect and treat its own water.

Build that system now. See Disinfecting Water.

#🦠 Floodwater, wells and disease

Treat floodwater like sewage. It can carry sewage and chemicals. Swallowing water or food it has contaminated causes diarrheal disease, such as E. coli and Salmonella infections.18

Private wells must be tested and disinfected after floodwaters go down. Check with your water utility or health department about boil water advisories.19

Boiling, disinfecting and filtering cannot remove chemical contamination.20 If floodwater may hold fuel or chemicals, use a different water source. See Floods.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Check the water notice

    Ask the water utility or health department whether a boil water advisory is in force.19

  2. Gear up before cleanup

    Wear rubber boots, rubber gloves and goggles.18

  3. Do not bathe in it

    Do not bathe in water that may be contaminated with floodwater.18

  4. Wash what it touched

    Wash clothes in hot water with detergent. Disinfect children's toys before they play with them.18

  5. Test the well

    Test and disinfect a private well before anyone drinks from it.19

Dead bodies left after a storm will start an epidemic.

There is no evidence that dead bodies cause epidemics after natural disasters.17 Outbreak risk comes from displacement, crowding, and unsafe water and sanitation.17

Disasters that do not displace people rarely lead to outbreaks. Diarrheal outbreaks can follow contamination of drinking water.17 Keeping your household housed and your water clean protects you most.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and formula

Mix formula with bottled water until officials declare the tap water safe.20 Boiling cannot remove chemicals, so water touched by floodwater is not a safe base for formula.20

Disinfect toys that touched floodwater before a baby mouths them.18

#⚡ Carbon monoxide: the after-storm killer

Generators poison people after hurricanes. After two major hurricanes in Alabama and Texas in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with carbon monoxide (CO) and killed 10.21

Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.21 "Outside" is not enough. Distance matters.

CO has no color and no smell. People who are asleep can die from it before they have any symptoms.22

Generators are not the only source. CO comes from burning fuel in cars, small engines, stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces, gas ranges and furnaces, and it builds up in enclosed spaces.22 After a storm, cook and run engines outdoors only.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Outside only

    Never run it in a home, garage or carport.4 Open doors and windows do not make it safe.23

  2. Measure the distance

    Place it at least 6.1 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4 Use a tape measure the first time.

  3. Aim the exhaust away

    Point the exhaust away from every building.23

  4. Alarm the sleeping areas

    Put battery or battery-backup CO alarms near sleeping areas. Replace each alarm every 5 years.22

  5. Act on symptoms fast

    Headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain or confusion: get everyone into fresh air, then get medical help.4

Do

  • Generator outside, 6.1 m (20 ft) or more from doors, windows and vents
  • Exhaust pointed away from the house
  • Battery CO alarms near sleeping areas
  • An extension cord longer than 6.1 m (20 ft)

Don't

  • Run it in a garage or carport, even with the door open
  • Set it just outside a door or window
  • Heat the home with a gas oven4
  • Run a car in a garage or carport4

A generator is safe in the garage if the big door is open.

Never use a generator inside a home or garage, even with doors and windows open.23 Keep it at least 6.1 m (20 ft) from doors, windows and vents.4

☠️ Danger

Who is at higher risk

Infants, older people, and people with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems are at higher risk from CO.22 CO poisons animals too, so dogs shut in with a running engine are in danger.22

Full details are in Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before storm season

  • Battery or battery-backup CO alarms for each sleeping area22
  • An extension cord longer than 6.1 m (20 ft), so the generator can stay far away
  • A tape measure and paint to mark the generator spot

#💧 Store water before landfall, then guard it

Fill your bathtub and large containers before the storm. Use the bathtub water for cleaning and flushing toilets only. Do not drink it.7

For drinking, store at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day for at least 3 days, and for 2 weeks if you can.14 Helene showed why: Asheville's water crisis lasted 53 days.10

Use food-grade containers, never old bleach or pesticide bottles. Label and date them, and replace stored tap water every 6 months.14 Keep them out of sunlight and away from gasoline and pesticides.14 See Storing Water for Months & Years.

Water calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

👶 Babies & children

A filled tub can drown a toddler

From 2006 to 2010, 434 children under 5 drowned at home in the US. 82% were under age 2, and 81% of the deaths involved bathtubs or bath products.8

Keep the bathroom door closed while the tub is full. Never leave a young child alone near a filled tub or bucket.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy and stored water

Store more water if anyone in the home is pregnant or sick, or if you live in a hot climate.14 Count the extra before the season, not after the taps stop.

💡 Tip

Food after the outage

When the power has been off for hours, sort the fridge and freezer before anyone eats. Use the rules in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

#🧓 The long tail: deaths after the storm passes

Most of a hurricane's deaths can come after the wind stops. After Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico in 2017, the official death count was 64.56

A study commissioned by Puerto Rico's governor found 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.6 That is more than 46 times the official count.

A survey of 3,299 households found homes went an average of 84 days without power, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell service.5 About one third of deaths came from interrupted medical care.5

Once the storm passes, the danger is over.

Maria's official toll was 64.5 Researchers later linked 2,975 excess deaths to it, counted from September 2017 to February 2018.6 About a third of deaths came from interrupted medical care.5

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older people and medical devices

The poor and the elderly were at highest risk after Maria. Older men had a 35% higher risk of death.6

In the US, over 3 million Medicare beneficiaries use electricity-dependent medical equipment. Counting dialysis, oxygen and home health, the number is over 4.6 million.24 Plan a backup for every device, and write down how long each battery lasts. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

📊 Key fact

Insulin without a fridge

Insulin vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, may be kept unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days. Pens and other products differ, so check the label.25

Replace insulin that has been exposed to extreme heat or cold.25 See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Maria's deaths came mostly in the months after the storm, and about a third came from interrupted medical care.65

In a grid-down life with no outside help, plan to be your own water supply and your own first line of medical care.

The 30-Year Plan

Lessons from real long blackouts and sieges, and a phased plan to feed, heal, teach and govern a community for three decades.

Real Long Blackouts: Lessons Learned

🟠 HighYear 1Long haul📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Plan for months, not days. Puerto Rico took about 11 months to reconnect the whole island after Hurricane Maria.1 Surveyed homes averaged 84 days without power.2
  • Missed medical care was a major killer. About one third of Maria's excess deaths were linked to delayed or interrupted health care.2
  • Cold caused most deaths in the Texas 2021 winter storm. About two-thirds of 246 deaths were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia.3
  • Water stops when the pumps stop. Water disruptions hit more than 14 million Texans in 2021.4 Fill containers the moment the power goes.
  • A generator near the house can kill. Most generator poisonings after Katrina and Rita came from generators outside but near homes.5
  • Grids can be broken faster than they are fixed. Ukraine's power capacity fell from about 38 GW to about 12 GW between 2022 and 2024.6

#🏝️ Puerto Rico after Maria: 11 months to reconnect Year 1

What happened

Hurricane Maria hit Puerto Rico on September 20, 2017.2 About 11 months later, officials said every part of the island had power again.1

A Harvard-led team surveyed 3,299 randomly chosen households. From landfall to December 31, 2017, homes averaged 84 days without electricity, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell phone service (NEJM, 2018).2

Remote homes waited longest. In remote areas, 83% of homes had no electricity for the whole period studied.2

How many people died

The first official death toll was 64. The household survey estimated 4,645 excess deaths from landfall to the end of 2017.2

A George Washington University (GWU) study, commissioned by Puerto Rico's governor, estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.7 "Excess deaths" are deaths above the number normally expected.

Missed care killed people for months. The survey linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted medical care.2 The GWU study tracked excess deaths through February 2018, about five months after landfall.7

The GWU team found that poor and elderly people had the highest risk of dying.7

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults carried the most risk

After Maria, older men had a death risk 35% higher than expected.7 Put the medicines, devices, warmth and cooling of older relatives at the top of your plan. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

⚠️ Caution

First counts can be far too low

The first Maria count was 64.2 The study commissioned by the governor found 2,975, about 46 times more.7 Texas raised its 2021 count from 210 to 246.3 Always check the date on a number.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Puerto Rico's island-wide restoration took about 11 months.1 Thirty years is about 33 times longer (360 months ÷ 11), and this book assumes no repair crews arrive. Plan the long haul with Year 1 to Year 30: A Phased Plan.

#❄️ Texas, February 2021: up to four days in the cold First 72 h

More than 4.5 million people in Texas lost power, some for up to 4 days. Federal regulators found that frozen generating equipment was the main cause.8

Texas linked 246 deaths to the storm. The count rose from 210 in an earlier report. About two-thirds of the deaths were from cold exposure, mostly hypothermia, which means body temperature falling dangerously low.3

Water failed at the same time. Water system disruptions hit more than 14 million Texans.4

The lesson: a blackout of a few days can kill when it is cold. Most of the Texas deaths came from cold, not from the dark.3 Heat for the most vulnerable person in the house comes first. See Winter Storms & Extreme Cold.

👶 Babies & children

Babies and young children

Ready.gov warns that older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures. If your home gets too cold or too hot, go to a place with heat or cooling.17 Plan the warmest spot in your home for the youngest child first: see Staying Warm Without Heat.

☠️ Danger

Never heat your home with a gas stove or oven

Ready.gov says never to use a gas stove or oven to heat your home.17 Read Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer before winter comes.

#🚰 When the pumps stop, the water stops First 72 h

Tap water runs on electricity. Water and wastewater plants often use about 30–40% of a town's energy (EPA, 2024).18 Losing power for more than 30 minutes can disrupt wastewater treatment.18

Cleveland and Detroit, August 2003

On August 14, 2003, about 50 million people in the US and Canada lost power. The outage cut 61,800 megawatts of load across eight US states and Ontario.9

In Cleveland, the four major water supply pumps lost power. Taps gave only a trickle.10 Residents were then warned to boil their water.19

In Detroit, a boil-water alert covered 4.3 million customers. It was not lifted until August 19, five days after the blackout began.119

Asheville, North Carolina, 2024

After Hurricane Helene, Asheville did not lift its boil water notice for all customers until November 18, 2024.16 Local public radio called it a 53-day water crisis. The notice was lifted after 120 water samples were tested.15

Why it matters for health

A review in a CDC journal found that diarrheal outbreaks after disasters can follow contamination of drinking water.20 Keep toilet waste far away from anything you drink. See Toilets Without Water.

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Fill clean containers at once

    Cleveland's taps dropped to a trickle when its pumps lost power.10 Fill every clean, lidded container while pressure lasts.

  2. Separate drinking water from washing water

    Label them. Keep drinking water covered and away from flushing and cleaning water.

  3. Treat tap water when it comes back

    Boil-water warnings followed the 2003 blackout in Cleveland and Detroit.1911 Boil or disinfect tap water until officials say it is safe. See Disinfecting Water.

  4. Count your days of water

    Asheville's water crisis lasted 53 days.15 Write down how many days your stored water covers each person.

When the water comes back on, it is safe to drink.

Not always. Cleveland residents were warned to boil water after the 2003 blackout.19 Asheville's boil notice ran until November 18, 2024.16 Treat tap water until officials say it is safe.

#🏭 Ukraine, 2022 to 2025: a grid under repeated attack Long haul

Before 2022, Ukraine had about 38 gigawatts (GW) of dispatchable power capacity.6 Dispatchable plants are the ones operators can turn up or down on demand.

Ukraine lost 19 GW to occupation, destruction and damage in the first year of the full-scale war. After more attacks in spring 2024, about 12 GW was left (IEA, 2025).6

That is about two-thirds of the capacity gone (38 − 12 = 26 GW; 26 ÷ 38 ≈ 68%). The attacks continued. On September 7–8, 2025, Russia carried out its largest air attack on Ukraine since February 2022, with major damage to energy infrastructure.6

The lesson: repeated damage kept capacity far below its pre-war level from 2022 into 2024, and major attacks were still hitting energy infrastructure in 2025.6

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

This book plans for a grid with no repairs at all. Build household systems that need no grid: see Low-Tech Power for the Long Haul and What Fails When: The 30-Year Timeline.

#🏧 Spain and Portugal, 2025: 16 hours without cash or trains

On April 28, 2025, a widespread blackout hit Spain and Portugal. Subway networks, traffic lights and ATMs stopped.13

Full restoration took about 16 hours. The expert panel's final report (2026) found no single trigger, with voltage management at the center of the failure.12

Even a 16-hour blackout was linked to deaths. Early reports linked at least three deaths to it. In Galicia, police investigated carbon monoxide (CO) from a generator after an older couple and their adult son died at home.14

Money and fuel stop first

Payments and fuel need power. FEMA lists fuel pumps, lighting and payment systems among the systems hit by power outages (2025).21 Ready.gov warns that ATMs and card machines may not work, and says to keep cash in your kit.17

Plan for a world without cards. See Barter, Trade & Money After Collapse.

☠️ Danger

"Outside" is not far enough for a generator

After Hurricanes Katrina and Rita in 2005, portable generators poisoned at least 78 people with CO and killed 10. Most of those generators were outside, but near the home.5

Keep generators outdoors and at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows. Fit CO alarms with battery backup.17 See Generators & Fuel Storage.

#🩺 What studies measured: how long blackouts hurt health

The studies and official counts behind these cases point to five killers. Each one is documented:

  • Missed medical care: about one third of Maria's excess deaths.2
  • Cold: about two-thirds of the 246 Texas deaths in 2021.3
  • Generator fumes: 10 deaths and at least 78 poisonings after Katrina and Rita.5
  • Unsafe water: diarrheal outbreaks can follow contamination of drinking water.20
  • Heat during evacuation: overheating in vehicles during the Hurricane Rita evacuation.22

Leaving can kill too

Nearly 3.7 million people left the Texas coast in the 4 days before Hurricane Rita in 2005. Over 100 of at least 119 deaths linked to Rita came from the evacuation itself.22

At least 10% of those evacuation deaths were linked to overheating in vehicles. A bus carrying nursing-home residents caught fire in the evacuation traffic, and about two dozen people died.22 Weigh both risks in Stay or Go?

People who need power to stay alive

In the US, more than 3 million Medicare patients have claims for electricity-dependent medical equipment. More than 4.6 million rely on that equipment or on services such as dialysis, oxygen or home health care (HHS emPOWER).23

Ready.gov says to make a plan for any medical device that needs power, and for medicines that must stay cold.17 It also says to discard refrigerated medicine after an outage of more than a day, unless the label says otherwise.17

⚠️ Caution

Do not throw away life-saving medicine

The one-day rule has an exception. If a life depends on a refrigerated medicine, Ready.gov says to ask a doctor or pharmacist and to use it only until a new supply is available.17 Insulin vials and cartridges can stay at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days.25

Displacement drives outbreaks

A review in CDC's journal Emerging Infectious Diseases linked disease outbreaks after disasters mainly to displacement. Disasters that did not displace people rarely led to outbreaks.20

The same review linked outbreak risk to crowding, water and sanitation, nutrition, vaccine immunity and access to health care.20 A safe home with clean water and a working toilet covers several of those.

A blackout kills in the first day or two. After that, it is just an inconvenience.

After Maria, excess deaths were counted from September 2017 to February 2018.7 About one third were linked to delayed or interrupted medical care.2

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Plan period supplies, pregnancy care and a birth plan for months without power, not days. Puerto Rico homes averaged 84 days without electricity and 68 without water.2 See Periods Without Stores and Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital.

#⏳ How long restoration took

Restoration ranged from hours to years. Here are the documented times, shortest first.

  1. 16 hours

    Spain and Portugal, April 2025: full restoration.12

  2. Up to 4 days

    Texas, February 2021: more than 4.5 million people without power.8 Parts of the US also waited 4 days in August 2003.9

  3. 5 days

    Detroit, August 2003: boil-water alert for 4.3 million customers, lifted August 19.11

  4. Over 1 week

    Ontario, 2003: rolling blackouts in parts of the province.9

  5. 41 days

    Puerto Rico, 2017: average home without cell phone service.2

  6. 53 days

    Asheville, NC, 2024: water crisis after Hurricane Helene.15

  7. 68 days

    Puerto Rico, 2017: average home without water.2

  8. 84 days

    Puerto Rico, 2017: average home without electricity, counted to December 31.2

  9. About 11 months

    Puerto Rico: power restored to the whole island in 2018.1

  10. 2022 to 2025

    Ukraine: about 12 GW of 38 GW left after spring 2024; the largest air attack of the war came on September 7–8, 2025.6

In Puerto Rico, phones and water came back before power, on average. Homes averaged 41 days without cell service and 68 without water, against 84 without electricity.2

📊 Key fact

Even the longest repair was short next to 30 years

Puerto Rico's whole-island restoration took about 11 months.1 That is about 3% of 30 years (11 ÷ 360 months). Every system in your plan has to last far longer than any outage on record.

#🧭 Lessons for a 30-year outage Long haul

Each lesson below comes straight from the cases above. Each one turns a documented failure into an action.

1. Plan in months, then years

The Red Cross advises a 2-week supply at home.24 Puerto Rico homes averaged 84 days without power.2 Two weeks covers one sixth of that average. Start there, then keep building.

2. Medicine runs out first

The Red Cross kit list says a 7-day supply of medications.24 The FDA says insulin vials and cartridges can stay at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days; pens differ, so read the label.25 The average Maria outage was 3 times longer than 28 days.2

Talk to your doctor now about each daily medicine. See Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

3. Water before everything

Cleveland's taps dropped to a trickle when the pumps lost power.10 Water problems hit more than 14 million Texans.4 Store water and know your nearest natural source: see Finding Water When the Taps Stop.

4. Warmth and cooling are life support

Cold caused about two-thirds of the Texas deaths.3 Overheating in vehicles killed Rita evacuees.22 Pick one warm room and one cool room now.

5. Fumes kill people who are trying to cope

Generator CO killed people after Katrina and Rita, and police investigated it after deaths in Spain.514 Most 2005 poisonings came from generators outside but near the home.5

6. Cash, paper and neighbors

ATMs stopped in Spain and Portugal.13 Ready.gov says to keep cash, use flashlights instead of candles, and check on your neighbors.17

Do

  • Plan for at least 84 days, then for years
  • Fill water containers the moment the power fails
  • Treat tap water until officials say it is safe
  • Keep a generator outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows
  • Keep cash in small notes
  • Check on older and disabled neighbors

Don't

  • Trust the first death toll or the first repair estimate
  • Run a generator in a garage or near a window
  • Heat your home with a gas stove or oven
  • Drink tap water the moment pressure returns
  • Sit in hot evacuation traffic without water and a plan to stay cool
  • Count on card payments working

Test your household against the record

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. List every powered medical device

    Oxygen, dialysis, powered wheelchairs, home health equipment. More than 4.6 million US Medicare patients rely on such equipment or services.23 Make an outage plan for each one.17

  2. Count medicine days

    The Red Cross minimum is 7 days.24 Compare your count with the 84-day average from Maria.2

  3. Count water days

    Asheville's water crisis lasted 53 days.15 Write down how long your stored water lasts. See Storing Water for Months & Years.

  4. Choose a warm room and a cool room

    Cold caused about two-thirds of the Texas 2021 deaths.3 Pick the room now, not during the storm.

  5. Mark the generator spot

    Outdoors, at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows, with CO alarms that have battery backup inside.17

  6. Put cash and paper in the kit

    ATMs and card machines may not work.17 Add printed phone numbers and a written medicine list.

  7. Name the neighbors you will check

    Poor and elderly people had the highest risk after Maria.7 Write down who you will visit first.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs live through the same outage

The Red Cross lists a collar, leash, ID, food, carrier and bowl for pets.24 Count your dog's food and water in every supply total. See Dogs in a Long Emergency.

🎯 Practice now

Run a one-day blackout drill

While help still exists, switch off the power at the main switch for one day. Note what fails first: water, cooking, light, phones or medicine. Fix those gaps before anything else.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

A CO alarm with battery backup,17 flashlights and spare batteries,17 lidded water containers, cash in small notes,24 and extra supplies of every daily medicine your doctor agrees to.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Download these while the internet works

Ready.gov: Power Outages, the HHS emPOWER FAQ on electricity-dependent patients, and the Hurricane Maria mortality study (NEJM, PDF).

#✅ Do this now

0 / 10 done

#🧠 Remember this

How long did Puerto Rico take to restore power to the whole island after Maria?

About 11 months (2017 to 2018).

How long did a surveyed Puerto Rico home go without power, on average?

84 days. Also 68 days without water and 41 without cell service.

What share of Maria's excess deaths came from missed medical care?

About one third.

What killed most people in the Texas 2021 winter storm?

Cold exposure, mostly hypothermia: about two-thirds of 246 deaths.

Where were most generators that poisoned people after Katrina and Rita?

Outside, but near the home. Keep them at least 6 m (20 ft) from windows.

Is tap water safe the moment pressure returns?

No. Treat it until officials say it is safe. Detroit's 2003 boil alert lasted 5 days.

How much of Ukraine's power capacity was left after spring 2024?

About 12 GW, down from about 38 GW before 2022.

Why keep cash?

ATMs and card machines stop without power, as in Spain and Portugal in 2025.

🏗️ Part 15 · The 30-Year PlanChapter 164
🗓️

Year 1 to Year 30: A Phased Plan

🔵 Long haulYear 1Long haul📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Plan in four phases, not one stockpile. Live on stores (year 0–1), build production (years 1–3), make it last (years 3–10), then rebuild and hand on (years 10–30). One person at 2,100 kcal a day eats about 23 million kcal in 30 years. No home can store that.10
  • Year 1 is the build year. Puerto Rico needed about 11 months just to restore power after Hurricane Maria.13 Start every long-term system while stored food still covers you.
  • Everything stored has an end date. Fridge food about 4 hours, insulin out of the fridge up to 28 days, home-bottled water 6 months, bleach 1 year, CO alarms 5 years.35267
  • Protect the children born after the grid fails. Diarrhea is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months worldwide.17 Clean water, toilets and handwashing are your child survival plan.
  • Skills outlast supplies. The AHA says children 12 and older can learn CPR.18 Drill twice a year, every year.19
23 Mkcal one person eats in 30 years at 2,100 kcal a day10
11 moto restore power to all of Puerto Rico after Maria13
1 in 3Maria excess deaths linked to delayed or interrupted health care12
5 yrsuntil CDC says to replace a carbon monoxide alarm7

#🗺️ The 30-year plan on one page

This chapter turns the whole book into a schedule. For each phase it shows what to work on, what runs out, which skills to master and how your family changes.

Stored supplies are a bridge, not a plan. At the planning figure of 2,100 kcal a day, one person eats 22,995,000 kcal in 30 years.10 At the CDC minimum of 1 gallon a day, they need 10,950 gallons (about 41,450 liters) of water.2

Real outages already last months. Homes surveyed in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria averaged 84 days without power.12 In Ukraine, attacks cut dispatchable power capacity from about 38 GW before 2022 to about 12 GW after spring 2024.14

This book plans for the longer case: 30 years with no grid and no repair crews. For the real events in detail, read Real Long Blackouts.

The four phases at a glance
PhaseMain jobMove on when
1. Stores
Year 0–1		Live on stores. Ration food, never water. Start water, toilet and garden systems.Your water comes from a system you run, and the first harvest is in.
2. Production
Years 1–3		Grow, raise and preserve food. Replace each store before it runs out.Food you produce covers most meals, and you saved seed for next year.
3. Make it last
Years 3–10		Keep tools, health, soil and skills working. Teach the children.At least two people can do every critical job.
4. Rebuild
Years 10–30		Trades, records and community health. Hand everything on.People born after the grid failed can run the systems.

Long outages end in a few days, so a 3-day kit is enough.

Puerto Rico homes averaged 84 days without power after Maria,12 and the whole island took about 11 months.13 The Red Cross 3-day supply is for evacuation; it advises 2 weeks at home.1

💡 Tip

How to use this chapter

Find your phase. Read that section. Tick its milestones at the end of this chapter. Then follow its links to the detailed chapters.

#📦 Phase 1 · Year 0–1: Live on stores, build systems Year 1

Your job in year 1 is to stretch what you have and start what replaces it. Do not wait for stores to run low. The first weeks are covered in The First 72 Hours and The First 30 Days.

What runs out in Phase 1

  1. Hour 0

    ATMs and card machines may not work. Ready.gov says to keep some cash.4

  2. Hour 4

    Food in a closed fridge stays safe for about 4 hours.3

  3. Day 1–2

    A full freezer holds about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.3 Refrigerated medicine: discard after more than a day without power unless the label says otherwise.4

  4. Day 14

    The end of a Red Cross 2-week home supply.1

  5. Day 28

    Insulin vials and cartridges can stay out of the fridge for up to 28 days, and only at 15–30°C (59–86°F).5

  6. Month 6

    Water you bottled yourself is due for replacement.2

  7. Month 12

    Bleach passes the 1-year age that EPA's water disinfection method uses.6

Ration food, never water. FEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can live on half their usual food for an extended period, but children and pregnant women should not be rationed.11

A normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (about 2 liters) a day. Drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow.11

Do the year math once, on paper. A family of 4 at 2,100 kcal each eats 3,066,000 kcal a year.10 Add up the kcal printed on your stored food, divide by your family's yearly number, and you know how much of the year your stores cover.

Food calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Set up the year-1 systems

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Count everything

    Food in kcal, water in liters, medicine in days. Write the totals on the wall.

  2. Set the ration

    Half portions for healthy adults only if needed. Full portions for children and pregnant women.11

  3. Build the water system

    A source, a way to treat it and clean storage. Read Rainwater Harvesting and Disinfecting Water.

  4. Build the toilet system

    Do it before stored supplies of bags and wipes run out. Read Composting Toilets.

  5. Plant the first beds

    Check days to harvest on each seed packet. Plan food for the gap until harvest. Read Survival Gardening.

  6. Write a plan for each daily medicine

    List the medicine, the dose and the days left. Read Chronic Conditions Without Pharmacies.

📊 Key fact

Missed medical care killed slowly in Puerto Rico

About one third of the excess deaths after Hurricane Maria were linked to delayed or interrupted health care.12 Researchers found the poor and the elderly at highest risk.25 Medical continuity is a Phase 1 job, not a later one.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Cold medicines and powered devices

If a person's life depends on a refrigerated medicine, Ready.gov says to ask a doctor or pharmacist and keep using it until a new supply is available.4

Make that plan with the doctor now, before the outage. Read Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

☠️ Danger

Carbon monoxide kills in every phase

Run generators outdoors, more than 20 feet (6 m) from windows, doors and vents, and never in a home or garage.7 Fit battery CO alarms near sleeping areas.7 Read Carbon Monoxide.

#🌱 Phase 2 · Years 1–3: Production replaces purchases Long haul

In Phase 2, anything you cannot grow, make or repair becomes a countdown. Your job is to replace each store with a working system before it reaches zero.

Rationing stretches a store. It never refills one. Only production refills it, so production gets your best hours.

Stores that run out, and what replaces them
Stored itemLimit in official guidanceWhat replaces itRead

BleachEPA's method uses bleach under 1 year old6Boiling, filters, biosandBiosand Filter

If we store enough, we will never need to farm.

At 2,100 kcal a day, a family of 4 eats about 92 million kcal in 30 years (91,980,000).10 Stores buy the time it takes to build production.

Production systems to start by year 2

  • Staple crops and seed: Survival Gardening and Seed Saving
  • Preserving the harvest: Drying, Smoking, Salting & Fermenting and Root Cellars
  • Eggs and meat: Chickens and Rabbits, Goats & Small Livestock
  • Fruit and nut trees: check how many years each tree takes to bear, and plant those first. Read Perennials & Fruit Trees.
⚠️ Caution

Bleach and iodine are first-year tools

EPA's method uses unscented bleach stored at room temperature for less than a year.6 CDC does not recommend iodine for continuous use beyond a few weeks, or for pregnant women or people with thyroid problems.9

For decades of safe water, plan on boiling, filtering and good sources.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs in the production years

CDC says to store extra water for pets.2 Carbon monoxide poisons animals as well as people.7 The Red Cross pet list includes a collar, leash, ID, food, a carrier and a bowl.1

By Phase 2, plan to feed dogs from your own production. Read Feeding Dogs Without Kibble.

#🔧 Phase 3 · Years 3–10: Make it last Long haul

Phase 3 is maintenance. Your systems now feed you. The danger shifts to things that wear out slowly: alarms, plastics, tools, skills and health.

What wears out in Phase 3

  • CO alarms: CDC says to replace them every 5 years.7 The alarms you fit in year 0 are due in year 5.
  • Plastic drums in the sun: Be Ready Utah says blue barrels in direct sun can start to fall apart within 5 years.8 Shade them from day one.
  • Medicines: every medicine has a date. The WHO 2025 Model Lists name 523 essential medicines for adults and 374 for children.24 Read Medicines: Shelf Life.
  • Kits: Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year and update the kit as your family changes.23 A newborn from year 0 is a school-age child by year 6.

Disease risk rises with crowding and poor sanitation. A CDC review of epidemics after disasters linked outbreak risk to displacement, crowding, water and sanitation, nutrition, vaccine immunity and access to health care.15

WHO reports that better water, sanitation and hygiene can save about 1.4 million lives a year (2019 estimates).16 Poor hand hygiene alone was linked to about 384,000 diarrhea deaths.16 Read Public Health for a Small Community.

Do

  • Train two people for every critical job
  • Keep a written log for each system
  • Shade plastic drums and tanks
  • Replace alarms on schedule
  • Teach children something every day

Don't

  • Let one person hold a skill nobody else has
  • Put off small repairs
  • Use food-grade drums for fuel or chemicals
  • Stop drilling once life feels normal
⏳ The 30-year view

Phase 3 builds the group, not just the farm

Shared work, shared food and disputes all need rules that everyone knows. Write your group's rules early, while things are calm. Read Group Rules, Decisions & Disputes and Tool Maintenance.

#🏗️ Phase 4 · Years 10–30: Rebuild and hand it on Long haul

Phase 4 is about handing knowledge on. The adults who learned skills before the grid failed are aging. The children born after it failed are growing into the workforce.

The math is simple addition. A baby born in year 1 turns 18 in year 19. An adult who is 50 at the start is 80 in year 30.

Older people need planned care, not leftover care. After Hurricane Maria, the poor and the elderly were at highest risk of death.25 Ready.gov says older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.4

Phase 4 jobs

  • Trades with apprentices: Rebuilding Local Trades
  • Power without the grid: Low-Tech Power
  • Records that last: Preserving Knowledge & Records
  • Teaching the next generation: Passing On Skills
⏳ The 30-year view

Year 30 is a checkpoint, not an end

At one replacement every 5 years,7 each sleeping area uses 6 CO alarms in 30 years. A home with 3 sleeping areas uses 18.

Every habit in this chapter, from the daily water log to the twice-yearly drill, carries on past year 30.

#👶 Children born after the grid fails

Plan for babies to be born in your group. Treat pregnancy, birth and childhood as core systems, not surprises. For methods and how well each works, read Contraception & Family Planning.

Add 10, 20 and 30 years to each person
PersonYear 0Year 10Year 20Year 30
Grandparent65758595
Parent35455565
Child8182838
Baby born in year 2not born81828

Young children die mostly of preventable causes. WHO lists diarrhea as the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months, with about 443,832 deaths in children under 5 each year.17

WHO estimates that unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene caused about 395,000 deaths of children under 5 in 2019.16 Your water and toilet systems are your children's survival systems.

Vaccinate everyone now and copy the records. After disasters, measles risk depends on vaccine coverage, especially among children under 15.15 The Red Cross says to keep copies of important documents.1 Read Vaccine-Preventable Diseases.

👶 Babies & children

Stored water drowns toddlers

From 2006 to 2010, CPSC counted 434 in-home drowning deaths of children under 5. 82% were under age 2, and 81% involved bathtubs or bath products.22 CPSC warns about buckets, too.22

A home that stores water for decades needs a lid on every bucket, drum and tank, every day.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy and breastfeeding come first

The protein RDA rises to 71 g a day in pregnancy and breastfeeding.21 FEMA and the Red Cross say not to ration food for pregnant women.11 CDC says to store extra water for them.2

Read Pregnancy Care, Emergency Childbirth and Breastfeeding before anyone in your group is pregnant.

A child's path through the 30 years

  • Ages 0–5: safe water, clean hands, toilets, warmth and full food rations.11
  • Ages 6–11: reading, writing, math and safe chores. Read Teaching Kids Without Schools.
  • Age 12 and up: CPR and first aid training.18 Read Survival Skills Kids Can Learn by Age.
  • Late teens: apprenticeship in one trade and one health skill.
🐕 Dogs & pets

Plan the dog line, too

The dogs you start with age along with everyone else. Decide early whether your group will breed dogs, and keep a record of each dog's parents. Read Breeding, Whelping & Dog Population Control.

#🎓 Skills to master in each phase

Supplies run out. Skills do not. Learn the Phase 1 skills now, while trainers, clinics and official courses still exist.

Skills to master, phase by phase
PhaseSkills to masterStart here
1. StoresCPR and choking, severe bleeding, water disinfection, CO safety, food safety, toilets and handwashingCPR & Choking, Severe Bleeding
2. ProductionGardening, seed saving, preserving food, small livestock, nursing the sickSeed Saving, Home Nursing
3. Make it lastTool repair, teaching reading and math, safe birth care, managing shared resourcesTool Maintenance, Childbirth
4. RebuildTrades, record keeping, low-tech power, training health workersTrades, Community Health
🎯 Practice now

Practice while help still exists

The AHA published its 2025 CPR guidelines on October 22, 2025, and says children 12 and older can learn CPR.18 NFPA says to practice a home escape plan twice a year, by day and at night.19

Most families do not practice. In 2023, only 37% of US adults had made an emergency plan in the past year, down from 41% in 2022.20

🛒 Get it before you need it

Buy for the long phases now

Choose things you can repair or reuse, such as hand tools, metal pots and wool clothing. Buy spare CO alarms and write the date on each one, because each lasts 5 years.7 Read What Fails When before you spend.

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Download and print while the internet works

Ready.gov Build a Kit, CDC How to Create an Emergency Water Supply, and WHO's 2025 essential medicines update. Keep paper copies with this book.

Tick these off in order. Each list is saved on this device. Review them at every drill, twice a year.19

#🧠 Remember this

What are the four phases?

Stores (year 0–1), production (1–3), make it last (3–10), rebuild and hand on (10–30).

How many kcal does one person need in 30 years?

About 23 million, at 2,100 kcal a day.

Who should never be put on short food rations?

Children and pregnant women. And nobody rations water.

How often do you replace a CO alarm?

Every 5 years: 6 alarms per sleeping area in 30 years.

How long can insulin vials stay out of the fridge?

Up to 28 days, at 15–30°C (59–86°F).

Third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months?

Diarrhea. Prevent it with safe water, toilets and handwashing.

From what age can children learn CPR?

12 and older (AHA, 2025).

Public Health for a Small Community
