⚡ The 30-second version

  • Water, latrines and soap come first. WHO linked at least 1.4 million deaths in 2019 to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene.1
  • Count on paper, every week. Tally new cases by sign, plus every birth and death. After Hurricane Maria the first official death count was 64; a study for the governor later estimated 2,975.45
  • Train health helpers in a few danger signs. Start with fast breathing in a child and dehydration from diarrhea.92
  • Mothers and young children first. FEMA and the Red Cross say food may be rationed, but not for children and pregnant women.18
  • When cases jump: separate, treat, find the source, block the route. Cholera can kill within hours, and most cases can be treated with oral rehydration solution (ORS).11
1.4Mdeaths in 2019 linked to unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene1
1 in 3Hurricane Maria excess deaths linked to delayed or interrupted care4
443,832children under 5 killed by diarrhea each year2
1 per 20people per shared latrine, the UNHCR target6

#📊 What really kills a community

Public health is the work of protecting everyone at once. A doctor treats one person at a time. A community that guards its water, latrines, food and records protects everyone together, and none of it needs electricity.

The numbers below come from WHO data and real disasters. They point to the same short list: dirty water, human waste, dirty hands, crowding and missed care.

Water, waste and hands

Unsafe water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) kill on a huge scale. A 2023 WHO report found that safe WASH could have prevented at least 1.4 million deaths in 2019. More than 1 million of them were from diarrhea.1

Hands alone matter. WHO linked about 384,000 diarrheal deaths and 356,000 deaths from respiratory infections in 2019 to poor hand hygiene.1

Young children pay the most. Diarrhea is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months. It kills about 443,832 children under 5 every year.2

Cholera is a current disease. In 2024, 60 countries reported 560,823 cholera cases and 6,028 deaths to WHO.12 Cholera deaths rose for a second year in a row, and by September 2025, 31 countries had reported outbreaks that year.25

Disasters: crowding and missed care

A review in the CDC journal Emerging Infectious Diseases studied outbreaks after natural disasters. Displacement was the main risk factor. Disasters that did not displace people rarely led to outbreaks.3

The same review tied outbreak risk to crowding, safe water and sanitation, nutrition, vaccination coverage and access to health care.3 A community can work on every one of these.

Missed care kills slowly. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, a household survey linked about one third of excess deaths to delayed or interrupted health care.4 Poor and elderly people had the highest risk of dying.5

Each threat has a community job
ThreatWhat the evidence showsCommunity job
Unsafe waterDiarrheal outbreaks after disasters can follow drinking-water contamination3One protected, treated water point
Waste and dirty hands384,000 diarrheal deaths linked to poor hand hygiene in 20191Enough latrines, with soap and water beside each
Crowding, displacementThe main outbreak risk factor after disasters3Keep people housed and spread out
Missed careAbout 1 in 3 Maria excess deaths4Health helpers, a register, a medicine plan

#🚰 Water, latrines and soap: the first medicine

Plan water by the head count. The Sphere humanitarian standard sets a minimum of 15 liters (about 4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene.7

Sphere splits basic needs into 2.5–3 L for drinking and food, 2–6 L for hygiene and 3–6 L for cooking.7 How to find and treat that much water is in Disinfecting Water.

One protected water point

No hands, cups or dippers in the water. CDC guidance says wide-mouth containers let hands, cups and dippers carry germs into treated water. Safe containers have a small opening, a lid and a tap.23

Big batches need measured bleach. The EPA dose is 2/3 teaspoon of 6% unscented bleach per 8 gallons (30 L) of clear water. Double it for cloudy, colored or very cold water, then wait 30 minutes.22

Chlorine does not stop every germ. CDC rates chlorine and iodine as not effective against Cryptosporidium, and boiling as very effective.21 Boil drinking water for babies and the sick whenever you have fuel.

Latrines and handwashing

Build enough latrines. UNHCR's target is 1 latrine per 20 people, or 1 per household. In the first phase of an emergency, no latrine should serve more than 50 people.6

Put soap and water beside every latrine. The Sphere standards call for handwashing facilities close to latrines.6 Building them is covered in Toilets Without Water.

Keep waste away from water. Diarrheal outbreaks after disasters can follow contamination of drinking water.3 Site latrines and garbage pits well away from the water point and the kitchen.

Field math for a community of 60 people
NeedStandardFor 60 people
Water per day15 L (4 gal) per person7900 L (238 gal)
Shared latrines1 per 20 people63 latrines
Hard limit, first phaseNo more than 50 per latrine6At least 2 latrines
6% bleach, clear water2/3 tsp per 8 gal (30 L)22About 20 tsp (100 mL) a day to treat all 900 L

Water calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

⏳ The 30-year view

Bleach is a first-year tool

EPA's method uses bleach stored for less than one year.22 At about 100 mL a day, 60 people would use about 36 L (9.5 gallons) of 6% bleach a year. Plan boiling, filters and pool shock for the decades after. See Disinfecting Water.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs and the water point

Keep dogs out of latrines, the kitchen, the water point and the sick room. CDC says to store extra water for pets, so count every dog in the water math.19 Rabies and other animal diseases are in Rabies & Diseases Animals Give Humans.

#🧑‍⚕️ Train your own community health helpers

Pick helpers, not heroes. A health helper is a trusted neighbor trained to spot danger signs, start simple care, keep records and send people on to a clinic whenever one works.

Teach a short list well. Drill the danger signs in the table below until every helper can recite them and act on them without looking.

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Choose at least two helpers

    Pick calm adults the community trusts, who can read and count. Two means one can rest or fall sick.

  2. Include a woman

    Women and girls can then choose a woman to talk to about periods, pregnancy and assault.

  3. Teach the danger signs

    Use the table below. Practice counting a child's breaths for a full minute.

  4. Teach a few safe actions

    ORS and continued feeding for diarrhea,8 CPR and bleeding control. Get formal courses while teachers exist.

  5. Give them tools

    A watch with a second hand, a thermometer, ORS sachets, soap, gloves, the tally sheet and the register.

  6. Meet every week

    Review each sick person, the tally sheet and the medicine count. Write down what you decided.

Danger signs every health helper learns first
SignWhat countsDo
Fast breathing, age 2–11 months50 or more breaths a minute9Pneumonia sign: get a clinician
Fast breathing, 12 months–5 years40 or more breaths a minute9Pneumonia sign: get a clinician
Chest indrawingWHO classes it with fast breathing as pneumonia9Get a clinician
Severe dehydrationLethargic or unconscious, sunken eyes, drinks poorly, skin pinch goes back slowly2ORS now, urgent care
Some dehydrationRestless, drinks eagerly2ORS, watch closely
Serious diarrhea signsBlood in stool, fever over 38.9°C (102°F), frequent vomiting, diarrhea over 3 days17Get medical care
Yellow skin or eyesWith dark urine or clay-colored stools14Separate toilet, get care

Full exams are in Assessing a Sick or Injured Person. For children, also learn Sick Baby & Child: Danger Signs.

⚠️ Caution

Helpers do not prescribe

Health helpers never hand out prescription drugs on their own, and never use veterinary, fish or aquarium antibiotics. Those decisions belong to a licensed prescriber. See Infections, Sepsis & Antibiotic Facts.

🎯 Practice now

Practice while teachers exist

Book every helper into a first aid and CPR course now. Once a year, count each child's breathing at rest for a full minute and write it in the register. A sick child's count means more when you know their healthy one.

🌸 Women & girls

Women as helpers

Train at least one woman as a helper and one as a birth assistant. Women's specific health needs are covered in Pregnancy Care Without a Hospital and the chapters that follow it.

#📋 Paper surveillance: count it, write it, compare it

Surveillance means counting the same things, the same way, every week. When one count jumps above your normal, that is your early warning. Paper and a pencil are enough.

Use fixed case definitions. WHO defines diarrhea as 3 or more loose or liquid stools in a day, and acute bloody diarrhea as dysentery.2 If every helper counts the same way, the numbers can be compared.

Cholera's typical sign is milky "rice-water" diarrhea, often with vomiting and leg cramps.10 Hepatitis A can cause yellow skin or eyes, dark urine and clay-colored stools.14

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Count new cases only

    Mark each sick person once, on the day the sign starts. A child sick for 5 days is 1 mark, not 5.

  2. Write one line per case

    The line list holds the details the tally sheet cannot (see the table below).

  3. Add every birth and death

    No exceptions. These two rows matter most over 30 years.

  4. Send even the zeros

    A sheet of zeros proves someone looked. A missing sheet tells you nothing.

  5. Compare with past weeks

    After a few weeks you know your normal. A clear jump starts the outbreak loop below.

  6. Keep every sheet dry

    Store them in a sealed container. See Preserving Knowledge & Records.

Line list: one line per sick person
ColumnWhy it matters
Date the first symptom startedLets you count back to the exposure. Cholera usually starts 2–3 days after exposure.10
HouseholdHepatitis A spreads by close contact,13 so cases cluster in homes
Water source usedA shared source points to the water
What they ate and drankTyphoid spreads through food, drinks and water contaminated by sewage15
Name, age, sex, signs, outcomeShows who is hit hardest and who died

Count every birth and every death

Death counts are easy to get wrong. After Hurricane Maria, Puerto Rico's first official death count was 64. A household survey estimated 4,645 excess deaths to the end of 2017.4

A study commissioned by the governor estimated 2,975 excess deaths from September 2017 to February 2018.5 Excess deaths are deaths above the number normally expected.5 You can only see them if you have been counting.

For each death, write the name, age, sex, date, household and the signs before death in plain words. For each birth, write the date, the mother, and whether the baby breathed and fed well.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults on the register

After Maria, poor and elderly people had the highest risk of dying, and older men had a 35% higher risk of death.5 Put every older adult on the health register with their medicines and the neighbor who checks on them. See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

🎯 Practice now

Run a practice month

Tally your own household's diarrhea, coughs and fevers for 4 weeks, starting now. You learn the form while mistakes cost nothing.

#🤰 Mothers, babies and young children first

Protect the people with the least reserve. CDC lists children under 5, pregnant people and adults 65 and older among those more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning.17

Feed them first. FEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can survive on half their usual food for an extended period. Food should not be rationed for children and pregnant women.18

Pregnant and breastfeeding women need more protein: 71 g a day in the US reference tables.20 CDC also says to store extra water for pregnant women.19

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy and water treatment

CDC does not recommend iodine-treated water during pregnancy.21 Give pregnant women boiled water, or water treated with bleach. Birth planning is in Emergency Childbirth: Step by Step.

The child health basics

Diarrhea: ORS, zinc and keep feeding. For children with diarrhea, WHO and UNICEF recommend low-osmolarity ORS, zinc supplements and continued feeding.8 Zinc shortens an episode of diarrhea by 25%.2

Take the zinc dose from a clinician or the package label. The full ORS method is in Diarrhea, Dehydration & Oral Rehydration.

Oral rehydration calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Healthy-looking children can spread germs. About 70% of hepatitis A infections in children under 6 cause no symptoms.13 Wash hands with soap after every diaper change.

Vaccination records are health records. Measles risk after disasters depends on how many people were already vaccinated, especially children under 15.3 Hepatitis A is also vaccine-preventable.13 See Vaccine-Preventable Diseases to Recognize.

The mother-and-child register

  • Every pregnant woman: due date, who will attend the birth, and the nearest working clinic
  • Every baby under 1: birth date, feeding (breast or other), weight checks, illnesses
  • Every child under 5: vaccination record and every episode of diarrhea or fast breathing
  • Every new mother: date of birth and any warning signs (see After Birth: Bleeding, Recovery & Warning Signs)
👶 Babies & children

Babies and diarrhea

Diarrhea is the third leading cause of death in children aged 1–59 months.2 In 2019, unsafe WASH caused 395,000 deaths of children under 5, including 273,000 from diarrhea.1 Babies keep breastfeeding through diarrhea.8 See Breastfeeding: The Survival Superpower.

#🚧 Outbreak plan: isolation, quarantine and response

Write the plan before the first case. Decide now where the sick will stay, who will care for them, and who tells everyone what to do.

Isolation separates people who are sick. Quarantine separates well people who were exposed, until the time when symptoms could start has passed. Infection control in the sick room is in Epidemics: Quarantine, Isolation & Infection Control.

Step by step · 7 steps

  1. Spot it

    One row of the tally sheet is clearly higher than your normal week.

  2. Check it

    Visit each family. Do the cases really match the case definition?

  3. Separate and treat

    Move the sick to the isolation room. For watery diarrhea, start ORS at once: cholera can kill within hours.11

  4. Find the source

    Count back from each first symptom with the table below. Look for a shared water source, meal or latrine.

  5. Block the route

    Close or treat the suspect water, fix latrines, add soap. Keep the sick out of food preparation.

  6. Tell everyone

    One short message from trusted people: what to watch for, what to do, where to bring the sick.

  7. Watch the window

    Keep tallying. New cases can still appear up to the longest incubation time after the last exposure.

Watch windows: when symptoms can still start
DiseaseSymptoms start after exposureLongest wait
CholeraA few hours to 5 days, usually 2–3105 days
Typhoid6–30 days1630 days
Hepatitis A15–50 days, average 281350 days

Do the arithmetic. If the last exposure to a hepatitis A case was on day 10, a new case can still start as late as day 60 (10 plus 50).13 For cholera, that window closes on day 15 (10 plus 5).10

☠️ Danger

Cholera can kill within hours

WHO says untreated cholera can kill within hours, and most cases can be treated with ORS.11 About 1 in 10 people get severe symptoms. With early, proper treatment, even people with severe cholera can survive.10 Start ORS at the first watery stools.

Setting up the isolation room

Do

  • Pick a room or tent away from the kitchen and water point
  • Name one carer per patient, and a backup
  • Put soap and water at the door
  • Give the patient their own cup, plate and toilet bucket
  • Write every patient on the line list

Don't

  • Let a person who had typhoid cook for others without a clinician's advice15
  • Let children visit or play near the room
  • Share cups, towels or bedding
  • Empty waste near the water point

The carer is the person most exposed. Hepatitis A spreads by close contact,13 and people who had typhoid can keep carrying and spreading it after their symptoms are gone.15 Care at home is in Nursing the Sick at Home.

Dead bodies left after a disaster start epidemics.

A 2007 review found no evidence that dead bodies cause epidemics. Deaths in rapid-onset disasters come mostly from blunt trauma, crush injuries and drowning.3 Still handle the dead with care and hygiene: see Death, Dying & Handling the Dead Safely.

If a child looks healthy, they cannot spread hepatitis A.

About 70% of hepatitis A infections in children under 6 cause no symptoms.13 Wash hands after every diaper change and every latrine visit.

💡 Tip

Coughs too

Hand hygiene is not only about diarrhea. WHO linked 356,000 deaths from respiratory infections in 2019 to poor hand hygiene.1 Put soap at the isolation room door for every kind of outbreak. See Handwashing & Personal Hygiene.

#💊 Medicines, chronic illness and records for 30 years

Missed care was a major killer after Maria. About one third of excess deaths were linked to delayed or interrupted health care.4 A community that knows who needs which medicine can act before supplies run out.

Keep one health register. For each person write: medicines and days of supply left, long-term conditions, allergies, devices that need power, vaccination record and any pregnancy due date. Update it at the weekly meeting.

Use the WHO Essential Medicines List as a planning map. The 2025 edition, published on 5 September 2025, lists 523 medicines for adults and 374 for children.24 Talk it through with a doctor or pharmacist while you can. See Building a Long-Term Medical Kit.

  1. Week 1

    Map the water point, latrines and isolation room. Start the health register.

  2. Month 1

    Two helpers trained in the danger signs. Weekly tally sheets start, zeros included.

  3. Year 1

    You know your normal week. Bleach bought before the outage is now over one year old.22

  4. Year 5+

    Helpers train new helpers. Birth and death registers show whether children are surviving.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Supplies run out; skills and records do not. Over decades, the jobs that last are the cheap ones: a protected water point, enough latrines, soap, a trained helper, and a notebook that counts births and deaths. Teach them to teenagers. See Passing On Skills to the Next Generation.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get this before you need it

#🧠 Remember this

What is diarrhea, by WHO's definition?

3 or more loose or liquid stools in a day. Bloody diarrhea is dysentery.

How many people per shared latrine?

Target 1 per 20 people, or 1 per household. Never more than 50 in the first phase.

Minimum water per person per day?

15 L (about 4 gal) for drinking, cooking and hygiene (Sphere).

Fast breathing in a child aged 1 to 5?

40 or more breaths a minute. 50 or more at 2–11 months.

Whose food is never rationed?

Children and pregnant women (FEMA and Red Cross).

How long can hepatitis A take to show?

15–50 days, 28 on average. Watch contacts that long.

What share of Maria's excess deaths came from missed care?

About one third.

Do dead bodies cause epidemics?

A 2007 review found no evidence. Still handle them safely.

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Build in tiers: 3 days, then 2 weeks, then 1 year. The Red Cross sizes a 3-day supply for evacuation and a 2-week supply for home.2
  • Water: at least 3.8 liters (1 gallon) per person per day. That is 53 L (14 gal) each for 2 weeks, plus extra for heat, pregnancy, illness and pets.3
  • Food: plan 2,100 kcal per person per day. That humanitarian planning minimum adds up to 766,500 kcal per person per year.7
  • At least 7 days of every person's medicines go in their bag, with a written medication list.2
  • Rotate on a paper calendar. Self-filled water every 6 months, kits every year, carbon monoxide alarms every 5 years.3113

#🗺️ How the lists fit together

This chapter is the packing and shopping list for the whole book. Every list is tickable, and your ticks are saved on this device. Print the chapter and tape it inside a cupboard door.

Work from the smallest tier up. First a 3-day bag, then a 2-week home supply, then a year of storage. The Red Cross uses the first two sizes: 3 days to carry when you evacuate, 2 weeks to keep at home.2

Long outages are real. After Hurricane Maria in 2017, surveyed households in Puerto Rico averaged 84 days without power, 68 days without water and 41 days without cell service.24 Two weeks is a start, not a finish.

Quantities per person

Multiply by people, then by days. Count babies, children and elders as full people. Give each pet its own line.

Store more water for hot climates, pregnant women, sick people and pets.3 In very hot weather, water needs can double.4 Why and how much is in How Much Water You Really Need.

One gallon a day covers all of a person's water needs.

The CDC calls 1 gallon a minimum.3 The Sphere humanitarian standard sets 15 L (about 4 gallons) per person per day for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene, and drinking and food alone take 2.5–3 L.5

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Count everyone

    Adults, children, babies and elders on one line each. Pets on separate lines.

  2. Pick the tier

    3 days, 14 days or 365 days.

  3. Multiply

    Amount per person per day × people × days. Use the table above.

  4. Write the total in pencil

    Families change. Ready.gov says to re-think your needs every year.1

  5. Tick what you have, buy the gaps

    Finish one tier before you start the next. Cheap ways to do it are in Prepping on a Budget.

#🎒 List 1: the 72-hour kit First 72 h

One bag per person, ready by the door. This list merges the Ready.gov and American Red Cross kit lists.12 Fit, weight limits and children's bags are in Go-Bags for Every Family Member.

Pack items in airtight plastic bags, in one or two easy-to-carry containers. Ready.gov also says to keep kits at home, at work and in the car.1

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Elders and disabled family members

The Red Cross lists hearing aids with extra batteries, glasses, contact lenses, syringes and a cane.2 Ready.gov adds contact lens solution and non-prescription medicines such as pain relievers, anti-diarrhea medicine, antacids and laxatives.1

Ask the medical provider now for a power outage plan for any device that runs on electricity.12 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

🌸 Women & girls

Women and girls

Pack menstrual products for every girl and woman who menstruates; Ready.gov lists feminine supplies in the basic kit.1 The CDC says to store extra water for pregnant women.3 Nursing mothers need more water too.6 Reusable options are in Periods Without Stores.

#🏠 List 2: the 2-week home supply First 30 days

This is what lets you stay home safely when power and water stop. The Red Cross sizes it at 2 weeks.2 The CDC asks for at least 3 days of water, and 2 weeks if possible.3

0 / 14 done

Cash matters because payment systems need power. The April 28, 2025 blackout in Spain and Portugal knocked out ATMs, traffic lights and subways.23 Ready.gov and the Red Cross both put cash in the basic kit.12

Ration your water from day one to make it last.

FEMA and Red Cross guidance says never ration water: drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow. A normally active person needs to drink at least 2 quarts (1.9 L) a day.6

👶 Babies & children

Never ration children's food

Healthy adults can live on half their usual food for a long time. Food may be rationed safely, except for children and pregnant women.6 Plan their full share first.

⚠️ Caution

Medicines that need cold

Insulin in vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, can stay unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days.11 For insulin pens, follow the label. For other cold medicines, Ready.gov says to discard them if the power is out more than a day, unless the label says otherwise.12

If a life depends on that medicine, ask a doctor or pharmacist and use it until a new supply arrives.12 See Medicines: Shelf Life & Expiration Facts.

Do

  • Store water at 10–21°C (50–70°F), out of sunlight3
  • Label each container "drinking water" with the date3
  • Keep boxed food in tightly closed plastic or metal containers1
  • Make sure everyone knows where the kits are1

Don't

  • Store water near gasoline or pesticides3
  • Reuse containers that held bleach or pesticides3
  • Keep the only kit in a car that might be gone
  • Hide supplies where only one person can find them

Containers, hidden water in the house and drum weights are in Storing Water for Months & Years. Fridge and freezer timings are in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

#📦 List 3: one year of storage Year 1

A year of storage is a bridge, not a destination. It buys time to get rain catchment, a garden and animals working. Build it slowly, from food your family already eats.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Read the label

    Find kcal per serving and grams per serving.

  2. Work out kcal per kilogram

    kcal per serving ÷ grams per serving × 1,000.

  3. Pick the share

    Decide what part of the 766,500 kcal this food will cover, for example half.

  4. Divide

    Example: half is 383,250 kcal. A label reading 350 kcal per 100 g gives 3,500 kcal per kg, so you need about 109.5 kg (241 lb).

  5. Write it on the list

    Repeat for each food until the shares add up to 100%.

Which foods keep for years, and how to pack them, is in Long-Term Food Storage and Shelf-Life Tables. Per-person calorie targets are in Calories & Nutrition.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view

Thirty years at the minimum is 10,950 gallons (41,450 L) of water per person.3 At 2,100 kcal a day it is 22,995,000 kcal per person.7 That water alone fills about 41 cubic meters (1,464 cubic feet) for each person.

Use stored supplies to buy time while you build production. See Year 1 to Year 30, Feeding a Family Forever and Rainwater Harvesting.

☠️ Danger

The kit aspirin is not for everyone

Never give aspirin to children or teenagers. Adults should not take it if they are allergic to aspirin, have bleeding problems or take another blood-thinning medicine.10 Keep all medicines locked away from children.

🎯 Practice now

Skills before supplies

Take a first aid and CPR class while classes still run. Then empty the kit on a table and name every item. Steps are in CPR & Choking and Stopping Severe Bleeding.

#👶 List 5: the baby kit

A baby's supplies run out fastest, and most cannot be improvised safely. Ready.gov lists infant formula, bottles, diapers, wipes and diaper rash cream.1 The Red Cross adds baby food.2

👶 Babies & children

Safe water for formula

The CDC says to use bottled water for powdered formula until officials say tap water is safe. With no bottled water, boil water for 1 minute and let it cool.16

For babies under 2 months, premature babies or babies with weak immune systems, the water must still be at least 70°C (158°F) when you mix it. Then cool the bottle to body temperature before feeding.16 Boiling does not remove chemicals.16 See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

💡 Tip

Count your own baby's numbers

Count diapers and feeds for 3 days. Divide by 3 for the daily number. Multiply by 14 for 2 weeks, or by 365 for a year. Babies change sizes, so buy ahead in the next sizes. Full lists by age are in The Baby & Toddler Prep Kit.

#🐕 List 6: the dog kit

Your dog eats and drinks from the same stores you do. The CDC says to store more water when you have pets.3 Ready.gov's basic kit includes pet food and extra water for your pet.1

🐕 Dogs & pets

Measure, do not guess

Fill the bowl from a measuring jug for 3 days and write down every top-up. Weigh one day's food. Repeat in the hottest month. Those numbers × 14 and × 365 are your dog's 2-week and 1-year lines.

Temporary public shelters may not allow animals, and vet clinics and shelters scan pets for microchips.18 Give a dog medicine only when a veterinarian has told you to. See Dogs in a Long Emergency and Feeding Dogs Without Kibble.

#🛠️ List 7: tools

Tools turn stored supplies into working systems. Start with the utility and safety tools on the official lists. Then add hand tools for the long haul.

☠️ Danger

Never run a generator indoors

Not in a home or garage, even with doors and windows open. Run it outdoors more than 6 m (20 feet) from windows, doors and vents, with a battery CO alarm inside.13 See Carbon Monoxide: The Blackout Killer.

Which hand tools matter most, and how to keep them working for decades, are in The Essential Hand Tools and Sharpening & Maintaining Tools.

#📄 List 8: documents and cash

Pack copies, not originals, sealed against water. Ready.gov says to save records electronically or keep them in a waterproof, portable container.1 Keep paper too, because phones need charging.

📊 Key fact

FEMA's free document kit

FEMA and Operation HOPE publish the Emergency Financial First Aid Kit (EFFAK). It has sections for household information, advisors and health care providers, and a checklist of documents.19 If a document is missing, contact the company or agency for a copy.20

Split copies across adult bags so one lost bag does not lose everything. Paper that lasts decades is covered in Preserving Knowledge & Records. The contact card is in The Family Emergency Plan.

#🔄 The rotation schedule Long haul

A list only works if the items on it still work. Write these dates on a paper calendar, not only in a phone.

  1. Every day

    Keep the car at half a tank of fuel or more.21

  2. After any use

    Refill what you took and re-tick the list the same day.

  3. Every 6 months

    Replace water you bottled yourself.34 Practice your home escape plan, once by day and once at night.22

  4. Every year

    Re-think your needs and update every kit.1 Buy fresh bleach, because the EPA water method uses bleach less than a year old.14

  5. By the label date

    Replace store-bought water by its date.3 Replace used or out-of-date first aid items.9

  6. Every 5 years

    Replace each carbon monoxide alarm.13

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Unpack one kit at a time

    Lay everything on a table with this chapter open.

  2. Check every date

    Replace expired items.1 Write the earliest date left in the kit on its lid.

  3. Use the oldest first

    Eat stored food in normal meals before it expires. New stock goes to the back.

  4. Refit for growth and age

    New clothes sizes, new medicines, a new baby, an older dog.

  5. Re-tick the list

    Write the next check date on the calendar before you close the box.

🎯 Practice now

Test it for one weekend

Switch off the main breaker and live from List 2 for 48 hours. Note every item you wished you had. Add those to your lists.

⏳ The 30-year view

When the stores never reopen

Rotation then means using and replacing from your own production: eat stored food in daily meals and refill from the harvest. Choose items that do not expire, such as metal tools, pots and wool. Ready.gov says to keep canned food in a cool, dry place.1

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Write the date on everything you store. Every limit in this chapter counts from a date or time you wrote down. The CDC says to label and date stored water.1
  • Replace water you bottled yourself every 6 months. Keep it at 10–21°C (50–70°F), in the dark, away from fuel and pesticides.12
  • No power: a closed fridge keeps food safe about 4 hours, a full freezer about 48. Perishable food above 4°C (40°F) for 2 hours goes in the trash.34
  • Insulin vials and cartridges last up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Other medicines labeled "refrigerate" are discarded after a day without power, unless the label says otherwise.56
  • Use bleach less than 1 year old for water. Replace carbon monoxide (CO) alarms every 5 years.78
  • Signs beat the calendar. Food that smells, looks or feels wrong, or is warm, gets thrown out. Never taste to test.93

#📏 How to read a shelf-life number

A shelf-life number is a limit under stated conditions. It tells you how long something stays safe or useful when it is stored the way the source describes.

Read the conditions, not just the number. EPA's bleach rule is for bleach stored at room temperature for less than one year.7 FDA's 28-day insulin rule is for 15–30°C (59–86°F).5 Outside those conditions, the number does not apply.

Every clock needs a start time

Label and date every water container when you fill it. The CDC asks for exactly that.1 Do the same for bleach, food boxes and medicine. A table cannot help you if you do not know when the clock started.

In an outage, write down the time the power went off. The fridge, freezer and medicine limits below all count from that moment. The first hours are covered step by step in The First 72 Hours.

Three kinds of numbers

  • Replace-by schedules. Water you bottled: every 6 months.1 CO alarm: every 5 years.8 Put these on a paper calendar.
  • Safety limits. Perishable food above 4°C (40°F): 2 hours.4 Past the limit, it goes.
  • Printed dates. Find out what a date means before you act on it. A CDC planning guide says the sell-by date on bottled water is mainly for stock rotation.10
⚠️ Caution

For medicine, the label wins

Ready.gov's one-day rule for refrigerated medicine applies unless the label says otherwise.6 If a medicine was stored outside its label temperature, the FDA says to check its storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, doctor or the maker.11

💡 Tip

Tables for other supplies

Dry staples, home-canned food, fuel, batteries and seeds each have their own chapter and storage rules: Long-Term Food Storage, Home Canning Safely, Generators & Fuel Storage, Small Solar & Batteries and Seed Saving & Seed Viability. Use the same three questions there.

#💧 Water and water containers

Store-bought bottled water is your safest stored water. The CDC calls unopened, commercially bottled water the safest and most reliable water in an emergency.1

Water you bottle yourself gets replaced every 6 months. The CDC and Ready.gov give the same schedule.12

Water: how long it keeps and when to replace it (CDC, Ready.gov, Utah)
ItemKeep forReplace sooner if
Store-bought bottled water, unopenedThe sell-by date is mainly for stock rotation10It sat in light: plastic turns brittle or leaky13
Tap water you bottled in clean, food-grade containers6 months12You see green growth (algae) from light13
Water you disinfected and bottled yourselfNot forever: check it for leftover chlorine10No chlorine is left: treat it again10
Blue plastic drum kept in direct sunCan start to fall apart within 5 years13The plastic is brittle, cracked or leaking13
Old milk or juice jugDo not use for water14Always: residue lets bacteria grow,14 and milk jugs also turn brittle15

What makes water last, or not

  • Cool: 10–21°C (50–70°F).1
  • Dark: out of sunlight.1 Light makes plastic brittle and lets algae grow.13
  • Away from fuel and pesticides: vapors from gasoline, kerosene and pesticides can pass through plastic.116
  • Off bare concrete or dirt: plastic absorbs odors there.17 Air flow underneath limits moisture and mold.13
  • Room to freeze: leave 5–8 cm (2–3 in) of headspace, and do not use glass.16
  • The right plastic: food-grade HDPE, marked with a 2 in the recycling triangle, is the best choice.15

Container choice, rotation and how much to store are in Storing Water for Months & Years.

👶 Babies & children

Babies, children and nursing mothers

University of Florida Extension says to store more water when there are children or nursing mothers at home.18 The CDC says to make powdered formula with bottled water until officials say the tap water is safe.19 Keep a few unopened bottles set aside for formula only.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Count the dog

The CDC says to store more water if you have pets.1 Ready.gov's pet kit includes a water bowl and several days of water.20 Put the dog's water on the same 6-month calendar as yours, and read the labels on any pet medicines for the word "refrigerate".

#🧴 Water-treatment chemicals

Your disinfectants have time limits too. Put them on the same calendar as the water they treat.

Water-treatment chemicals: time limits and checks (EPA, CDC)
ItemTime limitStorage and checks
Regular unscented liquid bleachEPA's method uses bleach stored at room temperature for less than 1 year7Write the purchase date. Scented, color-safe or "with cleaner" bleach is not for drinking water7
Chlorine dioxide tablets or dropsFollow the date on the packageKeep sealed and out of the sun: it is volatile and sensitive to sunlight21
Iodine tablets or solutionCDC does not recommend continuous use beyond a few weeks22Not for pregnancy, thyroid problems or iodine allergy22

Bleach keeps forever if the cap stays on.

EPA's emergency water method calls for bleach stored at room temperature for less than one year.7 Older bleach is outside the official method. Date every bottle when you buy it.

The smell test tells you the dose worked

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Measure the dose

    8 drops of 6% bleach, or 6 drops of 8.25%, per 3.8 L (1 gallon) of clear water.7

  2. Double it for hard cases

    Cloudy, colored or very cold water gets twice the dose.7

  3. Stir and wait 30 minutes

    Stir, then let the water stand for 30 minutes.7

  4. Smell it

    A faint chlorine smell means it is ready.7

  5. No smell? Repeat

    Add the same dose again and wait another 15 minutes.7

Bleach calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy and nursing

The CDC does not recommend iodine water treatment for pregnant women.22 The CDC also says to store more water during pregnancy,1 and Florida Extension says the same for nursing mothers.18 Other methods are in Disinfecting Water.

🎯 Practice now

Learn the smell now

Dose 3.8 L (1 gallon) of tap water with fresh bleach, wait 30 minutes and smell it.7 Then you will know the faint chlorine smell when it matters, even in the dark.

#🥩 Fridge and freezer food without power First 72 h

Keep the doors shut. The safe times assume the fridge and freezer stay closed.3

Use appliance thermometers. Safe readings are 4°C (40°F) or colder in the fridge and −18°C (0°F) or colder in the freezer.312

Fridge and freezer food when the power is off (USDA, CDC, FoodSafety.gov)
SituationSafe for aboutAfter that
Closed fridge4 hours312Discard meat, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers12
Full freezer, kept closed48 hours3Refreeze or cook food that has ice crystals or is at 4°C (40°F) or colder3
Half-full freezer, kept closed24 hours3Same rule; check each package3
Full 510 L (18 cu ft) freezer with 23 kg (50 lb) of dry ice2 days3Never touch dry ice with bare hands3
Perishable food above 4°C (40°F)2 hours, or 1 hour when the air is above 32°C (90°F)4Throw it out4
Hard cheese, butter, whole fruit, raw vegetables, bread, peanut butter, condimentsCan be kept after an outage9Unless they smell, look or feel wrong9

Why the limits are so short: bacteria grow fastest between 4°C and 60°C (40°F and 140°F) and can double in as little as 20 minutes.23

Signs it has gone bad

Throw out food with an unusual smell, color or texture, or food that feels warm.9 The CDC rule is short: when in doubt, throw it out.12

A small taste will tell you if food is still safe.

USDA says never taste food to decide whether it is safe.3 Use the thermometer, the clock and the sign check instead.9

▶️ Watch & save while the internet works

Print this chart while the internet works

FoodSafety.gov: printable chart of refrigerated food to keep or throw out after an outage.24 Tape it inside a cupboard door. The full method is in Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

#💊 Medicines that depend on cold

Read every medicine label for the word "refrigerate". Make the list now, while a pharmacist can still answer your questions.11

Medicines without a fridge (FDA, Ready.gov, Red Cross)
MedicineLimit without a fridgeWhat to do
Insulin vials and cartridges, opened or unopenedUp to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F)5Replace vials exposed to extreme conditions once properly stored insulin is available5
Insulin pens and other insulin productsRules differ by product5Read the package insert now and write the limit on the box
Other medicines labeled "refrigerate"Discard after more than a day without power, unless the label says otherwise6If a life depends on it, ask a doctor or pharmacist and use it until a new supply arrives6
Any medicine stored outside its label temperatureDepends on the medicineCheck the storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, doctor or the maker11
First-aid kit suppliesThe printed expiration dateCheck dates and replace out-of-date items25

Once the fridge stops, all insulin is ruined.

The FDA says insulin vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, can stay unrefrigerated at 15–30°C (59–86°F) for up to 28 days.5 Pens and other products have their own rules, so read the insert.5

Expiration dates on ordinary tablets are a separate topic with its own research. It is covered in Medicines: Shelf Life & Expiration Facts.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults and medical devices

Ready.gov says to talk to your medical provider now about a power-outage plan for refrigerated medicines and for medical devices that need electricity.6 Older adults and young children are especially vulnerable to extreme temperatures.6

👶 Babies & children

Children's medicines count too

The one-day rule covers every medicine that should be refrigerated, including children's medicines.6 Ask the pharmacist which of your child's medicines need cold, and write the answer on the bottle.

#🌡️ Storage conditions that add or cut time

Heat, light, air, fumes, damp floors and frost all shorten shelf life. Each row below comes from an official source.

What shortens shelf life, and the fix
EnemyWhat it doesDo this
HeatFood bacteria grow fastest at 4–60°C (40–140°F).23 Insulin's 28-day limit only covers up to 30°C (86°F)5Water at 10–21°C (50–70°F);1 fridge at 4°C (40°F) or colder3
LightMakes plastic brittle or leaky and grows algae.13 Chlorine dioxide is sensitive to sunlight21Store in the dark1
AirChlorine dioxide is volatile21Keep tablets sealed. Keep kit items in airtight plastic bags26
Fuel and pesticide fumesVapors pass through plastic16Store water away from gasoline and pesticides1
Bare concrete or dirtPlastic absorbs odors.17 Poor air flow lets moisture and mold build13Raise containers on boards or pallets
FreezingWater needs room in the container16Leave 5–8 cm (2–3 in) of headspace; no glass16

Do

  • Write the fill or purchase date on every item1
  • Keep water cool and dark1
  • Keep containers on boards, off concrete17
  • Seal kit items in airtight bags26
  • Check the bleach date before you dose7

Don't

  • Store water next to fuel or pesticides16
  • Leave plastic drums in the sun13
  • Reuse milk or juice jugs for water14
  • Taste food to test it3
  • Use a medicine stored outside its label temperature without checking11

#🗓️ Your replacement calendar Long haul

Turn every number into a date on paper. A wall calendar works without power. Here is the order in which the official limits arrive.

  1. Hour 4

    A closed fridge reaches its limit.3

  2. Day 1

    A half-full freezer reaches its limit. Refrigerated medicines are discarded unless the label says otherwise.36

  3. Day 2

    A full, closed freezer reaches its limit.3

  4. Day 28

    Insulin vials and cartridges kept at 15–30°C (59–86°F) reach their limit.5

  5. Month 6

    Replace the water you bottled yourself.1

  6. Year 1

    Replace bleach for the EPA method. Check every kit and re-think your needs.726

  7. Year 5

    Replace CO alarms.8 Inspect plastic drums that sat in light.13

Run a shelf-life audit

Step by step · 6 steps

  1. Pick one category

    Water, chemicals, cold food, medicine or gear. One shelf at a time is enough.

  2. Write the start date

    Fill date for water, purchase date for bleach and alarms. The CDC asks you to label and date stored water.1

  3. Write the replace-by date

    Water plus 6 months, bleach plus 1 year, CO alarm plus 5 years.178

  4. Check the signs

    Look for brittle plastic or algae,13 and for out-of-date first-aid supplies.25

  5. Fix the storage

    Move items somewhere cool, dark, off concrete and away from fuel.117

  6. Copy the dates to paper

    Put them on a wall calendar. Re-think your needs every year.26

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year arithmetic

At one swap every 6 months, 30 years is 60 rounds of water rotation.1 At 5 years per alarm, each alarm spot needs 6 alarms in 30 years.8 Bleach replaced every year is 30 replacements.7

Plan now for what you can renew yourself. Water treatment without bought bleach is in Disinfecting Water.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these before you need them

  • Permanent markers and labels for dates
  • Two appliance thermometers, for the fridge and the freezer3
  • A battery-powered CO alarm8
  • Food-grade HDPE #2 water containers15
  • Boards or pallets to keep supplies off concrete17

#✅ Do this now

0 / 10 done

#🧠 Remember this

How often do you replace water you bottled yourself?

Every 6 months. Store it at 10–21°C (50–70°F), in the dark.

How long does a closed fridge keep food safe with no power?

About 4 hours. A full freezer about 48 hours, a half-full one about 24.

Perishable food above 4°C (40°F): how long?

2 hours, or 1 hour above 32°C (90°F). Then throw it out.

Insulin vials without a fridge?

Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Pens differ: read the insert.

Other refrigerated medicine after a day without power?

Discard it unless the label says otherwise. If a life depends on it, ask a doctor or pharmacist.

How old can bleach be for EPA's water method?

Less than 1 year, stored at room temperature.

When do you replace a CO alarm?

Every 5 years.

Should you taste food to check it?

Never. When in doubt, throw it out.

Conversions & Field Math

🟢 CoreLong haul📚 25 sources

⚡ The 30-second version

  • 1 liter of water weighs 1 kg. A US gallon weighs 8.33 lb. So a full 208 L (55 gal) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb).1
  • Roof math: 1 mm of rain on 1 m² of roof gives 1 liter. In US units, 1 inch on 1 sq ft gives 0.62 gallon. Measure the roof from above, not along the slope.
  • Bleach: 8 drops of 6% (or 6 drops of 8.25%) per gallon of clear water. Double it only for cloudy, colored or very cold water.5
  • Plan 2,100 kcal per person per day. That is about 3.07 million kcal a year for a family of 4.8
  • Weigh first, then dose from the label in mL. kg = lb ÷ 2.2. Never give aspirin to children.13
  • Count breaths and pulse for a full 60 seconds. WHO calls 40 or more breaths a minute fast breathing in a child aged 1 to 5.22

💡 Tip

Shortcuts you can do in your head

  • kg × 2.2 = lb. lb ÷ 2.2 = kg.
  • 1 liter is a little more than 1 US quart (about 6% more).
  • 1 meter is about 3.3 feet. 5 miles is about 8 km.
  • 1 mL is 1 cubic centimeter (cc). 1,000 mL is 1 liter.
⚠️ Caution

Check which gallon

A US gallon is 3.785 L. A UK (imperial) gallon is 4.546 L, about 20% bigger. If a book or label says "imperial" or "UK" gallon, use the bigger number.

Water is its own scale. One liter of water weighs 1 kilogram, and one US gallon weighs 8.33 pounds.1 For water, liters and kilograms are the same number.

#🌡️ Temperature: one formula, five numbers

To get °F, multiply °C by 1.8 and add 32. To get °C, subtract 32 from °F and divide by 1.8. That is the whole method.

Step by step · 3 steps

  1. °C to °F: × 1.8, then + 32

    Example: 70°C × 1.8 = 126. Add 32 and you get 158°F.

  2. °F to °C: − 32, then ÷ 1.8

    Example: 40°F − 32 = 8. Divide by 1.8 and you get 4.4°C.

  3. Write both on your labels

    Your thermometer, your book and your medicine box may use different scales.

Keep food at 40°F (4°C) or colder, or 140°F (60°C) or hotter. Bacteria grow fastest between those two numbers.17 A cooler must stay at 40°F (4°C) or below.18

Insulin vials and cartridges can stay out of the fridge for up to 28 days at 59–86°F (15–30°C). Pens and other products differ, so read your own label.14

"Double it and add 30" converts °C to °F well enough.

It is close near room temperature but wrong when it matters. At 70°C, the shortcut gives 170°F; the real answer is 158°F. That is the CDC's formula-water temperature.21 Use × 1.8 + 32.

👶 Babies & children

Formula water and boiling

CDC advises boiling water for formula for 1 minute, and using water of about 70°C (158°F) for young or vulnerable babies.21 Above 6,500 ft (about 2,000 m), boil water for 3 minutes.20 See Feeding Babies When Formula Runs Out.

#🪣 How much water is in that container?

Volume = area of the bottom × depth of the water. It works for any container with straight sides: drums, tanks, buckets, troughs.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Measure the inside

    Use centimeters or inches. Measure inside the walls, not outside.

  2. Find the bottom area

    Box: length × width. Round tank: 0.785 × diameter × diameter.

  3. Multiply by the water depth

    Use the depth of the water, not the height of the tank, to see what is left.

  4. Convert to liters or gallons

    • cubic cm ÷ 1,000 = liters
    • cubic inches ÷ 231 = US gallons
    • cubic feet × 7.48 = US gallons

  5. Write it on the container

    Liters when full, liters per cm of depth, and the full weight.

Example, round drum: 60 cm across, 80 cm of water. 0.785 × 60 × 60 × 80 = 226,080 cubic cm, so 226 L (60 gal). Each 1 cm of depth holds 2.8 L.

Example, box tank: 100 × 80 × 50 cm = 400,000 cubic cm, so 400 L (106 gal). It weighs about 400 kg (880 lb) when full, because 1 L of water weighs 1 kg.1

☠️ Danger

Full containers are heavy

A full 208 L (55 gal) drum weighs about 208 kg (458 lb).1 University of Nebraska Extension advises sturdy shelving for stored water because of its weight.3 Fill big containers where they will stay.

Leave 5–8 cm (2–3 inches) of space at the top of any container that might freeze.3

Stored water at CDC's minimum of 1 gallon (3.8 L) per person per day
PeoplePer day2 weeks1 year
13.8 L (1 gal)53 L (14 gal)1,382 L (365 gal)
415 L (4 gal)212 L (56 gal)5,527 L (1,460 gal)
623 L (6 gal)318 L (84 gal)8,290 L (2,190 gal)

CDC sets 1 gallon per person per day as the minimum and asks for a 2-week supply if possible. Store more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates.2 See How Much Water You Really Need.

Water calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Ration drinking water to make it last longer.

FEMA and the Red Cross say never ration water. Drink what you need today and find more for tomorrow. A normally active person needs at least 2 quarts (about 1.9 L) a day to drink.7

👶 Babies & children

Every open container is a drowning risk

A child can drown in less than 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water. Never leave water containers open and unattended.24 Keep lids on buckets and tanks.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Count your dogs in the water math

A pet kit needs a water bowl and several days' supply of water.25 CDC says to store extra water for pets.2 Add a line for each dog in your table, and measure what each one drinks in a day.

#🌧️ Roof catchment math

1 mm of rain on 1 m² of roof gives 1 liter. The reason: 1 mm × 1 m² = 0.001 cubic meters, which is exactly 1 liter.

In US units, 1 inch of rain on 1 square foot gives 0.62 gallon. 1 inch × 144 square inches = 144 cubic inches. A US gallon is 231 cubic inches. 144 ÷ 231 = 0.623.

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Measure the footprint

    Length × width of the roof as seen from above, overhangs included. Slope does not add area.

  2. Multiply by the rainfall

    mm × m² = liters. Inches × sq ft × 0.623 = US gallons.

  3. Compare with your need

    4 people at 1 gallon a day need 1,460 gallons (5,527 L) a year.2

  4. Measure what you really catch

    After a measured rain, check how much the tank gained. Gained ÷ calculated = your roof's own ratio. Use it for future estimates.

Metric example: a 10 × 8 m footprint is 80 m². A 25 mm storm can give at most 2,000 L (528 gal). For 4 people at CDC's minimum, that roof must capture about 69 mm (2.7 in) of rain a year.2

US example: a 30 × 40 ft footprint is 1,200 sq ft. 1 inch of rain gives at most 748 gallons (2,831 L).

💡 Tip

Make a free rain gauge

Any container with straight, vertical sides measures rainfall. The depth of water in it equals the rain that fell, whatever its width. Check it at the same time each day and write the number down.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view: keep a rain log

One year of daily rain numbers shows your wettest and driest months. Size tanks to carry you through your longest dry stretch, not your average month. Treat roof water before drinking it: see Disinfecting Water. For gutters and first-flush diverters, see Rainwater Harvesting.

#🧴 Bleach and chlorine dilution math

Start from the EPA table, then multiply. Use only plain, unscented bleach that is less than 1 year old, and wait 30 minutes before drinking.5

Unscented bleach for clear water (EPA rates; bigger batches multiplied out)
Water6% bleach8.25% bleach
1 quart or 1 liter2 drops2 drops
1 gallon (3.8 L)8 drops6 drops
5 gallons (19 L)40 drops30 drops
20 L jerrycan (5.3 gal)42 drops32 drops
Cloudy, colored or very coldDouble itDouble it

The first two rows and the doubling rule are EPA's.5 The 5-gallon and 20 L rows are the 1-gallon dose multiplied. For a 55-gallon (208 L) drum, Oregon State Extension gives 2 tablespoons (30 mL).4

Bleach calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

A few extra drops make clear water extra safe.

EPA gives a set dose per strength, and doubles it only for cloudy, colored or very cold water.5 Measure; do not pour by eye.

To sanitize a container, use 1 teaspoon (5 mL) of bleach per quart (about 1 L) of water. Shake it to coat every surface, wait at least 30 seconds, then pour it out.2

The dilution formula

Strength before × amount before = strength after × amount after. Written short: C1 × V1 = C2 × V2. It works for any dilution.

EPA's dry-chlorine method: 1 heaping teaspoon (about ¼ oz, 7 g) of high-test calcium hypochlorite in 2 gallons (7.6 L) of water makes a stock of about 500 mg/L. You then add 1 part stock to 100 parts water.6

Check it with the formula: 500 mg/L × 1 part ÷ 101 parts = about 5 mg/L. Because 1 L of water weighs 1 kg (1,000,000 mg), 1 mg/L is the same as 1 part per million (ppm).1

☠️ Danger

Stock solution is not drinking water

At about 500 mg/L, the stock is 100 times stronger than the treated water.6 Label it, cap it and keep it away from children. Never mix chlorine with other cleaners.

#🍚 Calorie and protein math

Plan 2,100 kcal per person per day. That is the minimum planning figure for humanitarian food rations.8 Adult women need about 1,600–2,400 kcal and men about 2,000–3,000, depending on age and activity.9

Calories at 2,100 kcal per person per day, and the same calories as dry white rice
Peoplekcal per daykcal per yearAs rice per year
12,100766,500210 kg (463 lb)
48,4003,066,000840 kg (1,852 lb)
612,6004,599,0001,260 kg (2,778 lb)

The rice column uses USDA's figure of about 365 kcal per 100 g of dry white rice, which is 3,650 kcal per kg.10 Rice is only an example. Calories are not a full diet: see Deficiency Diseases.

Step by step · 3 steps

  1. Find kcal per kg

    From the label: kcal per serving ÷ grams per serving × 1,000.

  2. Find the total kcal you hold

    kg of food × kcal per kg.

  3. Divide by the daily need

    Total kcal ÷ (people × kcal per day) = days of food.

Example: a 25 kg (55 lb) sack of white rice holds about 91,250 kcal.10 A family of 4 at 2,100 kcal each uses 8,400 kcal a day. 91,250 ÷ 8,400 = about 11 days.

Oil carries 2.4 times the calories of rice, kilo for kilo. Vegetable oil has about 884 kcal per 100 g; dry white rice has about 365.10 That matters when you carry food. See Calories & Nutrition.

Food calculator. Interactive in the digital edition.

Cutting everyone's food in half hurts everyone the same.

FEMA and the Red Cross say healthy people can survive on half their usual food intake for an extended period. Food may be rationed safely, except for children and pregnant women.7

Protein by body weight

Protein targets are grams per kilogram of body weight. The adult RDA is 0.8 g/kg.11 The Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 set 1.2–1.6 g/kg a day.12

Daily protein by body weight (multiplication of the published g/kg figures)
Body weight0.8 g/kg (RDA)1.2–1.6 g/kg (2025–2030)Pregnancy, breastfeeding 1.1–1.3 g/kg
50 kg (110 lb)40 g60–80 g55–65 g
60 kg (132 lb)48 g72–96 g66–78 g
70 kg (154 lb)56 g84–112 g77–91 g
90 kg (198 lb)72 g108–144 g99–117 g
🌸 Women & girls

Pregnancy and breastfeeding

Protein needs in pregnancy and breastfeeding are 1.1–1.3 g/kg a day.11 CDC says to store more water for pregnant women.2 Do not cut food for pregnant women or children when you ration.7

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older adults

The 0.8 g/kg protein RDA applies from age 19 to over 70.11 Weigh older relatives each month. A falling weight is a number you can act on early.

#💊 Dosing and loads by body weight

Weight-based math needs a real weight. Guessing a child's weight puts every later number wrong.

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Weigh yourself

    Use a bathroom scale on a hard, flat floor.

  2. Weigh yourself holding the baby or dog

    Stand still and read the number.

  3. Subtract

    The difference is their weight. Convert: lb ÷ 2.2 = kg.

  4. Write it down with the date

    Children and dogs grow. Re-weigh before any weight-based dose.

Learn the unit ladder. 1 kg = 1,000 g. 1 g = 1,000 mg. 1 mg = 1,000 micrograms (mcg). 1 L = 1,000 mL. Mixing up mg and mcg is a 1,000-fold mistake.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Get the weight in kg

    Use the steps above.

  2. Find the dose on the label or from a clinician

    The dose comes from the label's chart or a written instruction, never from your own guess.

  3. Read the strength

    Labels give mg in a volume. "100 mg per 5 mL" means 20 mg in each mL.

  4. Measure in mL with the device that came with it

    Not a kitchen spoon.

  5. Write the time and amount

    Check the label's daily maximum before every dose.

Do

  • Weigh, then convert to kg
  • Measure liquids in mL
  • Use the device in the box
  • Log every dose and time

Don't

  • Guess a child's weight
  • Dose with kitchen spoons
  • Give aspirin to children
  • Work out a dog dose from a human one
☠️ Danger

Never give aspirin to children

Mayo Clinic's first-aid guidance is plain: never give aspirin to children.13 Use professional care whenever it exists. For what each medicine does, see Over-the-Counter Medicines.

🐕 Dogs & pets

Dogs are dosed by a vet, not by math

Do not convert a human dose for your dog. Weigh the dog with the hold-and-subtract method and give the weight to a veterinarian. See Dog Health.

Loads by body weight

A child's backpack should weigh 10–20% of the child's weight. An 80 lb (36 kg) child carries 8–16 lb (3.6–7.3 kg).15 For adults, a 2018 military study recommends loads of 30% of body mass or less.16

🌸 Women & girls

Loads scale with the body

At 30% of body mass, a 50 kg (110 lb) woman's limit is 15 kg (33 lb), and an 80 kg (176 lb) man's is 24 kg (53 lb).16 Split group loads by body weight, not evenly.

#⏱️ Estimating time: count it, don't guess

Count breaths and pulse for a full 60 seconds. WHO calls 50 or more breaths a minute fast breathing at 2–11 months, and 40 or more from 12 months to 5 years.22 See Assessing a Sick or Injured Person.

Timer: Count breaths or pulse: 60 seconds. Interactive in the digital edition.

🎯 Practice now

Calibrate your counting now

While you still have a watch, count "one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand" to 60 and check the clock. Repeat until you land within a few seconds. Then you have a timer that needs no battery.

  1. 1 minute

    Rolling boil makes water safe from germs; 3 minutes above 6,500 ft (about 2,000 m).20

  2. 20 minutes

    Bacteria can double in food between 40°F and 140°F.17

  3. 30 minutes

    Wait after adding bleach before drinking.5

  4. 1 hour

    Perishable food limit above 90°F (32°C).18

  5. 2 hours

    Perishable food limit above 40°F (4°C).18

  6. 4 hours

    A closed fridge keeps food safe with no power.19

  7. 24 / 48 hours

    A half-full / full closed freezer.19

  8. 28 days

    Insulin vials and cartridges out of the fridge at 59–86°F (15–30°C).14

  9. 6 months

    Replace water you bottled yourself.2

  10. 1 year

    Replace bleach you use for water.5

A half-full freezer keeps food as long as a full one.

A full closed freezer holds about 48 hours; a half-full one about 24 hours.19 Write down the time the power went off. See Food Safety Without a Refrigerator.

#🌳 Estimating distance and height

Your pace count

A pace count turns your legs into a tape measure. In this method, one pace is two steps: count each time the same foot lands.

Step by step · 5 steps

  1. Mark a measured 100 m

    Use a tape measure on flat ground. In feet, 100 m is 328 ft.

  2. Walk it normally and count

    Count every time your left foot lands.

  3. Repeat 3 times and average

    That average is your pace count per 100 m.

  4. Recalibrate for real conditions

    Walk the course again carrying your usual load, and on slopes, and keep a separate count for each.

  5. Use it

    Distance in meters = paces counted ÷ your pace count × 100.

Example: your count is 64 per 100 m and you counted 320 paces. 320 ÷ 64 × 100 = 500 m.

Use it for safety distances. CDC says to run a generator outdoors more than 20 feet (6.1 m) from windows, doors and vents.23 With a count of 64, 6.1 m is about 4 paces; pace it out and mark the spot.

Map scales: what 1 cm or 1 inch on the map means on the ground
Map scale1 cm on the map1 inch on the map
1:24,000240 m2,000 ft
1:25,000250 m2,083 ft (0.39 mi)
1:50,000500 m4,167 ft (0.79 mi)
1:100,0001 km1.58 mi

The rule: ground distance = map distance × the scale number. For route finding, see Map & Compass Navigation.

Height from shadows

A stick and two shadows give a tree's height. At the same moment, every upright object casts a shadow in the same ratio to its height.

Step by step · 3 steps

  1. Stand a straight stick upright

    Measure the part above the ground.

  2. Measure both shadows

    The stick's shadow and the tree's shadow, base to tip, at the same time.

  3. Do the math

    Tree height = tree shadow × stick height ÷ stick shadow.

No sun? Use the arm's-length stick method. Hold a stick upright at arm's length, with the part above your fist as long as the distance from your eye to your fist. Walk until the stick's tip lines up with the treetop and your fist with the base. Your distance to the tree now equals its height; pace it.

💡 Tip

Know the reach before you fell

A tree that falls reaches as far as it is tall. Measure the height first, and keep people, dogs and roofs out of that circle.

#🌾 Area and land measures

Area is length × width for a rectangle. A triangle is base × height ÷ 2. A circle is 0.785 × diameter × diameter.

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Pace or tape every side

    Sketch the plot on paper and write each length on it.

  2. Split the shape

    Cut odd shapes into rectangles and right-angle triangles.

  3. Work out each piece and add them

    Rectangles: length × width. Triangles: base × height ÷ 2.

  4. Convert

    m² ÷ 10,000 = hectares. m² ÷ 4,047 = acres. sq ft ÷ 43,560 = acres.

💡 Tip

Square corners with a 3-4-5 rope

Mark a rope at 3 m, 4 m and 5 m (or 3, 4 and 5 ft). Pull it into a triangle: the corner between the 3 and 4 sides is a perfect right angle, because 3² + 4² = 5². Use it for beds, sheds and fences.

Seed packets often give rates per 100 sq ft. 100 sq ft is 9.3 m², so "per 100 sq ft" is close to "per 10 m²". For yields and land per person, see Feeding a Family Forever.

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view: keep your own standards

Tools wear out, but water does not change. A 1-liter bottle full of water weighs 1 kg, so it can check a homemade balance scale.1 Keep one tape-measured 1 m stick, and recheck each child's pace count and weight every year.

🛒 Get it before you need it

Get these while stores exist

  • A tape measure marked in both cm and inches
  • A mechanical kitchen scale and a bathroom scale
  • Measuring cups and spoons marked in mL
  • Oral syringes marked in mL
  • A food thermometer marked in °C and °F
  • A notebook and pencils for logs

Print these official pages now

  • CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply

#🧠 Remember this

How much does 1 liter of water weigh?

1 kg. A US gallon weighs 8.33 lb.

1 mm of rain on 1 m² of roof?

1 liter. (1 inch on 1 sq ft = 0.62 gallon.)

°C to °F?

Multiply by 1.8, then add 32.

Pounds to kilograms?

Divide by 2.2.

Bleach for 1 gallon of clear water?

8 drops of 6% or 6 drops of 8.25%. Double for cloudy, colored or very cold water.

Planning calories per person per day?

2,100 kcal.

Tree height from shadows?

Tree shadow × stick height ÷ stick shadow.

How big is a hectare?

100 m × 100 m = 10,000 m² = 2.47 acres.

  3. University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension: Preparing Water for Use in an Emergency (n.d.). Sturdy shelving because of water's weight; leave 2–3 inches of headspace for freezing.

  6. EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (archived page) (2013, archived). 1 heaping teaspoon (about ¼ oz) of high-test calcium hypochlorite in 2 gallons makes about 500 mg/L stock; dilute 1 part stock to 100 parts water.

  12. USDA/HHS: Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2025–2030 (NMSU Extension copy) (2026). Protein 1.2–1.6 g per kg of body weight per day.

  14. FDA: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency (n.d.). Insulin vials and cartridges may be left unrefrigerated at 59–86°F (15–30°C) for up to 28 days; pens and products differ.
  15. Nemours KidsHealth: Backpack Safety (n.d.). Backpack 10–20% of body weight; an 80 lb child carries 8–16 lb.
  16. Military Medicine: Metabolic cost of soldiers carrying 30% and 45% of body mass over mixed terrain (2018). Loads of 30% of body mass or less recommended to avoid performance decrements.
  17. USDA FSIS: Danger Zone (40°F–140°F) (n.d.). Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F and can double in as little as 20 minutes.
  18. FoodSafety.gov: Food Safety in a Disaster or Emergency (n.d.). Discard perishable food above 40°F for 2 hours, or 1 hour above 90°F; keep coolers at 40°F (4°C) or below.
  19. CDC: Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency (2024). Closed fridge safe up to 4 hours; full freezer 48 hours, half-full 24 hours; fridge 40°F, freezer 0°F.

  21. CDC: Prepare and Store Powdered Infant Formula in an Emergency (2024). Boil water 1 minute; about 70°C water for young or vulnerable infants.
  22. World Health Organization: Pneumonia policy brief on the revised classification and treatment of childhood pneumonia (2014). Fast breathing: 50 or more a minute at 2–11 months, 40 or more at 12 months to 5 years.
  23. CDC: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics (2024). Run generators outdoors more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents; never in a home or garage.
  24. Nemours KidsHealth: Drowning Safety for Parents (n.d.). Drowning can happen in less than 1 inch of water; never leave water containers unattended.
  25. Ready.gov (FEMA): Prepare Your Pets for Disasters (n.d.). A pet kit includes a water bowl and several days' supply of water.

⚡ The 30-second version

  • Find a word by its first letter. Short forms in capitals, like CDC, ORS and CPR, have their own tables. Every entry links to the chapter with the full steps.
  • "Only gasping" means not breathing. That is cardiac arrest: start CPR and use an AED (automated external defibrillator).6
  • The Danger Zone is 4–60°C (40–140°F). Bacteria in that range can double in as little as 20 minutes.13

#🔤 How to use this glossary

This is the book's dictionary. When a word or a set of capital letters stops you, look it up here, read one line, then follow the link.

Each table runs A to Z. Short forms (letters like ORS or MARCH) have their own section. So do the organizations behind the facts.

Numbers and safety rules carry a source. Plain word meanings link to the chapter that covers the topic in depth, with its own sources.

Step by step · 4 steps

  1. Spot the type of word

    All capital letters? Go to Short forms. An organization? Go to Who's who. Anything else: go to its first letter.

  2. Find the row

    Terms run A to Z inside each table. The first column is bold.

  3. Read the one-line meaning

    A number in the meaning is a rule. Learn it together with the word.

  4. Follow the chapter link

    The last column takes you to the full steps, warnings and sources.

☠️ Danger

Five terms that mean act now, read later

  • Cardiac arrest: no response and not breathing, or only gasping. Start CPR and use an AED.6
  • Choking: for an adult or child, alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts. For a baby under 1, use back blows and chest thrusts.4
  • Carbon monoxide: headache, dizziness, weakness, vomiting or confusion near burning fuel. Get to fresh air, then get medical help.2
  • Massive bleeding: in an injured person, MARCH puts it first.7 See Stopping Severe Bleeding.
  • Cholera: untreated, it can kill within hours. Start oral rehydration solution (ORS).17
💡 Tip

Search instead of scrolling

In the online book, press / to search every chapter at once. On paper, use the letter headings in this chapter.

Do

  • Look up every short form on a medicine or chemical label
  • Use exact words with helpers, such as "not breathing, only gasping"
  • Write new words and their meanings at the back of the book

Don't

  • Guess what letters on a label mean
  • Call gasping "breathing"3
  • Use scented bleach on water just because the label says bleach11

#🌡️ Words that come with a number

Some words are rules with a number attached. Learn the number together with the word, because the number tells you what to do.

The thermometer below gathers the temperature words from across the book. The timeline after it gathers the time words.

Time words, from seconds to years

  1. 2 seconds

    Capillary refill: nail color should return in under this time.9

  2. 1 minute

    Rolling boil for clear water. Make it 3 minutes above 2,000 m (6,500 ft).10

  3. 20 minutes

    Bacteria in the Danger Zone can double this fast.13

  4. 30 minutes

    Wait this long after adding bleach before you drink.11

  5. 2 hours

    Perishable food above 4°C (40°F) for longer than this goes in the trash.14

  6. 4 hours

    A closed fridge keeps food safe this long without power.14

  7. 24 or 48 hours

    A half-full or full freezer, with the door shut.14

  8. 28 days

    Insulin vials and cartridges out of the fridge at 15–30°C (59–86°F).16

  9. 6 months

    Replace water you stored yourself.22

  10. 5 years

    Replace carbon monoxide alarms.1

Gasping means the person is still breathing.

Gasping can happen after the heart stops. Treat "only gasping" as not breathing and start CPR.36

Boiled water is safe from everything.

Boiling kills germs. It does not remove chemicals.15

Hands-Only CPR is right for everyone.

It is for teens and adults who suddenly collapse. Infants, children, and people who drowned, overdosed or had breathing problems need breaths too.5

👶 Babies & children

Baby words

In CPR and choking guidance, an infant is a baby under 1 year. A choking infant gets back blows and chest thrusts with the heel of one hand, never abdominal thrusts.4

🐕 Dogs & pets

Words that include your dog

CDC's carbon monoxide warning covers animals too: the gas builds up and poisons people and animals.1 CDC also says to store extra water for pets.22

A zoonosis is a disease that passes between animals and people, such as rabies. See Rabies & Zoonoses.

🌸 Women & girls

Women's and girls' health words

CDC says to store more water for pregnant women.22 Postpartum means the weeks after birth. A postpartum hemorrhage (PPH) is heavy bleeding after birth.

Other terms you will meet: pre-eclampsia, mastitis, LAM and toxic shock syndrome (TSS). Start with Pregnancy Care and After Birth.

🧓 Elderly & disabled

Older and disabled people

CDC lists older people, and people with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems, among those at higher risk from carbon monoxide.1

Normal vital signs differ with age and health, so write down each person's baseline while they are well.8 See Caring for Elderly & Disabled People.

🎯 Practice now

Teach the act-now words this week

Say a term and have each person tell you what to do: "only gasping", "choking baby", "CO alarm", "Danger Zone". The AHA says children 12 and older can learn CPR.4

⏳ The 30-year view

The 30-year view: keep the words alive

Write the full words, not only the short forms, in notes and medical records. Then anyone who reads them years from now, including a child who grew up without the internet, can follow them.

Add local words as you learn them: plant names, place names, radio call signs. See Preserving Knowledge & Records.

#🧠 Remember this

What does "only gasping" mean?

Not breathing. It is cardiac arrest: start CPR and use an AED.

What is the Danger Zone?

4–60°C (40–140°F). Bacteria can double in 20 minutes.

What does ORS stand for?

Oral rehydration solution: salts and sugar in clean water to replace fluid lost to diarrhea.

What does MARCH stand for?

Massive bleeding, Airway, Respiration, Circulation, Hypothermia and head injury. Bleeding comes first.

What does SAMPLE stand for?

Signs and symptoms, Allergies, Medicines, Past history, Last in and out, Events.

What is a normal capillary refill?

Nail color returns in under 2 seconds.

Which bleach goes in drinking water?

Plain unscented bleach, less than 1 year old.

How long can insulin vials stay out of the fridge?

Up to 28 days at 15–30°C (59–86°F). Pens differ.

#📚 Sources

  1. CDC: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics (2024). CO is colorless and odorless, made by burning fuel; builds up in enclosed spaces and poisons people and animals; higher risk for infants, older people and people with heart disease, anemia or breathing problems; battery or battery-backup alarms near sleeping areas, replaced every 5 years.
  2. CDC: Avoiding Carbon Monoxide Poisoning (n.d.). CO symptoms (headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, confusion); get to fresh air, then get medical help.
  3. American Heart Association: Part 7, Adult Basic Life Support, 2025 Guidelines for CPR and ECC (Circulation) (2025). Adult compressions at least 5 cm (2 in) deep at 100–120 a minute; recognizing cardiac arrest, including gasping.
  4. AHA Newsroom: Updated CPR guidelines tackle choking response, opioid-related emergencies and a revised chain of survival (2025). Published October 22, 2025; alternate 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts; infant back blows and heel-of-hand chest thrusts; single chain of survival; naloxone; children 12 and older can learn CPR.
  5. American Heart Association: FAQ, Hands-Only CPR (n.d.). Two steps; for teens and adults who suddenly collapse; breaths needed for infants, children, drowning, overdose and breathing problems.
  6. American Red Cross: How do I check a person who appears unresponsive? (n.d.). Unresponsive and not breathing, or only gasping, means cardiac arrest: start CPR and use an AED immediately.
  7. StatPearls: EMS Tactical Combat Casualty Care (n.d.). TCCC is the accepted battlefield prehospital standard; MARCH starts with massive hemorrhage.
  8. MedlinePlus (NIH): Vital signs (n.d.). Normal vital signs change with age, sex, weight, exercise capability and overall health; healthy adult blood pressure 90/60 to 120/80 mmHg.
  9. MedlinePlus (NIH): Capillary nail refill test (n.d.). Nail bed color should return in under 2 seconds after pressure is released.
  10. CDC: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency (2024). Boil 1 minute, 3 minutes above 6,500 ft; settle or cloth-filter cloudy water; bleach and iodine less effective against Cryptosporidium and Giardia; chlorine dioxide can kill Cryptosporidium if instructions are followed.
  11. EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (n.d.). Bottled water first; unscented bleach less than 1 year old; double for cloudy, colored or very cold water; 30-minute wait; aerate strong-tasting water.
  12. EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (archived page) (2013, archived). High-test granular calcium hypochlorite, about 70% available chlorine; 1 heaping teaspoon in 2 gallons makes a stock of about 500 mg/L; mix 1 part stock to 100 parts water.
  13. USDA FSIS: Danger Zone (40°F–140°F) (n.d.). Bacteria grow fastest between 40°F and 140°F and can double in as little as 20 minutes.
  14. USDA FSIS: Keep Your Food Safe During Emergencies (n.d.). Fridge 4 hours; full freezer 48 hours, half full 24; 40°F and 0°F targets; 50 lb of dry ice holds a full 18 cu ft freezer 2 days; do not touch dry ice; refreezing; discard perishables above 40°F for 2 hours.
  15. CDC: Prepare and Store Powdered Infant Formula in an Emergency (2024). Water at about 70°C for young or vulnerable infants; boiling does not remove chemicals.
  16. FDA: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency (n.d.). Vials and cartridges, opened or unopened, may stay unrefrigerated at 59–86°F for up to 28 days; pens differ.
  17. WHO: Cholera fact sheet (n.d.). Cholera can kill within hours if untreated; most cases can be treated with ORS.
  18. WHO/UNICEF: Clinical management of acute diarrhoea, joint statement (2004). Low-osmolarity ORS and zinc supplements for children with diarrhea, with continued feeding.
  19. WHO: WHO updates list of essential medicines to include key cancer, diabetes treatments (2025). 24th adult list and 10th children's list; 523 adult and 374 children's medicines.
  20. New England Journal of Medicine: Mortality in Puerto Rico after Hurricane Maria (Kishore et al.) (2018). Household survey; about one third of deaths linked to delayed or interrupted medical care.
  21. NASA: What NASA Is Learning From the Biggest Geomagnetic Storm in 20 Years (2025). May 2024 G5 storm, the first in over two decades; GPS-guided tractors thrown off course.
  22. CDC: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply (2024). At least 1 gallon per person per day, 2 weeks if possible; more for pregnant women, sick people, pets and hot climates; food-grade containers; replace every 6 months.
  23. Sphere Project: Water supply standard 1, access and water quantity (2011 edition). Minimum 15 L per person per day for drinking, cooking and personal hygiene.
  24. Global Food Security Cluster Handbook: 5.6.1 Food Assistance (n.d.). 2,100 kcal per person per day is the minimum planning figure for general food rations.
  25. CDC: What to Do in Radiation Emergencies (n.d.). Get inside, stay inside, stay tuned; go to the middle of the building or a basement.
